speaker: Al Roker
text: Wow. Ooh. That's a pretty boring story, but what the heck? No, you know, it was one of those things. I -- and I'm honest when I say, I had no plans of being on TV. I went to the State University of New York at Oswego. I was gonna be a cameraman or a producer or writer, something like that, something behind the scenes. In fact, this is a true story. I took a television performance class, and my department chairman, Lew O'Donnell, told me after my first class, he said, "Roker, you have the perfect face for radio." \[ Bracy laughs \] But yet, he put me up, actually, for a job doing weekend weather at the end of my sophomore year. And the only reason I was able to do it, and that's kind of part of my message, is that I'd taken a couple of classes in meteorology. Actually, one class in meteorology, one class in environmental science. Then it was called ecology in 1973. But I'd taken those classes just to fulfill a science requirement. It wasn't like I was that interested in doing the weather.

speaker: Al Roker
text: But I was able to put together a weather map at school. My department chairman actually had a part-time job at the station in Syracuse, and they were looking for a weekend weatherman, and I got the job. So I said, "I'll just do this until I get a real job." And the end of my junior year, I got the Monday through Friday job while I was a junior, and so six months after I graduated, I got a job in Washington, D.C.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Six months after graduation. I went to WTTG in Washington, D.C., which was the independent station there. And I was kind of naive. The news director told me, "We're not gonna be paying you a lot, but you'll be on the number one station at 10:00 in Washington." It wasn't until I was there for a couple of weeks, it was the only station on at 10:00 in Washington. It probably was one of the most important moves I'd ever made because I met the man who would become my mentor, Willard Scott. He kind of took me under his wing. He was at the NBC station, and at the time, in Washington, D.C., the only thing bigger than Willard Scott in Washington was the Washington Monument.

speaker: Al Roker
text: He created Ronald McDonald for McDonald's, and they ripped him off. \[ Both laugh \] So, there's a lesson for you, America. Anyway, but he gave me the two best bits of advice I ever got which was, never give up your day job. And my main job is doing the weather. That's what I love doing. Everything else I've done has sprung from that, and that's terrific, but that's my main gig. and then the other thing that he said to me was, always be yourself. Because at the end of the day, nobody can take that from you. And you can play a character, you can do whatever, but, eventually, people see through that. So, I met Willard, and I worked there for two years, and then I got a job at the NBC-owned station in Cleveland, WKYC. I worked there for five years. And at the end of the five years -- I'm from New York City. I was born in Brooklyn, lived in Queens, Brooklyn, and then Queens again. I still own a house in Cambria Heights -- I grew up.

speaker: Al Roker
text: And I got a weekend -- I got the weekend weather job at WNBC in New York, which was so exciting to me because my parents could finally see me on television, my mom and my dad, because when I got my job in Syracuse, it was Channel 5 in Syracuse. And I remember calling my mother, excited, I said, "Mom, I just got a job on TV." "Oh, what channel?" I said, "Well, you can't see me because it's up in Syracuse." She goes, "Well, what channel is it?" I said, "Well, it's Channel 5." "Oh, that's good. We have Channel 5 here." I said, "Yeah, but no, mom. It's a different Channel 5." She goes, "Well, how can a 5 be different?" I said, "Well, because it's on a different spectrum. My Channel 5 doesn't reach down here into New York." "Well, it must because I have Channel 5 on the TV." It was like a bad Abbott and Costello routine. It went on for about 15 minutes, and I still never quite got her. The first day I was on, she said, "I watched. I didn't see you," you know.

speaker: Al Roker
text: "No, you didn't see me, mom," you know. But then eventually, when I came here, she could see me, so that was -- And I was here for six months when Dr. Frank Field, who was the weatherman at the time, a legend, left to go to Channel 2 'cause he left in a contract dispute. And I worked for nine weeks in a row with two days off. And the I was given the Monday through Friday job, and I did that.

speaker: Al Roker
text: My mother's family's from the West Indies. My dad's from the Bahamas. He's still doing the birthdays, the 100-year-old birthdays for Smucker's. So, I've been doing this for television weather for -- full and part-time for 42 years.

speaker: Al Roker
text: I've worked for NBC for 38 years. And between WKYC in Cleveland, WNBC, and the "Today" show. And coming in March, I'll have been at the "Today" show for 20 years, full-time.

speaker: Al Roker
text: I don't know if there was any one point. I think -- some people -- I'm always amazed that people have, like, these five-year plans. I'm like, "Really?" I don't know what I'm having for lunch, you know? You got a five-year plan? Good luck with that. I think a lot of times, you fall into your passion. You may not even know what it is, and all of a sudden, you're in it. Like I said, I didn't plan to be a TV weatherman. I wasn't gonna do that. And it just -- you know, sometimes I think you have to go with the flow. You know, not to get too Zen about it, but sometimes, you know, there are forces out there that are pushing you into something. And you can fight it, but I think that's a lot of expended energy that could be channeled into other things. So, you know, I kept getting jobs doing TV weather, so I I guess I thought, "Well, I guess this is what I'm gonna do. And don't get me wrong, I love it. I love doing it.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Because it's different every day. Thank you. It's different every day. And at the "Today" show, we have audience members who come down. I get to do so many different interviews and segments. It feeds onto your passion, things that you don't realize. And so I've been very lucky. I've been very blessed. I just finished six years with the Weather Channel doing "Wake up with Al," a two-hour morning show. We're gonna be launching a new digital morning show, a 6-minute morning show on their app coming in October -- I think October 15th -- called "The Lift," which will be kind of a quick hit of news and weather and information. So, you know. I kind of like -- I just go with -- I don't know. You know, like, people say, "What's the next big thing?" Who knows? I don't know. Who knows? But I think it's -- I mean, this whole Periscope, Meerkat, Facebook mentions. I mean, you know, everybody's a broadcaster now.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Everybody can be on live. You could all be on live right now taping each other. Eventually, everybody will be live, nobody will be watching, but we'll all be live. We'll all be walking around live. "Are you live?" "I'm live." "Are you watching?" "I can't because I'm live."

speaker: Al Roker
text: As long as you're live, you know? Kid comes out of the womb, just put a GoPro on his head, let him go. People can watch. To actually bore people, you had to actually have them come over to your house and watch slide shows or home movies. Now you can bore a wide view of strangers by just putting stuff on Facebook and YouTube and Instagram. Instagram your food, what you had, what are you doing, where are you, who are you with.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Hello, Mr. Roker. My name is Vernon Roof. I attend Mercer University Penfield College in Atlanta, Georgia, a part of the NSLS. speaker: Al Roker
text: Hmm. Well, that's a good question in that, I think everybody has a different set of obstacles, a different set of challenges. You know, when I started in this business, there weren't a lot of African-Americans. I mean, I had some great role models to watch. Here in New York, there was Bill McCreery. There was Bob Teague. There was -- I'm blanking on her name now. Melba Tolliver. There were these people, these icons in local television that you got to see, and you went, "Wow, this is -- I could do that," you know, if that's what you wanted to do. But I think what people need to realize is that, they can't use the challenges as an excuse. You know, everybody's got hardships. Everybody's got obstacles. Everybody's got barriers. Do you let that define you or put boundaries around you, or do you use it as an impetus to break through? And I think if you do, you know, that makes you that much more individual and that much more unique. Look, I -- if you looked at me, and especially 10 or 15 years ago, I was the least likely person to be on national television.

speaker: Al Roker
text: I mean, I think the reason I was doing well was people watched and said, "Heck, if this guy can do it, I can," you know? But I realized that I needed to, you know, to improve. I needed to lose weight. I needed to -- And so, I stopped making excuses and finally went ahead and took care of it. I did a gastric bypass. Other people find other routes, but I think it's mainly -- the issue is not letting your obstacles define you.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Well, it is hard, and I was up to 340 pounds, and I lost 140. I thought I had it licked, and then I reali-- my mom got sick -- First my dad passed away, but I had -- he was the reason I went ahead and did the bypass because he was dying of lung cancer, and he'd said to me, "Look, we both know I'm not gonna be here to help raise my grandchildren. You've got to get healthy. You've got to swear to me right now." And that was my reason. And I had the bypass six months later. And then my mom got sick a few years after that, and driving -- she was at North Shore Long Island Jewish out on Long Island, and I had to drive about an hour each way, and I was going out there six days a week, pretty much, and I had fallen back into the old habits. I was eating in the car. And before I knew it, in three months, she had passed away, and I'd gained 40 pounds.

speaker: Al Roker
text: And then I realized I needed to really kind of buckle down. And I'm at the lowest. Right now, I'm at 180 pounds, and -- but I've made eating better a priority and working out and exercising, which just makes me a better person. People have said to me, "How can you do a broadcast and do all this stuff and do the Weather Channel and write a book and do this?" Because if you feel good, and if you're healthy, it makes that much easier to push through. I mean, look, I will admit, I'm kind of running on fumes right now. We had Hurricane Joaquin. We had the flooding in South Carolina. I was doing "Wake up with Al," the "Today" show, MSNBC, and "NBC Nightly News" five days in a row, and then I flew down to South Carolina and reported from there for the last three days, and then came back. I got in this morning at 2:00 A.M., did the "Today" show, and now we're here. I'm actually asleep right now.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Well, I started about a year and a half ago now. Yeah, I guess it would have been a year and a half ago. And I was thinking of actually writing a book on the 10th anniversary of Hurricane Katrina. And so when you start doing something like that, you want to kind of compare it to other storms. And so I started to do the research, and I'd been in Galveston in 2008 for Hurricane Ike, and I remember everybody talking about the hurricane in 1900. And then when I looked at some of the research, I thought, "This can't be right." This is the deadliest -- the hurricane of 1900 is still the deadliest natural disaster in America's history? That can't -- and then I looked, and sure enough, it is.

speaker: Al Roker
text: And so I thought, "Maybe this is the book." And I hired a great guy, Bill Hoglund, who is a terrific author in his own right, to do research for me. Because I'm not that bright. And that's another -- know your limitations. You know, a good leader knows what his strengths are, but most importantly, knows what his weaknesses are and bolsters those and works with those who augment them. You should not fear strong people who complement what you do. To me, that is knowing, you know, what your strength and weakness is critical because if you don't know that and don't acknowledge it -- A lot of people know it. They don't want to acknowledge it. They think that's weakness, that in itself is weakness. I don't think so. I think you make yourself stronger by surrounding yourself with people who complement you and bolster you because that makes you better. And in the meantime, helps them, as well. Because you want to foster good leadership because -- If you're confident in yourself -- if you're not confident in yourself, then by all means, keep good people away from you.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Because you will -- not that it won't help you, but you will always be worrying that they're going to supplant you. Look, after -- I've been doing this for a while, and so I now take two weeks off in July. And somebody said, "Oh, aren't you worried you're gonna be replaced?" I said, "Well, if they're gonna replace me, they're gonna replace me whether I take two weeks, or I take a week, or I don't take any time." So, you know, you've got to be confident in yourself, but you also have to be confident in your skills and bolster the ones that you don't have. Anyway, I think that -- I don't even remember what I was talking about.

speaker: Al Roker
text: I hired Bill Hoglund, and when this research started coming in, I was just blown away by the statistics. But more importantly than the statistics, he had found these troves of information about these oral histories of African-Americans at that time. And when you think about it, I mean, Galveston was a fairly diverse society in that they had blacks, they had whites, Hispanics, Asians, Jews, whites, Christians. Now, for blacks, obviously, it's still a segregated society. I mean, we're talking a little bit more than a generation from the end of slavery in this country at that point. But it was an interesting place. But in any event, Bill found all these great first-person accounts, newspaper clippings,

speaker: Al Roker
text: And in fact, I've had a number of people come up to me and say, "Those characters that you created, were they based on real people?" I said, "No, no, these were real people." And it's one of those things. It's like this disaster movie that you know something bad is going to happen and could have been -- if not avoided, and I don't think it could have been avoided. The death toll could have been mitigated quite a bit. The destruction probably would have -- but even the destruction might have been mitigated had there not been a certain hubris about, "We know what we know."

speaker: Al Roker
text: And whether it's 1900 or it's 2015, I think we still have a certain amount of hubris about we, as people, that we can have some sort of an affect on nature, which in some ways, we can. But in other ways -- There's a Muslim saying, "Man imposes, Allah disposes." You know, and you can see it time and time again with natural disasters that I think people are stunned. Look, I was just down in South Carolina, and the sheer power of moving water is something to be in awe of, but also to be terribly afraid of because it can -- I mean, two feet of water moving at about 3 to 4 miles per hour can move a 3,000-pound car. So, we found all these stories. And you start putting them up on a board, and it's like, "Now, how do we -- how do I weave this into a story?" Get some weather in there, as well. It's funny, I've written eight books -- nine books, but this was the first weather book or a book based on weather that I've done. I've done books on fatherhood. I've done cookbooks.

speaker: Al Roker
text: I've done some murder mysteries, but this was the first nonfiction weather book. And it was probably one of the harder ones to write because you want to tell a story. You want to do justice to the people whose story you're telling.

speaker: Al Roker
text: It took about eight months, going back and forth with the editor, and editing and going back and making sure, fact-checking and things like that. And so, it was -- it was very satisfying, and you realize, again, that there are a lot of parallels today that go back to 1900. It's -- you would think that, well, that was then, and this is now. But if we don't learn from history's mistakes, we're apt to repeat them, as a wise man once said.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Well, you know, it's funny. There was a great book written by the author Eric Larson called "Isaac's Storm." And the protagonist in it, the subject was Isaac Cline who was in Galveston in 1900, and was the head of the U.S. Weather Bureau Service there and was probably the foremost expert on hurricane forecasting in this country, if not the world. And there was a belief back then that you could -- that hurricanes of a certain magnitude wouldn't hit the Gulf Coast because they had to curve, and they wouldn't hit. They had been hit by storms before, and there had been flooding, but nothing of any great magnitude. And Cline believed this so much that, when they were contemplating a few years earlier about building a sea wall to protect the downtown, he said, "No, we don't have to worry about that. We don't need that." And so in my book, it starts off, he's in the middle of the hurricane. But when he realized his mistake -- because there was a series of events that led to a horrendously erroneous forecast. Some of them not of his making.

speaker: Al Roker
text: He did -- even though he knew that they were in for a horrible storm and could have easily gathered his family and gotten them out of town safely, he stayed and tried his best to warm people and to get them out of harm's way. To the point where he lost family members. I don't want to give too much away in the book. But I think he showed amazing heroism because he exemplified -- another thing that I believe is crucial in great leadership, and that's admitting when you're wrong. He realized he could have fled and just saved himself, but he admitted he was wrong, and he did his level best to try to correct that and to save people. And I remember -- you know, like we all -- if we're fortunate enough to have a leader and a hero in our own fathers, which I was. I was very fortunate in my dad. One of the things I always remember. I was I think 13 years old, and I know I always struggle with math. And I had gotten my report card. I was in seventh grade, I remember now.

speaker: Al Roker
text: And it said I had flunked math, and I knew I didn't flunk math. And he was furious, I mean, because he wanted his son to have a good education. And I was gonna be the first one to go to college. And he said, "Well, there's a parent-teacher meeting tonight, and I'm gonna find out." And I remember him coming home that night, and he said, "I should have listened to you. Your teacher, Sister Emmanuella wrote the wrong grade. She transposed your grade with somebody else. I was wrong. I was wrong, and I'm sorry." And I always remember that. It, was like, "Dad said he was sorry?" And that's -- I think, you know, I don't think that's weakness. I think a lot of leaders today, both in industry and business, and in the government are not willing or not capable of saying, "Sorry. I was wrong." And it does not diminish you as a leader. I think people respect it, and I think they value your leadership because they know that you will not lead them blindly. That you are not infallible.

speaker: Al Roker
text: I think that's why -- not to digress too much, but I think that's why so many people were and are still, no matter what your religion, are still taken by Pope Francis because here's a man who, in so many instances, has basically said, "Who am I to judge?" Look, I grew up Catholic, and you're taught that the Pope is God's voice on Earth and is infallible. And he has basically denied that, and that's what's made him an amazing leader because he's led by example, and he's led by faith, and he's led by a belief in humanity. And I think great leaders possess those same things.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Hi, there. My name is Brooke Rikishinowski, and I attend the Ohio State University. I am currently studying Atmospheric Sciences and Agriculture Communication, and I'm planning on graduating this spring. My career aspiration is to become an on-air meteorologist, like yourself, so I was wondering what steps you took when trying to find a job. I know this is a very competitive field, so I was also wondering what tips you had on how to stand out in an interview. Also on a related, but unrelated topic, why do you think Hurricane Joaquin was so hard to track this year?

speaker: Al Roker
text: Okay, the first question was -- I've already forgotten. The first question was, how do you stand out in trying to get a job? Look, and this is not any kind of a brag. I've been very fortunate in that I've never actually had to get a job. Well, I mean, my first job was doing weekend weather, and my college professor put me up for it, and I auditioned for it, and I got the job. And then each time other people had known about -- seen my work and offered me a job. So I never actually applied -- I never actually wrote a résumé.

speaker: Al Roker
text: I've been so blessed, it's crazy. For a relatively unattractive man, I've been very fortunate. But I do think that people -- When I talk to people, friends, talking about jobs, that -- And again, it goes back to Willard, that everybody -- \[ Sighs \] For example, in this business, when she was at the height of her popularity, Oprah Winfrey, or any great broadcaster. Everybody wants to know, "Who's the next Oprah? Who's the next Katie Couric? Who's the next Martha Stewart?" There is no next. They are them.

speaker: Al Roker
text: But you have to be the next you. And that's -- I mean, everybody -- Look, when I was in radio -- I did college radio, and I would come home from college, and I would listen to Frankie Crocker on WBLS and Dan Ingram on WABC. And I would try to emulate their -- what they did, I mean, to the point where I'd write down their stuff. And it didn't work because it wasn't me. It was them. It was me channeling them. So, until you find your voice, which is hard because until you get the job, it's hard for you to find the voice. And so it's kind of a Catch-22, but I would say that that's -- You've got to be you. You have to really be yourself.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Yeah, that's how you stand out. That's how you make you you. You know, I think that's vitally important. The second part of the question was... Was it -- Was what? Interview tips, interview tips. A good memory.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Crucial. Crucial. You know, I think -- I think being well-dressed, obviously, good personal hygiene. I think -- I think listening. And when I say a job interview, if you're going to go into this business or any business, listening is the most important thing. We are so -- and I've been guilty of it. I'm so thinking about, what am I going to say next that I'm not listening to what the person's saying. And so many times, I'd say, 80% to 90% of the time, your next question will come out of what that person is saying. And it does two things. It moves you along to the next thing. But it says to that person you were listening, and that you are valuing what they say. The other thing is, for God's sake, whatever you do, don't have your phone out on the desk. Turn your phone off, okay? I mean, off. No buzzing, no beeping, no nothing. Because it's like, am I not important enough that you've got it -- what's coming on there that you're getting? You're here to get a job, but you've got something coming in. So, don't do that.

speaker: Al Roker
text: But I would say listening, and you know, and look, it's a great world out there now. There's Google. You can find out about the person you're gonna interview with. Don't find out too much, and then start throwing that out. Because that then, you become, as my 17-year-old says, "Now you're a creeper." Okay?

speaker: Al Roker
text: Don't do that. And then the third thing was Hurricane Joaquin, thank you. And I -- you know, actually, it was interesting because in "Storm of the Century," in 1900, they didn't have the technology we have. We have satellites. We have radar. We have weather balloons that radio back instantaneously information real time. Back then, they had technology -- there's still some technology that we use. You know, temperature gauge, thermometer, barometer, anemometer, hygrometer. So that we can measure relative humidity, temperature, wind speed, wind direction, the barometric pressure. The difference is, it had to be collated all by hand, aggregated by hand. Whereas today, it's all done by computers. The interesting thing, back then, the forecast for this storm -- the most accurate forecast that put it within 100 miles of Galveston was not by the U.S. Weather Bureau, but was by the Cuban -- It was the Cuban Meteorological Society that was run by Jesuits. Cuban Jesuits. The Balin Meteorological Institute. And at the time, the U.S. Weather Bureau was run by this guy, Willis Moore, who was a petty bureaucrat. And back in 1900, there were some political differences with Cuba. Ooh, what a shock.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Good thing that hasn't gone on for too long. And they decided to cut off telegraphically because back then, the big communication was telegraph. Telephone was coming in, but telegraph was the state of the art at the time. And the Cuban Meteorological Institute had the best network of stations throughout the Caribbean so they got real-time information about a hurricane's whereabouts, how it was behaving, how it was strengthening. And so, they had an accurate forecast. It was going to go out into the Gulf. It was going to strengthen. It was probably gonna hit somewhere within 100 miles of Galveston. But they never got -- that forecast was never disseminated because they were cut off telegraphically to the mainland U.S. And so when Isaac Cline made his forecast -- And the other thing that Willis Moore did, he stopped allowing local offices to make their own forecasts. They wanted local offices to send them all their information, and the U.S. Weather Bureau from Washington would tell them what to say.

speaker: Al Roker
text: So, anyway, Hurricane Joaquin, we actually had the European model, and we had the National Hurricane Center model, and there are a bunch of other models we look at. There's about five or six main ones we look at. And the European model had it going off the coast, never touching land. And the American model had it kind of hugging the coats and maybe hitting New Jersey. But as time went on, the American model got closer. So, we have more information to be able to forecast. So, Joaquin, while some models had problems with it, other models didn't, and we had that information. I know I went a little off the mark there.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Well, look, it was a horrific time. I mean, 10,000 people, estimated, died in Galveston. The population on September 7th was about 38,000. On September 8th, at that night the hurricane hit. On September 9th, they had lost about a third of their population. Most of the buildings were destroyed. There were thousands of corpses in the street. And in a weird way, Galveston and the hurricane led to integrated workforces because in the beginning, they thought, well, the only way to get rid of the bodies was pile them onto barges and send them out into the ocean and dump them. And so they conscripted able-bodied black men to do it. The only problem was, the tide kept washing the bodies back in. So they realized they didn't have enough people to do the work. So they integrated. They had whites and blacks working together. The only way to get rid of the bodies was, sadly, to burn them. So, they had funeral pyres going 24/7.

speaker: Al Roker
text: But the city fathers and the elected officials and business owners got together and said, "What do we need to do to protect ourselves?" They, over four years' time, erected a 17-foot concrete and steel iron seawall that ran 3 miles to begin with, but eventually ran 10 miles. They elevated the level of the city, the downtown area, by upwards of 5 to 8 feet, which back then in 1900, you had to jack these buildings up. You had to dig out. It was really a feat -- an amazing feat of engineering. So, they didn't let this define them. But it was a horrific -- You know, there's survivor's guilt. You know, many people -- it was what was to worse, to perish that night or to have survived?

speaker: Al Roker
text: You know, I don't think about it that much. I just -- you put one foot in front of the other, and you make certain plans when it comes to your family and friends and things like that. But, you know, you've got to make sure you have your eye on what you want to achieve. Yes, there are long-term goals, and we all have long-term goals. I joke about it a bit, but to me, the medium term and short term lead to the long term. And you know, you've just got to make sure you stay focused on that. You know, it's sometimes, you're so focused on the long term that you can't -- your long game -- that your short game suffers.

speaker: Al Roker
text: Hello, my name is Justin Rowland. I'm from Texas A\&M of Commerce. Mr. Roker, I just want to thank you for your time and dedication for Society. I know time is one of the most valuable assets that we have, so I'll try to keep my question pretty brief. My question is somewhat of a two-part question. Life in business is filled with great storms. When faced with these periods of business and career development, how do you weather the storm? And secondly, how do you measure success in your own life?

speaker: Al Roker
text: Well, you know, I think you -- I mean, that's the trick. Everybody can do pretty well when things are going well. It's when things go badly, what do you do? Yeah, I used to watch my dad. text: \<v -\>Discrimination based on race, gender, and poverty was something that we thought those were our touch points. speaker: Anita Hill
text: \<v -\>Hello, my name is Michael Henkle from Western Governors University. And my question is what are the characteristics that separate out great leaders from good or average leaders? Thank you. \<v -\>Wow. Leadership, really, is almost a personal matter. I think one of the things that we have to avoid is stereotyping that person who is the good leader. But there's a process that I think of about leadership too, along with the personalities to go along with it. And one, a leader has to be a good listener. They have to, in fact, be able to listen and to actually hear the people who they're responsible to. They have to be able to analyze what they hear, take it and find common ground, because if they're leading broad constituents, there are many interests involved in that kind of leadership role. And then, they have to be able to propose solutions. And I say, propose solutions and not impose solutions. They need to bring people together in order to get to solutions that work and that work for a wide range of people. So those are the things that I think of when I think about leadership.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: By responsibility I mean, you have to be willing to take on the tasks that are assigned to you and those that aren't assigned to you, in many cases. You have to take responsibility for a wide variety of experiences that perhaps you haven't even imagined when you've gotten into a leadership role. I know that has happened to me, that I was very happy in a leadership role as a teacher. But when I expanded that, I had to be a much more public person than I had anticipated. But that's what's been my responsibility. Once I became a public figure and started to speak publicly about the issues that concerned me, my responsibility was to grow into that role. And then accountability is important too, because things don't always go right. And as a matter of fact, we make mistakes as a leader, and we have to own those mistakes. We have to be accountable to the people who are depending on us and at least, we acknowledge when we're not perfect and then be accountable for correcting the mistakes that we made and the harm that's caused by them.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: So those two things are really important to me, the willingness and ability to take responsibility for leading, for learning, for growing into a role. And then the accountability part, where it's sort of like the buck stops with the leader, and me taking that to heart and really working whenever you make a mistake or things don't go exactly right. It may not even be a colossal mistake, but learning from that and then finding solutions so that you can go the right way the next time. \<v -\>And sort of on the other hand, have you ever been in an experience with somebody in a leadership position that maybe was displaying not great leadership skills and ones that maybe that you learned, you know, that's not something that I ever want to display? That's not something I ever want to be as a leader? \<v -\>Yes, I have encountered that. I think one of the easiest things to fall into is to believe that, well, you know, I'm in this world, nothing that I can do is wrong. I'm the person who sets the standards for my own behavior. And I get to call all of the shots.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: And being a leader, as I was saying earlier, means listening and actually being responsive to the needs of the organization that you're put in charge of. So yeah, I don't ever wanna be that person who doesn't grow and isn't empathetic and isn't really in tune with the people who are counting on her to find solutions and to move an organization or a classroom or a school forward. \<v -\>All right. speaker: Anita Hill
text: And then they may approach people who they think will support them and end up feeling like they're being blamed for what has happened to them. Know Your IX is another national organization that provides information and information really can be a source of support, but it also allows you to connect with people who have been doing this work in sexual violence and other forms of abuse. So those are two organizations. And it's always good to have a group of support, if you have friends. But again, that doesn't always happen. And what I do tell people is that really, you don't have to have an army of support. If you have one or two people, someone who knows you, who loves you unconditionally, who knew you before the bad thing that happened to you and understands who you are at your core, then you should go to that person or those persons and find the support with them.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: It does help to have more than one, but even one person can be a great support. speaker: Anita Hill
text: And they really sort of have lived with me, many of the people. There was a caller who was an adult male who had experienced incest as a child. speaker: Anita Hill
text: I think about when I was asked that question, I don't think I've really felt as though I changed the world, but I felt inspired to try to, and I realized that the reason that I was doing it was for all of those people, but especially for a younger generation. That's really amazing. Okay, Anita. Social media and the use of hashtags like \#MeToo, \#WhyILeft, \#WhyIStayed has given a voice to countless women who have been otherwise silenced over the years. What are your thoughts on the role that social media plays when it comes to this issue, because it's a weighty one. \<v -\>Well, it's a mixed bag. I mean, right where we couldn't deny it when you had so many people participating.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: Social media has allowed people to organize and to protest issues of bias and abuse. Social media has created affinity groups, allowed people to get together under the hashtag, but to realize that they're not alone. But at the same time, I also know that social media has been used as a tool to actually bring about more abuse and more harassment to certain people. And studies show that young girls are sometimes targeted by older men for sexual purposes by social media. So it's a mixed bag, and I think we have to really get a handle on it. Some of the evidence about how social media is used to make young girls feel worse about their bodies is really troubling. And it's something that's doubly troubling, in a sense, because we can all be addicted to social media, even when it is doing bad things to us. So I think social media can have a positive purpose, but there are also negatives associated with it.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: And I don't know if the answer is the governmental control or for us as a society just to figure out how we wanna use it and when it is being harmful to us and how to stop using it. \<v -\>So something you hear a lot when speaking about problems in the country is that the next generation will fix it, right? However, you write in your book that 34% of Gen-Z middle and high schoolers have been cyber bullied by their peers. So this doesn't really sound like a fix to me. It sounds like we're passing the buck and repeating patterns and allowing young bullies to grow up to become older bullies. So what do we need to do as a country? Like what real steps do we need to take, no matter what your age, to effect positive change when it comes to gender violence?

speaker: Anita Hill
text: \<v -\>Well, first of all, we need to stop telling young people who are bullied, who are harassed, whether it's cyber bullying or bullying in person, I cannot tell you how many times I've heard from young people who've said that when they went and they complained about bullying that they were sort of told that that problem, whatever they were complaining about, wasn't so bad, that that behavior was just something that boys do or that girls do and that they were left thinking that what was happening to them didn't matter and nobody would ever do anything to address it. And that's what I believe has created and endorsed this culture of silence. If we tell people when they first come to us, that their problem isn't important, that the behavior they're describing isn't so bad, we aren't only diminishing the idea that they should step up, that they should complain and they have a right to do so, but we're also grooming the abusers and telling them that they have every right to behave in whatever way they want to, and that nothing will be done about it. I had read an email from Girls Inc.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: One girl wrote a short piece saying that when she was in the first grade, she had her experience with sexual assault. We've got to train people who are teaching our children to understand that boys don't pick on girls because they like them. And so we've got to do a lot of thinking about language, how we groom children to accept abuse, and then the systems that we provide for them to address don't have to be open to hearing them and responding in appropriate ways. \<v -\>It's so crazy, even hearing you say that.

speaker: Anita Hill
text: I mean, I remember that's what I was told as a child. "Oh, he must like you, if he's teasing you or picking on you." And that does just breed more of this behavior and you're right. In a lot of the way that we communicate across genders and to leadership, I think it needs to change. Something needs to give, because I feel like if I was told that then, and it's still happening now, that's really scary. It's really scary. \<v -\>Yeah, it is. It is. Elaborate on? \<v -\>Well, I thought, there were three of them that were really kind of close in terms of the percentage. speaker: Anita Hill
text: But I do, of course, as an educator, I love the fact that many people embrace the moment and they learn from it. They don't try to deny it or ignore it. It's not an easy one, but it helps so, so much. \<v -\>Absolutely, absolutely.
