speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Wow. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, guys. Good evening, National Society of Leadership and Success. And welcome to those members watching nationwide at nearly 500 campuses both live and In re-broadcast. We are coming to you live from New Jersey City University.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Michael, for being the executive producer and the host and getting me water and doing everything. And thank you all for being here and for watching us by remote. And I was finding out a little bit about you all, and I understand some of you have accents like me. So I just want to tell that you for me, that hasn't been easy. You know, it's been a little bit of the bane of my existence. I tried many times to lose my accent and finally, I met Henry Kissinger. And it wasn't just that he had an accent. He said to me, "don't worry about your accent." He said, "in American public life, you can never overestimate the advantages of complete and total incomprehensibility."

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: In fact, I did try to change it. I gave up. And now I'm kind of relaxed about it. I hope you are all relaxed about your accents if you have one, okay? Because after all, what matters is that we thrive, no matter what our accents or anything that we're dealing with. So I'm particularly excited to be speaking to you and to have so many young people in the audience. I have two daughters who just recently graduated from college. And I only wish that I knew what I know now about thriving when I was your age. And I'm often asked, what is the advice I would give to my 20-something self? And I say my advice would be very simple. Stop worrying and get more sleep. Because a lot of the time, we worry about so many things. And when you look back at your life, a lot of these things are really figments of our imagination. One of my favorite quotes is from Montaigne who said, "there were many terrible things in my life," he said, "but most of them never happened." So remember that.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Some of the worst things that happen in our lives happen in our heads. I wrote "Thrive," which incidentally just came out in paperback today, because of my own wake-up call. Eight years ago, I collapsed from exhaustion, sleep deprivation, and burnout, hit my head on my desk on the way down, broke my cheekbone, and got four stitches on my right eye. And that's how "Thrive" begins. You know, that's like the opening scene. And it's a little bit of a melodrama because I come to in my own pool of blood, and the first question I ask myself is, "is that what success is?" Because, you know, if you come to in a pool of blood of your own and nobody has shot you, clearly, by any sane definition of success you are not successful. Can we all agree on that? You did something wrong, in terms of what you prioritize in your life. And then on top of it, I had to go from doctor to doctor, from echocardiogram to MRI, to find out what was wrong with me.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And it turned out that what was wrong with me is that I had civilization disease and civilization disease is burnout. Millions upon millions of people are suffering from it. So basically, I almost wish that all these doctors would have come together and said to me, "you know, Arianna, here's your diagnosis. You have civilization disease and there's nothing we can do about it." Because really, doctors can do nothing about it. it's up to us to make different lifestyle choices. And so that's how my journey began, that led to "Thrive." And I wrote "Thrive" because i wanted, especially your generation, to learn that our generation has gotten it all wrong. That we have been living under the collective delusion that burnout is a necessary price of success. And it is not. And even now the question I most often get is "okay, it's very good for you now. You've succeeded. You can get enough sleep and not worry. But what about me? I'm just starting out in life?" And no, no, no, I want you to really listen to me. It doesn't matter where you are in life.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Whether you're struggling to put food on the table, graduating from college, or at the top of the world juggling multiple demands on your time, your highest and first priority is to do what they tell you in airplanes. Put your own oxygen mask first. Now, you know, when they tell you that on the airplane, it's not because they're nice. It's because that's how you're going to be the most effective for other passengers as well. So it's not selfish to put your own oxygen mask first. It means you are taking care of your own human capital and then you're going to be much more effective at your job, your family, and giving back to others. The way we have been running our lives is a little bit like trying to sit on a two-legged stool. Because we define success just in terms of the two metrics of money and power. And this is a two-legged stool. We need that third leg of the stool, the third metric, consists of these four pillars, and "Thrive" has a dedicated section for each pillar. The first is well-being. Listen, if we sacrifice our well-being, nothing else is really worth it.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And do you know that 75% of healthcare costs are because of preventable stress-related diseases? 75%. And it's not really surprising. Right now, I bet everybody here, approximately, knows how much battery remains on your smartphone. Because we take much better care of our smartphones than we take care of ourselves. Like, when, if you had asked me the night before my collapse, "how are you, Arianna?" I would have said "fine." Because I was not even conscious of how burnt out I was. And that's really what happens. Most of us are not even conscious because I have had so many people who came up to me during the last year of touring about "Thrive" and said to me, "I don't remember the last time I was not tired." We kind of forget. And we live in this new normal, which is being perpetually exhausted. I remember what it was like when I would go for a whole day and be so tired. You know that feeling when you really would look at a table across the room and I would want to go crawl under it and hope nobody would notice -- that kind of level of exhaustion.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And now, that I have actually prioritized my sleep -- you know, "Thrive" in each section has two steps, a total of 12 steps, Because we are addicted. I picked 12 steps deliberately. So through these 12 steps, if we integrate them in our lives, we actually get to the point where we truly move from simply surviving and succeeding to actually thriving. So the first step which is the most important one for me was sleep. I went from four to five hours to eight hours. And right now, 99% of the time, I get eight hours sleep. No matter what. If you look at my schedule, I'm not exactly chilling under a mango tree. But the fact that I get enough sleep makes me much more effective. It makes me better as a leader, knowing where we need to go, being clear about our vision. It makes me make better decisions. You know, I quote Bill Clinton in the book, who said, "the most important mistakes I made, I made when I was tired." Now, he didn't specify what mistakes he was referring to.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: But we can know and identify that it's when we are tired that we make our worst mistakes, that we overreact, that we become emotional, that we take things personally. And this is a huge shift. We now have amazing scientific findings about the importance of sleep. And the connection between sleep deprivation and diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease, Alzheimer's. And we see athletes -- that's one of the most exciting things is that athletes who only care about winning have prioritized sleep. Olympic Games now have nap rules. I did an interview recently with Kobe Bryant who said he rediscovered sleep and it made him better on the field and better as a family man. So sleep is the first step, and you know what? Because a lot of people have been coming up to me and saying, "you know, Arianna, we kind of agree with that, we agree that we need to change how we live our lives and what we prioritize," but it's really hard. It's really hard to change entrenched habits and build new habits. So I created and just finished taping an entire six-week course

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: you'll get that special offer and a free copy of "Thrive." And it starts on May 3rd. And each week, we will work through two steps together. We've taped it all. We have amazing guest teachers, including Kobe Bryant on sleep and meditation, including my own daughters, Christina and Isabella, talking about their own problems. My daughter Isabella dealt with eating disorders. My daughter Christina in her last year at college got involved with drugs. And I got the call that every parent dreads, "Mommy, I can't breathe." And driving to the emergency room to get her, I had to focus on what I was grateful for -- the fact that she was alive, the fact that she had reached out for help, the fact that she wanted to get well. But now that she's been sober for three years, she talks in the course about what helped her, and one of the things that helped her is one of the steps in "Thrive," and that's making every day a gratitude list. Because, you know, so often, we focus on all that is not working in our lives, And we forget the blessings.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: So for three years now, every night, she writes down three things she's grateful for and shares it with three friends, and they do the same with her. And gratitude is one of the most amazing emotions. And one of my favorite quotes about gratitude is from Rumi the poet who said, "live life as though everything is rigged in your favor," Which means even when things go really badly, when you look back, you'll be surprised. There's some reason for it. I remember when I wrote my second book in my 20s, and nobody wanted to publish it. It was rejected by 36 publishers. Now, that sounds fast, but it takes a while to be rejected by 36 publishers. By the time 36th rejection came, I had run out of money. I was living in London. And I remember walking kind of depressed down St. James' Street and I saw Barclays bank. And I walked in. And armed with nothing but a lot of Greek chutzpah, I asked to see the bank manager and asked for a loan. And for some reason, he gave it to me.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And that's what made it possible for to hold it together for a few more rejections, and finally, somebody published it. So, if you think of your own lives, there are always moments like that, when it's a little bit like in fairy tale, when the hero or the heroine is lost in a dark forest and everything seems dark. And then suddenly, these helpful animals come out to help them find their way out of the forest. Well, that bank manager as like my helpful animal, you know, disguised as a bank manager. I still send him a Christmas card. So in life, often, these magical things happen, and it's important to remember, because sometimes we live life as though we think we make everything happen. But life is a dance between making it happen and letting it happen. And in order to connect with that part of our ourselves, that wisdom, which is the second pillar, we need to make sure we leave a little bit of time for ourselves, to be by ourselves. Do you know how hard that is becoming? We're so bombarded with information, with notifications.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: They did a study at Harvard and the University of Virginia where they asked people to choose whether they wanted to spend 15 minutes alone in their room with no devices, no newspapers, nothing -- no TV -- or get electric shock. And 67% of men chose electric shock. I have to say that the superior sex -- women -- only --

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Only 25% of women chose electric shock. That gives you an idea of how hard it has become for us to have any silence in our lives. I, for example, now walk into my apartment and I don't automatically turn on the TV. And it's just kind of amazing to see how great it is to allow a little silence. You know, the iWatch, right, the Apple Watch -- is everybody dying to buy the Apple Watch? Okay, let me tell you why I'm not buying the Apple Watch. Because the last thing I want is something on my wrist giving me constant notifications, notifying me of every stupid text and every meaningless e-mail and every news alert from the Huffington Post...

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: ...Nonstop. I don't want that. Because let me give you one piece of career advice. The people who are going to win the future are not the people who are constantly being notified on their iWatches, or their smartphones. They're going to be the people who are capable of sitting alone in a room, with their own thoughts, to come up with creative ideas while the rest of us are futilely trying to deal with all the incoming communications. And Steve Jobs himself has said that the best ideas that led to the most iconic Apple products came after Zen meditation. So the irony is that if Steve Jobs was wearing the Apple Watch, maybe he would not have invented Apple.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: So that takes us to another big illusion, which is an illusion that multitasking makes us efficient. You know how now -- I live in New York, and you can hardly walk down the street and see anybody who is just walking. People are walking and talking on the phone, walking and texting. And, of course, if they're walking and texting, they expect you to get out of the way because you are clearly are not as important as they are because you can just walk. And when I stopped doing that, I started noticing things that I had completely missed. I remember walking with a friend by my apartment and saying to her, "you know, this building, it's so beautiful." And I said, "when did it go up?" She said, "1890."

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And I'm wondering, what else have I been missing, Under the illusion that by multitasking we are super efficient. Well, science now shows that there is no such thing as multitasking. It's actually task switching, and it's the most stressful thing you can do. My mother, who is this amazing, wise, Greek woman, the last time she got angry with me before she died was when she saw me answering my e-mail and talking to my children at the same time. And she said to me, "I abhor multitasking." And if you think I have an accent, you should have heard my mother. in fact, she talked about the power of unitasking, the power of giving your full attention to whatever it is that you're doing, including your children. including having a meal with a friend. There's a game that a lot of people are playing now in New York, where, when they go out to dinner, they put all the phones in the middle of the table, and the person who reaches for the phone first pays the bill. Because have you noticed how parents complain about their children being always on the phones? But then, they're modeling us.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: They're modeling the behavior that they see. So well-being, wisdom -- wonder is the third pillar. And multitasking is a big enemy of wonder. Because you need to be really present in order to be able to experience the mystery of life. And I was recently on Oprah's show, you know, "Super Soul Sunday," and she asks everybody the same question. She asks, "what do you know for sure?" And I said to her, "what I know for sure is that however magnificent your job is, Oprah, or my job or anybody's job, who we are in our essence is more magnificent." and that's the mystery of life. We try to shrink ourselves down to our jobs, our to-do lists, but we're so much more than that. And when we actually remember that, a lot of the pressures of daily lives away. So remember, there's more to life and that's really the mysterious journey we are on than doing incredibly well in our jobs. Trust me, I'm not saying that that's not important. But it's not the only thing that matters. And it doesn't matter how people enter this journey, this thriving journey.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Sometimes people enter this journey just because they want to be better at their jobs, and I say that's fine. Because in the course of doing that, you'll also discover that you are more than your job. And what is wonderful now is that's there's an enormous amount of scientific evidence that validates ancient wisdom about the importance of sleep, of meditation, of periods for renewal. I was recently speaking at a conference -- the Salesforce Conference in San Francisco. And they had put out this great new app, this great new cloud, Salesforce1 platform that has 99.9% uptime. And I thought to myself, human beings -- we're not designed to have 99.9% uptime. We try to act as though we have 99.9% uptime, but we don't. And the reason human beings were not designed that way is not because God got it wrong. After all, remember, he worked really hard for six days and created Heaven and Earth. That is a pretty big job, okay? And then he took a day off. You know, that is a hugely important metaphor. You know, he really didn't have to take a day off. I mean, the guy is omnipresent, omnipotent, omni-everything.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Right? He could have kept going. He took a day off to send us a message -- That we all need that day of completely disconnecting from whatever it is we're doing -- a day of digital detox, A digital Shabbat. I love the idea of the Shabbat, where you can actually connect with something more important than whatever it is that is on your to-do list. Because right now, we have shrunken everything down to our to-do list. And we have shrunken the definition of success down to these two magics of money and power, while if you look at any philosopher, spiritual teacher, they've all defined the good life in a much bigger way than that. And you know has anybody here been to a memorial recently? You know, a eulogy is very different than our LinkedIn profile. Have you ever heard anybody eulogize by saying, "you know, George was amazing. He increased market share by 1/3."

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And I'm not saying that in a morbid way. I actually think that talking about death is a really good thing. Because as The Onion headline puts it, "death rates holds steady at 100%." So it's part of life. And if we're lucky, we have 30,000 days to play the game of life. And how we play it will depend on what we value. So what I love right now is that because of social media, we can actually share each other's stories and learn from each other. You know, they say that you can only grow through pain. You've heard that, right? You have to, like, hit your head like I did, have some disease, lose someone, something bad happening in order to learn and grow. I want to change that. Can we change that? Why can't we learn from each other's pain? Why do you have to have your own collapse? Why can't you learn from mine? Because we can learn from each other's stories. And that's why I want to invite you to write your stories. And we'll publish them on the Huffington Post. The Huffington Post is now in 14 countries.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: We translate the best stuff, and we love being a powerful platform with 214 million unique visitors to get the word out. So write your stories of burnout or your wake-up calls or what you've learned, and you never know who is going to read it. And it may be exactly what they needed to read. And I'm going to make it super-easy for you. I'm going to give you my e-mail address, and you can send it directly to me. You can of course also tweet at me or follow me on Facebook or Instagram or Google Plus, or whatever has been invented, I'm on it. But if you also want to follow some old fashioned e-mail, Arianna -- with one R and two N's --

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And I love getting stories, especially from young people. But older people can participate too. But because I'm amazed by how much different it makes in the lives of others, and that's one of the magical things about a platform. You never know who is going to read it. We had a homeless teenager who write a beautiful post three years ago, and the Harvard Admissions Office read it and offered him a place at Harvard. And he's now in his third year. And I love stories like that. I love the story of a Special-Ed teacher who wrote a piece called "The Day I Stopped Saying 'Hurry-up' to My Daughter." And she wrote this beautiful piece about how she has this daughter who was 6 years old, and she discovered that the two words that she would speak to her more often than any other words every day were "hurry up." "Hurry up and get up." "Hurry up and eat breakfast." "Hurry up and go to school." "Hurry up and go to bed." And it so resonated with people, it got 7 million page views and a 1.2 million likes.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And I think the reason is that we all do this to ourselves. We don't just do it to our children. We do it to ourselves. We live life in this breathless way. They call it "time famine," rushing from one thing to the next, always feeling as though we are running out of time. And it's time to come back to the center. You know, Archimedes, the Greek mathematician said, "Give me a place to stand, and I can move the world." And when we find that centered place in us, it is just amazing how time expands and we create space in our lives instead of contracting as though we are constantly running out of space and running out of time. So the final pillar is giving. You know modern science shows that giving is actually a shortcut to happiness. It is really amazing how much happier it makes us and it doesn't have to involve giving money or giving time. It can just involve giving of our presence to someone, not looking at people and taking them for granted.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: It starts -- and this is one of the steps in "Thrive" -- with making a personal connection with someone that otherwise You would take for granted. Like the barista in the coffee shop, or somebody cleaning your office or your school -- Making a personal connection. You know, I had a mother who was incapable of making any personal connection. I remember when I lived in London, I was dating a member of Parliament, who brought Ed Heath, who was then Prime Minster, to the dinner one night. My mother was in the kitchen. My mother was always in the kitchen. I think my mother thought if you didn't eat every 20 minutes something terrible would happen to you. And something happened to the stove. So she called in the plumber and she said to the plumber, "you know, what do you think of the Prime Minister? And the plumber said, "not much. he hasn't been good for working people." So immediately my mother, not even giving it a second thought, said to him, "hold on a second.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Let me go bring him here so you can tell him directly." And she went to the dining room and brought in the Prime Minister so the Prime Minister and the plumber could have it out. And for her, there's no hierarchy. As far as she's concerned, human beings are all equally magical and wonderful. It doesn't matter whether they're Prime Minister or the plumber. And I think if you approach life with that sense of no hierarchy, life is constantly surprises you. Something pretty amazing happens. And that's one of the most wonderful things that I love about at the Huffington Post. We have a platform where you can have a Prime Minister like Francois Hollande, who is the Prime Minister of France, writing next to a student, or someone who is unemployed. It doesn't matter. All that matters is having something interesting to say. And that's the most wonderful thing about what we have created online and what modern platforms make possible. We see a real perfect storm. We see that the way we've been living our lives is no longer sustainable.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: You know how we talk a lot about the environment and climate change and how what is happening in the environment is not sustainable? Well, my prediction is that burned-out people will continue to burn up the planet. We need to start with ourselves. We need to start dealing with our own burnout, because that's when we'll be able to look ahead and move beyond just the short term and be able to look beyond that. I was in Pompeii recently. And it's kind of amazing to see how they missed all the warning signs before the Vesuvius exploded. I mean, they had plenty of warning signs. They had dogs that were running away, birds that had stopped singing, white smoke bellowing out of Mount Vesuvius, and they missed it all until they were buried under 60 feet of lava and rock. So we look around, and we see, "what are we missing?" But in order not to miss the signs, we need to be reconnected with ourselves, and that means learning to unplug from our devices And recharge. Disconnect from our technology and reconnect with ourselves.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Let me just start with a very simple step here, which Is actually step number two in "Thrive." Which is at the end of your day, pick a time when you collect all you devices and gently escort them out of your bedroom.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: You will find them in the morning, I promise. But if you charge them by your bed, admit it. if you wake up in the middle of the night, you are going to be tempted to go to your devices, lest some terribly important text arrives in the night. And then your sleep is not going to be as recharging. My children will tell you I'm the device police. I go around, collect devices, take them out of their bedrooms if they're at my home or if we're in a hotel together. And they have actually grown to see the value of that. And when you wake up in the morning, do me another favor. Do not rush first to your phones. Give yourself one minute. I promise, you have one minute to set your intention for the day. Remember what you're grateful for. And then go to your phone. You know why? Because if you first go to your phone, it's like telling the world, "whatever you want me to know is more important than what I've set as my priority.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: "So I will let you, world, whoever you may be, determine what matters to me." That doesn't make sense. You need to start with what matters to you. Do you know the word priority was first invented in 1400. And between 1400 and 1900, it was singular. It was one priority. What's your priority? What's the most important thing in your life? And then suddenly, it became priorities. It became a lot of priorities. I think just about everything is a priority. And really, all the people who actually get stuff done and change the world have learned to prioritize. And learning to prioritize means learning to say "no." Did you know that no is a complete sentence? And the way to learn to say no is to recognize that... you can complete a project by dropping it. Let me explain what I mean by that. We all start a lot of projects in our heads. Like, in my case, I thought I would learn to become a good skier. I'm a lousy skier. My children like to ski. I thought it would be great if I can learn to become a good skier.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: I thought I wanted to become a good cook, or at least any kind of cook. I wanted to learn German. And then I did a life audit, and I realized, you know what? I was never going to invest enough time and energy to get that stuff done. So I completed these projects by dropping them. So as far as I'm concerned, skiing is done. I'm still a lousy skier. But it's no longer on my to-do list. Cooking -- I still can't cook, no longer on my to-do list. German -- no longer on my to-do list. So look at your list And decide what do you want to complete. Right now, tonight, by dropping it, and you'll see how liberated you are going to be. Then you're going to be left with the things that you are really going to spend time and energy on, as opposed to all the things that you started, somehow, maybe some day, but realistically, they're not going to be part of your life.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: So that's one of the great things we're going to be working on on the Oprah course -- learning to do regular life audits, completing projects by dropping them, and being able to focus your energy on what really matters in your life. And what that also means is learning to observe but not take seriously that voice in your head that I call in "Thrive," "the obnoxious roommate living in my head." It's the voice of doubt, the voice of judgment. I was recently on Steven Colbert's show, and I said to Steven, "you know what? my obnoxious roommate, Steven, sounds exactly like you -- Really sardonic." And he said to me, "I had to find a place to crash." But when you learn to distance yourself from your obnoxious roommate, you suddenly have so much energy available to you. Because that voice of judgment is the most exhausting thing. You can all identify with that. That voice was so strong in me when I was younger that it took me a while to actually learn to recognize that that voice is not the truth.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: So I could give a speech like that and really love it and enjoy being with you. Then I would step off the stage and the voice would start, "oh, I didn't like at all what you said there, that wasn't right." "Now, you forget to say this and you forgot to say that." "And, you know, really, you were not really on. No, that wasn't right. And I didn't like what you wore either." You know that voice? So, basically, that voice could go on for days, long after I left the stage. And that's really what we need to learn to deal with, by treating it like something which is not who we are. It is not the truth. You know, sometimes I wish you could recall what that voice says about us. Because our worst enemy doesn't talk about us the way that voice talks about us. Another thing that I do, another exercise that we do on the Oprah course, is to write down what the obnoxious roommate is saying and then take it to the sink with a candle and burn it. It's incredibly cathartic. I love it.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And it's basically saying, "okay, that's what I think of what you're saying." Gone. The important thing is to come back fully present in your life, because that's all we really have for sure. The past is gone, never to come back. The future, nobody really knows about. And yet, we spend so much of our life either judging ourselves in the past or worrying about the future. And yet, the only time when life can actually happen is right now in this very moment. So let me just wrap up by saying, this is an extraordinary moment to be alive, with these unprecedented, scientific findings that validate ancient wisdom. With greater awareness about the dangers of technology, as well as the joys of technology, and the recognition that each one of us has it in our power to live our lives every day with more gratitude, more joy, more compassion, and yes, more sleep. Thank you.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Is she the coolest? She's the coolest. Let's find out who our trivia winner is. The trivia question, as a reminder, was "in what year did Arianna Huffington found the Huffington Post?" And the answer to that question was 2005. Our trivia winner is Kim Snyder from Mitchell Community College. Congratulations, Kim.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: A supportive group. It's a supportive audience this evening. Our poll question was, could you be without your cellphone and digital devices for one hour each day? 46% of you said, "yes, I could unplug and be totally fine for an hour a day." 2% of you said, "no, I can't be without my phone or devices." I'm impressed. 9% of you said, "I think I could but I'm not going to enjoy it." and 43% of you said, this is something I can already do."

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: That's pretty cool. So let's get to our Q\&A. These are the questions that came through Twitter. Members, if you would like to hear your questions asked in a future broadcast, and you're watching in a rebroadcast, you can always e-mail questions to

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Here's the first question from Twitter. Michael from Lane Community College in Eugene, Oregon, said, "when you're against a deadline and you really need to catch up, would you prefer to crunch at night and wake up right before you have to go to your meeting, Or go to sleep early, wake up extra early in the morning and prepare then?"

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: I would say, first of all is, look at what did you make more important than preparing for that meeting? And there will be the time when this is a new request or something you have to do that you didn't know in advance, or you were sick or you had a sick child or any of those things. Then 1,000%, no question about it, you go to sleep and wake up recharged and work then. You're going to be so much more effective and productive at getting what you want to get done, because in the end, what matters is not time but energy. And if your energy is low because you are tired, it can take you five times as long to achieve the same result. I mean, how many of you -- it's happened to all of us in college. Our studying -- and you can't even remember a thing you read because you're so tired. And yet, you keep powering through and having another Red Bull or another cup of coffee to keep going even though the returns are increasingly diminishing.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: This question comes from Allie. "In the quest for mindful living, how much, if at all, do you think that your social circle and your environment influence your ability to thrive?"

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Oh. that's a very good question. In fact, I should have mentioned that. I can hear my obnoxious roommate. Because you really need a support group in order to change, It can be a support group of one. It doesn't have to be a large group. We call it a "thrive tribe" in the Oprah course. You need your little thrive tribe. I introduced my thrive tribe during the course which consists of my sister and my two daughters. And basically, your thrive tribe is there for you, no matter what. Let's say you are tempted to binge-watch "House of Cards" instead of going to sleep. You can call a member of your thrive tribe, and they can talk you down. They can tell you to close your laptop, and you can watch it over the weekend. We all, as we are creating new habits, we all need someone who can support us, who can hold us accountable, who can track our progress with us.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And one thing to remember is that when we don't do things right -- and that's going to happen all the time -- not to judge ourselves, because we have the next moment available to us to fix whatever it is we want.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Great question. Yes, great question. In fact, we have gone into colleges, and Jessica Kane who is here, who is in charge of our Millennial Outreach at the Huffington Post ave created what we call Oasis, A place in college where even in the middle of an exam, even in the middle of a more -- a particularly stressful time, you can have a respite. You can have a time where you can do some yoga postures, you can meditate, or just have a nap, have something healthy to eat. So that's the kind of environment which you can create for each other in your college, in your dorm, where you can support each other to actually get some respite, to get some renewal period. And then whatever it is you are doing, whether you're just passing an exam or launching a start-up, if you are a budding entrepreneur, you are going to be better at it. Basically, everything I'm telling you -- sleep, meditation, renewal, are performance-enhancement tools. They're not like trade-offs between doing well at what you're doing and practicing these things that help you take care of yourself.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Well, it's always about things that I care passionately about. Like "Thrive" is a book that I really wanted to write for my daughters and their generation more than anything because I feel we've screwed up the world for you guys, and it's now up to us to help you figure it out and not to make all the same mistakes that we made. And, unfortunately, you look around, and you see so many people who've succeeded and have burned out along the way and you may think, hey, that's the only way to succeed." And I'm telling you "no." There are many, many new role models who are succeeding differently and who are prioritizing their own well-being and wisdom and wonder along the way.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Hello. My name is Diane Bass. And I go to Marygrove College in Detroit, Michigan. And I'm wondering, do you think that technology will be a hindrance to people gaining more wisdom, or will it help them or benefit them more? Thank you.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Yes. I think that technology can be a big hindrance, but we are learning to recognize that. And in fact, the paradox is that we are actually now finding ways for technology to help us disconnect from technology. I know it sounds paradoxical, but at the back of the "Thrive" book, you have an appendix with 12 meditation apps -- one of my favorites is Headspace -- that help you try to meditate by using technology, which sounds paradoxical, but it works. There's another appendix that has 12 apps that help you disconnect from all your notifications and all your distractions and concentrate on what it is you are doing. And one of my favorites is called antisocial. It puts everything on hold while you're writing an essay or writing a memo because you know how impossible it is to be really be undistracted if you're constantly checking your e-mail and your texts. If you look at history, some of the best and most significant creations took place when people were completely undistracted. Why do you think people have their best ideas in the shower?

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: \[ Audience murmurs \] It's probably the last place left where you can't take your smartphone, and I bet they're going to create an Apple Watch that you can take to the shower and that will be the end of that.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: It's about picking and choosing the right ways to use technology, folks. Scott from Temple University wants to know, "are there any regrets that you have in your professional life?"

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: No, really not. I feel that my professional life was...full of zigzags and coincidences and strange things happening along the way. But I think that's really what is so wonderful about life. It doesn't go in a linear way. It's not from "a" to "b" to "c." That's why it's important to be open to all the unexpected things that happen in life.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Very interesting woman. She's the chief technology officer of Cisco. She oversees tens of thousands of engineers. She's Indian. Her name is Padma Warrior. And she talks proudly about the fact that she gets eight hours of sleep. She writes haikus. She meditates. And every Saturday, she does a digital detox. So I say to myself, and everyone else I know, if the woman who runs technology for Cisco and oversees tens of thousands of engineers can do a digital detox every Saturday, so can I.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Hi. My name is Alexandra Yurish. I'm a senior and an English major at Auburn University in Montgomery. And as a young woman graduating soon and hoping to work in the media and the press, I'd like to ask how you were able to overcome barriers to make your presence known in a predominantly male field, and what you think we, as women, can do to make it possible for people of all genders to be equally represented in the workplace. Thank you.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Thank you. Great. So there obviously still is traditional barriers for women, but I think also there are barriers in our own heads. I think women have that obnoxious roommate speaking more loudly than men. And I think it's really important for us to speak up for ourselves. I mean, I know how often, you know, you can be in a room, and the men have no problem speaking up for themselves and thinking that what they're saying is incredibly profound. And the women are often holding back and being nervous about expressing themselves. So the lesson here for me has been to just say it, even if I'm nervous. You know, fearlessness is not the absence of fear. Fearlessness is really doing something even while you're afraid. If you wait to stop being afraid, I mean, you probably will do -- you will not do a lot. When I started speaking at Cambridge, you know, I was terrified. I was terrible. I mean, you have no idea. But I just made myself speak even though I was afraid, and it's like a muscle. You know, it gets stronger and stronger and stronger.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And you know, they say that public speaking is the worst fear that people have. The second worst fear is death by mutilation. And one of these reasons is because of how we are constantly judging ourselves and what we're saying and doing. But whatever it is that your fear is, take that step. and the minute you realize you are alive, you will grow that strength in that new muscle, so it will be easier the next time.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: We have two more questions for you. Andre from Temple university wants to know, "who influenced you to be the best at what you do, and what was their approach?"

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: I don't know if I'm the best at what I do, but I don't even know what that means. And, you know what? I like what Mikhail Baryshnikov, the ballet dancer said. I quote him in "Thrive." He said, "I don't try to dance better than anyone else. I just try to dance better than myself." And I think that's a real important way to approach life, not to just constantly compete and compare, but to look at what is it that you can keep doing that I can keep doing that makes me better and better. And there's no question that my biggest influence was my mother because she always made me believe in myself, by which way she didn't mean that I would not fail. She used to say to me, "failure is not the opposite of success. Failure is a stepping stone to success." And so failure is just fine. It's not a problem. In fact, trust me. There is nobody, nobody who has succeeded who has not failed along the way. You know, I mentioned to you my second book being rejected by 36 publishers.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: This is just one of the many, many failures in my life. In fact, I think people who have succeeded need to start talking more about their failures to remind everybody else that that's just an inevitable part of life.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: That's a good lesson to learn. Last question for you. Why do you think that it's important for students to join an organization like the National Society of Leadership and Success?

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: And they can come and hear great speakers. And they can also be there to support each other and learn from each other. From everything Michael has been telling me, this is an organization that is always going to be there for you. And I love the fact that it has leadership in the title, because we all need to discover that leadership potential in us, and that it has success in the title because now we have learned to redefine success, right? You know, "redefine success."

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: So when you hear the name of the organization and you hear the word "success," it isn't just going to mean for you money and power, okay? It's going to mean taking care of yourself, reaching out to the others, giving back, and really enjoying the mystery and the wonder of life instead of taking it all for granted. So that way you can have true success as opposed to the shallow kind of success that is costing such a heavy price. Thank you.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: This has been wonderful. My friends, the book is called "Thrive." It is out in paperback today. Check out the Oprah course, as well. And this concludes our broadcast lineup for the spring semester. So I'd like to thank our previous speakers. I want to thank Dan Harris. I want to thank Debbi Fields. I'd like to thank Arianna Huffington. And I really want to thank our host, Kevin Bracy. We miss you, we'll see you soon. We will be back for our next broadcast lineup on October 6th. And I'm happy to announce that we will be joined by the host and weather man of the "Today" show on NBC, Mr. Al Roker.

speaker: Arianna Huffington
text: Yeah, you can clap. Yeah. It's exciting. It is. Al's going to be talking about his upcoming book release "The Storm of the Century." It's true story of heroism and survival. But until then, I want to thank all of you for watching for this semester. And once again, let's thank Arianna Huffington.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: \<v -\>Hello, NSLS members. Watching a rebroadcast doesn't mean you can't be involved. We wanna hear your thoughts. Tweet us your favorite quote from today's rebroadcast using \#theNSLS for your chance to win $100 Amazon gift card. Enjoy the broadcast. (upbeat music) \<v -\>What kind of choices will you make from this day forth to live your life so that your life will be infinite? The contribution you will make to the lives of others will outlive you. \<v -\>I mean, first of all, you've gotta have an idea that is gonna make a positive difference in other people's lives. Otherwise, what's the point? \<v -\>Oftentimes in life, we spent so much time being afraid of what won't happen, that we never try and pursue the idea of, it will happen. \<v -\>You can do anything if you can envision it. \<v Narrator\>This is the NSLS national speaker broadcast with President Barack Obama. Here's your host, Charles Knippen. \<v -\>Hello, I'm Charles Knippen, president of The National Society of Leadership and Success. And I'm honored to be your host for tonight's special edition to the spring broadcast lineup. And I wanna encourage you to participate along with us.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: You can earn one of 100 copies of President Obama's book "A Promised Land," simply by going on social media and sharing with us an accomplishment that you're proud of. Make sure to hashtag \#theNSLS, include your name and your college name. Now, before we introduce our special guest, let's take a moment to watch this video. \<v Barack\>I want to tell a more personal story that might inspire young people considering a life of public service. How my career in politics really started with a search for a place to fit in, a way to explain the different strands of my mixed up heritage and how it was only by hitching my wagon to something larger than myself, that I was ultimately able to locate a community and purpose for my life. \<v -\>NSLS members watching across the country, I am pleased to welcome the 44th President of the United States, President Barack Obama. \<v -\>Chuck, thank you so much for having me. \<v -\>Mr. President, it is great to have you here and on behalf of 1.4 million members at over 700 colleges, I would like to welcome you.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And also thank you for spending some time with us here today. \<v -\>Right, yeah, I can't think of a better way to spend time than with young leaders from across the country. That's what I spend a lot of time working on is how can I be helpful to all those folks in colleges, universities, community colleges, and in neighborhoods across the country, we're making a difference. \<v -\>Excellent. Well, you've got the right group of motivated students. Each of these students are completing a certain step to building their leadership skills and you are a part of that process with them today. And I'd love to talk about leadership and success with you. And I don't think there's a better place to start than with your book "A Promised Land." Now, you put out this book and it has a call to action that's specific to the next generation. That call to action to remake the world. Could you share with our members the meaning behind that? \<v -\>Well, look, when you look at human history, when you look at American history, what has consistently moved society forward is the next generation, our founding fathers.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: At the time of the revolution, we tend to think of them as real old guys 'cause they got the wigs and all that. But Thomas Jefferson was 33 years old at the heart of the civil rights movement. Dr. King, at the Montgomery bus boycott. He's in his early to mid twenties. John Lewis was barely into his twenties when he led a march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge that helped to transform America to make it more just. So, every major step of progress that we've made has been brought about by a generation that comes in and starts asking questions. Why do we allow children to labor in dangerous settings? Why shouldn't women have the right to vote? Why are we still dividing our society on the basis of race? And you're seeing that today with many of the questions that have been asked around social justice issues. So, when I think of what's the great engine of progress, here in the United States and around the world, it's usually young people who haven't grown complacent about wrongs that need to be righted and improvements that need to be made for all of us.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And we greatly benefit from this and this generation, I think, is no exception. \<v -\>And I think you put that call to action in the book, very importantly, but also very succinctly. In terms of saying, this is in their hands. And I'd love to go first to one of our students who submitted a video question for you. His name is Darryl Johnson from Southern New Hampshire University. \<v -\>Hi, my name is Darryl Johnson with Southern New Hampshire University. In 2009, you came to my base in NAS Jax, and you showed all of the sailors that you cared. You showed me that you cared. That moment will stick with me for the rest of my life. Thank you for your service. And my question for you, Mr. President, is this, what advice do you have for someone that is facing a perceived impossibility? \<v -\>Well, first of all, thank you for your service. One of the great honors of being president of the United States is seeing our men and women in uniform and the extraordinary competence, sacrifice, discipline that they display every single day.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And you talk about young folks, sometimes you'll see like a 22 year old or 25 year old corporal who's in charge of billions of dollars of equipment, or more profoundly the lives of his fellow soldiers. When I think about the question of impossibility, look, I do think that as you get older, you start realizing there's some things that probably aren't gonna happen. I figured out that I was not gonna be an NBA player fairly early. It was around sophomore year in high school I figured I'm not on anybody's top 50 charts for major recruits. So I'm probably not gonna make a living doing that. But, once you get past certain highly specialized professions that require extraordinary skills or genetic blessings, I don't believe that things are impossible if you recognize two things and they're companion thoughts. One is that any great project has to be broken up into its component parts. I write about in "A Promised Land," I didn't go directly from, I'd like to maybe go into public service to, so let me be president of the United States. There were stages involved, right?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And I first started as a community organizer, and I described the learning process of being a leader at a local level. Then I went to the state legislature, went to the United States Senate. By the time I started running for president I had already accumulated a set of skills, a set of experiences, understanding of basic policy and I knew who I was. So there was a certain confidence and set of core values that I could operate off of. And that's true in business. Occasionally you'll get, the Mark Zuckerbergs of the world who make a big splash very young, but more often they're building blocks in place and somebody creating something of value. And so, learning how to break your longterm goal into a series of manageable pieces with realistic timeframes, I think is important. And then, related to that is taking a long perspective on things. I think that we live particularly now in a immediate gratification, Twitter speed society. The things that last, the things that matter take time. If you care about climate change, we're not gonna reverse our entire economy and how we use energy overnight.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: But if we start now and systematically move towards clean energy, if we are able to create the kinds of international cooperation that I write about in the book with respect to the Paris Accords, then we can make progress. We don't have to feel discouraged that it's impossible to do it can be done but it's gonna operate on a 20 year timeframe. And so, that I think is just as important because what that requires you then to do individually is figure out how do I sustain effort? How do I create resiliency when I have setbacks? Those are important skills to cultivate, because if you're doing something big and hard, you're gonna, by definition, confront setbacks. And you've gotta be able to figure out how do I learn from that? And how do I bounce back from that? \<v -\>All good points, Mr. President. And I think for a lot of students it starts with figuring out what their passion is that they can get through and have that grit of getting through those walls that they're going to hit along the way.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And it was interesting to read in your book about how you discovered your own passions. And that at first in your book, you're described as, you described yourself as not a top notch student, as a self-professed partier, but that a pile of books at a garage sale changed the direction of your life and helped you find your passion. I'm hoping you can share that story because it is the first step, like you're referring to it, it's the first step for students to find that passion. What was that pile of books? How did it impact you? And what tips would you give for our students in finding that passion that they can have that grit for? \<v -\>I think that's a great point, Chuck, look, as I describe in the book and my first book dreams from my father. I write a lot about this. I had a father who left when I was two, who I didn't know very well. I was an African-American in a place, Hawaii at the time, that didn't have a lot of African-Americans, didn't have a lot of male role models who looked like me.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: So I had to kind of piece together what it meant to be a man, what it meant to be an African-American. And initially I think I reacted to that by rebelling, which a lot of teenagers do. In high school, I, even though I was, as you said, spending a lot of time in extracurricular activities and not focused on my schoolwork, my mother had given me a set of values, core values, my mother and grandparents who raised me had given me a set of core values that were there, even if I wasn't always living up to them. And they had planted in me a love of reading. And in high school, something around my sophomore year clicked where I happened to be at a garage sale, I write about this and I come to a big bin full of old books, and it was everything from "The Autobiography of Malcolm X" to Dostoevsky's "Crime and Punishment." And, I just, for whatever reason, decided, let me buy, they're a nickel a piece or dime a piece, let me gather a few of these. Maybe I'll pick one up, see what's in them.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And it created, while I was still playing basketball and chasing girls and all that, it created this part of my life in which I dove deep into books and into study. And the books that I read, I read not for technical skills, they weren't how to manuals, they weren't on any particular subject. They were really books about who are we as human beings? How do we live a good life? How do we understand tragedy? How do we think about issues like war or poverty? What are the stories we tell ourselves about our relationships to our families and the people we love and how do we overcome our blind spots and our bigotries? And I told that story in "A Promised Land" because I think that for so many of us in school we're trained to be good at math, or write a term paper, or get through the chemistry exam. We don't spend a lot of time just reflecting on what does it mean to live a good life? What's important to us? How do we ask ourselves questions about being intentional and setting a direction for ourselves?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And those aren't typically found in how to manuals or self-help books, as much as they're in great literature and great stories. And the myths that have grown up around our society. And that kind of deep dive is something that, hopefully, particularly when you're in college, you spend some time doing it and it becomes a lifelong habit because here's one thing I'm absolutely certain of, that the people who do great things, it is not so much because they did everything perfectly as they had clarity about direction and what mattered to them. And in my case, it was through this exploration that I discovered that what I cared deeply about was issues of social justice and activism and social change. And I also learned that it was important to me not in an abstract way, but in part because of it was connected to my own story, as I knew what it was like not to have a father. I had to figure out my own identity. I had to figure out what it means to be an American in a big multiracial, multicultural society.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And how do we bring ourselves together and find what's common in all of us? Those are the kinds of things that you don't get all the time in a classroom. But you can get in books if you dedicate yourself to it. \<v -\>And I think it starts with that exploration. I love that word, that you have to explore your own values. You have to explore your own desires. You have to explore what's your background and how that impacts your world view. And so, again, I think it's a great call to action for all of our members watching today to pick up those books, to explore different things, to find those passions. So thank you, Mr. President. Excellent, well, let's go over to our second student video question today. This one is from Katarina Garcia. She is from Texas A\&M-Corpus Christi. \<v -\>Hello, President Obama. My name is Katarina Garcia from Texas A\&M University-Corpus Christi. It is an absolute honor to be able to ask you a question today.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: My question for you is, being that you accomplished so much at such a young age, how did you ensure that your voice was heard when working with older, more experienced colleagues? \<v -\>Well, that is a great question, Katarina. When I write about when I arrived in Chicago as a community organizer, I was working with a bunch of churches on the south side of Chicago, the pastors and the community leaders that I was working with they were all my parents' age, sometimes older. So they'd look at this kid and they'd say, "What does he know? How's this guy gonna help us on anything?" At that time I was getting a haircut maybe once a month to save money, so the hair was kinda mussed up, the clothes were a little raggedy. But a couple of things, I think when I advise my own daughters, when I advise younger staff, number one is leadership sometimes we portray as you doing all the talking. It turns out actually the best leadership is listening and being predisposed to other people's skills, power, talent.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: One of the things I found as a young person in a room, but with some leadership responsibilities was, the most useful thing I could do sometimes was not so much to speak a lot myself as to direct traffic, to be a conductor, to identify who else in the room was saying something smart, important, giving good guidance and highlighting that. And I think that's a broader principle of leadership. We have a tendency to think the person who's speaking all the time, who's making the speeches, who's kind of hogging the spotlight, that that automatically is the leader. And that may not be the case. So that was, that's point number one. And that makes you, I think, more palatable to older folks if they see that you're not trying to take all the credit yourself, but in fact, you're just trying to facilitate others to be their best selves and a team to work together as best they can. Second thing though, was, knowing your stuff.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I think if you are young and you walk in and you've done your homework and you have good information and you have data, and you've got research, so that you are useful to the problem that's trying to be solved. At the end of the day, you can feel confident about offering your opinion and having your voice heard. Because you know what you know. And a little secret about any kind of group dynamic is, a lot of people haven't done their homework and a lot of people aren't paying attention to and preparing. And if you out prepare and out work folks, then you can come in with a certain amount of confidence, not cockiness, but confidence that what you have to say matters, particularly if you're picking and choosing your spots.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And this is particularly important, 'cause Katarina asked, for women, young women like my daughters where, let's face it, although we've made some progress on this front, oftentimes the guys in a meeting are talking over people or, a woman will make a point, and then suddenly the guy comes 10 minutes later, and makes the same point and acts like it's his point that's being made. So I think it's important for women in particular to not fall into some of the social constructs that have been set up where they're expected to defer all the time. It doesn't mean that you have to overdo it, but you should push up and maybe overcompensate a little bit, if there's a voice inside you saying, well, maybe it's not my turn, or maybe I should just wait until I'm called on or, if you've got something to say that's important, you've got to kind of blow through that. \<v -\>So respect and listen and make sure your voice is heard in that room. I think again, as a young person walking in, as these students are emerging out, I think those are very valuable tips for them, Mr. President.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Thank you for sharing that with Katarina's question. Much appreciated. All right, sir, well, I wanna shift gears on you a little bit. In your book you talk a bit and make a meaningful share, a short but meaningful share about how early on in your campaigns you had the tendency to be a little wordy. I think the exact quote, I think the exact quote was, "I was just plain wordy "and that was a real problem. "If there were two sides of an argument, you would find the fourth." And I love that. but I am wondering today, if you would be up for a little game, because we wanna get the most out of every minute with you today for our members and all that learning. \<v -\>Lightning round. \<v -\>Lightning round with President Obama. (dramatic music) All right, sir, simple rules today. Eight questions, 90 seconds. Are you up for the challenge? \<v -\>Let's do it. \<v -\>All right. Let's put 90 seconds up on the board here. I wanna start with, we'll start the timer with my first question. Here we go. All right, number one. Your favorite book?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: \<v -\>"A Fire Next Time" by James Baldwin, very timely right now. \<v -\>A leader every student should know about? \<v -\>Ella Baker. One of the unsung heroes of the civil rights movement. \<v -\>A pump up or motivational song on your playlist? \<v -\>"My First Song" by Jay-Z. \<v -\>A favorite quote? \<v -\>Favorite quote. Now that one's a little tough. "Don't worry about doing things right, as much as doing the right thing." \<v -\>A stress reliever? \<v -\>Exercise. \<v -\>Place that makes you happy? \<v -\>Hawaii. \<v -\>A movie that impacted your life? \<v -\>"The Godfather." Just 'cause I love it. (crosstalk) \<v -\>An important lesson you learned outside the classroom? \<v -\>Be useful and be kind. \<v -\>With 12 seconds left, Mr. President, I can say you've got the brevity thing down now. Congratulations. And thank you for- \<v -\>I will say that my wife and my daughters might contest that I've completely got it down, but they may wanna try this contest at the dinner table. To edit me a little bit. \<v -\>Well, I tell you what, you have now mastered the lightning round with President Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: (dramatic music) And you've now got this to share with them for the rest of your life. So, all right, sir, well, let's shift gears to our final student video question today. This one is coming from Shakira Jackson at the University of Pittsburgh at Bradford. \<v -\>Greetings and salutations. My name is Shakira Jackson. And I am a history political science student at the University of Pittsburgh. President Obama, one day, I want to lead this country. So what was your inspiration for continuing to move forward with running for president when you had many either not wanting you to or doubting your campaign? \<v -\>Well, Shakira, great question. And I can tell you got energy. So that's one thing you need if you're gonna run for president. Look, I think, I try to emphasize to young people who have expressed some interest in public service, that one of the things that was good for me was, I didn't go into it saying to myself, I wanna be this, or I wanna be that, I wanna be a mayor, or I wanna be a senator, or I wanna be president.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: What I said to myself is, I wanna get healthcare for folks who didn't have it. How do I do that? I want kids who don't have a good education to get a better education. What tools or what position can I get that might make a difference there? I guess one way of thinking about it is, I worried less about what I was gonna be than what I was gonna do or get done. The by-product of that was for me to go into public service. And as I moved through my career, the opportunity presented itself then to be president, and I said, okay, well, given the things I wanna do, this would be a worthwhile goal to try it out. And I think that the reason I was able to do it was A, I knew why I wanted to do it, and it wasn't just about ego and I was happy and doing well before I ran for president and I would have been happy not being president, but it was also a willingness to take some risks which I think you always have to be prepared to take. There was no guarantee of victory.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And I think a lot of times fear of failure, fear of loss, fear of embarrassment stops us from taking calculated risks. I would not have run for president if I had no chance of winning. I had some chance of winning. I had done enough preparation and work where it was a plausible possibility that I could get the nomination and win. And still, there is an element of why not? Let's try something that hasn't been done before. And I would urge everybody who's listening to, don't always ask yourself all the reasons why you shouldn't do something. Your life is a great experiment. And if you know who you are and what you care about, then there are gonna be some risks involved in, whether it's starting a business or getting involved in a career as a writer or deciding you wanna go into public service, whatever you do, including by the way, choosing a partner to live your life with, they're always gonna be some risks. But there are great rewards and so, go ahead and take them.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: \<v -\>Fantastic, again, going back to that whole part of, starting with your passion, knowing your why, getting you through, when those walls hit, and you've gotta have the grit to make it happen. I think definitely Shakira has demonstrated she's got the energy to make that happen for herself. So, for all of our students, we wanna make sure that they have that leadership not only potential, but they have that grit to continue on towards their passions. All right, Mr. President, we are down to our last question today, and it is one that we like to ask all of our guests. And we'd like to know from you, why do you feel it's important for students to develop themselves as leaders? With organizations like the NSLS or others, to build those leadership skills, to build communication skills, identify their passions, why do you believe that's important? \<v -\>Well, a lot of times, as I said before, we have stereotypes about who leaders are.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Some of the greatest leaders I know are folks who are almost shy, they're quiet, they don't seek out the limelight, but they know how to work with other people and motivate and inspire them in ways that brings out the best in them. And that's a talent and a gift that applies in any setting. You are a leader if in your own neighborhood and your own community you are helping to do something about a homeless problem there. You are a leader if you're in our military, and you may not have rank, but the unit that you're in, they're looking at you to set an example in terms of performance that may have to do with saving lives. You're a leader if you care passionately about our environment and are making a commitment to get other young people involved in doing something about issues of climate change or environmental degradation. Whatever it is you're doing, the point is that for you to have impact involves being with other people, and working with other people and mobilizing ideas and energy in a direction that meets the moment.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And that is something that all of us have a capacity to do. Now, we have to recognize that a part of being a good leader is also being a good follower. And there are times where our role is to support people who are trying to get stuff done. And you're not always gonna be out front, you're not always gonna be in the limelight, but we all have a role to play, particularly here in the United States where the whole premise of our government is self-government. This place only works if all of us are active citizens who are informed and care and are willing to participate and have our voices heard. \<v -\>And I think that that is giving that call to action that you have done so well in this book to go out there and remake this world and get students involved in being an active part of that process. So, I can't think of a better way to wrap up this conversation. So I wanna say thank you for sharing your knowledge and insights with our members across the country today. It has been an honor and privilege being with you here today.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: To our members, I want to express appreciation for each of you for continuing on the journey and being committed to being a leader who makes a better world. And as President Obama has said today, we wanna encourage each of you to stand up, step forward and remake the world. Thanks for being here with us today. Take care. \<v -\>Thank you so much, Chuck. Take care of yourself. (upbeat music)

speaker: Blake Mycoskie
text: And in this one café, I met a couple of women that were also in Argentina for about a month. But instead of goofing around like I was and having vacation, they were doing volunteer work. speaker: Blake Mycoskie

text: Thank you. So, that summer, we sold 10,000 pairs out of my apartment -- 10,000. My goal was 250. And now we just sold 10,000 pairs in one summer. Leadership is something to be learned. It is not automatic. You don't just jump into it and think you're a leader. And so it's really important to understand not just the fundamentals, but then put it into practice, into action. And as I said earlier, leadership happens at every level. It is not when you get the title. That is not when you become a leader. Leadership is also about influence. And so how is it that you are influencing your colleagues, your peers? How are you leading in those scenarios?

speaker: Bozoma Saint John
text: You'll be a much better leader if you take a combination of the learnings and the practices which you're being taught, and then applying them in your current role wherever you are, however you sit, and then you'll become a better leader. \<v -\>Thank you. Thank you so much. Boz, I want to thank you for being with us tonight. I had a great time speaking with you. It was incredibly insightful and a lot of fun. So, thank you so much. \<v -\>Thank you so much. And now, I mean, I think folks heard me call you Dev a couple times. I would encourage everyone to just call you Dev from now on. \<v -\>I'll take it I vote for Dev. It's perfect. \<v -\>I love it, I love it. I'll take it. All right, NSLS members, I'd like to thank you for watching this evening and look forward to being with you on March 7th with our special guest, Daymond John. But before we go, I want to say thank you once again to Bozoma Saint John. \<v -\>Thank you so much. Appreciate it. Bye\! (upbeat music)
