speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Good evening, everyone. And thank you, Kevin, for that very generous introduction. It is great to be with all of you all across the country to talk about leadership 'cause that really is what I want to talk about tonight. But before I do that, I need to sort of correct perhaps a misimpression that Kevin gave you. You know, it was a very generous introduction. Although he said I started at the bottom and I worked my way up, it sounds kind of smooth, you know? It wasn't. Success never is. My life certainly wasn't and hasn't been. And so I want to fill in a couple of the blanks in that quick story he told. I grew up in a family with a stay-at-home mom. My dad was a professor. And my parents pushed really hard that we should get a good education and that we could be anything we wanted to be and that we should work hard to fulfill our potential, whatever that was. And in fact, when I was 8, my mother gave me a little plaque, and it said, "What you are is God's gift to you.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: What you make of yourself is your gift to God." And I thought that made a lot of sense. It made a big impression on me when I was 8 years old. But I also really had no idea what I should make of myself. And so I was one of these kids. I was a middle child. I was sort of the peacemaker in the family. And I was one of these kids that sort of had a dream a day. You know, I was going to be a fireman and then I was going to be a ballerina, and then I didn't know what the heck I was going to be. But I turned into kind of a Goody-Two-Shoes, you know? My sister was rebellious. My brother was sort of rebellious in another way, as well. And I was the faithful, good middle child. So I go off to college. And I graduate from college. I work two jobs. I thankfully knew how to type. I know no one has to type anymore, but when I came up in school, there actually were things called typewriters.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I date myself because the big technology innovation when I was working my way through undergraduate school as a secretary was something called the IBM Selectric typewriter. Okay? When I was in college, I was something called a Kelly Girl. We don't call them that anymore. We call them Kelly Temporary Personnel. But Kelly Girls were mostly women who would go into offices and be temporary administrator personnel. We would go in for a week or two and type or answer phones, and so that's what I did to put myself through school. I graduated with a degree in medieval history and philosophy, which meant, honestly, that I was all dressed up and nowhere to go. I graduated in the middle of a recession. There weren't a lot of jobs, and there certainly weren't a lot of jobs for people who had degrees in medieval history and philosophy. So I didn't know what to do with myself. And my dad was a professor of law, so I thought, "Well, I'll go to law school." And I had to work my way through that, too. But here's the thing. I got to law school, and I hated it.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I absolutely hated it. And I agonized over the fact that I hated it 'cause I wasn't a quitter and I'd always kind of done what everybody expected me to do. But I finally came to what was at that time the most important and the most difficult decision I had ever yet made. And I was 22 at the time. It was an incredibly hard decision. I decided that I was going to quit. I decided to go home and tell my parents, "I hate this. I quit." I felt like a quitter, and worse than that, I had no idea what I was going to do. And, in fact, as you might expect, my mother and dad said, "Well, what are your plans?" And my answer was, "I don't know." But I needed to pay the rent, and I needed to make a living. And so I went to the want ads, and I answered the first ad that I saw, and that ad was for a receptionist, someone who would sit in the front of an office of a small company. It was nine people. It was a commercial Realtor.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And my job, it said in the want ad, was to sit in the front and type and file and answer the phones. I got that job. I didn't think it was beneath me. I was grateful to have it. And every day, I came in to work determined to do the best job I could. And that went on for about six months. And after about six months, two men who worked in that office came to my desk, and they said, "We've been watching you, and we think maybe you could do more than type and file and answer the phones. Do you want to know what we do?" And that was my introduction to business. Now, that very first job -- it was a modest job. There was no runway. There was no plan. There was no apparent future in that job. But here's the thing -- I learned three really important things in that job -- actually, four, probably.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: The first thing I learned was what it feels like to be at the bottom in an organization, and that was a really important thing for me to learn, and it's something I hope I will never forget. The second thing I learned was that even someone at the very bottom of an organization can make a difference -- particularly, anyone in an organization can make a difference for the people that the organization is supposed to be serving, whether those people are customers or students or citizens. Anyone can make a difference for the people an organization is serving. And I learned that because, one day, a gentleman came in through the front door, and he said, "I'd like to meet with one of your brokers. I'm a new client." And I said, "Well, that's wonderful, sir. May I ask you why you've chosen to come to Marcus \& Millichap?" That was the name of the firm.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And he said, "Well, I chose because of you, because every time you answered the phone, you were professional, you were cheerful, you asked questions about what I needed, and I figured that was a good reflection on the firm." And that was a really important lesson and something that I would remember all through my career. And the final lesson I learned was about leadership... because those two men showed leadership. Why? Why do I say that? Because those two gentlemen saw possibilities in me. They saw possibilities in me that I didn't see in myself. They saw potential in me that I didn't know I had. And because they saw possibilities in me, because they saw potential I didn't know I had, they helped me seize those possibilities. They helped me believe in that potential. And that, actually, is what leadership is about. People get confused, I think, about leadership. People think that leadership is about power or a title or a position. I mean, I used to think that.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I thought, as I was coming up in the ranks -- I went to work after that -- By the way, after I left that small firm, I ran away to Italy to teach English for a year -- another great plan. \[ Scoffs \] Finally buckled down and went and got an MBA and began working in the huge company called AT\&T -- a million employees. I started at the very, very bottom. And I thought, when I started at the very bottom of that huge firm with a million employees -- I thought that leadership was about the guy who had the big office. I thought leadership was about the person with the title. I thought leadership was about whoever had the biggest budget or the most people reporting to them or the best perks or maybe even the biggest paycheck. For a long time, I thought leadership was about power. But leadership is about none of those things. Leadership is about seeing possibilities. Leadership is about seizing possibilities. And leadership, most especially, is about unlocking potential in others. That is the highest calling of leadership.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And I think about those two men a lot because they saw possibilities, because they unlocked possibilities in me, because, by doing that, they made a positive difference in my life. Well, fast-forward. People ask me all the time, "Well, did you have a plan to become a C.E.O.? And the truth is, I never had a plan to become a C.E.O. I didn't have a plan that I was gonna work my way up. What I learned about myself was that I liked challenges. The harder the job, the better I liked it. What I learned about myself was that if you gave me a job, I saw possibilities. What I learned about myself is when people said, "Ohh, don't take that job. It's too hard," I would say, "Ooh, that looks interesting." And in the course of learning that about myself, I would take on harder and harder and harder things. And guess what I learned. When you take on hard things, people take notice. And if you accomplish something in a really difficult situation, people take notice. But along the way, I learned something else, as well. I liked challenges.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I liked doing something that I felt, "Wow, I really made a difference here." The thing that I figured out is most people were just like me. The thing I figured out is that most people actually want to do something worthwhile. Most people want to come to work every day and say, "You know what? I made a difference." Most people want to be challenged. Most people would prefer to put their energies towards something that's worthy of them, not just, you know, spend every day going through the same old, same old. And so, over time, I learned not just to have faith in myself that I could take on tough challenges -- no. What I learned is to have faith in others. What I learned is that, if I could collaborate with other people and take on a tough challenge together, that we could get it done. And I also learned what, for me, was the joy of the situation. And I actually think joy is important in life. Why did I quit law school? Just back to that for a second. Because there was no joy. I hated it.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And I don't think anyone can be good at something unless they find joy in it. If you want to tap your own potential, if you want to make your own positive difference, there has to be joy in it for you, as well as challenge. And so taking on the hard things was challenging, but seeing how people reacted when they accomplished something, that was the joy. Think back to your own experiences. I can remember going into a situation where I was going to have a team of three people working for me. And given the time that I came up in the business world and given the kinds of businesses that I worked for, technology-based businesses, the truth of the matter is most of the time, the people who were working for me were men a lot older than me. And you can imagine that a lot of times, those men would look at me and say, "Why is she our boss?" It's not that they were bad people. It's just that they were skeptical.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And one of the ways that I would overcome skepticism in every job that I went into, was I would pay them the respect of letting them know that I knew that they probably knew more about the situation I had just stepped into than I did. And so I'd ask a lot of questions. One of the things I learned over and over and over by asking questions is that people always know what's wrong. They're just rarely asked. And because people always know what's wrong, they also always can figure out how to fix it if they're asked, if given the opportunity. Anyway, we had this very difficult situation here. These three far older men. They're all engineers. I'm not. And we have this big, difficult engineering problem, and they hadn't been able to solve it. I wasn't an engineer. So I had to think very carefully about, "How do I add value? How do I make a positive difference?" Because I can't tell them how to be engineers. But maybe I could help apply their capability, their expertise, their potential to solving a problem that they hadn't been able to solve.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Make a long story short, we did solve that problem. But here's where the joy comes in. There is a certain look that people get when they accomplish something they didn't think they could accomplish. And that look is the same the world over. I have worked with women in desperate situations and places in the world, women who have nothing except their own potential and their own determination to make a better life for themselves and their families. And they face a difficult and desperate situation and yet, if someone takes a chance on them, if someone gives them the opportunity to utilize their potential they accomplish something they didn't think they could accomplish. I don't care whether it's a middle-aged male engineer or a young woman in a desperate situation in Afghanistan, people get the same look every time they accomplish more than they thought was possible. There's a look people get in their eyes when they realize, "Yes, I can do this. "Yes, I can make a difference. "Yes, I had more potential than I realized. Yes, I can solve this problem." There's a look. And that, for me, is the joy of leadership.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: One of the things I had to learn the hard way is not to pay too much attention to what everybody thought about me, 'cause everybody thought all kinds of things about me. All of you know, whatever situation you're in, if you make a difference, if you make waves, if you do things differently, if you take on the hard things, if you're a little bit different than people around you, you're going to get scrutinized, criticized. People are going to talk. And for a lot of us, when we're coming up, that talk is the most important thing. What are people saying about me? Ooh, I'm rattled by the fact that people are saying, "You shouldn't do that. "You can't do that. Why are you doing that?" And I've learned over time that what people say about you isn't what counts. What counts is how you choose to live your life. And I also learned that no matter what you do, if you're having an impact at all, people will say things. One of the highest compliments I ever received was from a reporter who I don't think actually thought much of me.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: But this reporter said to me, "You know, Carly, you are the most ferociously self-determined person I've ever met." And that to me was the highest compliment I could be given. Because each of us must determine ourselves. We can't let other people do it for us. And that means finding what brings you joy, finding how you like to make a difference, finding what gives you a challenge, finding a way to tap your own potential. Now, a lot of you listening today are coming of age or building a family at a different time than the time I'm talking about. We've gone way beyond IBM Selectric typewriters. In fact, remember I was a history major, so forgive me if I talk in historic terms for a moment. But I believe that we now are living in a transformational time in human history. And I use that term "transformational" very deliberately. Why do I say that?

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Because throughout all of human history, the millennia of human history, it has only been in the last 15 years that any person, anywhere could get ahold of any piece of information or communicate with anyone else at a time and a place of their choosing. Any person, anywhere can get any piece of information and can communicate with anyone else at a time and a place of their choosing. That is transformational. Indeed, I would tell you, it is revolutionary, and in fact, revolutions have started because people suddenly realize, "Ooh, I can communicate with others who think what I do. Oh, people are watching what we're doing." I don't think we yet fully understand the impact of this transformational era in human history. Any person, anywhere can get any piece of information and can communicate with anyone else. And we're proving it here this evening.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And that means, I believe, the reason I think this is the most fantastic era in human history, the reason I have such optimism despite all the problems we have in the world and in our communities and in our nation -- The reason I am optimistic is because this era is a time where more things are more possible for more people than at any time in human history, when more human potential can be unlocked. There's only one limitless resource in this world, and that is human potential. And most people have far more than they ever realize. Most people have far more than they ever utilize. And it takes leadership and opportunity to unlock people's potential. It takes challenge to unlock people's potential. But as phenomenal as this time is, and it is phenomenal, this is also a difficult time. And it's a difficult time because the same technology that allows you to get any piece of information, anytime, anywhere or communicate with anyone about any subject at any time, it's also true that this is a really complicated world now. Everything is interconnected. And that means that all of our problems are more complex.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Because of technology, our timeframes have shrunk dramatically, and so there's less time to figure out what to do. Things are happening all the time. The pace of change is accelerating. All of this makes it hard. And I believe, also, the technology, as wonderful as it is, as empowering as it is, it's also -- let's face it -- a huge distraction. How many of us spend sort of all day long responding to stuff, reacting to stuff? How much of it is actually important? Probably about 15% if we're lucky. And I also think because of all this stuff that we see, that we hear, that we can gain access to every day, there's a tendency towards, dare I say, superficiality. You know, we can kind of skim along the surface of things all day long. As much as things have changed for people because of this brave new world that we're in and because of the capabilities of technology, it is still true that the most profoundly human things are the most important things... in defining success, in making a good life, in fulfilling potential. Those things haven't changed.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: So let's talk a minute about what those things are. What are the profound human things that make a difference? Well, first, one we've been talking about -- leadership. And leadership, again, it's not about power, position, or title. You know and I know. We all know people who have big titles, lots of power, positions, budgets. Lots of folks reporting to them. And guess what. A lot of those people have never led a day in their lives. And then there are people who have nothing. Nothing. And they lead every single day. Because leadership is about making a positive difference. Leadership is about unlocking potential in others. Here's another misconception about leadership -- It's not the same as management. You know what management is in business? Management in business or in a university or in any situation. A good manager is someone who produces acceptable results within known constraints and conditions. Management's really important. You need to manage your time. You need to manage your budget. You need to manage your household. You need to manage your organization. But that's not leadership.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: If management is the production of acceptable results within known constraints and conditions, leadership is about changing those conditions. Leadership is about changing the order of things. Leadership is about seeing possibilities, seizing possibilities. Helping others see possibilities. Helping other seize possibilities. Leaders say, "Here is where we are, but here is where we must go." And leaders capture the potential of the people that they work with and motivate people to go somewhere else. By the way, that's always been what leadership is about. My favorite quote about leadership is from a philosopher of thousands of years ago, a Chinese philosopher named Sun Tzu. And Sun Tzu said this -- "A good leader is he who men revere. An evil leader is he who men despise. A great leader is he of whom the people say, 'We did it ourselves.'" Because, you see, great leaders unlock potential. Great leaders build capability. And that was true when Sun Tzu said it thousands of years ago. And it is true to this day. What's another thing that doesn't change? It's important for success. It's important to live a good life.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: It's important to make a positive difference in any setting -- a family, a community, a company, a nation, a world. Judgment. Judgment. What's judgment? Judgment is the ability to take on a really complicated problem where there's no black-and-white answer, where it's not clearly right or wrong, and make some decisions about how to proceed. I have worked with lots of people who tend to approach a problem and say, "I'm here at A, and I need to get to Z," and the only way some people can get there is to proceed A, B, C, D, E... but they get stymied when they don't know where F is. They get stymied when the path ahead isn't straight and clear. And most problems today, the path ahead isn't straight and clear. Judgment is the ability to make decisions in a very uncertain environment. And judgment comes from interacting with lots of different kinds of people, learning and trying lots of different things, having a world view, being broad in your point of view, not narrow in your point of view. Judgment is not the same as expertise.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: There are a lot of experts in the world, but I would not trust them to solve a difficult problem. Have you ever listened to experts, you know, and they'll say something about a problem? And you sit there and listen to them, and you think, "Yeah, but it won't ever work, because the world isn't perfect like that and because people don't react like that." Perspective. Another thing. Leadership, judgment. What's perspective? Perspective is the ability to distinguish between what's really important and what actually isn't important at all. And in a complicated world, where information is flying at you all the time, it's hard to learn how to have perspective. But, again, the only way you gain perspective -- You know what? "That's actually not important, and this actually really is important." The only way to gain that perspective is, again, to raise your sights, lift your eyes, get a broad view, not a narrow view. And how do you get a broad view? You get a broad view by talking to lots of people who aren't like you, trying a lot of different things.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And there's one more thing that's really important in success and in life that hasn't changed for thousands of years. It's the most fundamental perhaps of all. Leadership, judgment, perspective...and ethics. Having a moral compass. Being able to go home and say, "You know what? That's not the right thing to do." I will tell you that the more successful people become in their lives, the more opportunities there are to do the wrong thing. That's just a fact. And it's why we see so many people in high positions do obviously wrong things. They have more opportunity. And what I have found in my own life and in observing the lives of others is that if you don't have a pretty strong moral compass, if you don't have a pretty strong sense that you develop over time -- "This isn't right, this isn't what I should be doing" -- If you don't take the time to listen to that little voice inside you saying, "Is this really what I ought to be doing?" Then people barrel along and do the wrong thing.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: So, I'm going to -- Based on all that, there are a couple things -- I wouldn't presume to say "advice." But a couple of suggestions I would make to you. First, have the courage and take the time to find your own way. Find your own way. There's a lot of pressure on people to go a certain way. Maybe that pressure comes from your family. It came from my family. "Well, you know, you're going to go to law school." Maybe the pressure comes from your family. Maybe the pressure comes from a partner. Maybe the pressure comes from your community. Maybe the pressure comes from a job where you currently are, where people say, "No, no, no. Do this. Do this. Go this way." Sometimes the pressure is simply to conform, to do it the way everybody else does it. But if you want to tap your own potential, if you want to make the most positive difference you can in your life, if you want to have the biggest impact you can in your life, you must have the courage and find the time, take the time to find your own way.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Put another way, you have to choose your own path. People sometimes ask me, what's my definition of success? My definition of success is when someone has led the life they chose. Choose your own path. To choose your own path, to have the courage to find your own way means you have to take risks. All of us have to take risks. And, you know, people hear the term "risk taking," and theoretically it sounds great. People say, "Yeah, yeah. I'm a risk taker." But here's the truth. What does risk taking really require? It requires mistake making. If you're not making mistakes, you're not taking risks. You're not trying new things. You're not learning new things. So, in order to find your own way, you have to take risks. In order to tap your full potential, you must take risks, and if you're going to take risks, you will make mistakes. I've made loads of mistakes. The goal is not to make the same mistake twice. Sometimes -- I think this is particularly true, sometimes of women. We feel like we have to be perfect. We have to be perfect.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And of course, none of us are, and none of us can be, and the goal is not perfection. The goal is progress. So take the risks. Be prepared to make the mistakes. When you lead an organization or you lead a team, you have to let people make mistakes. For those of you out there who are parents, you know that as a parent sometimes you have to let your child make a mistake. You know how it's going to turn out, but you also know they got to go ahead and do it, because that's how they grow. And it's true of adults, as well. Third, there is no substitute for hard work and the pursuit of excellence. Every single job, it doesn't matter how humble -- Every single job can be done well and should be done well. And to do anything well takes hard work. There is no substitute for hard work and the pursuit of excellence. And every job -- every job can be seen as series of possibilities or it can be seen as a series of limitations.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And the people who see possibilities in a job are going to do better in that job. And the people who see limitations -- You know people like this. People say, "I can't do this. "I shouldn't do this. No one will let me do that." They don't get much done. And the people who say, Yeah, but I could do this. "Maybe I ought to do that. And nobody's telling me I can't do this." They get a lot done. To all the folks who are getting ready to graduate or are worrying about their job, you know, I said I graduated in the middle of a recession with a degree in medieval history and philosophy -- not exactly hirable. Don't wait for the perfect job. Just get a job. Just get started. Any job you get, you'll learn something important. Any job you get will offer you possibilities. Any job you get will offer opportunities to you if you do that job well. So don't worry about the perfect job. I see a lot of kids with a lot of potential who say, "I don't want to do this.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I don't want to do that." They're waiting for that perfect job. Don't wait. Just start. Just start. What happens when you get a job -- even if it's not the perfect job. Remember my first secretarial job. What happens when you get a job and you do it really well -- And this happens over and over and over. It's happened in every job I've ever had. if you get a job and you see the possibilities and you exploit those possibilities and you work hard at that job, and you do the best job you can and you pursue excellence, guess what. People will notice. And opportunity will knock. And when it does, you have to have the guts to walk through the door. You can't at that moment when opportunity knocks say, "I've never done that before." You can't, when opportunity knocks, say, "Maybe I'm not ready for that." When opportunity knocks, you have to walk through that door. I have seen a lot of people in my career who had great potential, but they were so worried about the next job that they forgot to do the job they had.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And the truth is, everyone who is offered an opportunity, everyone who is offered a promotion, is offered that opportunity or that promotion because of the job they're doing today. Not because of the job they might do tomorrow. So do the job you have to the absolute best of your ability. Fifth, I'm going to quote someone else. I'm going to quote a scientist this time. Charles Darwin, father of the theory of evolution. What did Charles Darwin say? He said it is not the strongest of the species that survives nor the most intelligent, but those most adaptive to change. And it is true. It is true of people. It is true of organizations. You know people who get really good at something. They become experts at something. They're comfortable with something. And at a certain point, they stop learning. They stop adapting. They kind of stick to what they know. And what happens when people stop adapting, when people stop learning -- I don't care if they are 21 or 81 -- is they get old before their time and they definitely never fulfill their potential. There is a term in bullfighting, and it's called querencia.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And in a Spanish bullfight -- I don't know how many of you have ever seen a bullfight -- But in a bullfight, there is a place in the ring where the bull will always return. So, as the bull goes through the fight and he is more and more threatened, there's a certain spot that the bull will go. And that spot -- Every bull's spot is different, but that spot is called querencia. And of course, what happens as the bullfight goes on, and the bull is more and more threatened, and he keeps returning to the same spot, what happens? He is more and more vulnerable. Well, guess what. people have querencias, too. People have spots that they keep returning to. Maybe we call it a comfort zone. Maybe we call it something we know we're good at. But when you stop learning and you stop adapting and you keep going back to your querencia, you won't achieve your full potential. Sixth, learn how to problem solve and collaborate with other people. Learn how to problem solve and collaborate with other people. It sounds so basic, but it's actually quite a difficult skill.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: If you think about the dialogue that goes on in our political process today -- Think about what happens. You know, I do a lot of commentary on television, but what's frustrating to me about the political process is one side will say one thing -- "Here's the problem" -- then the other side will say the other thing -- "Here's the problem" -- It's a totally different problem. And they never start problem solving. They just talk at each other back and forth. They are not problem solving, and they are not collaborating. There are some basic things you have to do to problem solve and collaborate with other people. And one of them is you have to ask questions. Any time you have a problem, the best way to start solving that problem and collaborating with other people is to come to the situation informed, but with an open mind. And then ask questions. Remember, I told you that job where I had those three engineers. What did I do? I spent so much of my time asking questions. People are usually really smart. And importantly, people have different points of view.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: It's one of the reasons why it's important to surround yourself sometimes with people not like you because they know things you don't know. And all the complexities of the problems we have today in our communities, in our companies, in our countries -- We need lots of smart people with lots of different points of view. There is not a single person who is smart enough to solve any problem all by themselves. And, by the way, success is never achieved by a single person acting alone. It's always a team effort. Every success story in the world is a team effort, whether the person who gets the glory is prepared to acknowledge it or not. And last but not least, never sell your soul. Maybe it's an odd thing to say. Never sell your soul.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: There are loads of opportunities in life to sell your soul, to sell your soul by becoming somebody you don't much like, to sell your soul by doing something you know is wrong, to sell your soul by letting somebody else define you, to sell your soul by deciding not to take on something that's worthy of you because of something somebody else might say. Figure out who you are. Own who you are. And then don't sell it out, ever. Because if you sell your soul, no one will ever pay you back. I'm going to stop here in a minute, because I want to take your questions, but let me just close by saying this. You know, sometimes, the greatest lessons in life are learned in the toughest times. I've tried to say explicitly that people learn their potential, fulfill their potential, people tap their potential when they have to work on something really hard. And sometimes we learn the most during difficult times. We've all had difficult times in our lives. In the last several years, I've had difficult times. I'm a cancer survivor. We lost our younger daughter several years ago.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And when you go through profound things -- When any of us go through struggles or profound things, it reminds us of something fundamental. There's very little that we actually control. Very little that we actually control. But here's something we do control. We control our choices. We control how we choose to live our lives. We control whether we choose to lead. We control whether we choose to say, "You know what? "I had more potential than this. I'm going to go tackle something hard." And so I would say aim high. Aim high because you are in the most incredible time in history. Aim high. Choose to do the things that bring you joy and make a positive difference. And choose leadership, because it is a choice. The one thing I know, having traveled and worked all over the world, having worked in many different settings in poor villages in Africa, to the corporate boardroom, to not-for-profits, to political campaigns -- I've worked in all kinds of settings with all kinds of people, and here's what I know. Everyone has potential. Everyone can lead. Leadership is about making a positive difference. Leadership is about seeing and seizing possibilities.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And our Facebook poll results. "What do you think is the most important trait in a leader? 2% of you said persuasion. 6% said quick decision making. 29% said conflict resolution. 10% said delegation. And 53% said taking action. That's really good. That's really good. I like that. Let's get to the questions. First question is -- "Your book is called 'Tough Choices.' What is the toughest choice you ever made?"

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Well, there are three that come to mind. It's always hard to come up with just one. One I've already talked about. Quitting law school was one of the toughest choices I ever made. Of course, now with the benefit of hindsight and perspective, it didn't seem that hard. But, boy, at the time, it was hard and it was self-defining. A second really tough choice I made -- I had a subordinate who worked for me, and they had lots of potential. In fact, I thought one day they could take my job. This was when I was the chief executive. But one day it became clear that this particular individual lacked a moral compass. They lacked ethics. They were doing things as an executive that we would have fired a lower-level employee for. And the thing about ethics is, you can have all kinds of value statements up on a wall. You can say "higher standards of integrity." Nobody listens to the talk. Everybody watches the walk. So, if higher standards of integrity were really important, this guy had to go.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Because the kind of people that are in an organization and whether they have a moral compass or not is everything to an organization. So I had to let him go. That was a really hard decision. And I guess the last one that I would say is, any time you have a dilemma, where you have to balance what people are going to say on the outside with what you know on the inside, that's a tough choice. So, as an example, and I talk about this in my book, when I -- the circumstances under which I left Hewlett-Packard. People ask me, "What are values?" Values, real values, are the things that guide you when no one is looking and when no one may ever find out. And when you become a person of prominence, people say all kinds of things, so a tough choice is always - People say all kinds of things for all kinds of reasons, and half of it's B.S., and some of it you should listen to. But in the end, values are the things that have to guide your decision making when maybe no one will ever find out.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Yes. My parents both came from very troubled homes and difficult upbringings. And for them, education was, you know, an escape. And so, there was no question, I was going to go to college.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: First, when any group comes together, the first really good thing that happens out of that is you learn things from each other. I mean, all of us learn things from other people. That's a really important thing. When you learn things from other people, you gain perspective. I talked about how important perspective is, and it's not the same thing as expertise. Perspective is being able to make decisions about what's really important and what's not and what makes sense and what doesn't. And the only way you gain perspective is to learn new things from different kinds of people, so that's one thing. Second, you learn hopefully how to collaborate with other people to achieve a goal. Have you ever been in a meeting -- I keep using this term "collaboration," but I'll tell you an easy way to know when you're doing it and when you're not doing it. Have you ever been in a meeting with a group of people and it just feels like this big spiral down? You know, where, I mean, you're just not getting anywhere. Maybe everybody's arguing. Maybe you feel like you're wasting your time.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: This isn't a really important problem -- whatever it is. You know how that feels, and everybody kind of walks away from that feeling frustrated. And then there are situations where you're with a group of people and you start spiraling up. You're feeding on each other and you're throwing ideas off and everybody is getting smarter and better as you do that. That's a mark of real collaboration -- when people spiral up and at the end of that meeting, that group, that experience, people walk away saying, "Wow. We're all better. We're all better as a result of that." And the final thing that I would say is, what's good about it, is all of us need help sometimes. Everybody gets down. Everybody needs a helping hand. You know, you mentioned Opportunity International. Opportunity International, in brief, is a microfinance organization. 96% of our clients are women. Women are the most subjugated and underutilized resource in the world today. 70% of the women that -- 70% of the people that live on less than $2 a day are women. So what we do is give very small loans to these women, but it's a chance.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: Now, why do I tell you all that? Because one of the important aspects of somebody being given a chance and succeeding with that chance is having support, having people around them who, when they get down, when they feel like giving up -- and let's face it -- all of us have felt like that -- there are people around them who can say, "No, no, no. "We're here for you. "No, no, no. You can do this. No, no, no. Don't give up." That support, whether it's in business or it's in life or you're having a family crisis -- all of us need that. So those are really important things. By the way, there's just one other thing -- it's interesting. All success is team -- these groups of people.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: It's a scientific fact that the human brain -- the human brain functions -- the synapses fire on two sources of fuel -- glucose and human interaction. That's a fact. The more people interact with other people, the more their synapses fire. We're all smarter and better if we're interacting with other people.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: So, when I was -- It's a great question. When I was coming up -- this will date me -- but the term "mentor" wasn't as...fashionable or ubiquitous as it is today. And so, when I started out, we didn't know what mentors were. So, here's the kind of people that I always look to. First, I looked to people who knew more about a situation than I did. I looked to people who knew more about a situation than I did. And one of the things I discovered is, frequently, that wasn't the boss. That wasn't the boss. Frequently, it was maybe a peer, and as I continued to go up the ladder, frequently, it was subordinates. Who knows the most about this situation? So I would go to them for advice. Another kind of person I would go to -- advice is someone who I thought understood me. And sometimes, that would be other women. Sometimes, it would be other men. A third kind of person I would go to are people who would take a chance on me. And I was not a likely person to take a chance on for a lot of people.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I mean, you know, I could tell you horror stories. I can remember the very first time I became a boss. I had two people who reported to me. I was really proud of that. And my boss introduced me to my new subordinates by saying, "This is Carly. She's our token bimbo." Okay, now, we would know that isn't correct today. But back then, that was sort of -- it was like, "Who is this young woman? "I mean, why do we think she can do anything?" So, I would look really hard for people who would take a chance and give me a chance. And they're always out there. They're always out there, 'cause there are people who are prejudiced and narrow-minded and pigheaded, but most people aren't those things. Most people will give you a chance. And the final kind of people I would look to -- still look to -- mentors, if you will -- are people who will tell me the truth -- people who will tell me the truth.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And as you become more and more successful in life, the funny thing is, there are fewer and fewer people who will tell you the truth. So the ones who will, the ones who will tell you the truth, the ones who know more about the situation than you do, the ones that you think understand what you're going through, and the ones who will take a chance on you -- those are the people that can help you out.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: You know, the basics of leadership are the same for everyone -- doesn't matter what your gender is. It doesn't matter what your ethnicity is. It doesn't matter what you look like. It doesn't matter where you come from -- none of that matters. The essence of leadership is profoundly human -- seeing possibilities, seizing possibilities, unlocking potential in others. On the other hand, it is also true that leaders who are different -- women, people of color -- have higher hurdles, unfortunately. So, I guess the advice that I would give women leaders is, do not let other people tell you what you should be. Define yourself. Find your own path. But I would give that advice to anybody, as you know, 'cause I have.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I think that's one of the reasons that I said, "Find what gives you joy," because, yeah, you know, life can be hard sometimes. And sometimes, in everyone's life, there are times when you feel as though, "Wow, you know, it's two steps forward and three steps back."

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: And in those times, you have to have something that gives you joy. What gives me joy is working with other people to tackle something difficult. That gives me joy. But that's not what gives everybody joy. So, know what gives you joy and go back to that because, when you feel joy, you are rejuvenated. Second, when you're feeling down and low, don't -- don't go in to yourself. And...you know, solitude is important sometimes. Reflection is important sometimes. But when you're feeling like that, seek out people who know you, who know what it's like, who -- to support you. Be vulnerable enough to say, "You know what? I feel just terrible today, and here's why." Find people who will lift you up because they're there. And the third thing I would say is honestly, truly, and it's -- I didn't know this when I was starting out. I was -- When I was starting out, honestly, I think I was kind of afraid of the tough times. I have been through tough times. Personally, I've been through tough times.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: You know, people say, "Oh, it's so cool to be famous." It's not all that cool to be famous. I mean, it's great when people are saying good things about you. It's terrible when people are saying terrible things about you. I learned that from Oprah, by the way. I remember having a conversation with Oprah Winfrey. And the headlines about her at this particular time were really bad. And I said, "Oprah, how do you deal with it?" she said, "You know, "I never read any of it. "'cause if believe the good, I got to believe the bad." I thought that was really good advice, you know? You just put it away. But I digress. The point is, when you feel like that, when you're going through those really tough times, it turns out the toughest times sometimes bring the greatest blessings. I was terrified of cancer, as most of us are.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I was terrified the day my doctor said, "You have cancer, and we don't know what kind." But -- and I honestly can say this truly -- having survived, I can also sit here and say, "Cancer turned out to be a great blessing," because my faith was renewed. I learned the power of love and a family. I learned the power of friendship. I learned, once again, the kindness of strangers. I gained perspective on what's really important in life. So all of that is probably a too-long way of saying, when you're in the tough times, when things aren't going your way, there is a blessing in there. There is a blessing in there. There is a lesson in there. Find it. And it will make you stronger and better the next time.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I mean, look, a degree may get you in a door, but it will not keep you there. If you think about a degree as a piece of paper, a box to check, and, "That's gonna "get me in the door and get me on my way," maybe it will, maybe it won't. If you think about an education as an opportunity to learn things that will help you later, as an opportunity to meet people that you can learn things from, then a degree can take you a long way. Let me give you a really simple example -- a Medieval history and philosophy degree? Not exactly, you know, a degree that's gonna take me places. But let me tell you something -- and, yes, I had to go on and get many other degrees -- two master's degrees. So getting skills is important, but the most valuable class I ever took, ever, was a course in Medieval philosophy, where we had to read a book every week by a Medieval philosopher. Don't worry if these are names that don't mean much to you -- Maimonides, Aquinas -- you know, big -- and those guys were long-winded, man.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: I mean, these were long books, okay? And we had to read one every week, and at the end of each week, our professor said to us, "You have to write "a two-page paper about that work of philosophy." So, I would read hundreds, maybe thousands of pages each week in that class, and then I would write. And first, I would get it down to 20 pages. Then I would get it down to 10. Then I would get it down to five. And finally, I would get it down to two. Now, does that sound tedious? Maybe. But I'll tell you what that process taught me, and I have used it all my life. I took that class 'cause it was interesting, not because I thought it would get me somewhere. I actually knew it wouldn't take me anywhere, except what I learned in that class was this -- how to distil a lot of complicated stuff down to the essence. This is the heart of the matter. And that skill is actually really important.

speaker: Carly Fiorina
text: If you want to lead a big organization, solve a complicated problem, then you have to figure out, what's important in all this, and what's the heart of the matter? What's the thing we really have to focus on?

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Many of our chapters will facilitate a discussion following our broadcast and we'd like to encourage you to stick around to participate.
