He's here tonight to answer your questions and talk about the lessons you could learn from his new book, Losing Isn't Everything: The untold stories of the greatest losses in sports history.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Society members watching live across the country and those watching re-broadcast, please give a warm society welcome to Mr. Curt Menefee. (audience applauding) - Thank you. Thanks Shon. - Thank you so much. - My pleasure. Thank you so much. This day and age, you've gotta get the technology out of your pocket, so there goes the phone and other things you don't need to know about. And the gum. How is everybody? (audience yells affirmatively) Good, good, good. Thank you for coming out. Thank you for those of you who are watching online. And I wanna make sure that we leave time to answer any questions that you may have. 'Cause I'm sure you have some and I wanna make sure that we make the best use of time. But one of the things I wanna talk about is that whenever I introduce somewhere, or people recognize me as the host of Fox NFL Sunday, they always ask me two questions. One, how's my team gonna do this year? Two, how can I get your job? So, depending on who your favorite team is, the first answer will always vary.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Some teams are gonna do well, some teams, I mean, ya gotta be honest. Not every team's gonna win. But the answer for the second one always remains consistent. How do I get your job? One, hopefully wait until I retire and don't rush me out of the door, but secondly, you gotta be willing to work hard for a lot of years at very little money. And that's not the answer that everybody wants to hear. 'Cause everybody looks at the end game. And they see me as host of Fox NFL Sunday. As Shon said, the number one pre-game show in all of sports. Number one for 23 years. I've been hosting it for 11 years. But I'm also the same kid who was 16 years old, grew up in Atlanta, worked in the Mayor's media office just so I could try to learn a little bit about that side of the business. Then, when I was 18, I interned at CNN where I was the only paid intern, And I got paid $5. for every three hours that I worked. All right? I don't know if that's even legal, but that's what they did, okay.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Then when I was 19, I started on the air for the first time in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. And I was willing to carry cable and do whatever it was for no money, just to get my foot in the door. The first job I had after I graduated from college, I was 22 years old, working in Des Moines, Iowa. I made so little money that I wound up having to have a roommate. It turned out he was the local pot dealer. I didn't know that, but you know, sometimes you gotta do what you gotta do, right? So I had to have a roommate just to get through because I knew I wanted to do this. I knew I wanted to be in this business. And I talk about internships with a lot of people because they say well should I do an internship? How much should I do? I think there are many good reasons to do them. Because a lot of times you can do an internship and you find out that maybe that's not what you wanna do with the rest of your life or your career.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: You thought at a young age you did. But for me, having done internships solidified that I wanted to do this. I wanted to be in this business. I didn't know I wanted to be on the air, to be honest with you. When I started out I thought I wanted to be a producer, be behind the scenes. But the one thing I did know, that whatever I did and wherever I was, I just wanted to be the best. When I was a kid who was interning at CNN, I was the one paid intern they had, that $5 for every three hours he worked, but the reason I got to do that is because we all went there as interns at the start of the summer. The summer between my freshman and sophomore year in college. And all the other kids, when our broadcast that we were part of, when CNN did sports back then, it was finished at 11 o'clock at night. They'd all get together and go out and have a good time, and have drinks. Ya know, back then, I'm a little older than you, so you could drink at 18.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: But I would stay there and learn from the editors. And I would seriously just sit down and say hey, can you teach me how to edit? I wanna learn how to do this. Especially then, I wanted to learn this entire business. So I stayed there. A couple of weeks after the summer had begun, the one paid intern they had needed to leave because he had to make money to go back to school. So he couldn't afford to stay there and do the $5 for every three hours you work, but in order to have that job, you had to know how to edit. I said, hey, guess what\! I've been staying here at 11, 12, one o'clock in the morning learning how to edit. So I told the producer who was in charge. Wound up getting that internship and it gave me a lot of experience because they let me produce cut in segments and things that went on throughout the day. So when I went back to school that fall for my sophomore year at Coe College in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, I called up all the local stations.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: I said, "Hey, I interned at CNN this summer. "I'm willing to do anything, anything." Sometimes you need good fortune to come your way as well. Nobody needed anything at that time. But one guy, John Campbell, who I am still friends with to this day, he just retired after more than 30 years there, wrote my number down and four months later, called me up. Said, hey, you still willing to do anything? Oh yeah. He said, well, I just need someone to carry some gear at the University of Iowa spring football game. You don't get paid, you don't get to be on TV, you're not gonna get famous. I said, I'm in. Because I knew I wanted to do this. So I went and did that. And the next week he called me up again, said hey, Iowa State's playing their spring game, you willing to do the same thing? And I did it. Now, a lot of people look at it say, well why you giving away free labor? For me, look at the life I've gotten because of that. Because I was able to take advantage of a free opportunity.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: That's what it was to me. That second time I did it with him, John said, well, what do you want to do? Why are you volunteering? What do you want to do in this business? And so I told him at that time I thought I wanted to be a producer. And he kinda literally took me under his wing. Because at that point, I wasn't officially an intern, I was just volunteering to help this guy work the local television station. So I knew how to edit already, he taught me how to shoot a camera. Then I wound up doing an internship through school to make it official, then I wound up working at the station. Five days a week while I was going to school. While I was doing that, and I was going out and shooting high school games and local college games, John said to me, "Ya know, you've got a nice voice, why don't you "put your voice down on tape?

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: "Take the highlights we do at night and just read the script "and put it down on tape and we'll see how it goes." So I did that for a while, and unbeknownst to me, he took it to the news director and said why don't we have this kid start reporting on local high school and college? And there, I was 19 years old. Wound up being on the air. Again, if this guy hadn't called me back, my life may be different. If I hadn't been in Cedar Rapids, Iowa my life may be different. So sometimes you do need fortune, but you do need to be willing to step through the door when the opportunity comes. Don't complain that you don't get paid, or that maybe they've asked you for two weeks in a row to do the same thing for free and you're not advancing. These things take time sometimes. So my goal was just to be the best, everywhere I was. I wanted to be the best intern at CNN. I wanted to be the best volunteer that John Campbell ever hired.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And then once I started reporting, I wanted to be the best reporting in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. That was simply my goal. My goal was never looking at the end of the road saying I want to be host of Fox NFL Sunday or on a national network some day. I always kept it to being the best wherever I was. When I took that job and had to be roommates with that pot dealer, I was making $13,000 a year. After six months probation, I got a raise to 16,000. I thought I'd made it, 'cause I didn't need the pot dealer anymore, ya know? So sometimes you've gotta just take advantage, especially when you're young, of those opportunities. I was 22 years old, I had no family. I could do those kinds of things. That's the time to take advantage and find out. Is this for you? Because you're not gonna get rich, especially at a young age, but if it's your passion, then you're never gonna be disappointed by it. I honestly don't feel that I've worked a day in my life.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: I've been blessed, I've been fortunate to do what I want to do and have someone pay me for it. A little bit in the beginning and then over the years, I went from Des Moines, Iowa, where I started there, Madison, Wisconsin, Jacksonville, Florida, Washington D.C., Dallas, Texas. But I was in Dallas as the number one guy in sports at the number one station on the market when I was 26 years old. Because I'd done all those things and took advantage of those opportunities and kept my goal focused on where I was and what I was doing, not worried about where it would lead me. I wound up being the number one guy at the number one station here in New York at the age of 29. Very same reason. So once I got here, I kept that goal. How can I be the best guy in New York? Not worried about down the road and national. 'Cause at the age of 29, I know that's older than everybody in this room pretty much, except Shon, I don't know.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: (laughs) Ya know, but, it's one of those things that you've still got a long life ahead of you, all right? So at 29, I'm still a young man, by far the youngest person in the New York City market. But I was only focused on being the best I could be in that market. After doing sports there for a number of years, Fox had me do play by play for NFL games. I'd never done play by play before. But they gave me an opportunity. And back then they had NFL Europe. I went over there and did a couple games just to get the experience. They liked what they saw, two years, two summers of doing it. Came back, had a full time NFL schedule. Was a play by play guy in the NFL for 10 years. And then the opening came in the studio at Fox. They knew I had a studio background, I wound up coming in and working with Terry Bradshaw, Howie Long, Michael Strahan and Jimmy Johnson. So I've been doing that for 11 years.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And at that point, that's when you start to go wow, I made this little journey from the guy who volunteered in Cedar Rapids, Iowa to hosting a network pre-game show. And that's when you can let it all become too big for ya. You tend to forget the steps you took to get there. All the things that got you there, The work on being the best only where you were, and keeping this focus, all the sudden the whole world's there and you're like oh my gosh, now I'm here. What do I do? So the guy who promoted me, was the president of Fox Sports, David Hill, a potty-mouthed Australian, let's just say it that way. So, I said David, hey you made me host of the pre-game show, any advice for me? He goes, "Yeah, don't F it up." (audience laughing) So with that, my job was not to F it up. The show had been number one for 12 years, and I'm going well, there's only one way to go is down. And if it goes down the only change they made was making me host.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: So I felt an enormous amount of pressure to make sure this train kept rolling, to make sure it's still succeeding. And again, because you start looking at the big picture, rather than staying focused on where you are, that's when you lose control. First show we do, Terry Bradshaw, I don't know how many people realize, he's been public about it, he's had multiple divorces. He's on his fourth marriage. The woman he's married to now is the perfect woman for him, they've known each other 20 years, he should have married her to begin with, but the first week, I'm trying to fit in with these guys. They've been together for 12 years. So I make fun of Terry and his three divorces. (audience chuckles nervously) Exactly, right. That was not the wisest thing to do. So I found out, ya know, later on that week from the producer, oh you know, you probably shouldn't have done that, Terry wasn't happy. Now at this point, I'm not even sure Terry Bradshaw knows my last name.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Ya know, I'm just some guy who's sitting there, and replaced the guy who was there before, so, I'm thinking about it, I'm like yeah, it's not comfortable, but I've gotta prove that my bosses were right in hiring me and giving me this job. I felt a responsibility to them to not fail. So that second week, I go out and I do something just equally as dumb. People say, well what'd you do? It's one of those things, ya know how like they say when you have a traumatic experience, you kinda purge it from your memory so that you can kinda survive? I think I did that. (audience laughing) So I can't tell you what it was, but I knew it wasn't right, and I felt bad. But I'm trying to make it work. I wanna succeed at this thing.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And I remember I'm walking down the hallway at Fox, this guy who's not even affiliated with our pre-game show, just another executive at Fox says, "Hey Curt, you got a moment?" I said, "Yeah." He says, "Come sit in my office." And I sat down, he goes, "Look, you got the job, "Just be yourself, just do your own thing. "They hired you because of who you are. "They hired you because everywhere you've been, "you've been the best. "You've focused on succeeding at that job "and not worrying about the big picture." And it was like the hallelujah chorus went off. It was like, ah, now I understand. And for me, that's the foundation of success. It's really, I like to call it the three know's that equal yes. As in the ultimate success. And the first thing is to know yourself. And more importantly trust yourself. And that's what I had lost for a little bit. I didn't trust who I was. I didn't trust who had gotten me there. If you know yourself and you trust yourself, you will continue to succeed because step by step, you will do the right things.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And when you don't do the right things, you'll learn from them, hopefully. The thing is is that a lot of times, people try to do something that they're not. They see someone else do it and they pretend to be them. You can't get away with that for long. It's like anything else, you can't act your whole life. You've got to know yourself. In order to be successful, you've gotta do what you know. And the one thing you know is you. So just do you. That's the first "know". The second one is to know your role. And when I say that people say, well does that mean stay in your place? No, there's a whole difference. Knowing your role is not only knowing yourself and trusting yourself, but how it fits in to whatever your job is. For me, I'm the host of Fox NFL Sunday, Terry Bradshaw's a four time Super Bowl winning quarterback who's in the Hall of Fame. Howie Long's a defensive end, defensive tackle who won a Super Bowl and is in the Hall of Fame. Michael Strahan is Mr.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Everything who is in the Hall of Fame and Jimmy Johnson is a coach who won a National Championship as a player, as a coach and two Super Bowls in the National Football League. So when it comes to football, what am I gonna tell these guys, right? My job and my role on this show is to know names, help out Terry when he screws up, stats, stories, but to bring out of those guys the qualities that make them special. You know, coaching stories from Jimmy or defensive stories from Howie. And also knowing their strengths and weaknesses. That's my role. Doesn't mean that I'm subservient to them. But in order to make this whole thing work, I have to know my role. I have to know their role. I have to understand how they all fit into it. So besides knowing yourself and trusting yourself, you have to know your role in order to be successful. And the third one, is know at some point, you're gonna face adversity. And you gotta overcome it. Nobody wins every single time. Nobody succeeds every single time. In your personal life, your private life, your professional life.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: You're gonna have days where it sucks. Where whatever you did was a colossal failure. But you don't get to spend the next 20 years going I had a bad day back in 2017, therefore I don't have to be productive for the rest of my life. And that's something that I learned at a young age, thankfully. I talk about all these local stops I made, when I was 25 years old, I had gone from Madison, Wisconsin to this all sports network that was based out of Washington D.C. and it was basically what ESPN news is now. But it was a precursor to it. Well, that gig only lasted eight months because they went bankrupt and out of business. So then I was unemployed for nine months. And at the age of 25, you're not quite sure, you're like, hm, am I unemployed because I'm not good enough to be in this business, that I'm not gonna get hired again? Part of what happened was, it was 1991, the first Gulf War broke out and nobody was hiring sportscasters.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: So you put your nose down, or I did, went back to Madison, Wisconsin, did more volunteer work, slept on a friend's couch until I found another job. And that's when I wound up finding the job in Jacksonville. But it taught me to go back to believing in myself. And trusting the process, and trusting that I know what it takes to succeed. And ever since thing, luckily, I've been employed. And here I am, the hose of Fox NFL Sunday. But it's also been a lesson, I think, that people don't talk enough about, is their failures. And about overcoming adversity. Because we all see people that succeed. But we don't see the stumbles they make. We don't see the failures. The bad grades they got in school. The jobs they got fired from or they just lost because they went out of business. We only see the end result.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: You see me, you see the host of Fox NFL Sunday, you have no idea that I was unemployed, or that I lived with a pot dealer or those kinds of things, because those are parts of our background, but those things are what make us who we are today. And that was kinda the premise behind the book. Because I'm a big believer in everything in life you need to know, you can learn from sports. I've always thought that. Because it teaches you how to handle winning. It teaches you how to be a part of a team. It teaches you how to handle losses and adversity. It teaches you self discipline, you name it. I believe everything you can learn in sports. And the biggest lesson, I think, is overcoming adversity. Because when you look at every sporting event, barring the rare ties in hockey and soccer, one side wins, one side loses. 50/50, so you're not gonna win all the time.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And with the book, I wanted to find out from people who have been part of major sports losses, that for us, at the general public, that's the only reason we identify them, as being a part of a loss, part of a team or an individual that had a major loss. How do you go on with your life? How does it affect you? How do you rebound? How do you bounce back? Because for most these people, when you're an athlete at that level, professionally or in the Olympics, most the time, you're in your early 20's, maybe mid-20's, you still have a lot of life to live after that day is over, and everywhere you go, people are like, hey aren't you that guy who lost that event? And I found out that these events affect not only the people involved, it affects their families. There are lots of good stories, but there are lots of bad ones as well. So then the challenge became, well why are some people able to overcome it and succeed and continue with a prosperous life and others still struggle with it?

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And I found out it's really about how you handle adversity because there are many ways, obviously to try and deal with it. I'll go back to Craig Ehlo who's a guy, Michael Jordan hit the shot over him, ya know, in 1989 NBA playoffs. Jordan hadn't won an NBA championship at that point, but he had lead the league in scoring, I believe three years in a row. But he was Michael Jordan so everybody knew it, but he hadn't won that title yet. Cleveland lead that game. Ehlo scored 24 points in the game including what would have been the game winner with three seconds left. Chicago calls a time out, they go back down the other end of the court, Ehlo is assigned to defend, as part of a double team, Michael Jordan. One of the things they do on the sideline, is that Lenny Wilkens, who is the head coach, says we're gonna double team Jordan. And at that point, Ehlo says we haven't double teamed anybody all year. So that's again where that moment becomes bigger than you should make it. You get outside of your element.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: You stop doing what you know how to do. Well, they go back, and because he and the other guy that was defending him, Larry Nance, couldn't figured out the spacing, because they'd never done it. Jordan winds up hitting the shot, Ehlo was trying to defend him, Ehlo's on every poster in the world, Jordan hits the shot, he's doing the pump, it's in the Gatorade commercials, it's everywhere. Ehlo goes from being the hero to the goat just like that. 24 points didn't matter, they lost the game on a buzzer winner in the deciding game five of that series. Well he said that his way of dealing with it was just to move on. Nobody else talked to him about it, so he's like the off season happened, my wife talked about vacation, my family didn't talk about it, so I figured the way that I need to deal with this is just to pretend it didn't happen, just to move on. Well that turned out to be a disastrous move for him.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: He played in the NBA another eight years, but he wound up with a drug problem that he and his therapist relate directly with not having dealt with the emotions of that shot. Another guy, Calvin Schiraldi, who was a pitcher for the Boston Red Sox when they lost the 1986 World Series. Everybody seen the ball go through Bill Buckner's leg, but what they didn't see, unless you were watching the series back then, and I know nobody who was born back then in this room, but Schiraldi blew a one run lead in the eighth inning, and a two run lead in the tenth inning. Gave up three straight hits, the ball goes through Buckner's leg, they lose game six. He comes in in game seven, a three-three tie in the seventh inning, gives up a home run the first batter, they lose game seven. So he loses game six and seven. Same thing, season ended, he said, nobody talked to him about it, he figured he'd just bury it. The next year, the fans gave him a hard time whenever he was on the road. But he tried to deal with it by not dealing with it.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Only pitched in the majors three more years, he's been coaching high school baseball down in Texas. Finally in 2013, his wife said to him, "Look, you buried this thing, but you haven't gotten "over it." From 1986 to 2013, we're gonna get a divorce if you don't go to a therapist. And he said she was 100% right. He had a 27 year old daughter whose life he had never been involved in, that he knew that he had buried this thing because he didn't know how to deal with it. So between the stories of Ehlo and Schiraldi, I think those are good examples that not dealing with whatever adversity you have is not the way to deal with whatever adversity you have. For guys like Rodney Harrison who's a member of the New England Patriots, The season they had, the perfect season, and then they lost the Super Bowl to the Giants on the famous David Tyree helmet catch. I see a Giant fan there. Well Rodney Harrison's the guy in every picture you look, who's the defender. He was the safety on the play. When Tyree catches the ball here, he's trying to swat it away.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And when you talk to Rodney, Rodney says, "I physically thought I'd knocked it away." He goes, "I thought I'd swatted the ball away, "and we're down on the ground, and I see Steve Smith," another Giant receiver, "come over and say, hey, get off "my guy, good catch, good catch. "Good catch?" He says, "I look at the jumbo tron and I see he catches it "in his helmet." He's like, "I couldn't believe it, "but it's a miracle bowl miracle." And what people forget is there's still a minute and a half left in that game. The game was not over. The ball was on the 25 yard line. And he said he knew that there was still time to win this game. Three plays later is when the game was decided. The defensive coordinator, Dean Pees of the New England Patriots calls a blitz. Go back to when Rodney Harrison is drafted in 1994, in the fifth round by the San Diego Chargers. Barely played his rookie year. Couldn't get on the field.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Junior Seau was a linebacker, a Hall of Fame linebacker, with the San Diego Chargers, but he saw how hard Rodney worked and took him under his wing. And said, you're gonna be something someday, just keep at it kid, just keep at it. Well, almost 20 years later, Rodney Harrison's on the New England Patriots, he's already won two Super Bowls, but Junior Seau comes over as a free agent. He's never won a Super Bowl. So the defensive coordinator calls in the blitz. Rodney's in charge of the defense, he's the safety. He's sitting back here, he says we call the blitz in the huddle, we go out and line up. I look over, I see six foot five Plaxico Burress lined up against five foot nine Ellis Hobbs. He goes, I know we got no shot in that play. I've been in the league 14 years. I should know. So he says, we're not gonna blitz. Call the blitz off. Junior goes, no, let's run it. Now he's not blaming Junior.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: But his love and respect, and I go back to the moment becoming bigger than it needs to be, he says, no, let's call off the blitz. And Junior's like, let's run it. And he said he respected Junior so much, because Junior was the guy who believed in him, that he trusted Junior, rather than trusting himself, even though he knew it was the wrong decision. The ball was snapped, he said he didn't even turn around. Once he saw the ball in the air, he knew touch down, game over. He didn't care about being beaten on the helmet catch, because that's just a play that happens. What haunted him was the fact that he went against his own judgment, against what he knew was right. He didn't trust himself, and that's what he had a hard time living with. Now he went and tried to process for while. He said for six weeks he was in bed, he didn't go play golf, he didn't do anything until his wife and mother had basically come to Jesus meeting and said look, look at the blessings you've got.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: You won a couple Super Bowls, your children are healthy, all these things. And eventually he was able to process it through. He dealt with it in his own terms, and it took a while, but he dealt with it. And that allowed him to move forward. And I think the process of trusting and believing yourself is probably the most important message I can give you. Because you see Rodney didn't do it, and how it affected him. You see other people that didn't do it and how it affected them. The flip side, there's a golfer by the name of Jean Van de Velde, he lead the 1999 British Open. One of the four major golf tournaments. Going into the final hole in the tournament, par is four, all he needed to do is get a six and he wins. So he could mess up and still be fine. He hits an initial T shot, almost goes into the stands. The next one out of the brush. It was just a disaster. He hit it into the water. I mean, it was one thing after another.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And people to this day, in the golf world, whenever a guy blows up, they call it pulling a Van de Velde 'cause it was that bad, it was that embarrassing. People couldn't believe this guy. He wound up shooting a seven. Wound up going to a play off and wound up losing the British Open when all he needed was just a six on the final hole. And I talked to him and part of it is, I think, he's French, he goes, "Eh, I went out and had some wine, "everything was good." Six months later he was doing commercials making fun of it. But part of what he talked about was he was okay with it, because he had processed it. In the moment. One of the things that golf allows you to do is you think about the shots before you hit it. So he said he was okay living with it, because he did what he believed was right. He trusted himself.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: And as long as you trust yourself, every decision's not gonna go your way, you're gonna hit bad shots, but if you know that you did it for the right reasons, or what you thought was the right reason at that time, then you can move forward. He said if he had listened to his caddy or someone else and taken their advice and blown up, he'd never be able to live with himself. But because he blew up, if you will, but on his own terms, he was able to heal. He was able to move forward because he knew that he did what he believed to be the right thing at that moment. So you're gonna have these moments in your life. Not everything is gonna be perfect. It's okay to fail. It's about learning from those failures. It's about rebounding from those failures 'cause they're gonna happen and they're gonna happen time and time and time again. The thing is all scars eventually heal. And they usually give a great story to tell in the end. It's about what you learned from having gotten those scars. And as long as you learn something, then you're a success.

speaker: Curt Menefee
text: Thank you very much. (audience applauding) And now I guess, we'll take any questions that anybody may have. text: Thank you very much. Very kind. Appreciate it. How is it going, everybody? Thanks for coming out on a not-so-warm evening. It's nice to be in Jersey City. My father actually grew up here. I'm going to apologize in --

speaker: Dan Harris
text: Thank you. Thank you. He's lived in Boston ever since. Still has a Jersey accent. I am going to apologize in advance because I may be a little bit rusty. I haven't been giving this talk that much lately because a couple of weeks ago my wife and I had our first kid. Thank you.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: I found myself a couple of days into it holding this screaming child covered in poop and thinking to myself that the title of my next book is going to be "Everything in My Last Book Was Baloney.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: So, if you had told me a couple years ago that I was ever going to be, like, a traveling evangelist for meditation, I could have coughed my beer up through my nose. This is not something I ever thought was going to happen, but strange things happen in people's lives. And for me it all started, as Kevin said with a panic attack on national television live on a little show you may have heard of called "Good Morning America." Because I'm a total masochist, I actually asked our research department to find out exactly how many people were watching when I lost my mind, and they came back with the number 5.019 million. So it was not a big deal.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: Good morning, Charlie and Diane. This is me 10 years ago, and the reason why this is the most embarrassing day of my life is not that it looks like I've been attacked by a blow dryer and a can of hair spray. No, it's that I am about to freak out on national television. Health news now. One of the world's most commonly prescribed meditations may be providing a big bonus. Researchers report people who take cholesterol-lowering drugs called statins for at least five years may also lower their risk for cancer, but it's too early to -- to prescribe statins slowly for cancer production. At this point I realize I'm helpless, so I bail right in the middle. That does it for news. We're going to go back now to Robin and Charlie.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: Once the fear subsided, humiliation rushed in. I knew with rock-solid certainty that I had just had a panic attack on national television. I've watched that clip 1,000 times, and it sucks every time. I get -- I get different reactions to it, because anybody who's ever had just a little taste of panic, when they watch that clip, they know exactly what they're seeing. Some people actually watch that clip and say, "Hey, it wasn't that bad." And I agree with that, but I think that if I hadn't had the luxury of being able to toss it back to the main hosts of the show, Diane Sawyer and Charlie Gibson, what you would have seen is flop sweat and maybe a Tourette-ic outburst and me ripping the mike off and running away because that was the scariest moment of my entire life. Interestingly, though, that very embarrassing moment, in a weird and windy way, ultimately led me to something that vastly improved my life.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: I'll talk about that much more in a second, but I want to give you the backstory to the panic attack because I think at the root of it is something that certainly everybody in this room and everybody watching on the other side of those cameras -- anybody who is a member of this society -- shares, which is a desire to be great at whatever you do. I arrived at ABC News at age 28. This is the picture they took of me on my first day. It is still, despite repeated begging and pleading, on my security I.D. A friend of mine has joked that if you take a wide shot, it looks like I might be holding a balloon. I was, as I said, 28 years old. I was terrified. I was working with giants like Diane Sawyer, Barbara Walters, and Peter Jennings. And I was really insecure about the fact that I was green, and my way of coping was to become a workaholic. I just threw myself into the job. I had a motto that I inherited from my dad -- again, from right here in Jersey City.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: His motto was, "The price of security is insecurity." "The price of security is insecurity." So I was a huge -- and still am, really -- worrier, and I believe that the secret to my success was that I was going to out-worry everybody else. And when 9/11 happened, not long after I got the job at ABC, I saw an opportunity of sorts. I volunteered and raised my hand to go overseas and cover whatever happened next. And frankly, I didn't think much about the psychological consequences. This is me with some nice gentleman from the Taliban several weeks after 9/11 in Southern Afghanistan in Kandahar. And I'll be honest with you, this was my first time in a war zone, and I liked it. I found it thrilling and spent many, many subsequent years in places like Afghanistan, Pakistan, Israel, the West Bank, Gaza. I made six trips to Iraq, as Kevin said. And when I came home from a particularly long and hairy run in Iraq in 2003, I got depressed.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: Embarrassingly, I didn't even know I was depressed, although I was exhibiting what I now know to be some of the classic signs and symptoms of depression, including the fact that I was having trouble getting out of bed and I felt like I had a low-grade fever all the time. And at this point, I did a phenomenally stupid thing, which is that I started to self-medicate with recreational drugs, including cocaine and ecstasy. I hear that usually when I say that, there's, like, a low murmur in the room. Let me just hasten to add that it wasn't like "The Wolf of Wall Street."

speaker: Dan Harris
text: It was reasonably sporadic. It was always on my own time. It was on the weekends, never when I was working, never when I was on the air. As I like to say, I was stupid but not that stupid. After the panic attack, I went to go see a shrink who is an expert in panic, and he asked me a bunch of questions to try to get to the bottom of my panic attack. And one of them was, "Do you do drugs?" And I kind of sheepishly said, "Yeah, I do." And he leaned back in his chair and gave me a look that said something to the effect of, "Okay, moron. Mystery solved." And he explained that even though I hadn't been using every day or anything like that, it was enough to artificially raise the level of adrenaline in my brain and prime me to have a panic attack, which is just a giant rush of adrenaline. So, in that moment, I realized quite powerfully what a dummy I had been and that I needed to make some changes in my life. So right there, I made two big ones.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: One, I quit doing drugs, which is kind of a no-brainer. The other one was I agreed to go see this shrink once or twice a week indefinitely. This is not, however, a neat, tidy story where I quit doing drugs, start meditating, and then my life is a non-stop parade of rainbows and unicorns. Something else had to happen -- something completely unforeseen, which was that this guy, Peter Jennings, who was my mentor at the time -- Some of you may be too young to remember him, but he was a giant in the field of journalism. He was the number-one news anchor for many, many years. I had grown up watching him and emulating him and was lucky enough to have him as my mentor and boss. And he took me aside one day and gave me an assignment that I did not want. He told me that I was going to start covering faith and spirituality for ABC News. I grew up in the People's Republic of Massachusetts.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: So I had no interest in or knowledge of faith and spirituality. Just was not my thing. And I tried to explain this to Peter. I was like, "Look, you got the wrong guy. Find somebody else." And he said, "I don't care. You're going to do it, anyway." And it turned out to be a great thing for me. I spent the following years hanging out in mosques and megachurches and Mormon temples and I made a lot of really good friends and I realized how ignorant I was on this issue. And I really saw the value of having a world view that transcends your own narrow interests, which was very useful for an ambitious, young guy. That said, none of what I encountered spoke to me personally. I didn't, you know, go kosher or anything like that until the year 2008. So many years after I started covering religion and many years after my panic attack, a producer with whom I was working recommended that I read a book by this guy. Does anybody know who this is? Okay. So, a few hands going up. Don't feel bad because I had no idea know who he was.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: But his name is Eckhart Tolle. He is a massively successful self-help guru. He has sold tens of millions of books. As my producer at the time was explaining to me, he has a lot of celebrity fans. Paris Hilton carried one of his books into jail when she did time for drunk driving or something. Oprah loves this guy. She had him on a bunch. Anyway, he's very, very popular. And my producer thought I should read the book and maybe we should go do a story on him. So I ordered his book, and I started to read it. And at first, I thought it was complete garbage. Like, complete garbage. All this weird language in there about vibrational fields, pseudoscientific claims, grandiose assertions about how his book is going to provoke "in you, the reader, a spiritual awakening," whatever that means, and how after his own spiritual awakening he claims that he lived on park benches in the city of London for two years in a state of bliss. I am not a meteorologist, but last I checked, they actually have winter in London.

speaker: Dan Harris
text: So I was not impressed by this dude at all, but I kept reading. And I ultimately stumbled upon, a couple pages in, some material that I found extremely compelling. So in trying to figure out how it does happen, I thought maybe I'd take a little bit of my life and try to share it with you guys, so you could see that somebody like me that looks like they might have hit the jackpot, worked really hard, and also didn't know what they were doing. And I had no idea what I was really going to be in life. But I had an idea of what I wanted to be. So anyway, I grew up in DC, Washington, DC, and I was a dancer. And I had a mom and a dad and a sister, and I lived in a duplex house and with very, very humble means. So, pulling everything down to the common denominator, I'm pretty much like you guys. Some of you grew up with more money, some less, some different social stratas, religions, races, all that stuff. But basically, we're people, and I did not grow up with a silver spoon in my mouth, right?

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: So I grew up on a dead-end street in a duplex house, so not a whole house, half a house. It was a palace to me. And my dad was a musician, and my mom ran dancing schools and things like that. And we rubbed two sticks together, and daddy worked hard, and mom did. We had a living. But just a living to get by. What I did is I became a dancer, and I danced at the age of three, and I loved dancing. Dancing was my life. I wasn't that good in school. I wasn't a great student, as I said before . I'm not proud of it, but I certainly continued a great lust for learning, but we'll get to that in a minute. But anyway, I guess I had just this sort of love of being alive, loved to dance to music, loved what I did. School, I went to kindergarten, I went to first grade, I went to second grade. Second grade, I hit a stumbling block. I was put into a reading group called the Purple Balls.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And I liked myself so much, and I was so happy with myself that I thought it was the best reading group in the class because no one else was in it. So I came home, and I told my mom, I said, "Mom, I'm so lucky. I'm in a new reading group called the Purple Balls." She said, "Really? Is that good?" She said, "Why?" I said, "Because I'm the only one in it." She said, "Really?" I said, "Yeah." She says, "And where's your book?" I said, "I'm so good, I don't get to have a book." She said, "Okay. Goldie, I think you need to learn to read." So I said, "Oh, well, okay." So she taught me how to read. My mother taught me how to read, and that's a whole other story about the value of mothers and the importance of women in our society. But we'll skip that one. And I used to do things like they'd teach me, they'd say, the banana and the apple and the grape and all these things, and you have to color everything purple and yellow, and all these things.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And I turned mine in, and the teacher said to me, "Goldie, why did you color everything yellow?" A banana is yellow, but an apple isn't yellow, and grapes are green and whatever. And I said, "Because I like yellow." And so I was sort of one of these people that just enjoyed yellow. I enjoyed my life. And I signed everything, "Love, Goldie." All my papers, everything. I never finished one thing. My math, I never finished. My English, I never finished. But I did have a lovely salutation because I loved my teachers, and I signed, "Love, Goldie." So, of course, I didn't fail. Anyway, I had another interesting story when I was in third grade because we were doing a talent show, and of course, this is where I shined. I was a dancer. I would dance to music. I danced to anything you'd put on. And my family would say, "Goldie, dance for us." And I would dance, and I would do stuff into music. I never knew where I was going next, but I always improvised, and I was always feeling good about it.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: So this teacher said, "Okay, you're going to be in a talent show." I said, "Great." So me and all these other guys are going to be in the talent show, and everybody was there, and it was like a big deal. So Mrs. Toomey, who was my third-grade teacher, she said to me, "Now, I want everyone to be perfect."And I went completely, my head just spun around. I said, "Mrs. Toomey, I can't do this." She said, "Why, Goldie?" I said, "Because I'm not perfect." She said, "Well, when I say perfect, I mean you have to be on and do your very best and whatever." I said, "No, I'm not going to do the talent show." So I went home. Mrs. Toomey got completely crazy. My mother went more insane. She said, "What are you doing? You're not perfect. I mean, what are you saying?" I said, "Mommy, I'm not perfect, and I know I'm not perfect, and I won't be perfect when I go up there. So I don't know what I'm doing, and I'm only improvising to this music. And this is great, but I don't want Mrs.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: Toomey to be angry with me because I'm not perfect." So Mrs. Toomey then cried. She did this whole thing. "Please, Goldie, I didn't mean perfect. None of us are perfect, honey," and all this stuff. And of course, at the end of the day, I had my 78 record, and it was Sleigh Ride. It goes . And it was the most uplifting music, and it was music where I was just flying with joy. And I said, "Okay, I'll do it if I don't have to be perfect." So my mother was so relieved, she sat down on the chair and broke the record. Anyway, she took her pointy shoes, and she went out to go buy the record, and she found another 78 or whatever, and I did the show. And I think that perfection and fear of failure and wanting to be perfect, I mean, I was a very young child, and I think we all kind of have this fear of not being perfect or not wanting to step out and say it because somebody's going to judge us or whatever. And of course, what business do I go into?

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: I go into show business, which is where you are rejected up, down, and in the middle. But I'll get to that in a minute. So anyway, so now I'm in school, and I do my thing or whatever. My sister just didn't know what I was going to do for a living. In fact, she gave me no vote of confidence, God love her. She sat at the dinner table, and she said, "Mom, what's Goldie going to do when she grows up? I mean, she can't even type." And I actually thought, oh, yeah. Well, I knew I was going to be a dancer, but I thought, well, I better enroll in a typing class. Well, thanks to her, I'm at 65 words a minute. And I've written a book and a script and a thing, and I have to thank her for that challenge. But nevertheless, I knew in my heart that I wasn't going to be a typist, or I wasn't going to be an assistant, even though that was one of my fun things of being a secretary when I was little. So my mother said, "Goldie's going to dance.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: That's what Goldie's going to do." And I went, "Yeah, that's what I'm going to do for a living." I brought Cs home, and if I brought a B home, it was a big celebration. But I wasn't going to be an academic. And I thought, going to school and college, and that's going to be hard, but dancing was my life. So I end up teaching dancing in a dancing school. At 17, I had my own dancing school. I worked for the government. I taught in recreation centers. I had my own school. I advertised in my father's watch shop. I was entrepreneurial at 17. I'm thinking, boy, this is by nature. I'm having a business. So at 17, of course, this was after high school, I then went on, and I kept dancing, and I went to an audition. And as my mother said, "You know what, Goldie? Just be ready when the time comes. Be prepared. Do what you do well, love what you do, and when the door opens, just be prepared. That's all you need to be.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And the rest of it is up to the people that hire you." So I did, and I got a call, and it was a world's fair, and I could go do a dance there. So I thought, oh, great, so I'm going to audition. So I take my car, I go down, and I audition for this show. And it was in New York, and I lived in DC, and lo and behold, I got a job. I left LA. I mean, sorry, I left Washington. Whoo. It's been too long since I lived there. I left Washington, and I moved to New York City. And I had two shopping bags and a suitcase, and some guy that my mother knew drove me to New York and left me literally on 10th Avenue in Hell's Kitchen. And I looked around, I said, "Let's see. Where am I supposed to go?" There was a guy I would talk to. He said I could stay at his apartment. And I went up into the worst rat-infested-- By the way, guys, back then, Hell's Kitchen was Hell's Kitchen. And I went up, and they were gone.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And so the guy, little weird guy, opens the door. He said, "Oh, they left weeks ago. They're on a job somewhere." And I went, "Really?" So I now have to find another place to live in New York, and I only know one person, and that's my dancing teacher. So I had to go to the choreographer/dancing teacher, stay with him for a few days, and then finally got an apartment on Needle Park, which was a horrible place. It was between Amsterdam and, I don't know, Broadway. And it was lots and lots of roaches and so forth. So this is the beginning, right? But I must tell you that when I was 11 years old, the one thing I wanted to be, I was very clear. I loved to dance, but people would come up to me when I was little, and they'd say, "Goldie, what do you want to be when you grow up?" And I said, "Happy." And they looked at me like I had six heads. And I'll never forget this. It was so weird. I'd look up, and they'd look, and they go, "No, no, no. What we're-- No.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: We don't mean that." "Do you want to be a ballerina or a movie star or be on Broadway?" And I looked at them, and I thought, you know what? They didn't understand me. And I looked, I said, "No, I want to be happy," which is all I really wanted to be. Because I felt that I would be able to dance. I didn't have any worries about that. And I didn't dream about being a movie star because that was way out of the question. I lived in a very real world. I had a father who was a great realist, who never let me believe in fantasy.Meaning fantasy that expectations, was his line, is greater than realization. So in fact, if expectation is greater than realization, then let's not expect too much because it's never going to work out that way. So keeping that in mind and my wish for happiness, open a dancing school, get married, have a lovely house, and be happy. And that's all I wanted to do. Go home, get married, open a dancing school, and be happy. And that was my dream. And that was a pretty cool dream. I was 19.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: I liked that dream. Have children, have a white picket fence. I had a whole life designed for what I thought I was going to do. So I go to New York, I go to the World's Fair, danced on a stage that's nine feet deep, and I had to do cartwheels. I thought for sure I was going to end up in the bartender's lap because he was underneath us, so we were 12 feet high. It was the scariest job I've ever done. Hopping and hollering and cartwheeling on a nine-inch thing, whatever. I mean, nine foot. It was crazy. But I got through that job, and then I started auditioning for Broadway. Didn't make it. So to make my money, going to dancing school and paying for rent and dancing school, I did go-go. So all of my hopes and dreams of being on the Broadway stage wasn't exactly the way it turned out. And I said, "Where do I dance?" "On that pedestal." Or, "Excuse me, I'm here. I brought my fishnet tights and my high-cut leotard, my high-heeled shoes. Where do I go?" "In that cage." And it was just terrible.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: I mean, it was cool. I liked dancing and the music and so forth, but it was so like-- I don't know. It didn't feel right. It's not what I studied. It's not-- It was like years of ballet and my training and my sweating and my dreams of being on Broadway. And I would get just as close to a Broadway show, and I'd hear, "Number 10, thank you very much. You're just a little too short." So this is what my life was like. A lot of rejection, a lot of guys putting their nose up to the go-go thing, like, "Ugh." And people looking and oohing and aahing. And I tell you, and a few lewd things, which we're not going to discuss because-- But life is crazy. It gives you these things. I mean, one time I got stuck in a place, and I had to go to four men sitting at a bar and say, "Gee, excuse me, would you mind if you gave me a ride home to the city? I was in Jersey." Oh. I was far from here, though. Far from the university.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: I would have taken great respite had I been able to be here. But anyway, so I rode home in an 18-wheeler. Thank heaven, an 18-wheeler. These two guys, thank heavens, they were really nice guys, and they took me back to the city. So I called my dad. I said, "Daddy, is it time for me to come home, get married, open a dancing school, and be happy?" I mean, right? He said, "Goldie..." He was in the business. He was a musician. He said, "You know what? You're young. You should stay at it, have some fun." And I thought, "God, it's me and the cockroaches." I mean, can you imagine? I was 19. I was living alone. I mean, it was scary. I have a very close family. I was very close to my mom and dad. And so leaving home was not easy. But I was like, there I was, out on my own, sink or swim. And I was going to swim no matter what. So I then get a call from a woman named Zoya Laporska. I was just about ready to go home.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And she said, "Goldie, I worked with you here." We did a little summer stock, which was kind of Broadway, but not. I just went around little places in the East Coast, danced. She said, "I'd like you to come to LA and be one of my dancers." So I was like, "I thought great." So I got on the plane. I'd never been to California. That was another first. I called my mom and dad. I did the stupidest thing. I had $200 in my pocket that I'd saved up from go-going. I went past a dog on First Avenue, and I bought a poodle for $200. I always needed a friend. So I had a poodle, a little toy poodle, $200. I had $50 left in my pocket. Thank heavens, my mom sent me the ticket to go to LA. Anyway, I go to LA. I do this. I'm happy. Everything is perfect. Life is working out. The dog, I got a great roommate, I kind of liked LA. I thought Hollywood was Anaheim. I mean, literally, I'd only seen Anaheim. I had no idea what Beverly Hills and Hollywood was about.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: Then I got another audition for a TV show. And now it just shows you guys that you follow your path, you do your choices, you don't know if they're going to be right or wrong, but whatever they are, they will take you to the next step of your life. When you don't make the choice is when you don't get the knowledge, you don't get the wisdom by either the win or by either the mistake, right? So I made some mistakes by go-going. But at the same time, I stayed there, and I made some wins, and I learned a lot. I learned a lot about people, and that's a whole other speech. But anyway, so now I'm there, and I get this job, and I'm on a TV show, "The Andy Griffith Special." And I'm one of 12 girls, and it was really great. And I was Mecca. I had literally found my spot in life. I knew exactly I was doing just what I wanted to do. So I get in the line, five, six, seven, eight, and some-- That's the countdown for a dance, if you didn't know.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And this guy comes up to me, and he says, "Excuse me, are you represented by an agency?" And I said, "No, I'm not." Ugh, I thought, "This guy, he's going to come out with a number." I was just so used to this. I didn't trust anybody. And I mean, just because I was a girl alone in New York, right? So when he comes up, he says, "Well, I'd like to see you in my office, you know, on Wednesday," da, da, da. And I said, "Sure. Well, thank you very much. I'm not represented. I'd love to," whatever. And I take his card, I put it on my leotard, and I go back to dancing.So the show is over, it was great. It was a blast. I was going to do all these shows. I had my life lined up, and he calls me, and this secretary says, "Ms. Han, we're expecting you to be here at this agency, at this meeting, and you're not here. We were wondering if you were not coming, and we're from the William Morris office." I went, "Wait a minute.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: William Morris Agency?" This is like the biggest agency in the world. And now I'm in my little apartment and I said, "You mean he really, really meant this?" I said, "Well, okay. I'm definitely coming. I had another appointment," whatever, "And I'll be right there. Okay, where is it? El Camino Drive, no problem." So I get on this little-- I remember it was an orange mini dress. I threw it on. I go downstairs, I jump in my car. I was in a '54 Ford. It had no floor. Literally, I could see the road. So it was sort of this 360 view of life. It was good. And then I would turn, a right-hand turn, but my door didn't close, so every time I'd turn, my door would fly open. So I had to do this to hold the door. It was a jaunt anywhere I went. It was exciting. I never knew when I'd run out of oil. Gas wasn't a problem. It was oil. Anyway, so I go in and I meet these people.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: There's all these agents that are sitting there, and God love them, I don't know, William Morris Agency only hired agents that were five feet and under. They were all sitting there in their suits, and they were looking at me, and this one guy was this young junior agent. He said, "I don't know. I just have like a hunch, I have a feeling about her." And they're all talking about me like I'm just sitting there, like I was, had no mind or nothing. Just like, "So what do you think about her?" "Well, I don't know. I mean, I don't think-- She's too young for this and she's too young for that." "Yeah, but she put up for that show. I mean, she's not going to make that show." And I'm just watching them back and forth like this. They all got up and they went, "Well, whatever you think, Art. If you want to sign her, no problem. We won't stand in your way." So now they walk out of the room, and Art says, "Great. Now I want to get you to this audition.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: You're much too young for the role, but I really want them to meet you," blah, blah, blah. So I go. I've got this new agent. I've got another job that I'm doing, dancing. My life's starting to get a little crazy, so I get dressed up for this audition. I pack all of my stuff, all of my tea-- what do you call it? Props. Which you do not do in Hollywood. I mean, it's so not cool. But I didn't know that, right? I just came from a little town. So I get my props, my corny tea pot and everything, and I go in, I do the read. I was terrible. The props made them laugh. I knew that I made a mistake. I go home, I apologize to this guy I met. I said, "Look, you don't have to represent me. I totally get it. Whatever. I'm a dancer." I said, "That's what I do." He said, "What are you saying?" I said, "I'm just sorry. You don't have to represent me." He said, "Goldie, you got the job." And I said, "I got the job?" He said, "Yeah, you got the job." This is great.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: He was like, "Man, you could be big." I said, "Wait, but I'm too young for that role." Now I'm arguing with him. "I'm too young for that role." And they said, "No, they wrote a part in for you." I said, "You mean that didn't exist?" They went, "Yeah." He said, "Goldie, this is really great." I went, "Yeah, but does that mean I'm not dancing anymore? Does that mean that I'm not a dancer and that my life is not what I thought it was going to be, and that I'm going to be one of those screwed-up movie stars that I hated?" "That I never wanted to be in my life?" Which is why anybody wanted it, said, "Oh my God, you're going to be a movie star." I was like, "Oh yeah, I want to do that. I want to be miserable, and divorce people, and drugs and the alcohol," whatever. Whatever those magazines would tell you, which of course, by the way, most of them are lies. But I believed them. I believed them, too.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: So I had this whole notion on top of that I'd just gotten to do what I wanted to do, that I had trained all my life for. So it's like any of you guys. You're training to do something. You love what you're doing. Suddenly, you find yourself interested in something else or plucked out of the world that you thought you were going to be in, and all I can say is take the dive. Take the jump. Go off the precipice. Don't be afraid, right? I was so afraid, and it manifested in a very interesting way because, yes, I got this show. Yes, they wrote in a part for me. Yeah, it was great. And everybody was going, "Goldie, this is amazing." Meanwhile, my dancer friends were going, "Oh, that's really great." "That's so great. Good luck." "Thanks." "Okay, why not me? Why not me? Why not me?" And I kind of lost friends. Well, I didn't lose friends. I was always guilty. And I'm still guilty, by the way, trying to work through it. But I'm sorry I got the part. I'm sorry that they chose me. I'm sorry about all that stuff.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: I'm sorry for my success, and I apologize for everything I got. I didn't deserve it. These are bad things to feel guilty about. So by the way, you guys get successful, do not apologize for your success. You got there because you worked hard for it. But anyway, at that point in time, I was still learning those things. So now, where am I? So I go and I do this job, and I start to get anxiety attacks. And I was in my 20s. I was just 21 years old, and I was not doing what I wanted to do. I was living away from home. My business plan was not working. Open up dancing school, be happy, and get married, and all that stuff wasn't working. And I was alone, and I felt very isolated and very alone. I left "A Chorus Line." I went into a dark room, except lights and a camera and a live audience, and they said action, and my voice went up eight octaves and a character was born. "Hi\!" I was so nervous. But what's more important is that I becameAnxious and scared. I couldn't go out in public without vomiting.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: I was really a mess. I had what you would call non-specific anxiety attacks. I would stay home. I didn't know what was going on. I felt lost. I felt like I was in a world that I didn't belong in. And with that came this agitation and this fear. So what did I do about it? I didn't go out and drink. I didn't take drugs. I didn't try to forget things. I didn't got into the mainstream of being cool, saying, "Oh boy, I've got money. I'm going to have some fame here." People were asking me for my autograph. I didn't even know who I was yet. I'm signing my name saying, "Goldie Hawn. That looks vaguely familiar." So I saw a psychologist, because if I didn't see a psychologist, I couldn't get my joy back, because I lost my joy. Because I was put in an environment in a work that I wasn't prepared for or didn't think I was, and I was scared. So I saw this doctor regularly for nine years, all through the time of becoming successful. I went to the College of Goldie Hawn. I went to American University for one year.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: That was great. I majored in drama, and then I left because I got this audition. But this kind of university, of learning who you are, was the greatest tool I ever could have. I learned what made me scared. I learned what I was made of. I learned what my relationship with my mother and father was. I learned to cut through illusion. Not to dream of what I wanted it to be, but be able to look at what it really was so then I could deal with it. And I realized that fear and all these things in our own brains, we put things away. We try to make them okay. We try to cover them up with all kinds of things. We delude ourselves sometimes to think that we think one thing, but we really feel something else. Have any of you ever said, "Oh, I think this, but I feel this?" Isn't that just amazing how we can think one thing and feel something else? I know I do. So the idea is thinking and feeling and having it learn to come together so you can be a whole person.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: You can literally get out there and challenge yourself, take responsibility, which is what I learned to do through this process, is take responsibility for who I was. But you can't take responsibility for who you are and what you can do unless you know who you are, and you know what you can do, and you know what you can't do, and you know how far to push it. And these are the things that I learned, and this is why it's so important to me to be here today. It's one of the reasons why I want to do this, is to try to compare, just sort of say, look, you guys are at the beginning. You are at a time in your lives when you have a choice. You can either pretend you know who you are, or you can actually pay attention to who you are and what you want. To have honesty about your relationships, about your family, about your loved ones, your lovers, your boyfriends. For women to be able to be strong enough to declare what it is they want without feeling male, without feeling too tough. Just learn the graciousness of truth.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And this is what I went so hard these years to learn. And I'll tell you something, what I approached was a big, big role of stardom. That is a really tough road. It's great. It's money, it's success, it's fame. Guys, I promise you. By the way, I did get my joy back, just in case you were wondering. Money, all this stuff does not buy happiness. It just doesn't. It doesn't buy joy. It doesn't buy any of these things. I've traveled the world. I have met people in third world countries who have nothing, who are way, way happier inside and with the quality of their life than people are in the mall. I look at faces in the mall and it just looks like a dirge. Their eyes have lost the wonder. They've seen it all before, and it's just, "What can I buy now to make me feel good?" And yet people in India by the side of the road are sitting with their families. They're making chapatis. They're inviting you to sit with their family, to eat with them, and you don't even speak the same language.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: One time I was in Africa, and I was driving in the Turkana region, and it's very, very empty. It's just high desert. And I was with the Rendille tribes, and I was with the Turkana tribe. And we were in this Jeep, and I said, "Let's go over there." There was literally nothing. And we drove and hit this manyatta where there was just nothing but men. It was kind of extraordinary that there were just men there. But I'm telling you this because it shows you the amount of joy you can have when you have nothing. It means joy lives inside. So these men are all there, and they're squatting, and they're talking, and uhuhuhuh, in Rendille, and I thought, "What in the world?" And I have these cut-offs, and what they looked at me like, "Who in the world is this coming out of a Jeep?" It's like, "What?" There were rocks and escarpment and whatever, and the desert was going like . Truly, there was nothing there, except these guys. And all their huts and everything, and the goats and the chickens and everything, and me.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: And so now I go up and I say, "Hello," and so, "We don't speak your language," duh duh duh duh. And I had the guy talking to them, my whatever, the Rendille was like sharing them. So then I just sort of sat there.And I smiled a lot, and I stooped down. Well, when I stooped down, I was on a bit of an incline, didn't I know it? And I went head over teakettle backwards. And now I'm laughing. I'm pretty embarrassed. Although it's hard for me to get embarrassed because that's what's fun about life are those crazy, stupid mistakes. But I thought, "Oh my God, this is what..." They started laughing. Now, I'm not joking. That laugh lasted about seven minutes. They laughed, I laughed. We laughed, I laughed. They laughed. The guys over here laughed. The baby little boys were laughing, the seven-year-olds. I thought, "This is the coolest moment in my life." I am sitting with men. We do not speak the same language. We are not the same religion, the same thing, the same color, the same thing, whatever, same country, can't speak, and we are laughing together.

speaker: Goldie Hawn
text: We're sharing this amazing dialogue of joy. So this is one of the reasons why when I travel the world and I look around and I come back, and I see the potential of the human condition, the human spirit. What we have to work with is that we can either look at a glass that's half full or half empty, and we know those people who say, "Oh, God, it's raining again today." Or, "You know what? The sun is still shining above the clouds." It's so cool because I close my eyes, and I can just go up there. And the sun is there, and I feel, and it's warm. There's a difference in that mentality. And what I've learned through my studies and my-- obviously, I wasn't a great student, but we talked about thirst for knowledge. I have a big thirst for knowledge.
