His parents are just divorced. And his mother wants to still go out to fancy restaurants, but they don't have the money from the father anymore. But as part of the divorce settlement, the father said, "Well, I'll pay for anything you do with the boy." So this mother drags her son out to these fancy restaurants. And I thought it would be funny to kind of juxtapose bream, which is, like, a fish I've seen on fancy restaurant menus with hiccups.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: I'm not lying, yeah. Lie to 500 schools... about my title? No, so, anyway, so, hiccups is kind of like a thing that you associate with kind of like a childish reaction to something, and bream is this fancy fish. So it's never referenced in the book, but I thought it was kind of a funny description of that boy's plight.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Above everything else, I hope people laugh, 'cause, to me, that's what it's mainly intended to do. But, then, I also hope that people kind of question their own lives in relation to this book because that's what I did. When I'm writing it, I'm questioning all of my behavior and realizing the silly things I do and the kind of dumb things I do and trying to channel them in the book.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Hey, what's up? My name is Dylan Daniel, and I attend the University of Arizona. And my question is, when we're on our journey, we discover our purpose in life. And our purpose is to bring something good and great to society. So I was just wondering -- when along your journey did you discover your purpose in life, and what is that purpose? What is that good, great thing that you want to bring to society and leave with society?

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: The only -- You know, when I hear people say, like, "What is the meaning of life?" The only time I've ever read somebody give their opinion of the meaning of life and the only time I've ever thought it had any relevance was I read -- They asked Mother Teresa, "What do you think the meaning of life is?" at the end of her life. And she said, "Oh, to help other people." And that's the only time I've ever thought, "Oh, that's actually a good answer," 'cause most of the time, the answers are self-serving, like, "I want to, you know, have jellybeans." Well, you can go do that. So, her answer seemed to be outward thinking. She was thinking about other people. And she was saying that, you know, kind of we're on the Earth for a brief period of time, and we are necessarily social creatures. We're wired to engage with other people. And if you can walk away from those interactions and the other person is made better in some way by that interaction, that's the important thing to do. Now, I'm not, like, good at -- My best friend's a teacher.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: My girlfriend's a teacher. Like, I'm not good at that. I've tried teaching with them, and I'm just not wired to. So I found what I'm good at, and then I tried to kind of use that to affect those same changes. So, for example, when I do my plays, I bring school groups to my plays, or I do, like -- you know, I go into my friend's school, and I work with them on creative-writing projects. So I try to do the thing I do well and then bring it to kind of people who, you know, maybe require a bit of a boost in life.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: It's amazing. Okay, this is from @racquelrocky on Twitter. She asks, "Have people tried to discourage you from your passions? And what would you say to anyone who's experiencing such negativity?"

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Well, I think there's two kinds of discouragement. One kind of discouragement is bad, which is, "You shouldn't do that," for some not-good reason. The other kind of discouragement is helpful, which is kind of giving somebody a realistic world view. I am an actor who wanted to do, like, kind of small theater, you know, with friends. That's a kind of realistic goal. It's a less realistic goal to kind of want to be in the biggest movies because it just -- it's like a kind of weird -- like a winning of the lottery.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: It just is really, really hard, because you could be the most wonderful actor in the world -- and I know a lot of wonderful actors who are kind of struggling to find parts, 'cause a lot of it -- it depends on, you know, what you look like and if you're in the right place at the right time. And there are so many people -- So, some discouragement is helpful, because it says, "I will discourage -- So, when people say, "I want to be in a movie like that, like, you know, that's a big, popular movie," I try to -- Well, first of all, I'm not a great person to give advice 'cause who am I? But I know about this, and I know that some discouragement for that person is helpful. But there's a flip side of that, which is encouragement for realistic goals, which is, if you really like acting, if that's what it is that you love, and you'd be willing to do it for free or for very little money, 'cause most actors -- 99. 9% of actors -- do it for free or very little money.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: I've learned that, like, the kind of concern for doing well never goes away, and I'll just give a brief example. Like, my second play, the actress Vanessa Redgrave was in the play, and for those of you who know the 1992 Phoenix Suns and are a little older -- are my age or older, Vanessa Redgrave is, like, the greatest living actress. She's 77 years old -- the greatest actress of all time. And she was in this play. We did a show every night at 8:00. We did like 90 performances. And she would be at the theater at 4:00 every day, like, in a panic about the night's performance.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: And I thought -- I had stage fright, but I thought it would go away. I thought, you know -- I'm 28 years old at the time. I thought my stage fright would go away. It's just a lack of experience, a lack of confidence in myself. And here's this person who's absolutely incredible panicking. And I thought, "Oh, so it's just -- so maybe it's not stage fright. Maybe it's just concern for doing good, you know, and she just wants to do a good job every night, and it doesn't end." And so I thought, "Oh, really successful people still worry about doing a good job." And I think, maybe once you stop worrying about that, maybe you stop doing a good job. Now, not that you have to be a wreck -- it's probably not the best way to live, but that if you can kind of try to -- if you can always kind of treat things like it's the first time, you know, always treat decisions with the respect as that you treat the first decision you make.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: That's great advice. Part of the Society's program has its members setting S.M.A.R.T. goals -- "smart" being the operative word here. Since you like to pursue multiple projects, multiple passions, how do you go about setting goals for yourself and then, you know, holding yourself accountable for those goals?

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah, that's -- I guess I don't think of it that way. I think I just get really worried if I can't finish stuff. Like, I get really concerned if I can't, like, finish writing a play. Then I think, "Well, then, I will have not written this play." Or if I can't finish putting together a book that I think is good, then I have the fear that I won't have done that. So it's more kind of -- I mean, this is probably not the best advice to give, but it's like a fear-based -- it's like an anxiety that, if I don't do it, it won't happen. And I can't live with that, I guess.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Not because, like, I think the world needs it -- It's just 'cause I think, like, it should be done. I don't know why. It's strange. I guess that's maybe what ambition is or desperation.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Like, do you write lists of things that you want to accomplish, and it's like you put it out there? It's like "The Secret" -- you put it out there in the universe -- maybe it'll happen.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Really? No, no, it can be great, but anytime I put anything out into the universe, they usually say, "No, stop putting that out here. No, here. Take that dream back." No, I don't, like, put out a thing that I hope, then, people will come to, like, give me. I, like -- I do the thing, and then, like, I send it to everybody I know and say, "Can you please, you know, publish this or put this on, or can we do this somewhere?"

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: That seems more productive than the other thing. Yeah, I think that seems like the best way to do it. The other thing's great, too, but I just can't imagine, like, the universe being like, "Oh, okay, this stranger just asked for something. Let's give in to it." Like, it seems like, no, you got to go, like, do the thing, and then maybe the universe will be like, "Oh, you've done the thing. Well, let's give it to you, as opposed to this stranger who just asked for it."

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Hello. I'm Chesari Uchafu from St. Mary's University in San Antonio, Texas. And I was wondering what you think of people having a backup plan and pursuing that because they don't believe that their dreams would be financially viable.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah, which it won't. You know, that's like every parent tells their actor kid that. And, okay, I actually do know one athlete -- this guy Andre Drummond. He plays for the Pistons. And he's like the sweetest guy. Now, he's like a 21-year-old guy. He's humongous. He's a great basketball player. And he and I talk about, like, what he's going to do next, like -- and he's 21. He's at the beginning of the most illustrious career somebody will have, 'cause he's fantastic. And so, like, it's good to, like -- but it doesn't mean he doesn't focus on basketball.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: And he was just getting his degree in Connecticut this summer. Like, so, it's good to do that. But I think, like -- I think, like, the kind of secret of the whole thing is that, when you kind of also pursue the backup plan, I think the front plan benefits. I discovered that 'cause I had a backup plan 'cause I didn't know if I could act, so I studied anthropology, 'cause I thought I would teach. My parents are teachers. And then, what I discovered is, actually, by studying anthropology, which is the study of other cultures and other people, it actually helped me as an actor. And when I was not getting acting jobs, I would write a play. And as I said, my last play, Kunal Nayyar played a Nepalese immigrant, 'cause I got to meet, through my studies, a Nepalese immigrant. And so, like, it actually helped the front plan -- the backup plan helped the front plan. And the front plan helps the backup plan, too, because -- because I know about him, I could maybe go into teaching if the front plan doesn't work.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: So, this is to say that, if we think about the backup plan like, "If my dream doesn't work out, then I'll do this other thing" -- I think that's probably a wrong way to think about it. I think the best way to think about it is to kind of open yourself up to the opportunities and options that are around you. If you're going to one of the wonderful universities that are watching tonight, like, you have a million different opportunities.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: And if you pursue those things and find different interests, then all those plans may work out, or your backup plan may change, or your front plan may actually morph into something else.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: But what I've also seen is really talented people who don't have the motivation or discipline fall off, and you think, "God, that's such a tragedy." You see it all the time -- you know, the great actor who then succumbs to a kind of drug habit or alcohol, but, you know, 'cause they didn't have the kind of motivation and people surrounding them to -- or, really, the passion to go out there and do the great things with the talents they have. You see that a lot. It's almost more heartbreaking than the kind of... than the passionate person with no talent.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: So, when I work in theater, a lot of people you meet -- Say I started out wanting to be an actor, but I realized pretty quickly I couldn't do it. You know, I didn't get parts, or I realized I wasn't that good or I didn't like it that much. And so, they're doing other things in the theater, and they love it, and they're so happy that they didn't pursue the path of acting 'cause they realize how unstable it is. Being on the other side of it, you realize. So, passion with no talent usually leads to, like, kind of good things. Talent with no passion is really hard. It's really hard if you can't wake up in the morning, but you're the greatest artist in the world.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: I think this is -- Yes. I'm usually simultaneously terrified by the thing, like, "I'm gonna do terribly. I don't know how to do this," and, also, the exhilarating feeling of, "My God. This feels, like, real and interesting to me." And so I always feel like, "Oh, the last thing I did was the most interesting. I feel so lucky to have gotten to do that." The most interesting part I got, probably, on paper to play was on this movie called "The Double." And it was a very unusual movie, but I got to play two characters. It's about this kind of timid, shy, nervous man, who then meets his doppelgaenger, who I also play, and that character is this kind of brash, arrogant guy. And the movie's really funny, and it's very creative. It's very strange and interesting. But as an actor, it's like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity because it's just such an odd task, to get to play two parts.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: And when you love each part the way that you just described it, do you have trouble when it does come to an end, when the movie is over? Because I just feel like, when you're on a set, that it becomes a family.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: And I feel like it's hard to walk away. And I think, in real life, when you're at a job or if you're, you know, working on a project with people at school, it's hard, right?

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yes, I've become a lot more callous just because I've done it so much now. When I was younger and I was doing theater, I would just, like, weep for a month. I'd go into some kind of like postpartum depression. After you do a play, it feels like you gave birth, but you'll never see your kid again. Like, it's like the saddest thing, and I would just weep. And my family just thought it was hysterical, because, "I'm not gonna be in 'Peter Pan' anymore." Like, "Who cares? It's 'Peter Pan. '" And now I've become, like, callous now because I finish a thing, and I don't cry anymore. And I feel like, "Why am I not crying?" Like, that was so great when you felt the thing and you expressed it. The problem is, adults can't cry all the time. I've discovered that. You're not supposed to. You're supposed to just ask for your coffee and then walk away with it. You're not supposed to weep and maybe leave a tip if you can afford it.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Well, it's interesting. I would read the comic books, 'cause when you take on a different part, you think, "Well, what applies to this thing?" And so, a movie like "Batman" has this, like -- more history than, like, real history. Like, if you were playing, like, Alexander the Great, there would be less written about him than Batman. Like, there's just been more written about those characters than any human person. So, I had a lot to read. I found it to be, like, not helpful. And, like, the more I would read, the less helpful I thought it was.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Because what I'm reading is like somebody else's interesting concept of these characters, and it's interesting to read, but it doesn't apply to what I have to do. What I have to do is, like, go to a set and think, "What is driving -- Like, what is emotionally driving this person to, like, not like these superheroes?" Do you know what I mean? It sounds like a kind of silly thing when I say it that way, but that's my job to, like, take this thing that can sound silly and take it more seriously, take it -- treat it as though it's life and death. And then, so, I think, like, well, what in my life do I not like that I think has too much power, like the way Lex Luthor thinks Superman has power? So, I think, "Well, what do I, Jesse, think has too much power?" So I think about, you know, bosses I've worked with that have exploited his employees. And I think, "What did I feel during that time?

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: What anger did I feel -- how unjust that is, that that person should be in charge?" And so I take those feelings, and I bring it to that character, which is far more relevant than reading a comic book and being entertained by it and then going and doing something based on that.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Hi. My name is Anna, and I go to Cal State University, Northridge. I was wondering if you have ever had to turn down a role because you felt that it conflicted with personal beliefs or didn't want to be portrayed in a certain way. And if not, then would you? Thank you.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah, that's a great question. I don't love the -- I don't love how violent movies are, and I don't love that as an audience member, but I feel strange for me to kind of take -- get on a soapbox and say it shouldn't be there, and I've been in very violent movies. So I feel like I haven't earned the right to say they shouldn't exist, 'cause I don't think they should -- I think they should exist, in the same way all -- anything that kind of seems like a real self-expression should exist, and then it's up to maybe parents or schools or society to kind of figure out how to contextualize violence in movies and video games to make a safe environment. The only thing I really object to is when something seems unartful. So, I'd rather do a movie that is like a violent movie than a movie that seems like politically right, but not good, because, to me, those will never get that message across. Those will never be successful in getting that message across, and it's masquerading as art, but it's not -- it's a political statement.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: He's politically a very caring person. He cares about the -- You know, he cares about the struggling. He cares about, you know, rights for immigrants. He cares about all the things I care about -- healthcare for everybody. He cares about all the things that, if you care about the struggling people in the world, he cares about. But I asked him, "What is your main goal in making a movie? 'Cause you have these very specific agendas with your movie." He said, "I want to make a good movie -- that's the first thing. And then the second thing is the agenda." And he says, "There's no way to reach people and tell them your agenda if the art is bad, 'cause no one's gonna watch it."

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Exactly, exactly. And so my main goal is, like, to do things that I think are original and that are interesting, and then, secondarily, I want to, you know, affect change in the way that I'm interested in. But I would rather -- Like, I work with a domestic-violence shelter in Indiana -- raising money for it and working there. And to me, I'd rather, like, make money from a violent movie and give it to the domestic-violence shelter, as opposed to making a movie about how horrible domestic violence is, 'cause I just don't think that's the right -- to me, it just doesn't feel like the right way to do it.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: No, I have -- I set no goals, because I feel like I'll be totally discouraged. So I just -- I try to, like -- Yeah, I don't set a goal, no.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah, one day at a time. I mean, I loved Woody Allen movies growing up. He was, like, my hero. And I never, ever once thought I would get to be in a movie of his, because it just seemed like a weird thing to think about. I worked with a guy when I was like 22. I was just starting out. And he was like 24. And he said, by the time he was 25, he was going to win an Academy Award. I was like, "Oh, you got to get on that. Like, you have like six months." And I just thought -- And from that moment on, I just thought, "It's so foolish to, like, plan for that." Now, it's great to have goals -- personal goals for yourself. I want to kind of express myself. I want to, you know, work in the literary world. But I think it's probably a mistake to say, "I want to sell a lot of books, " or, "I want to be in a movie that makes a lot of money." It just seems like you're setting yourself up for some kind of failure.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Oh, geez. Probably the thing about kind of never stop having concern for your work. It's really just incredible to see, like -- Just across the board, the only thing that unites successful people, in my opinion -- and I'm not including myself in that bucket -- is that they're really concerned for doing a good job. It doesn't stop because they've been successful.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: No, if anything, it's the opposite. It spurs them on to kind of make sure that they -- and that transcends any industry. That could be in any industry, in any field -- just kind of putting pressure on yourself -- a healthy pressure, but a pressure on yourself to do well.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Absolutely. So, our viewers tonight are college students nationwide, and they're dealing with balancing their classes, relationships, part-time jobs -- all sorts of things. What sort of things stressed you out or make you feel pressure or nervous or fearful, and how do you manage all of those feelings and then overcome them?

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: I do something that I've only learned about recently, which is that I don't criticize other people. I don't criticize other movie. I don't criticize books because I have this weird, nagging voice in my head that, if I do that, somebody's doing it to me. And so I stopped doing it, and then I stopped worrying about getting criticized. I realize a lot of the kind of terror we have about getting criticized or made fun of comes from the fact that we are often doing that to other people, even if we're doing it silently, even if we think, "God, that guy looks stupid." I think the kind of dangerous related reverse of that is, "What if he thinks I look stupid?" And I just stopped thinking that. I just tried to think -- And it's hard. It's hard. It's taken me a long time, and I still have those feeling sometimes.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: But I try to think, "Oh, no, that guy looks the way he looks for all the same reasons I look the way I look, which is a series of decisions made for real reasons." And he might think I look like an idiot, and he might be right, or I might be right. But it doesn't really matter. But the less I kind of think those things, the less I worry that other people are thinking them about me. And it's the only thing that has worked. It's the only thing that has made me feel less worried about kind of rejection or criticism or being made fun of.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yes, and the best advice I heard in this regard was it's better to be nice than right. It's not so important that you got it right, that that guy looks like an idiot. Maybe he does. But it's more important that you're nice to the guy because what is it accomplishing by thinking he looks like an idiot? So, that's what I've discovered -- I'm happier being nice than right.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: That works. Who were some of your earliest supporters and confidantes, and how important was and is having, you know, the support system of people around you, people that you can trust and, you know, people to keep you balanced and grounded?

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah, it's great that I have friends that are not in the arts because there's a kind of like special neurotic personality that is in the arts that, if I'm around it too much, then it just reinforces all the horrible feelings I have.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: So, well, 'cause every artist feels like, "Oh, I've just finished this thing. Now I'm a failure." And, like, you know, you want to be around people that have a normal job, that say, "I finished teaching for the day, but, luckily, I get to go back tomorrow." So, I try to have, like, a kind of broad-in-scope group of people. You know, if you stay with people who are all on your same bubble, you end up having a kind of small world view, and if you try to meet people that are unusual, people that, you know, your parents wouldn't have, you know, put you in the same group together when you're little kids, that's great. It broadens your world view, unless you had these kind of interesting parents that thought, "You guys should be friends, " but most of us don't have that situation. We're 2 years old. They say, "Oh, you should be friends with this kid who looks exactly like you."

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Hi. I'm Zana Dako from Texas A\&M University-Central Texas. My question is, choices like writing your play "The Spoils" helped you capitalize on your strengths in order to work through difficult aspects of your life. Do you have practical tips to help us learn how to use our strengths to turn perceived weaknesses into opportunities?

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah. That's a great question. What I always try to write about, especially in, like, my last play, was trying to kind of find a part of myself that I feel uncomfortable about or find a part of myself that I think is not fully formed yet, like, and then try to write about that in an honest way. Like, if I think I do something stupid, and I know I do many stupid things, I try to write about them. So, my last play was about this kind of selfish guy who -- his selfishness takes over, and he ruins other people's lives. And that's 'cause I'm kind of working on, like not being self-centered. That said, like, doing an event like this, with a lot of people listening to me, it reinforces being self-centered. So this is probably not the best place for me to be. So, thanks so much, but... No, but I'm gonna go to therapy.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: But -- But, anyway, so, if I think I have that, then I could write about it, and then not only is it entertaining, because it's honest, 'cause people can relate to it -- they can say, "I do that, too," or, "I do that," or, "That reminds me of my friend or my brother" -- sometimes like that. And then, it also helps me, 'cause it makes me step back and view my -- And so I try to write about things like that. And then it does this other thing, which is that no one's ever written about that before, because I'm writing about myself.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Some people can do it, but it's really hard. The best thing to do, I think, as a young kind of writer, a young artist, is to, like, do the thing that you know well, and then, as you get experience with that, to kind of branch out. This great writer, John Patrick Shanley, who -- he's a great playwright, a Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright. He wrote the play "Doubt" that they turned into a movie, "Doubt." He said he spent the first half of his career writing about himself and the second half writing about other things.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: And so it's like he got the kind of experience enough writing about -- And he's a great writer. And now he has kind of like earned the talent to write about other things.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah, but the alternative is horrible, because the alternative is like you're writing about this great thing. You know, I mean, who wants to go watch a play written by a guy who thinks he's great showing how great he is? It just seems like the worst play.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: I don't even know what that would be. Yeah, like, a guy who's flying and calling his parents. Like, no one wants to watch that. You know, you want to watch about the guy who can't call his parents. And you think, "Well, that's -- Why can't this guy call his mother back?" And you think, like, it's such a bizarre thing. He's nervous about calling his -- You know, and that's interesting. And suddenly, you have a character. You have a situation. You have a scenario. And no one else is writing about that, 'cause it's so personal.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah. So, when you are writing a book or a play, you're putting yourself out there, obviously, like we're saying, that's far more personal -- that's far more personal than playing a role, like, in a movie.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Yeah, but acting in movies are personal, too, in a different way, 'cause they're like looking at your face. And I'm sure all of us have, like, you know, 9/10 of our face we think like, "That just didn't come out good. "

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: Like, that's how I feel. I feel like 1/10 of my face -- like, "Oh, good, yeah, I would have done that, too, if I were drawing it." But 9/10, you think like, "Now, if they just, like, rearranged it, like a half a millimeter... But, so, like, in movies, it's really personal, 'cause even though I'm playing a character and it's not me and, you know, somebody else is directing it or something, like, you're still -- your face is there, and then people write about, "Why does his face look like that?" And you're like, "I know. I feel the same way. I agree with you." You know, no one's ever told me anything about my face that I also didn't agree with. Like, "Yeah, I know that. I'm also disappointed." So, as personal as my book is, as personal as my plays are, like, it's just words, and it's Times New Roman, which I did not invent.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: I try to, like, have the tough times inspire me. Like, I try to think, like, "Well, why am I feeling so bad about this particular thing?" I oftentimes will, like, obsess with world news. And I have been to a lot of countries that are really struggling in ways that make anything that I will ever go through seem like the greatest day in the world. And so I'm obsessed with world news. I read world news all day. I know about all the tragedies that are occurring in the world. And yet, I still think, "Why do I feel bad about myself today? I haven't earned the right to feel bad about myself. They didn't have my doughnut?" You know, and, like, you think like -- Or, "Why am I nervous about this thing? Bombs are not falling on my head. Why am I nervous about this particular thing?" And so I try to kind of put my life in perspective. And by doing that, you start to kind of relieve yourself because you realize that it's gonna be okay.

speaker: Jesse Eisenberg
text: And then, also, I find it kind of amusing to think that I have any reason to feel one millionth of the anxiety that a lot of people in hard situations really feel. That's helpful. So, it's helpful to stay connected with the world, to read things that are going on, to try to interact with, if you can, you know, people in more difficult situations and try to help out. It'll end up making you feel a little better about yourself, if that's your goal.

speaker: Jim Cramer
text: And three, and here's where I'll get a little harsh because there are many professors and many salespeople and many promoters and a TV host or two who think that I'm totally full of it with my view and that you should just own an index fund because you're not smart enough to beat the market. speaker: Jim Cramer
text: I'm not in that phase of my life anymore. I'm done with that. Don't want it. What's my motive? Maybe I believe. Maybe I believe in you. speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: We are in charge of preserving all the memories of the time we had together here at school. We, we, we. Our, our, our. One of the ways you can tell when somebody is likely to be a leader is if you have them talk about their dream of the future, you have them talk about their own leadership, and you count the number of I's and we's. If every sentence starts with I, this person is not as likely to be a leader who uses at least as many we's as I's in their conversation. Leadership is also about what we aspire to achieve. We are making something that will be treasured for the rest of our lives. Just think how every time you look at it, it will remind you of those times. Now, maybe there's a better way to illustrate this. This is a Snoopy cartoon, obviously. It's Peanuts. He's the leader because he has an explorer cap on his head. And he gathers the troops around. "Okay, troops gather around." "Who is it?" "It's me. I'm the leader, so I get my picture on the flag.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Just think how it will inspire you as we march along." Well, Woodstock speaks up. He has some comment to make. And so Snoopy says, "Well, all right then. Does anyone have a better idea?" We are more likely to align ourselves with a leader's vision when we can see our own picture in the flag. One of our challenges as leaders is to be able to articulate that vision of the future in such a way that other people can see themselves in the picture. Another way to illustrate this is imagine I brought in a jigsaw puzzle. It had, let's say, 1,000 pieces. And I divided all the pieces evenly amongst you, and I said, "Put the puzzle together." What do you need to put the puzzle together? What do you want right now? With just the pieces in your lap, what do you need? What do you want? You want to see the picture on the box top. What's it look like when we're done? I have these things to contribute, but where do my pieces go? I want to see the whole thing so that I know where I fit in. Inspire a shared vision.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: The third of the five practices is what we call challenge the process. Challenge the process is essentially about searching for opportunities to change, grow, innovate, and improve, and then experimenting and taking risks. I love this comment from Allison Avon, another of the student leaders we had the chance to interview. She said, "When the process challenges you, challenge back."One of the things that when we did our own research on leadership, we found that students who rate high on proactivity are seen by their peers as more transformational leaders. Leaders are not people who sit around and wait for somebody else to do something. They are people who take the initiative. Remember Melissa Poe at eight years old? She had a problem with the environment, and she took initiative. She wrote a letter to then President George Bush, the first one, and she didn't get an answer. Now, so did she wait around for the United States government to do something about the problem and the president of the United States, the leader, to do something about the problem? No. She started her own organization, Kids' Face, and they did something about the problem.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: And down the road, some 17 years later, no, that's about 11 years later, one million trees were planted by one million kids. Leaders are proactive. They take initiative. They get out and do something. If they're unhappy with the problem, they figure out a way to fix it themselves. Another story about this same kind of issue, Gail Mayville. Gail Mayville worked at Ben \& Jerry's. Ben \& Jerry's Ice Cream. Some of you may have even tasted their product. At Ben \& Jerry's Ice Cream, they had a problem. The problem was at the time Gail was there, they were expanding so rapidly that the effluent from the factory was overloading the local waste treatment facility, and they didn't know how they were going to deal with this particular problem. And in fact, the local township in Vermont threatened to shut the factory down if they didn't do something about the problem. Now, Gail heard about this problem as the administrative assistant in the office of the president. Now, she was an administrative assistant. Now, most of us might, as administrative assistants, sit around and say, "Well, I'm not the factory manager. I'm not the environmental manager.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: I don't have a title in this organization. I'm just an administrative assistant," and wait around for somebody to do something about it. But she wasn't satisfied with that. So she went to the president, and she said, "I have a solution. I have a solution that I believe will work." And he said, "Well, what is it?" And she said, "Pigs." "Gail, you'll have to tell me a little bit more about the... I don't understand. Pigs? How are pigs going to help solve our waste treatment problem?" And she said, "Well, I grew up on a farm in Vermont, and what do pigs like to eat?" They'll eat anything, right? They'll eat anything. "So why don't we buy pigs for the local farmers? And we'll take them out there and give them to them, so they don't have to spend any of their own money. Then we'll take the waste from the factory, we'll put it in little barrels, and we'll take those barrels out on trucks and pour it into the troughs and see what happens." Guess what? It worked. It worked. It worked. The pigs absolutely loved it. Except for mint Oreo.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: They weren't particularly fond of mint Oreo. Think about that sometime when you go to the store. But again, here's a situation where somebody, no title, no official responsibility to do anything at all about this problem, had an idea, was proactive, took initiative, and got that rather odd and weird solution presented to the organization. It was accepted, and it wasn't a permanent solution, but it temporarily helped them keep the factory open till they could come up with a more permanent solution to the problem. So we asked Gail, why did you do this? This is an interesting story. It's a fun story. But her answer to that question is even more significant. We asked her, why did you do this, Gail? And she said, "For me personally, I am driven by my concerns for the environment, by concerns for my children, my three little children, and the legacy I am leaving for them, the environmental legacy." Remember, go back to model. What's the first step in the process? Modeling. In modeling, there's two pieces. Do what you say you will do. What's the first thing you got to do?

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Be clear about what it is you value and believe in, because then you're more likely to act on it. She was clear what's important to her. I am concerned for the legacy I am leaving my children, the environmental legacy. Because she was clear, she was able to act in a situation where she had no title, had no direct responsibility. That is the kind of contribution all of us in this room can make when we be clear, when we become clear about what we value and believe in. We can take more initiative. We can be more proactive. And when we do this kind of thing, we're going to make mistakes. We're not going to do it perfectly. It's not going to be exactly right the first time. So we need to understand that when we're doing something innovative, when we're doing something creative, when we're doing something for the first time, we're going to make mistakes.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: I had more failures than successesSaid James West, who holds 50 domestic and a couple of hundred foreign patents, and he's talking about his own work, and he says, "I make more mistakes, and I have more failures than successes." But the important thing is that he learns from them. And what Barry Posner and I and Lilas Brown found in research we did with both students at university and also in the working population, found that individuals who put more time and energy into their learning make better leaders than those who put less time and energy into it. There's actually a quantitative piece to this. It doesn't matter how you learn. What matters is how much time you put into it. I'm going to give you a little metric to be thinking about for your own development. How much time does it take to become world-class at something? Let's take music. Let's say via being a violinist. 15 years. 15 years, and about how many hours would you say? About- It's 10,000 hours. 10 years, 10,000 hours is the metric. Anders Ericsson, Florida State University, has been doing this research for well over 25 years now.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: It was popularized by Malcolm Gladwell in a recent book he wrote. Other people have used this metric, but Anders Ericsson deserves the credit for doing the original research. And what they found is to get to the highest level of expertise, be able to play on a concert stage in New York City or in Orange County or in San Francisco, 10,000 hours, 10 years. That's 2.7 hours a day, every day, seven days a week for 10 years. You want to get really good at something, you have to have the perseverance and the passion to stick with it over a long period of time. Think about that. Think about your own aspirations, wanting to be really great at something. It ain't going to happen tomorrow. It's not going to happen in a weekend course. It's not going to happen next year. It's not going to happen the year after that or the year after that or the year after that or the year after that. It's going to take you 10 years and 10,000 hours if you practice 2.7 hours a day. That's practice. That's not performance. I had the opportunity to interview Lang Lang.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Lang Lang is the Chinese pianist. If you ever have the chance to listen to any of his albums or download some music, listen to Lang Lang. It's absolutely beautiful music. Well, I happened to have the opportunity to interview him, and I said, "Lang Lang, when did you start playing the piano?" And he said, "At three." Three years old. It also helps to start early, by the way. It's a good thing you're starting here now, because to wait till you get to work is almost too late. The earlier you start, the better. I said, "How many hours did you practice?" He said, "Well, when I was first learning, before I became a professional, I practiced six to eight hours a day. Now that I am a professional, I only practice three." If you ever want to play on the world stage, think about Lang Lang. Our son Nicholas is a tennis player. Plays number one men's tennis, NCAA Division I school, UC Davis. When he was being recruited to play, we had the opportunity to interview a number of coaches. And we were interviewing a number one, and Glenn Michibata at Princeton was one of them.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: And I said essentially the same thing to Glenn, "Well, how much time do your players practice, and what do you provide for them in terms of tutors and other opportunities for learning because they have to travel and so on?" He said, "Practice. Well, let's see. I tell them they have to practice two hours a day just to stay the same, more if you want to get better." Whoever I've talked to, whether it's Lang Lang or read the research from Anders Ericsson or whether just talking to a tennis coach at Princeton University, what we learn is that there is a quantitative part to this. Better leaders are made from better learners. And you have to put in the time to get really good at it. The next thing is enabling others to act. It's about teamwork and trust, and it's about strengthening other people. This is a photograph from 25 years ago, and I picked it intentionally because I wanted to show you that when we first began this research, and I'll show you another slide of just last year, people have been saying exactly the same thing.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: We asked them to tell us a story about their personal best leadership experience. Tell me about a time when you did your best as a leader. Tell me about a time when you performed at your best. And we asked this of Bill Flanagan. He's the guy there at the chalkboard. And we said, "Bill, tell us your personal best leadership experience." And he said, "I can't." And we said, "Bill, you're a director of manufacturing." Since went on to be vice president of manufacturing, then division president. So obviously, he had a lot of experiences, and we were kind of shocked that he would say, "I can't tell you my personal best." So we said, "You must have done something in your career that was extraordinary, exemplary." And he said, "Well, that's not the problem. The problem is it wasn't my personal best, it was our personal best. It wasn't me, it was us." Everyone we talked to said that it was due to the other people that they were successful. No leader-By him or herself has ever gotten anything extraordinary done.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Leadership is a relationship, and in order to get anything extraordinary done as a leader, you have to have good relationships with other people. We make heroes out of leaders as if they are going to ride in and save all of us. But in fact, those who play well with others are the ones who become great leaders. Those who are able to build strong relationships with other people are the ones who make great leaders. Jill Cleveland at Apple essentially said the same thing last year to us in talking about her personal best leadership experience. She said, "To be successful, I needed to develop a cohesive team and a collaborative team, beginning with that really secret sauce, that secret ingredient of trust as the framework." And it's another thing. Take this example of trust. Here's an example of trust. Have you ever done the trust fall? How many have even done the trust fall? How many of us have done trust fall? So those of you who haven't, this person on the ladder is going to fall over backwards into the arms of the people behind, and they're going to catch this individual.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: When done perfectly, it looks like this. Now, I want you to imagine that you're the third person in line. First person in line goes up to the top of the ladder, falls over backwards, and the group does its job perfectly and catches the person. Everybody applauds. A great job, great teamwork, great, and we can all trust each other. Terrific. The second person goes up to the top of the ladder, and remember, you're the third person, so you're now going to be following this second person. The second person goes up to the top of the ladder, falls over backwards, but the group forgets to do its job, drops that individual down on the ground on top of the person lying down looking up. They're both hauled off to the hospital, and you're next. How are you feeling at this moment? Oh, you go. I'll wait. We'll see if they learn. We are more likely to challenge, to take initiative, to be proactive, to take risks, when we can trust that the group is going to catch us when we fall.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Trust is such an important ingredient, not only in situations like that, but out in the battlefield. Some of you may have friends who are fighting in a war. The three researchers at West Point did some research in the battlefield in Iraq, and they wanted to know the role that trust played in the influence of a leader. And they found that, most importantly, the level of trust subordinates had in their leaders determined the amount of influence from their officers that the soldiers would accept. Now, these are key words here. Accept. Now, this is the military. Now, isn't the military an organization where people are supposed to salute and do what the commanding officer says? But in fact, what they found in their research is people who were the rank and file were only willing to accept the influence from that captain or that commander if they trusted that person. Trust is absolutely essential in a group of people, and it's also about how we make other people feel.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: "I contend, however, that all other things being equal, we will work harder and more effectively for people we like, and we will like them in direct proportion to how they make us feel," said Erwin Federman, one of the first people we interviewed, and we continue to follow him year by year as he's moved throughout his career. I love that comment. People are going to be more willing to work harder and more effectively for people they like, and they will like them in direct proportion to how they make them feel. Part of our job as leaders is to make people feel positive, upbeat, encouraged, strong, capable, efficacious, like the origin of their own experiences. I mean, just think about this in relationship for one moment to say, a leader you admire and look up to. Just think about this for a minute. What are the feelings you have when you are around somebody as a leader you look up to, you admire, you would willingly follow? What words come to mind as how you feel? Inspired. So you feel inspired. I won't be disappointed. That you won't be disappointed. Cared about. You feel cared about.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: How else do you feel? Motivated. Important. Important. Safe. Empowered. What-- Are those mostly positive words or mostly negative? Positive. Mostly positive feelings. Part of our job as a leader is to instill in others positive feelings about themselves and about the group and about the organization. How do you feel when you're around some leader who is kind of bossy and who, if you didn't have to, you probably wouldn't be hanging out, and you would like to distance yourself from? How do you feel? Give me some words like... How do you feel? Uncomfortable. Pardon? Uncomfortable. Uncomfortable. Annoyed. Annoyed. Not happy. Not happy. Scared. Irritated. Scared. Irritated. Yeah. Unmotivated. What are those? Mostly positive or negative?Negative. This is a pretty simple exercise really, isn't it? And it's very telling because we get consistency every time we ask the question. When people are around leaders they respect, they admire, they look up to, they would want to follow, they have positive feelings. When people are around leaders they would rather not be around, when they're forced to be there, when they wish they weren't there, they have all these negative feelings.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Part of the job of a leader is to encourage the heart, is to tell other people, show other people that they care about them. Here's a little quiz. Do you need encouragement to perform at your best? How many of you would raise your hand and say, I need it? The key word is need. Now, so we don't get everybody's hands, right? But we were doing research on encouraging the heart, and we expected, well, everybody to raise their hand. Yeah, I need it. But the majority didn't. We were kind of, how is this possible? This was something that leaders who we want to be around do, but people aren't saying they need it. So like good researchers, we just changed the question. When you get it, does it help you perform at a higher level? Yes. Yes. How many would raise your hands? Yeah, well, it helps. See, this proves that most of us are in denial. We say we don't need it, but when we get it, it makes us perform at a higher level.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: So if it makes us perform at a higher level, we need it, because what's the job of a leader anyway? To keep people the same, make them better, or make them worse? Better. Make them better. And if people perform at a higher level because you give them encouragement, you need to give it to them. And they need it. "I found that encouraging my teammates," said Kristen Cornell, who was captain of her volleyball team, found that encouraging her teammates was one of the easiest and most beneficial things that she could do to get her team to perform at its highest level. There's a magic ratio to this, by the way, if some of you want to quantify this. Well, how much of this do I have to do? Okay. Let's say one is the negative, okay? One is the number of negatives. What's the number of positives have to be in order for you to perform at your very best? Three. Three? Yeah. Well, actually, the number is three. Thank you very much. You've read the same research I have. The number is three, and some people say it's 5.6.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: So somewhere between three and six is the right number, depending on which study you read, but a minimum of three. At home, by the way, it has to be more, or in a significant relationship or relationship with somebody you care deeply about and would like that relationship to last, has to be more than three, minimum of five. And those people who study this stuff, who actually videotape couples interacting over something like money, which is kind of a difficult subject to talk about, and then they videotape it and count the emotions, positive, negative, they find that if it's not at least five to one, they can predict with 95% accuracy that this couple is likely to split up. Now, all of you are doing a little serious review here, see. You can't make it up all at once, by the way. You can't do 25 tomorrow because you didn't do any at all last week. So on a regular basis, we have to do this. Three to one is the magic ratio. And it's also finally about being genuine. We have to be genuine when we're doing this.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Keep up the good work, whatever it is, whoever you are, is not exactly a genuine statement. It has to be genuine. And I just want to say one last thing about this individual right here as I close my comments before we take questions. This is Don Bennett, first amputee to climb Mount Rainier, 14,410 feet on one leg and two crutches. Don kind of summarizes all of this for us. Don said when I asked him to describe what it was that enabled him to get to the top of the mountain, he said, "Well, I could see myself up at the top of that mountain 1,000 times in my mind every day." That's having a vision. "But when I started to climb it, I looked at my feet, and I said anybody can climb from here to there, hop from here to there. So I did.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: I got to the top one hop at a time, one little step at a time." I said, "What was the most important lesson you ever learned, Don?" And he said, "The most important lesson I learned is you can't do it alone." Now, here's a guy that's the first to do something that no one else had ever done before, and who does he attribute his success to? To his team of people. And then he told me the following story. He said, "When I was making this climb, my daughter was with me. She was 16 years old at the time. Her name was Kathy. And we got to an ice field, and we were trying to get across this ice field, and as a two-legged person, we can get across ice field by putting crampons on the bottom of our boots, and then we stick the poles in so we're stable, and then we lift one leg out, and we move it forward, and then we shift our weight, and then we pull the back one out, and we push that down." So you can get across an ice field with crampons on your boot that way.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: But if you're a one-legged person, what happens? You put a crampon on the one boot, you stick it in the ice, you stick the two poles in the ice, what happens? You get stuck. You get stuck. So Don said, "I was standing there stuck. How am I going to get across this ice field? The rest of the team is up in front, and I'm trying to get across, and so what am I going to do?"So he falls forward, starts to crawl across the ice. He's crawling across the ice. His daughter, Kathy, 16 years old, sees her dad lying on the ground behind her, and she runs down to him, says, "Dad, what's wrong?" And he tells her what's wrong. He says, "I can't get across the ice field because I'm stuck, and I have to fall and crawl." She said, "Well, let me get somebody over here to help you." So she brought another member of the team who got an ice ax to cut holes in the ice so that Don could hop into the fresh snow and not be stuck.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: So he would use his pole for leverage and just swing himself forward and put his foot in the fresh snow. For four hours on his hands and his knees, this team member cut holes in the ice so Don could hop. You can't do it alone. And then he said, "For those same four hours, my daughter, Kathy, stood beside me every hop of the way and shouted in my ear, 'Come on, Dad, you can do it. I know you can do it, Dad. You are the best dad in the world.'" And he said, "There was absolutely no way I was not going to make it across that ice field with my daughter shouting that in my ear." You want to know what leadership is? What she did is leadership. Each and every one of us in this room can do what Kathy did. You can do it. You are the best in the world. We're going to take some time for questions now, but thank you all very much. Appreciate the opportunity to talk. We're going to take questions. Thank you. Have a seat. Have a seat. Thank you.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Thank you all for your patience with the technical difficulties. Well, you gave me goosebumps. Thank you, sir. What we're going to do right now is we're going to announce the trivia winner, and that winner is... It's Emily Pasquiero from Marist College. Congratulations, Emily. And also what I wanted to mention in the introduction, those of you who didn't have a chance to win that great package, you have a chance to get a copy of Jim's book. If you go to

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: purchase any one of his books, and you can get a society member discount. But right when you go to pay for that book, you could type in this promotional code, HAE20, and you'll get a 20% discount. So be sure to follow up on the great information content that we had today. Thanks. And thanks so much, Jim, for doing that. So now let's go to our first text question of the night, and it's this: If you could give a student one piece of advice today, what would it be? Eric from Michigan Technological University. Boiling it down to one. If people had only one... If you could do just one thing- Mm-hmm. Eric? Mm-hmm. I'd say you need to, and all of us need to, begin with that first practice, model the way, and the first behavior of building credibility, which is clarify what you value and believe and clarify what is important to you. Because what you'll find, what all of us will find, is it'll make us more committed to whatever we choose to do. It'll enable us to persevere.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Arlene Blum once said, "If what you're doing is meaningful to you, you can cut through the fear and exhaustion and take the next step." So it's really important that we clarify what's important to us, what's meaningful to us. That's excellent. That's the first step. Thank you. We have a second text question. Let's go to it. What was the first leadership role in your life, and did this instigate your passion for studying effective leadership? Lauren from Marist College. I had the opportunity to be an Eagle Scout, and if I had to say there was one leadership role which trained me early in my life, it was becoming an Eagle Scout, going through that process, and earning that. And as a consequence of doing that, I was selected to be in John F. Kennedy's honor guard when he was inaugurated President of the United States. Wow. That's amazing. I wish I could do that. Well, he's no longer with us, but he was an inspiration. Yeah. All right. Here's the next question. At what point in your life did you discover what your personal values were? Was there a time when they were challenged? Good question.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Good question. Thank you. Joanna from Texas State University. Joanna Marie, thank you. I would say that my values were shaped early in my life by my parents, and I think that's where most of us get our early messages. And I think also because my parents took me to church every Sunday in downtown Washington, DC, that was also a major influence in my life. Very consistent messages once a week. I got reminded of what's important. I also had the opportunity to live and work in Washington, DC, early in my life because my father worked for the federal government. Now, many of you don't think Washington, DC, is a place where you learn values, but- At least those you might want to emulate. But at least at the time I was growing up, because of my father, I had the opportunity to be around a number of people who were in the federal government, who were in the military, who were in civilian roles, who had very strong values and beliefs about service, about community. My mother was a member of the United Nations Association, served as our local chapter president in our local area.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: So I learned the value of being very global in my outlook. Well, my mother's 92, and she's still alive. Wow. And up till last year, there was a foreign student living in our home. That's from about 1960 until last year. Over 100 foreign students have lived in our home. So very early on, which is not to say that we don't learn values as we grow and get older, but the early exposure was what shaped my event. She asked about challenges. And a couple of times, and my wife and I were just having a conversation about this the other night. I joined a fraternity when I went to university. And I joined a fraternity because I felt rather repressed as a kid. Any of you feel this way? Like at home, your parents didn't let you do stuff. So I wanted... Yeah, some of you feel that way. So I joined a fraternity, and after about two years, I got to feeling really uncomfortable. The parties were great. The girls were great. Just wonderful. And it met a certain need that I had at the time, but after a while, I got really uncomfortable. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Because I just felt that we didn't share the same values and principles. And so I quit. Wow. Because I just felt that some of you said you were in the wrong place because you just feel uncomfortable. There was a real tension going on, and I had to make a choice of who I was, what I really valued and believed in. It doesn't mean that those of you who are fraternity members should quit, but that was my personal experience because there was a tension there. Well, we have a few minutes left, and before, I know that you wanted to say some words, but on behalf of the National Society of Leadership and Success, we wanted to give you an honorary membership for all the great work that you're doing. It is consistent with our mission. Please give Jim a warm round of applause. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you all. Thank you. Now, at this point, Jim, I know that you had some last-minute words that you'd like to share with everybody.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Yeah, I always like to share the secret to success in life at the end of any opportunity to talk with a group. Would that be of interest to you, the secret to- Take some notes, people. Take some notes. So I was interviewing Major General John Stanford. He was one of the people we had the opportunity to interview early on. And we asked him the same question we ask everybody else at the end of these interviews when we're talking to them about their personal best leadership experience, and we're gathering our data. And the question is, how would you develop leaders for the future? What advice would you give, given your own experience, what advice would you give? And John gave us the most memorable response. He said, "Whenever anyone asks me that question, I tell them I have the secret to success in life." Well, now I am really taking notes. I'm making sure the recorder is capturing every word. I'm taking them down by hand. And he says, "The secret to success is stay in love.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
text: Staying in love gives you the fire to really ignite other people, to see inside other people, to have a greater desire to get things done than other people. A person who is not in love doesn't really feel the kind of excitement that helps them to get ahead and lead others and to achieve. I don't know any other fire, any other thing in life that is more positive and exhilarating a feeling than love is." Blew me away. I didn't expect to hear that. And yet, as I thought about all the other people we had the chance to talk to and have had the chance to talk to since, that leadership, when they are, and we are, performing at our best as leaders is not an affair of the head. Leadership is an affair of the heart. So I leave you with just one last bit of advice, which is to love them and lead them. Wow. All right. Thank you all very much. Pleasure to be with you. Thank you. Thank you. Well, on November 10th is our next broadcast. We're going to have Mark Keilberger. He is the founder of Free the Children.

speaker: Jim Kouzes
