text: My life is over." And it was only then that I was also taking a political science class, and I got an "A+" And I won a political science prize. And I thought, "Huh. I could do something else other than be the next Steve Jobs." And it was there that my broadcast journalism career was born. I became the news director at Stanford Radio. I started writing for the paper at school. I started telling stories in the way that I thought was interesting, and I was deeply interested and moved by the political landscape all the time. But, you know, when I got to Stanford, I remember thinking -- There's something called the imposter syndrome. Have you heard of that? Where you feel like you can't, again, measure up to the next guy. "I'm not as good as that guy. I didn't go to that private school. I didn't have that, you know, silver spoon in my mouth." And it's only when you kick that aside and have the confidence in your own ability that you can start working your way up the ladder. I landed at ABC News 10 days after graduating.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: I was a Vacation Relief Desk Assistant. I had the most tenuous hold on the bottom rung on the ladder that you could imagine. And over the next 20 years, I traveled to every state in the country, to countless countries in far-flung places, inside maximum-security prisons with juvenile offenders, in rural villages in Africa where teenagers were giving birth in a dark tent, miles and miles from electricity or running water. I've been backstage at the Ed Sheeran concert and up close with Nicki Minaj, who told me a really interesting think, by the way, just to digress for a moment. I said something about like, "Why are you -- Why are you using 'F' words all the time? Why are you dr--" You know, and she said, "You know, a woman speaks with power and she's called --" Am I allowed to say "bitch?" "...a bitch, right? But a man asks to get paid and he asks for power and he's, you know, called boss. Why is that?" Back to the question of, like, why has there never been a female president of the United States.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: And she talked about how she aims her lyrics at being female empowerment where you don't need a man to help you get ahead. But that's my Nicki digression. So, I've been all over the world. You get that, right? We all tell stories at "Nightline" that have policy implications, too, and for every Chris Pine -- actor, fascinating, talented guy -- to, you know, the Tom Hankses or the Channing Tatums that were mentioned earlier, I enjoy meeting everyday people with everyday struggles who can tell me their stories, because those are the lessons that we can learn from. And sometimes when celebrities have troubles, we learn from their troubles, as well, whether it's postpartum depression for Hayden Panettiere or it's, you know, some -- whatever it is that you share -- a breast cancer struggle, a this -- you know, that's when people's stories start to matter to others. I think that, you know, I spent a week in a hospital in Tennessee where young newborns were born dependent on opioids. And I remember interviewing a teenage girl who talked about the first party drug that she took was a painkiller -- you know, Oxycontin.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: And one painkiller turned into three painkillers. And three painkillers turned into seven. And seven turned into I'm gonna crush them up and snort it. And then that couldn't be enough, and then, the next thing she knows, the only way she could get that big a high was to go to heroin. And we start talking about that slippery slope, and you see it in their eyes. And when people share these stories is when the impact really hits home. We have a saying at "Nightline" -- "Don't tell me. Show me." And so, we show these stories of people. We sometimes tell stories that spark anger. We point out injustices like the death of young black men dying in police custody. It triggers protests sometimes or riots. And it's not just anger at police behavior. Sometimes, there's an anger that there's a rush to judgment against the police officers, who are all painted with the same brush. You know, there are stories where I went recently to Indiana and told the story of Zach Anderson. He's a 19-year-old boy, was in college like you guys.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: He was on an app called Hot or Not, started swiping for a date. Next thing you know, he meets a girl online, they meet at a playground. She says she's 17. They have sex. Turns out the girl was not 17. She was 14. Her dad was not happy. The police were called. And even though she admitted that she lied on the website to register, she lied to him in person, she lied via text, the judge threw the book at him and was very angry at the "mores of young people" and sent him to jail and put him on the sex-offender register list for 25 years. And what that means is you have to register everywhere you live. You have no smartphones, no -- You can't live in a home with an Internet. You can't go to an establishment that serves alcohol. This kid wanted to be a computer programmer, and he wasn't allowed to touch computers. I mean, this was a story that was picked up by The New York Times. When "Nightline" did it, it got picked up by Reddit and others.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: to have the case re-evaluated. And after a lot of hue and cry and a lot of pickup, the -- the case was re-examined and the charges were changed. He was taken off the sex-offender registry list. But is there a moral to the story? I mean, what's the moral? That you have to ask for I.D. before engaging in sexual relations with somebody? Or is it something more fundamental that we, as a society, need to examine our courtship practices and ask ourselves, should you really be having sex with somebody that you don't really know their age? It's a good question. I told the story recently of Kalief Browder. I was with his mom telling the story of criminal juvenile justice. He was a high school senior in New York arrested and accused of stealing a backpack, right? He was sent to Rikers Island. Imagine -- A high school sophomore. He refused to plead guilty on principle, because he said, "I didn't steal the backpack. I'm not gonna plead guilty. I'm not gonna have a record and have that follow me." So, after delay, after court delay, weeks turned into months. Months turned into years.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: He spent a total of 1,000 days -- almost three years -- on Rikers Island without a trial. He was sent to solitary confinement for what nearly ended up being two years. One could argue he went mad. On surveillance footage, you see him being beaten by guards, not just a little bit, beaten repeatedly by gang members on Rikers Island. He actually was cited by President Obama when he talked about this recent executive action to stop solitary confinement for juvenile offenders. Imagine -- This young man hadn't even been seen -- hadn't even seen a trial yet, right? Eventually, after three years, the charges were dropped for not enough evidence. And he had, along the way, been told to "plead guilty, and then you'll get time served. You'll get out. The door's right there." And he said, "No. I'm not gonna plead guilty." He got his G.E.D. He went to school. He got good grades. He tried. But he was hampered by PTSD. He had nightmares, he was paranoid, he was afraid people were gonna, you know, attack him. And some number of months after he got out, his mother found him dead. He had committed suicide.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: And so, it is that kind of story -- You can look it up -- Kalief Browder -- that stirs the collective conscience in our society. And we ignore it to our detriment. There was a muckraking journalist back -- back in the old days who said, you know, "The duty of the press is to comfort the afflicted and to afflict the comfortable." And we have to give voice to those who are powerless and be unafraid, unflinching in the face of controversy. And one of the issues that I face a lot, we talk about a lot, is racism, right? I'm, you know, a non-- a woman of color in a largely still mainstream white industry. And I think about issues of race all the time, and I think that we are all at a stage now where we realize it's not out and out overt racism that we face, right? A lot of times, there's no segregation. There's no apartheid. But what we do face a lot of times is stereotyping and subtle racism. So, I want to call your attention to a study that I found while surfing Facebook a while back.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Wharton School of Business at University of Penn -- The University of Pennsylvania -- did a study that I actually found startling. It was research that was led by Wharton's Katherine Milkman. They e-mailed a bunch of professors, and when I say " a bunch," I mean 6,500 professors from 89 different subjects, 89 different disciplines, at 259 schools, right? I actually love that The National Society of Leadership and Success is at 500 schools. This e-mail went out to 250. But the e-mails had the same message, and the only variable that was different in the e-mail was the sender's name. Okay? So, for example, Brad Anderson, Lamar Washington, Latoya Brown, Juanita Martinez, Deepak Patel, Sonali Desai, Chang Huang. You get where I'm going with this, right? They were deliberately crafted in order to test the racial and gender biases of the professor's response, right? And you think, "Professors. They're intellectuals. They're, you know -- They're open-minded." And so, the type of student who garnered the most responses? The white male.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: As Milkman told NPR, professors "ignored requests from women and minorities at a higher rate than requests from white males." We see a 25-percentage-point gap in the response rate to Caucasian males versus women and minorities, right? All they were measuring was how often professors wrote back, agreeing to meet with students. They found very large, statistically significant disparities. Women and minorities were systematically less likely to get responses from professors and less likely to get positive responses from the professors. Now, the faculty at private universities, business schools, and those in "lucrative" fields, right, read "non-liberal-arts," were more likely to discriminate than those at public schools or those who work in the humanities. This research illustrates how white men continue to be recipients of academic privilege despite all the post-racial angst and paranoia directed at legally institutionalized methods of redressing gender and racial inequalities from Title IX to affirmative action. So, now, what are the implications? What are the implications? Uh, I'm sure that the professors, if you asked them, "Are you racist?" they would say absolutely not, right? And I think that they would be rightfully right in saying that, right?

speaker: Juju Chang
text: But when I hear older successful C.E.O.s give inspirational talks, right, what do they often say? They often say that the key to success is having a good mentor -- having somebody pull you up, right? But what this data suggests is that it's harder for women and minorities to garner those mentors, at least in the world of academia. But think about it. Would it surprise you at all if these types of biases -- old boys' networks -- existed in the corporate culture, as well? I mean, this is not a very old study. It's, like, from maybe last year. I mean, my Facebook feed is old, but it's not that old. It is therefore, think about it, essential, in my view, that we at least be aware of these potential biases and potential footfalls. So, what do you do about this? Let's take this e-mail and professors as a metaphor for something in the corporate world, right? Let's say you send an e-mail to a colleague you get out there and you don't hear back from them, right? You don't, like, barge into the meeting and go, "Aha\!

speaker: Juju Chang
text: You're a racist\!" Because, by noon, everyone would think that you're paranoid, and they might be right about that. On the flip side, you can't bury your head and say, "Well, I tried. I guess it was a bad idea." That's not the way to go, either, right? What I would argue is, instead, you might want to show up, talk to your boss/professor during office hours. Try to just ensure that you are being seen as an individual for who you are. I mean, just to poke fun at myself, I will tell you that, about a year or so ago, ABC's Outlook e-mail system had a system upgrade, right? When you opened your e-mail, all of a sudden, there was a photo of the sender. Right? First of all, nobody looks good in their employee photo. It's sort of like the DMV photo. Like, you just, like, "Ugh," cringe. And it's not like the selfies that you take backstage. Like you're perfect in those. Like, these, you look like a mass murderer or something. And also, they were from the original employment date.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: So, like, mine made me look like a teenager, and I could barely get any work done, 'cause I was too busy laughing at everybody's employee photos in the e-mail. Like, I would e-mail people and tell them, like, "Upgrade your photo." But then it occurred to me slowly that some of those little subtle biases were entering into my thinking, right? Just like the professors had, when I would see somebody's photo and they were younger than I expected, and then, suddenly, you know, I was looking at their gender, and I was, like, weighing this into the way that I was -- Instead of just looking at the information in the e-mail, I was suddenly catching myself with these biases. And so, what I say to you and I would challenge you to do is to be alert for your own biases, because we all have them. Let's face it, right? And all of those are amplified in your in-box or in your day-to-day interactions.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: And I think that when you look at it in that context, not so much as malicious racism, but as subtle biases that we are all guilty of, it's an easier way to break down those barriers and to really work together to kill those stereotypes, right, that we all carry with us. Because we are at a college campus and I'm winding down and I want to take your questions, so I want you to continue on the hashtag -- \#theNSLS -- I want to think about -- leave you with one thought, which is The New York Times columnist David Brooks talks in his book about "Road to Character" about the life you live between the span of two pieces of paper. And one is your résumé and one is your obituary. And to really give thought, because when you're building your résumé, you're selling yourself. You're marketing yourself and your qualities and all of what makes you good. But when you think about what's written in your obituary, think about what's lasting and what's important.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: You know, when you go to a funeral and it's somebody's life is really uplifting and it's a life well-lived, it means they built good connections with people, they gave back to their community, they did something that was meaningful, that had purpose, they were part of something that was larger than themselves. And that is what I would like to leave you with -- Between those two pieces of paper lies our lives. I want to thank you for inviting me here. I will take your questions, both in person and online. My hashtag is @JujuChangABC. And I will be, as I say, anchoring "Nightline" tonight, so I encourage you all to watch, to tweet, to check out my Instagram. It's all the same hashtag. Thank you so much.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Thank you, Kevin. My name is Betty Lo, Vice President of Community Alliances and Consumer Engagement with Neilsen, and I am privileged tonight to represent NAAAP, the National Association of Asian American Professionals. And tonight, we have the honor, D.A. and I -- D.A. is the Chief Diversity and Inclusion Officer for the USTA, which is the United States Tennis Association. He and I serve on the National Board of Directors for NAAAP, and we have the distinct pleasure to confer Juju Chang with NAAAP's 100 Award, which is the highest distinction. This particular award is actually presented by Buick, and we thank Buick for its continued support for this recognition program. NAAAP is the premiere leadership organization for Asian American professionals in the U.S. and also in Canada with nearly 30 chapters and several thousand members. Since 1982, NAAAP has operated as a non-profit organization to inspire, develop, and connect leaders in all major industries and countless communities. The NAAAP 100 Awards, presented by Buick, recognizes the most exemplary leaders in the Asian American community, and each year, exceptional candidates are nominated by members, selected by an independent committee, and ratified by NAAAP's National Board of Directors.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: The award is presented annually to the most influential leaders who have made significant contributions to their profession and to the community. In August of every year, we celebrate NAAAP 100 awardees at a gala event coinciding with NAAAP's annual convention. And this year, it will be held from August 11th through the 13th at Caesars Palace Hotel in Las Vegas. Tonight, in our ninth year of this recognition program, we add Ms. Juju Chang's name to this award's company of luminary and unsung heroes who include the late Senator Daniel Inouye, Canadian Senator Vivienne Poy, Super Bowl MVP Hines Ward, and playwright David Henry Hwang, just to name a few. Ms. Chang joins her colleagues Sachi Koto and Richard Lui as the third journalist in receiving this award. So, at this time, we certainly appreciate the collaboration with, of course, this distinguished organization, and please join me in welcoming back Ms. Juju Chang as she accepts her NAAAP 100 Award.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Thank you so much. This is fabulous. Thank you. Completely honored by it. Thank you. Thank you so much. Sure. That'd be awesome. Okay. Thank you so much. It was fabulous. Thank you. Ready to chat?

speaker: Juju Chang
text: I think it's a clear and concise message. And I-I mean, you know, look, I don't think there's a wrong answer in there, right? That's what's lovely, and I think it's a combination of all those things, but a clear and concise message where, you know, you talk about something thematically is when you leave a good impression and a clear communication.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: That is such a good question, and it has evolved for me over time. I mean, initially, I would practice and, you know, face up to my nervousness, 'cause I confided in you guys that I really was very insecure and shy, at least I felt that way on the inside. I may not have projected that always. So, I would practice and sort of overcompensate, right? And as I got older, I realized it's not so much the other person, but it's my own confidence that needs to grow before -- It's not just about practice. It's about literally, deep down inside, feeling like my idea matters, what i have to say matters, so I'm gonna communicate it clearly and concisely in a cogent message. And then, I think that, you know, over time, you start -- And again, it's evolved, and I think that, ultimately, what's important is being able to stand your ground when you need to but not, you know, try to bulldoze people. And building consensus is a really great way to approach somebody who's a superior, because you sort of bring -- you go in equipped with data and information, practice, and then confidence.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Huh. That's a really good one. I think that -- It turns out that I'm Jewish. I know that I don't really look Jewish, but, uh, I am. And -- And -- But I'm fascinated by the life of Jesus, and I've studied, you know, a lot of his teachings, and I'd be kind of -- I'd be very interested to sit and have a conversation. And, um, you know, again, this would be no cameras. Just a conversation about, sort of, philosophy, thinking, and... outlook, world view.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Oh, that is such a good question, Finn. 'Cause it happens a lot. I'm just kidding. Um, so, what happens is, a lot of times, you do a story that you're less than interested in or it feels a little, I don't know, not -- not high-minded and important and big or whatever, you know, sort of notions that you have -- high and mighty notions that you have. And then you realize that almost any story has, at its core, something that we can all relate to, even if its through the eyes of somebody you find less than, you know, palatable or less than respectful. And I think that that is always the case, whether it's a journalism story that you're doing or a project that you're doing with somebody who you think is a certain way. I find that when I then, you know, sort of drop the pretense and just try to meet somebody, you know, nose to nose, human being to human being, that I can always find something enlightening that I can share that could help others, even if it comes in an unlikely package.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Hello, Ms. Chang. My name is Jacob Jackson, and I am from Isothermal Community College in Spindale, North Carolina. My questions for you are in regards to our own hidden biases. What are some steps that we might take to not only become aware of but also to overcome our own hidden biases? And in your own experience, what are some steps that you have taken to overcome yours in your own life? Thank you.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: That is such a good question, and you know, I touched on some of that in my speech, right, about something as simple as e-mail, because that is something that the professors at UPenn were testing -- our response to e-mail. The biases that are sometimes the most damaging are the biases that we hold within ourselves. There's a professor at Stanford named Claude Steele, and he talks about stereotype bias. And when you are faced with a stereotype, you psych yourself out, right? So, he tested female students who were living under the stereotype of, you know, girls aren't as good at math, right? So, they were both given the exact same test, but before taking the test, they were told, "Oh, this measures your natural, raw ability to do math." And another group of girls were told, "Oh, this is just a basic, generic test." And the girls who were told, "Oh, this is just a basic, generic test" tested higher than the ones who were given the exact same test but were told that it measured their natural math ability.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: So, I think what we all need to do is constantly look at the terrain, look at the people that we're meeting, and not make assumptions and not sort of live up to our own expectations of those assumptions, whether it's a stereotype of ourselves or a stereotype of others. And I think that there are all sorts of hidden biases, especially in the workplace, that you don't even think about, whether, you know, it's a way somebody's dressed or -- You know, like, half the time, I run around with, like, sweat pants and a scrunchie in my hair, and you know, I'm treated a slightly different way than when I have six-inch heels on and a lot of makeup on, and yet I'm the same person, right? And so, we treat others based on biases, and we need to see our own biases, you know, whether -- whether it's race, ethnicity, religion, or, frankly, you know, the socioeconomic group that you assume someone is from for whatever reasons -- the car they drive, the clothes they wear, the bag they carry, whatever it is.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Well, the advice that I would give -- And, again, it's so refreshing that you guys aren't rolling your eyes at me like my son. Um, the advice that I would give is to increase your skills to the best that you can while you're still in college, right? So, whether it's building your brand on social media, writing your little blogs or whatever it is, even a tweet. If you write clever tweets and you pick up followers, that says something about your ability to communicate, right? Read newspapers. Read, you know -- What I find fascinating is adults who aren't on social media, and they're like, "Ah, Twitter. It's for idiots, you know?" Well, you're only as idiotic as the people you follow on Twitter, right? So, if you follow smart, interesting, thoughtful people on Twitter, it's actually a great forum to -- Now, I'm also following a few people that are less... But the truth is, you know, that's very important, and then, when it comes to whatever job you're looking for, whether it's consulting or banking or science or journalism, your first employer is taking a risk on you.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: So you have to do whatever you can to mitigate that risk, to reduce that risk, and the way you reduce the risk for that first potential employer is to demonstrate that you have the skills to perform the job that he's about to take a risk and offer you, right? So, if you're a journalist, demonstrate your ability to write, demonstrate your ability to shoot a camera, edit a video tape, do the things that, you know, on deadline, that are required of journalists. If you're going into nursing, you have to demonstrate those skills. If you want to go into, you know, whatever line of work it is, demonstrate those skills now. Polish those skills now while you're in college so that you can bring them to the table when you ask for that first job.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: The support system is critical, and there are two types of support systems that I lean on heavily. One is my friends and family, right? And the other is my nuclear family. So, whenever something -- Another thing I say to my kids all the time is everything in life is better when you share. And of course, they think that means their ice cream cone. But that's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about sharing your fears and sharing your insecurities and sharing your disappointments. Because that is just as important as sharing your, you know, "I scored 8 points in the game\! I'm the best\! I got an "A+" on my thing\!" Like, yes, that's fun to share and that's wonderful, but it's only when you share the pain that sharing the pleasure is that much more enriching, right And so, whether that is with your friends and family, whether you go out with your girlfriends and you, you know, complain about your boyfriend or your boss or whatever it is, that actually reduces your stress level and helps you live a longer life.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: But for me, that's always been key, because you will -- No matter how fabulous a career you have, your ups, your downs, you know, they will come. You will definitely have highs and you will definitely have lows. And it's in those moments where you realize, "This is your career, and then this is life." And don't get the two confused, because you can use your support system to help you in your career, but there's always this family life that's separate and important.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Hi. My name is Angela Grant, and I'm a student at Wake Technical Community College in Raleigh, North Carolina. Ms. Chang, you have an amazing career and life journey. My question to you is how can a student avoid being burnt out and what's the secret to your success?

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Ooh. That's such a good question. I think students get burnt out -- at least I did -- when I hid in a library and hid from, you know, the sorority parties or whatever. I was afraid, right? I was afraid of getting a bad grade. I was afraid of being rejected at the party, so I didn't do either. All I did was study, study, study with blinders on. So, the way to not get burnt out, I think, as a student, is to get your nose out of the book when you can and recharge in the way that you can. Go to that party. Do something that scares you a little bit, right? Because then you recharge and you go back. I find that in life now, too. Like, I can't -- The nature of my job is such that I could literally stay at the office 24 hours a day and there would still be work to do. At some point, you have to turn it off and say, "Enough," and walk out and feed the rest of your soul that allows you to do that grinding work later.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: I think that -- I think that part of it -- There's so many answers to that question. I think that part of it is having the confidence to know that you are never alone. There are so many times I do stories and I talk to people and they say, you know, "I was so ashamed. I didn't think anyone felt the way that I did. I didn't think anyone had the same affliction that I did." And I guarantee you, whatever it is that you're so deeply ashamed of, there are others that feel the same way...

speaker: Juju Chang
text: ...and that if you have the confidence that, you knows, as A.A. says, "You're only as sick as your secrets." Secrets are corrosive. And shame is corrosive. And you just have to dig yourself out of it and know that, in the clear light of day, you will be embraced. And you just need to find the right people who can understand and give you some compassion and love and obviously the support that you so deserve.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Ooh, that's a good question. I over-prepare, which helps, because then you -- For me, anyway, it makes me feel like, "Okay. I got this. I got this." I over-prepare, and then I kind of throw away my notes. And then I try to listen, right? I think that that's probably true in high-pressure negotiations, right? over-prepare, know your facts, know what the contingencies are to the 18 things that you might encounter, and that way, you -- I mean, half the time, I walk in, I'm like, "Whew\! That was easier. That was so much easier than I expected." But that's -- that's the key. And I think that's also probably the key in taking tests, right? When you over-prepare and you have confidence, you can go in calm and keep your nerves, you know, steady, and I think that that's a lot of it. I mean, and then, at some point, you just kind of let it have to go -- you have to let it go.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Right. And now I've gotten to the point in life where, like, I-I sometimes have to wing it, you know, a little bit, and I realize that I don't always have to over-prepare. Like, in fact, sort of the whole body of my work is such that, like, I can go off instincts more for sure.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Hi. Andrea Hall here from Tarleton State in Texas, and I would love to hear tips on condensing my personal story down to its most important points. My personal story is an epic novel, and I don't want to share that with people. I want to share them just a pamphlet-sized amount of information that will make them want to come back to me and ask for more. Thank you so much.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: That is such a good question. I don't know how you condense your thing. I mean, like, what do I do? I mean, obviously, I could drone on and on and bore you to tears about my life, but what I try to do is hit the points that I think other people can relate to, right? So, fine, I was a nationally ranked swimmer. That was great. I worked really hard. It was really hard. But it was only in the failure that people, you know, I think understand that you're human and that you're not -- that you're like them in many ways because you, too, know sort of the downs as well as the ups. You know, Princess Diana -- You guys are -- I'm showing my age again, but Princess Diana was, like, one of the biggest, you know, celebrities on the planet. And I would argue that it wasn't her crown and it wasn't her perfect skin or her flawless hair. It was when she started admitting just how difficult her personal struggles were with eating disorders, with, you know, feeling insecure, with feeling unloved. That's when people started to respond to her.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: And I think that that's, you know -- It's -- You don't want to just put on a big façade, because that's not the real you. I think sharing the real you and distilling it down to a certain essence, you know, helps people -- It's called a hook in television. It's like what's the hook, what makes people want to be drawn into your story. It's something that people can relate to, it's something that makes you real. I mean, everybody -- The buzz word in dot-com is "authenticity," right? You have to be authentic. It's like, "Okay, how do I -- how do I muster up authenticity?" It's like you just -- It's a little bit like, you know, the Supreme Court used to say, "How do you know pornography? Well, you know it when you see it." Same thing with authenticity. It's like you know it. You can smell it.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Well, a journalist's job is to not have their views be front and center all the time or ever, frankly. You are not supposed to root for a candidate. You're not supposed to -- So, I don't -- I try not to vote except for in the general election, because I don't want my -- You know, and it's a good thing that curtain closes. And I really try not to express my views. But there are times when we do stories where, you know, I leave something on the cutting room floor or I wish we had more time to follow that up, and at some point, you just have to get, you know -- get it done and hit the deadline and streamline the narrative. And so, yes, there are times, and it sticks in my craw, sometimes, but then I move on. I interviewed a school principal recently about college admissions, and she had something that I thought was really interesting and I took with me. She called it the 34-hour pout rule. That was that when you didn't get into the college of your choice, you're allowed to pout for 36 hours.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: You're allowed to grieve and feel bad and mourn, you know, all those hours that you poured into trying to get in to that college, but then you move on, right? And I think that's the same thing with, like, disappoints that you -- and how do you cope with these kinds of things. You -- You -- I thought it was an interesting thing. Like, yes, you grieve it. Yes, you're allowed to feel bad. But then move on. Dust yourself off, stand up, keep going.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Wow. There is so much there. I mean, you know, I try really hard to leave people with a good impression, right? And that doesn't mean that I need to look good, you know, in their eyes. It just means that I like to meet somebody, look them in the eye, and let them know that I see them as a person, right? And I like to be seen as a person in that way. And it kind of reminds me of the Maya Angelou quote, which is "People will forget what you say, but they'll never forget how you made them feel." And so, I work in an industry with words, where it's all about words, but at the end of the day, I hope that my story and my message leaves you with a certain feeling and that that endures.

speaker: Juju Chang
text: Why. Because it's like joining a synagogue or being part of a-a club, whatever it is. To be able to have a community, to work with people in an endeavor that's, as I said earlier, bigger than yourself, working as a team, working with a goal in mind -- That is the essence of life. That is why we toil and trouble. And I think being a part of an organization like this, which has such lofty goals of leadership and empowerment and, you know, giving people an opportunity to make and pave their own way to success -- It's fantastic. It's fantastic that you're affording yourselves that opportunity, that you're taking your nose out of your book for an hour tonight and looking around at the people around you, locking arms and marching in a a direction that will hopefully leave you all better.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Thank you so much. That was awesome. I would love to have that introduction every time I walk into a room. Good evening, everyone, and I'm pumped to be joining all of you folks that are out there in so many places around the country. Over 500 campuses. That's pretty impressive. So, I want to share with you a couple of lessons from pretty unexpected places. You just heard a little bit about what I do. I am the group president of FOCUS Brands, and basically we've got a business that does a couple billion dollars a year bringing some of the world's most disturbingly delicious products to countries all around the world. And you heard some of the brands. Cinnabon -- really sweet, indulgent. Amazing, delicious products. Moe's -- more on the healthy, Fresh-Mex side, and many other brands. And it's a ton of fun. I have a very complex job. We manage people all over the world. It's a franchise system. It's a global multi-channel business where we bring over $1 billion worth of product to the marketplace in consumer packaged goods and retail.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And all of that sounds pretty fancy, and I could tell you a lot of tips and tricks around managing big businesses and teams, but what's probably more relevant to you are the stories around what I've learned on the journey to get where I am today. And I have learned that in order to generally practice bad-assery in your life and be pretty resilient, there are three kind of main areas where, if you reflect on your own life, you learn some pretty big lessons. And one is around always having perspective. Just keeping things in perspective. So I hope my stories help give you a little bit of perspective. The second is around performance, and that's really kind of the thinking around having a bias for action. So, when do you take that step when someone else hasn't? When do you step back and listen and evaluate an opportunity? So, how you view performance, and your ability to step up and show up and then, as a result, move up is an incredible part of being the best version of you and a great leader. And then finally, priorities.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Because there's a whole lot you can spend your time doing, and we have a million distractions in the world, but you only have so much energy and so much time and so much heart and so much love. And so where do you spend your time as a person, in your personal relationships, and then how does that play out in business or in your community as a leader? And I've made some pretty big mistakes in those areas, and have learned some important lessons that I think have helped me be more successful over time. So, you've heard where I am. I'll rewind back a little bit to talk about where I started. So, when I was 9 years old -- I grew up in Jacksonville, Florida, and I'm the oldest of three girls. I have two awesome younger sisters that are three and six years younger than I am. And when I was 9, my mom came to me and said, "That's it. I'm done. We're leaving." What she meant was we were leaving my father. I grew up in Jacksonville, Florida. Kind of middle-class family up to that point.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: But the rest of my family -- my dad's side, my mom's side -- for the most part, were incredibly poor, and worked really good, solid, kind of blue-collar jobs. And we really had sort of the nicest house and the nicest cars. And my mom had a very entry-level job and didn't go to college, was a secretary, and she said, "We're leaving." My mom and three girls, with no financial resources, no really place to go. She said, "That's it. I'm done. We're leaving." And the reason we were leaving is my father, although an awesome man, super sweet, was a terrible husband and father because he had been an alcoholic for many, many years. And so basically my mom had been doing it on her own, anyway, and she just got to the point where she had to reflect on our situation, and had to determine that if we stayed, it was worse off than if we left. And my first lesson in life around perspective is what happened that moment when she told me we were leaving. So, imagine you. Not too long ago, you were 9 years old.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And imagine your mom coming to you and telling you this. Some of you may have had a very similar experience. And when she told me, "That's it. I'm done. We're leaving," at the age of 9, I didn't cry, I didn't get upset. I looked at her, at the age of 9, and thought, "What took you so long?" And the lesson in that is that the people, whoever the people are, the students who are in a class, the people of a community, the employees in a business, those people know what the right thing to do is long before the leader ever makes the call. I knew it was bad. I was the one waiting for my dad to come home when he didn't come home. I was the one seeing my mom have to deal with everything on her own. I was the one that was being disappointed, and seeing my sisters disappointed, for years. It was not a surprise to me that we were leaving.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: But as the young person -- and so think of this in your life, as the employee, as the student, as the individual contributor in a community -- I didn't have the power to lift us up and move us out. But I knew that it was bad. And as I grew up and I reflected on that moment, I realized how important it is for the leader to stay as close to the action as possible. In business, that means staying as close to the transaction or to the employee. In the community, if you're in government, that means staying as close to the majority of your people as you can. In your family, that means spending as much time with your family as you can, or your friends, because the more time you spend with them, the closer you stay with them, the fewer days and minutes and weeks go by between when they know what the right thing to do is and when you know when the right thing to do is.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: As a leader, it is your role -- even if you're just the person who has a point of view in your friend group, it is your role to make the call. The people around you sometimes can't. And if my mom had not have made that decision to get us out of that situation, I assure you, I would not be standing here today, and things would have turned out much, much differently for my father, my mother, and my sisters, and certainly for myself. And so the perspective I now have in looking back and thinking about what it must have taken for my mom to make that call. She didn't have the ability to raise us on her own financially. She didn't know how she was going to do it. There was no class. There was no certification. There was no support group. Yet she said, "I know this is right. I'm the only one that can make this call. We're leaving." And she packed us up and we left.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: What followed the next few years, also, were some of the lessons from an unexpected place that gave me great perspective as I would grow up and go on to do these really crazy business things at such a young age. First, when we left, she ended up having to, of course, work multiple jobs to support us. So I saw that as a child. That became my definition of what you do when you need to figure something out. You just figure it out. And she did it with such grace and such beauty and such positivity. I don't really remember her ever complaining about my father, speaking ill of him, or complaining about working all the jobs she had to work. I just remember her getting it done. My mom, for three years, fed my sisters and myself on a food budget of $10 a week. And this is not 1945 or 1952. These are the late '80s. On $10 a week as a food budget. She did that for three years.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And, so, again, I had this example of how to do things where others find it complicated, you have to just figure it out and make it happen. We ate a lot of beanie weenies, we ate a lot of potted meat. If you don't know what that is, look it up. It's kind of gross. And a lot of frozen lasagna. And I just don't remember anything other than it being generally pretty good. Of course, I had to take on more responsibility as a child, as you can imagine. Staying home, helping with my sisters when my mom couldn't be there. But I have to believe that that helped build who I am today. And certainly having the perspective of what my mom went through, how she was able to just raise three girls. And when I look at the pictures of my mom and these three little girls following her around, and thinking about all that she had to trade off and all the compromise, trust me, I still use that example today when I'm talking to franchisees or business partners or people like that.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: I'll say, "If my mom can raise three girls on her own and feed us on a food budget of $10 a week for three years, surely you can figure this problem out." And I don't think that my story, as you hear it, is really unique. Sadly. A lot of people who can relate, and there's a ton of people who have it a lot worse. The question is, how do you use that for good? How do you use that for your own perspective, and do you take the lessons out of your own life that you can, just like you might be thinking about lessons from mine that I'm sharing with you? And so think about the importance of perspective in becoming an incredible leader and dealing with change. My mom had to deal with change she could not control. She couldn't control my father. She couldn't change the circumstances, yet she had this incredible responsibility. And for her, the consequences of not doing something were far too great.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And I asked my mom as I grew up, "Why did it take you so long?" It was bad since the little one was born, since I was 6. And it was interesting, her answer. She said, "You know, there were so many people around me," because we did have a nice house when it was back in the day. We actually had a car. We even had a playhouse out back. That was fancy-shmancy. And so there were so many people that looked at our lives from the outside and said, "You've got it good. How dare you trade that off? Do you know what I would give to have your house and your car and your life?" And it's really easy to look at things from the outside and mistakenly give it value it actually doesn't have. Be careful what you glamorize. Be careful what you say is positive, and the things you strive for. Be careful who your idols are, and the people you look up to unless you know the whole story. And so my mom had all these people, even her own mother, and the family of my father saying, "Don't leave.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: You don't want to have to deal with what the rest of us have to." And so for years she listened to them. And she thought, "Wow, would I be being crazy to give all this up." And eventually my mom made an important realization that I've tried to make sure I can make in my personal life and in business, and it is this -- On one hand, one of the most powerful behaviors to have, as I've just shared, is perspective. Stated another way, to be grateful for what you have. Because it can always be so much worse. But my mom finally realized that just because things could be worse does not mean that you do not have the right, and in some cases the responsibility, to work to make things better. Think about that. Just because things could be worse doesn't mean you don't still have the right and the opportunity and sometimes the obligation to try to make them better. That plays out in business and in life all the time. Yeah, things could be worse. So I think daily how grateful I am.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: I think how grateful I am for the people that mean the most to me in my life. I'm so grateful for the work opportunities I have, for the ability to do things like this and impact people's lives. I am grateful. But that doesn't mean I just sit still and believe that this is all I should be doing. That would not be doing justice to the gifts that I'm given or the responsibilities that I have. So, remember the phrase. Just because things could be worse does not mean you do not have the obligation or at least the right to try to keep making them better. Companies wouldn't innovate if they didn't believe that. Families wouldn't grow. Individuals wouldn't learn. They wouldn't progress if they believed that. And I learned all that from just the perspective from my mom. And I really challenge you to think about what can you look back on in your own life? Don't just listen to other people's stories. You have your own lessons. And then, if you've got some great stories to share, you don't have to be on a stage or talk to 500 campuses to impact other people's lives.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Share your story. You are an inspiration to someone, and it gives someone else perspective. Over coffee. Over a beer. In class. On a break. Whatever it is, be comfortable enough sharing the things you've experienced. You'll be shocked how common your stories are. And so I learned that from my mom, and as a result, I got to grow up and see this awesome example of what a leader really looks like, with humility and grace and hustle, and the ability to just figure it out and make it happen. And my mom really learned to ask herself this question. I want you to think about this question, and ask yourself as often as you can, "If not me, who? If not now, when?" That's it. If not me, who? If not now, when? So, if you're sitting in Kansas or Illinois or California or Florida and you're watching this, try to just write that down or tweet it or find an opportunity tomorrow or next week to ask yourself that question when you're faced with a decision.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: The minute you feel like you need to complain or you've got an issue or you're disappointed in someone else or some situation, look at yourself and ask, "If not me, who? If not now, when?" My mom did that and it turned out pretty well, and I've tried to honor her by living up to that as often as I can. So, fast-forward. Now I'm growing up. Mom's working a bunch of jobs. I'm kind of having to stay at home and help with my sisters. We had to start working very young, so I started working when I was 15 years old, as soon as I legally could work in the state of Florida, where I grew up, and started selling clothes in a mall like a bunch of people do when they're in junior high and high school. And then I got another job being a hostess at Hooters. And it just wasn't a big deal in Florida. It started there, and people wear less on the beach. You know, when you grow up on the beach. And it was a cool concept. And so I was a hostess.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: So, I would open the door and say, "Welcome to Hooters." I would clean the bathrooms, I would keep the waiting list, I would bus tables. I would do anything I could do while I worked other jobs. And then I turned 18. I'm a senior in high school. And I became old enough to become a Hooters Girl. So I rocked the orange shorts. They were fantastic. Lot of fun. And it was just a cool job. I thought, "You know, this is fun. I can make great money," as anyone knows in the hospitality business, and being a waitress or a waiter or a bartender, you can make great money. It's a service industry. But it wasn't my dream to stay in the restaurant business. I had a dream. And my dream for my career was to go on and get my engineering degree, go to law school, and become an attorney for DuPont Chemicals.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: When I was young, I had seen a paint can in a garage that said DuPont on it, and I thought, "That must be a really big company, so I should go work for them." And my teachers told me I talked too much, and I should be an attorney. And so you put those two things together and it leads to being an attorney for a chemical company. And so that's really what I always thought I was going to do. I was the first person in my family to go to college, on either side of my family. Started as an engineering major at the University of North Florida after I graduated high school, while I was still working at Hooters. And a few things just changed, as sort of happens in life every day. It's important to have a plan, just also have the second plan be that that plan will for sure be different within minutes, if not days. And I was loving what I was doing at work, but I was saving up for college and paying for school. I only had a partial scholarship.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And when I was 19 -- so now I'm a year and a half into college, totally crushing it, having a great time, but still working full time on weekends, setting the record for close/opens. If you don't know what that means, it means you literally work the night shift, and then you come back and you work the day shift, and then you stay for the night shift and you do it again. I did that every stint in between semesters. So I was working as hard as a human being can work before school, after school, and in between classes. And when I was 19, I got a phone call, and the phone call was from the corporate office for Hooters Restaurants out of Atlanta, Georgia. And they said, "Hey, we've talked to your manager, and we're opening our first-ever Hooters franchise in Sydney, Australia, and you have been nominated to be one of the team to go and be the trainers," the employees who go and train the other employees, "for this restaurant.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: So, basically, we want to ask you, and your general manager is going to talk to you, if you would like to go to Sydney, Australia, and go help us open the first-ever franchise." What would you say if you were asked that? "Hell yeah." Like, "I am all over that." So I said yes. However, I didn't have a passport, I had never been on a plane, I'd only been out of the state of Florida twice in my life for cheerleading competitions. And so this was the first example in my life that I can look back on and get to that second group, that second bucket I talked about, performance, where I had a bias for action and I said yes long before I ever had the technical capabilities to do the job. I couldn't legally exit the country, yet I said yes. So, the first flight I ever took was to fly to Miami from Jacksonville to stand in line with all my paperwork and get a passport. But I said yes before I ever had a passport. And they didn't know. I didn't lie.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: It was just a slight sin of omission so that they wouldn't be scared that I couldn't do the job. So, I said yes before I had the technical skill. I had never opened a restaurant, but I believed I could figure it out. I had never been on a plane, but I believed I'd be fine. I didn't have a passport, but I believed I could get it. So, here's the trick. If you're gonna step up and raise your hand and have a bias for performance, a bias for action, you should always say yes before you have all the skills. Always. Do not think you need to know everything before you do something, because if that's what you think, you are far too late, and there's a bunch of people in line in front of you. However, there is a caveat to that. Say yes before you have the skills, but you had better have the hustle muscle to figure the gap out between what you have and what you need. \#HustleMuscle. Totally. One of my favorite hashtags. I use it all the time. And so think about that.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Step up, go to the edge, go to the edge of the stage, raise your hand, say, "Yes, I want that opportunity." But then what? You just stand there and think the world is owed to you because you said yes? No. What you have to do then is close the gap. Don't expect anybody else to do it for you. You just stepped up and opened the door. Now there's a distance you actually have to run to get things done. I went around and asked the questions, "How do I get a passport when I don't have one?" I asked people who had been to Australia, did all the research that I could on the culture and the country and everything that I could. I talked to other people that had opened restaurants. So when I went, I was as prepared as possible. And then when I got there, I was prepared to fail over and over. Failure is really just practicing at your first attempt. Think about it that way. Everybody has a first in everything. You got to do something once. It's your first. You're not gonna be awesome. If you are, good for you.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: It won't happen all the time. And so I knew when I got there I wouldn't know everything. So, the trick to closing the gap and having the hustle muscle really is about having humility. It's about believing you don't know everything, but believing you can figure it out at the same time. And those two things are a little bit in conflict. If you get too convinced that you don't know everything then you'll step back and be quiet and expect everything to come to you. But if you get too convinced that, "Oh, I can do it all. I know everything," trust me, nobody's gonna want to be on your team. And so it's a balance. And so I had the hustle muscle and the confidence and the courage to just go. But I had the humility and the curiosity to ask the questions I needed to when I got there. So, either I learned what I needed to know or I developed enough friendships and partnerships that when I screwed it up, there was a group of people that actually wanted to help me out and wanted to see me succeed.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: When you lead with only courage and confidence, you are a bull in a china shop. Even if people follow you temporarily, they will not be there for you when you need them. And if you're only humble and curious, you're just a student. Nothing wrong with being a student, for all you people on 500 campuses. But if you want others to follow you, being a student alone is not enough. You have to have both. And so think about performance, this second group of characteristics that you must have to be a successful leading change and having grit and practicing bad-assery and leading in your community or for your family. Think about your view of performance and having a bias for action as really being a combination of these two things. Courage and confidence on this side, where you lead and you take risks and you just say yes before you have all the skills. But on the other side, committing to the humility, acknowledging you don't know everything, and having the deep curiosity where you just want to know the answers and you ask.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And, by the way, that also means helping others when they're on that journey, as well. And I learned that from just traveling around the world. So, I go to Australia. I'm a part of this team. I stay there for 40 days. I was 19 years old. It changed my life, as you can imagine. But even when I got back, I still had the dream of being that attorney for a chemical-engineering company. But that quickly changed, because about 30 to 45 days later, the company calls and said, "Hey, we're opening another Hooters in Central America. First one ever in Central America. We want you to go to Mexico City since you speak enough Spanish to be dangerous and go open Hooters in Insurgentes in Mexico City in Zona Rosa." And I said, "Great\!" And so I went down and went to Mexico City and lived there for 30 to 40 days and opened up the restaurant there. And then I noticed things started to change. Then I got the phone call to open a few restaurants across the U.S. while I was still going to school and still working shifts in between that.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And at that point, it was manager shifts and bartender shifts, and I was doing all kinds of things. I remember one day, all the cooks quit. And so I went in the back to help cook. I don't know why they quit. Somebody stole their weed and they got upset and protested and left or something. But I was in our restaurant, and they literally all walked out. And if you've never been in a Hooters or a restaurant with an open kitchen, when the people who are cooking your food exit the building, it's, like, kind of obvious. And so the customers get a little antsy and nervous. And so you have a choice as a person. You can either be the one that steps back and says, "Well, what are we gonna do? We don't have food." Or you can be the person that literally rushes into the fire and says, "Well, I can figure out how to cook. I know enough about the menu to be dangerous. I'll figure it out." And chicken wings are easy. When they float, they're done. So it's not that hard.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And so I literally went in the back with a couple of other employees who were like-minded, and a manager, and we cooked, and we figured it out, and the customers loved it, and we had a great time. And it wasn't perfect, but it was fine. And it was things like that happened every day in the restaurant -- the bartender needed to go home early, so I'm like, "Hey, I'll help out." And the manager needed to do something for her kid whenever she left, and I said, "Yeah, I'll stay and count the cash." And it was just saying yes and raising my hand and being helpful, that's how I learned how to run restaurants. Nobody taught me a class. No one said, "Let me teach you every single step of running a restaurant." When people needed help, I was there. And then even though I didn't know everything, I was willing to ask questions and figure it out. And so every time I came back from a new country or a new opening, I was taking on more and more leadership roles in my own company.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And literally two years passed by, and all of a sudden I've opened up businesses on three continents and multiple countries, and multiple businesses inside of the United States, and learned the franchising model, and literally worked every job in the restaurant. I wasn't trying to build a resumé, I just did. And that's the way it works. I wasn't doing it because I thought, "You know, if I build this awesome resumé, one day, when I'm 26 years old, I'll be a vice president of an $800 million company, which I was. I didn't think, "Oh, if I just raise my hand a little more here, I'll be a president of a billion-dollar company when I'm 30 years old," which I was. I didn't think any of that. I just thought, "I want to be helpful. I want to have fun. I want to do a really good job." And so I literally busted my ass every day, and I just wanted to help other people, and I was so curious. And that's what led to people saying, "Will you help me here?

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Will you help me here?" And that gave me opportunities to learn, and that gave me opportunities to step up, it gave me opportunities to show up, it gave me opportunities, then, to move up. You don't move up without stepping up and showing up. Does not happen out of order. You have to earn it. And when I look back and people ask me, "Why you? Why were you able to run this big of a group or a department or a company at such a young age?" Of course, you never know. It's some combination of timing and events an talent and opportunity and all that jazz. Certainly I wouldn't be where I am without killer people who gave me a chance, who took a chance on a kid. But without question, the part that I know I own is that I had the hustle muscle to close the gap between what I didn't know and what I needed to know. And what I couldn't close the gap on, I had built enough community around me where people wanted to see me succeed. And at the same time, I was willing to take risks.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And the simple fact, also, is that I joined a growing company. I wouldn't have been able to open businesses in Australia and Central America and all over the world if I hadn't joined a growing company, and that's a huge part of it. Forget the fact that it's Hooters. It's a company that was growing. And so look for growth. Look for opportunity. So, I learned these really interesting lessons. And now I'm 19 years old, just about to turn 20. I'm traveling a ton all over the world. And, oh, by the way, if you do the math on all the countries I just said I was in for that small amount of time, I was also failing college. Because I was never there. And I remember the meeting with my professor, when I sat down, and my counselor at school, and they said, "You're failing. You're not just kind of failing. You are literally about to be expelled. Like, there's no amount of work, there's no amount of making up that you can do. You need to start all over.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: You'd have to literally stop working and go to school full time, and stop traveling so you can make up all of this that you've missed." And so for the first time in my young life, I was faced with a pretty important fork in the road. Either continue down the academic path, which my mother desperately wanted me to do. She was so proud, as you can imagine. Or follow this -- I don't know what I would call it -- passion project, traveling around the world and opening franchises for Hooters. And I quit. I dropped out of school. So, now, I'm 20 years old, I'm the child of alcoholic, single parent, worked for Hooters my whole life, and I'm a college dropout. Not exactly a stellar resumé. But I wasn't worried. And when people ask me, "So, does that mean you don't believe in college? Does that mean you think people should drop out of school?" And I speak to a lot of students, and I mentor a lot of students, and I do a lot of speaking around the world at universities, and so here's my response.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: The response is if you have a compelling alternative, which I obviously did, follow the compelling alternative. If you do not have a compelling alternative and you are still figuring it out, stay in school. It is your alternative. I got the job. I packed up a U-Haul -- I had to have someone else sign for it because I couldn't even legally rent a car -- and moved from Jacksonville, Florida, to Atlanta, Georgia, and took my first-ever corporate job.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: I made somewhere around $38,000 or $40,000 -- I don't remember exactly -- my last full year as a Hooters Girl. That's a lot of money for a 19- and 20-year-old. Back then. speaker: Kat Cole
text: And so I ended up, now as a 20-year-old, in my first corporate gig, and learned so many lessons along the way at Hooters. speaker: Kat Cole
text: I stayed in the office literally all night multiple nights just to do that job. And they help you build a reputation and trust. And they help you really understand the businesses that you're in. And eventually those jobs, that work that everyone looked at as menial, became my foundational learning, my opportunity for visibility, and they're the reasons that I was a director at 23, and that I was a vice president at 26, and I was a president of a company that does business in 45 countries just after I was 31 years old. speaker: Kat Cole
text: And, quite honestly, because there were people who gave me the chance, who trusted me. And I wasn't perfect all the time, because I was doing a lot of firsts. speaker: Kat Cole
text: Who else was gonna give a child of a single parent, alcoholic, college dropout, worked for Hooters her whole life the opportunity to go open businesses around the world at the age of 19 and become a vice president at the age of 26? It's not gonna happen at a bank. Maybe today. Tech companies, or other companies where there's more forward-thinking leadership. But the practical matter was I stayed where the opportunities were, and they gave me those chances, and I will always be grateful. And so my level of gratitude was through the roof. The other reason I stayed is my level of pride in what we built was tremendous. I remember opening a Hooters in Salt Lake City, Utah. Which is an interesting place to open a Hooters in the '90s. And I loved it. I fell in love with the city and the community. But the reality was the laws and the social structure and social norms there were even less welcoming of a Hooters than in many other cities around the world. And there was a woman who came on the radio and said, "We don't want you here.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: We disagree with what you stand for, and we think you are a hypocrite." Me. That I'm a hypocrite. "We think you're a hypocrite because you go around saying that you stand for women's rights and that you're a feminist and that you believe in opportunities for women," which, at the time, I was very visible in many women's organizations, as I am now. Clearly, the daughter of a single parent, oldest of three girls, I'm kind of into the, like, women's being awesome thing. And she said I was a hypocrite. And she said, "You're a hypocrite because you say you're for the advancement of women, yet you're running a concept that we believe exploits women." And I learned a lesson from a mentor of mine in Argentina when I opened one of the Hooters down there. And he taught me this lesson. Whenever you're criticized, take one moment, just a second, to consider that they might be right. Allow that to be your first thought. Whatever the criticism is, from the public, a friend, a family member, an employee, something you just hear through back channels. Take a second to consider that they might be right.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And not only is that incredibly humbling, but it causes you to pause before you react. Before you say, "Absolutely not. That's not me," or, "You're wrong." And when I thought about it -- it's a split second, but when I thought about it, I thought, "Is she right?" Because I totally saw where she was coming from. We're running around in tiny little clothes, and yet I'm talking about the importance of women being considered equals in the workplace. So, I respected her question. But instantly, because I considered she might be right instead of reacting, I actually came up with the reasons that I disagreed. I didn't just say, "I disagree." I came up with the reasons. And the reasons were, one, which I just shared, I'm so grateful for the opportunities that I've been given. How can I not advocate for a company that gives people like me a chance? And now I'm in a position to give other people like me a chance. But second, I am so proud of what we've built. It might not be on a billboard, but we had built literally the most aggressive, powerful tuition-reimbursement program in all of hospitality.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: The number of women that we put through college, I couldn't even begin to count. We had an incredible formula for hours worked and grades earned, and it was an amazing program. I was so proud of that program. I was proud of people like me who moved up in management, the women who became franchisees in the system. And so my answer to her was simply that my level of pride in what we've built, and my level of gratitude for my opportunities far outweigh my concern over what you think. Bam. And it just came to me like that. And afterward, I realized that that is a little bit of secret sauce, if you can figure out how to always be proud and grateful. And if you want to build a company, you can figure out how to help your people always be proud of what you're doing and grateful for the opportunities you are giving them, you can survive any economic challenge, any competitive threat, and any criticism. But if they are not proud and they are not grateful, you won't survive.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And I learned that just by dealing with the controversy and the head winds and the judgment that I faced not just working for Hooters, but when people would say, "Oh, you're an executive?" I learned that I had to be so sure of what I wanted to do on the inside that no matter what other people thought, I could keep going. Criticism, judgment, bias, in some ways, it's like water on a rock. It shapes you.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And it certainly allowed me to be the confident person I am today, to take other risks, and to be more adventurous, and to take bigger leaps, and to take more time to help carry on some of these messages. And it was an incredible opportunity. And then I stayed there for about four years helping to build that concept, turn it around. And then, over the last about year and a half, have been working in a new role as group president of the parent company at FOCUS Brands. And I will tell you, there is one huge mistake that I made when I first became the president of Cinnabon that I want you to learn from, especially as a young person. If you're the youngest in the room, you may do what I made the mistake of doing.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: So, I take over as president of Cinnabon, and I'm the youngest -- I'm probably the youngest person that has ever been the president of a company anywhere near that size. And there's, "Look at all these people I can learn from." And there were some things going on in the company, and I asked myself this question, which is both important and dangerous. Something was going on in the company, and I thought it didn't quite look right, and I wasn't sure exactly how it was gonna play out. And so what happened in my head was I said, "Who am I to question them? Who am I to question them? I'm so much younger.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: They've been doing this longer than me." And that was back to, What if my mom had asked that question? What if my mom had said, "Who am I to take these girls away?" It would've been bad. And the answer to the "Who am I?" question is I'm the freaking president. If I don't ask the questions, who's going to? But I didn't. And as a result, a particular initiative evolved in a way that it shouldn't have, and it completely killed my trust and credibility with my franchisees and my team that I had worked so hard to build trust with. And it put me in the position to have to kill a business initiative that had been budgeted, that was really planned on providing a great amount of revenue and profitability for the company, which meant affecting jobs and raises and people's compensation because I didn't ask the right questions on the front end. And I did the right thing, and I stepped up, and I owned it and said, "I should have asked these questions. I should have stayed closer to this," and repaired the relationship.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And I remember the president of the Franchise Advisory Council, the co-founder of Cinnabon, came up to me afterward and gave me a hug. And I'm short-cutting how emotional and horrible this really was. And he gave me a hug, and he said, "That's why I stay in this business. It's all about the relationships." And I learned then that business without trust is just a transaction, and transactions are so easily replaced. And make that broader. Not just business without trust. Life without trust. Relationships without trust are just transactions. And you are easily replaced when you are just a transaction. Trust is everything. And I learned that lesson, and it helped me develop that as my lead priority in business. Trust as the foundation of building teams and building change and taking risks. From my work in Eastern Africa -- and I do a lot of work in villages in Rwanda and Ethiopia, and we were working with a particular village. And they were not trusting us because people come in from the outside all the time and make promises. They build wells and they build schools and they bring books and they bring shirts.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And you know what? Where are you when those wells break? They got nothing. And so they give you a hug and they say yes and they're so excited you're there, and then you leave and they're just as screwed a year later. It doesn't mean it was a bad intention, it means you're not actually driving the outcome. And so we go to this village, and one of the village leaders was sick. And we ended up helping the village leader get to the hospital and become well. And the minute we did that, everything in the village changed, because we evidenced that we were there for them when it counted. 18 months later, I go back, and all of the work around agriculture and water and education had progressed farther than I ever thought possible. And when we asked the villagers why, they pointed to these two men, Ibrahim and Lemmy, and said, "Because Ibrahim and Lemmy are here. They eat what we eat. They sleep where we sleep. They live what we live. We trust them.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And because you showed up for them when they needed you, we trust you." And as a result, literally tens of thousands of lives all in this area have changed for the better, just because we were there for somebody when they needed it. Your priority should be being there for people when they need you, and not pushing back when someone's trying to be there for you. I learned this is business, in my personal relationships. The love of my life, the person that I want to make my priority, I am so clear on my priorities. I will be there for him whenever he needs me. That is first. I may run big companies. That is first. And then I'll be there for my companies when they need me, just like my mom was there for her family when we needed her. So, if you think about these lessons around having perspective, having a bias for action, driving performance, and then finally being reflective around your priorities, I want you to take away this one best practice.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: I call it the hot-shot rule. And the hot-shot rule simply means that once in a while -- I do it every quarter. My teams do this with me, also. -- I sit back and ask myself, "If a hot shot took over my job today," so, your job as a student, your job as a brother, your job as a girlfriend, your job as a friend, your job as a C.E.O. If someone came in your seat today and took your job over, what's one thing they would do better immediately? And the question is why can't that be you? Why can't that be me? Why can't I do things just a little bit better? If I know what awesome looks like for my personal relationships, for my business, for my friends, why can't I just do that one thing? Only one thing, 'cause you don't want to overwhelm yourself. And just do that one thing. That's the hot-shot rule. And if you think about doing that, being your own biggest coach, and then you reflect and ask yourself, "If not me, who?

speaker: Kat Cole
text: If not now, when?" And you raise your hand for opportunities that you're not quite ready for, but you have the \#HustleMuscle to figure it all out, I promise you, you will go so much farther than most others in life and in business. Thank you very much.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Absolutely. So, you have seen both of these in your life, whether you are 10, 18, or 50. And so a productive achiever is someone who is a giver, who builds as they move up. And instead of believing that they can be better by shining a light on others, or another way to say it, bringing others along with you, they sort of want all the light on themselves. speaker: Kat Cole
text: They just are. I mean, it is a way to achieve. My advice, though, is that if you're around those people, usually they end up working themselves out of a system. Not always. Technically, the destructive achievers I've seen stay in leadership positions have to move around a lot, because they don't succeed in one place very long. People kind of figure them out, and the reality is nobody wants to be on their team. Productive achievers can have their pick. They can stay rooted and build a community around them, and people hate to see them go but they're happy for their growth and evolution, or they can hop to other places and keep winning trust -- Back to this trust thing -- you know, over and over again. And destructive achievers can't. And I would say that there are far more long-term successful people that are productive achievers than destructive achievers.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Great question. So, what was interesting about "Undercover Boss" for me, I was in season three, youngest by a long stretch.
