speaker: Kat Cole
text: It wasn't that long ago that I was slinging wings and washing dishes. So, when I was undercover, they're like, "This should be harder for you." speaker: Kat Cole

speaker: Kat Cole
text: Hi. My name is Jacqueline Harkis. I'm currently a student at San Antonio College in San Antonio, Texas. It's extremely impressive to me how you've been so successful at each company. speaker: Kat Cole
text: Wow. Awesome question. A couple of ways. One, I was really involved in a group called the Women's Foodservice Forum. And I'd never seen 3,000 women in a room, much less 3,000 women in suits when I was 24 years old. speaker: Kat Cole
text: Whether it's a church group, a college group, whatever it is, go be with other people that are successful, because in your brain, it literally plants these little seeds that helps you be more of a believer and take more risks. The other thing that she brought up was, you know, how can you be successful and break through glass ceilings? Going back to being a productive achiever. I always tried to build teams. speaker: Kat Cole
text: And when things were tough for me at work, which they would be for me as kind of the only women, and much younger, on the executive team, I didn't have my whole sense of self sunk into my work. And so being straight up on my priorities as I've gotten older, instead of feeling like "Well, I'm the only woman," or "I'm the youngest one, and so I should sacrifice everything in order to show up," you don't have to do that. You do need to work harder than others when you don't have the earned credibility yet, but as you build that credibility, start setting a really good example of your priorities. And I've tried to do that.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And I think that makes people respect me as a woman and as a businessperson and as a businesswoman, and I think that builds trust and followership, and certainly my legacy for leadership.

speaker: Kat Cole
text: So, on the trust thing -- be there for people when it counts. Be the one that asks the question, not the one that holds back information so you have to be asked the question. speaker: Kat Cole

speaker: Kat Cole
text: And I have seen people either totally cower from mistakes they've made, which doesn't build trust, or wallow in the mistake for so long that no one wants to work with them, and doesn't trust their ability to be confident and lead. So, there's a delicate balance between those two things.

speaker: Kat Cole

text: We had no idea that was happening. It just got written in the script. Thank goodness. And he said, "If I'm lucky, I'll be a manager at a Cinnabon in Omaha." speaker: Kat Cole
text: And who doesn't love to get giant cinnamon rolls the size of your face in the mail? speaker: Kat Cole
text: The pilot's getting picked up and they've asked for more episodes, and there's a scene, but we don't know how long." speaker: Kat Cole
text: people. Don't try to put on a front. I mean, they could see the tears behind my eyes. And then we also need to understand what precipitated that. It was lots of conversations. It was lots of people who weren't part of that gathering, who were not there for the 20th anniversary. It wasn't just George Bush Senior or Helmut Kohl or others. It was young people. It was young people raising their voice, young people in colleges, universities across East and West Germany at the time, who were saying, "You know what? This is wrong, and we need to have a united humanitarian front." And that conversation was so important, and that's the theme which I'd like to share with you today. The topic of the speech per se is me to we, but it's actually a lot more than that. It's really how to shift from me to we, but it's really how to create a more just and humanitarian society.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: So what I want to do is tonight is share with you a little bit about why I'm here and what I do and what we do and why we're so proud of it. But more importantly, I really want to have a conversation with you. I really want to say, you know what? This world that we're all inheriting is really screwed up. We know that. But is really, really, really badly in need of our help, and especially badly in need of our leadership. So provide you with some stats, some facts, some figures, some ideas, and more specifically, some very tangible things. Some very tangible things that we can do as people who obviously care about the world, and how we can now create that massive social change. So as we get going, what I wanted to do first is share with you a little bit about why I'm here this evening, and my story was alluded to quickly in the introduction. But part of what I do is represent an organization called Free the Children. Free the Children is the world's largest network of children helping children, but I'll talk about that in a minute.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: But what I'd like to first reference is why I'm here. When I was 17 going on 18 years old, I went to do my first year of university. And for those of you who can't tell, I'm Canadian by my accent. And I'm Canadian, and I did my first year of university at the University of Ottawa, which is our nation's capital. And I got to work here as something called a parliamentary page in the House of Commons. Now, the House of Commons is kind of our version of Congress. And basically, for those of you who don't know Canadian politics, who haven't taken Canadian politics, or don't know anything about Canadian politics, that's cool. But in Canada, parliamentary page is this job I had. They actually technically run the government. Now, I'm very serious about this because they do two critical things. Number one is they get Members of Parliament water. You know when you see these guys on television, also in Congress, when they're debating and discussing, they're talking about these really important issues of the day, they yell a lot. And somebody has to make sure their voices don't go hoarse, and that was us.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: That was parliamentary pages. So we got them water, sometimes with ice, sometimes without ice. This was a really important factor. And the second thing we used to do is get them notes. Now, I was coming out of high school. Now, for those of you who are recent high school graduates, you're going to appreciate this. Now, I always used to get in trouble for delivering notes. So the teacher would call me up in front of the class and say, "Mark, would you like to read your note?" And in Canada, in Ottawa, in our nation's capital, these guys got paid way, way too much taxpayer money, and they had people like us deliver notes for them. It was an amazing, amazing job. So one day, a Member of Parliament called me over, and I walked over. I was like, "Water, note, what would you like?" And he asked me this question, this question I really want to ask all of you here this evening. And he said, "Mark, what type of legacy do you want to leave?" And I'd never been asked that question before. And maybe some of you have, and probably some of you haven't.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And I said, "You know what? I don't know." And I said, "If I dedicate myself and I work really hard, maybe I'll get a future here in Ottawa. I can become a senior page, tell the little pages where to go with the water and the stationery." He was really unimpressed. And he asked me this question again, this question again I really want to ask all of you here in the audience and those watching via live web broadcast, what type of legacy do you want to leave? And until I finally said, "You know what? I don't know." And he said, "I sit on the board of directors of this amazing international organization that works in the slums of Thailand that's so desperately looking for volunteers." And he said, "I think you should leave your job in Ottawa and go all the way to Thailand to change the world." And he said, "What do you think?" And I stopped.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And I was like, "Wow, you mean I could leave my job here in Ottawa and go all the way to Thailand and create massive social change?" I said, "No way." I explained to him that I was having a great time. I was delivering notes for Members of Parliament. I was spilling water on world leaders. I was having this amazing experience. And I also explained to him that I went to an all-boys high school, and now there was 40 young people in the parliamentary page program, 28 of whom were girls. And I had great odds, right? So I was like, "There's no way I'm leaving. I'm set up here. This is crazy." So what he did is he didn't take no for an answer. And every single day, he'd call me over, and he never wanted water, never wanted stationery, and always asked me this legacy question, "What type of legacy do you want to leave? What type of legacy do you want to leave?" Until I finally gave up. And I said, "Fine, I'll go two weeks." He got all excited. And I went off. And I went to my new home.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And this my new home was the Khlong Toei slums, made up of dilapidated row housing, corrugated iron roofing, the kind of thing you see on those Sunday morning commercials. And what I understood about poverty up to this point was what I saw looking for the football game on Sunday mornings. I would always pick up the remote control, and the kids with extended bellies, and there'd be somebody asking for money, and I would immediately pick up the remote control, and I would change the channel because that's what I did. But now, of course, I was on television and didn't have a remote control, and I was surrounded by poverty. And I walked in to the volunteer coordinator, and the volunteer coordinator said, "Mark, what are you going to do? What can you do? What do you want to do?" And I explained that I used to be a parliamentary page. She's like, "Okay. Hmm." She said, "Please go report to the AIDS ward." And I walked into the AIDS ward, and two nurses came up, and one literally hugged me. She was so happy to see me.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And they were both talking, and they had this broken English, but they had this thick accent, but they said, "Mark, thank goodness you're here. You're a doctor, right?" And I was like, "Uh, no, maybe you got me mixed up with another volunteer." She said, "Oh, there's another volunteer?" I was like, "I hope so." She said, "Okay. So Mark, you understand something basic about medicine. You understand basic medicine?" And I explained to her that I watch "ER" every Thursday. Discussion in Thai. They were getting a little agitated at this point. So they said, "Mark, we're going to teach you medical school, and we have about four hours." And I explained I was from Canada. Medical school in my country is a minimum of four years. So she looked down at her watch and talked to her friend and said, "Well, we better start right away." And I was like, "Okay." So guys, I learned medical school in four hours. I moved people with bedsores, I administered types of IVs and medication, the craziest stuff you can imagine.In literally four hours. It was four hours of extensive medical training.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: At the end of my extensive medical training, I was given a white lab coat, and I was told two things. One is on the left-hand side of the ward, there's an area separated by these removable curtains called the exit area. So when people get really, really sick and they're about to pass on, the patients get wheeled, wheeled, if that's even a word, to the left-hand side of the ward where the other patients don't have to see them die. And so this is a separate area from everybody else for culturally appropriate reasons they explained. And they said, "This is a very important thing you need to know just in case somebody passes away here. This is why." And I said, "Okay. Really sad, but thank you for telling me." And they said, "The second thing we need to tell you is that we literally haven't had a volunteer in three months, so we're so excited you're here. We're so excited that you're here especially. We're so excited that you're trained now.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: So what we're going to do is take the next shift off to get some groceries and relieve you of the ward." And I was like, "Oh, this isn't so good. I'm not feeling really good yet." And they said, "No, Mark. No, no. You'll be fine." They said, "Think of this as the beginning of your residency." And they literally walked out. So now guys, I was in charge of 24 AIDS patients. I was maybe your age, a little bit older, a little younger, it doesn't matter. And I had no idea what to do, so I started to hyperventilate. And I was hyperventilating, and I was... You know when you're supposed to then breathe through in your nose and out through your mouth to try to calm yourself down, like that's what they tell you? Wasn't working. So I was trying to breathe in through my nose and out through my mouth, and I was like, "Okay, Mark, you know how to do this. You can do this. Go back. What do you know how to do? What do you know how to do?

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: What do you know how to do?" I started asking myself that question over and over again. And I said, "Okay." Light bulb goes off. The first thing I did is I went back to my extensive training, and I got everybody a glass of water. And I was like, "What else do I know how to do?" And that was totally the end of my list. So what I did was I walked around and I gave everybody high fives or high tens, and a whole bunch of people laughed with me, but most laughed at me. But that was cool because at least they were laughing. And everything was going fine into that inaugural shift until a couple of hours in. One of the gentlemen in the exit area, again, that left-hand side of the ward separated by those curtains, was obviously very, very sick. And for those of you who study biology or potentially pre-med or any of that kind of stuff, you know that AIDS is not what kills you.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: It's the fact that your CD4 count, your white blood cell count goes down so low that you can't fight off infections, and this man had an opportunistic infection. He had pneumonia and had fluid in his lungs, and he was choking. And I did what I was supposed to do. I was supposed to administer this medication to help him. And he literally couldn't even swallow it. So I needed somebody to help me just to give him this medication. It was something really basic. So I went outside in that main street in the slum community separated by those windows there, and I needed somebody to come help me. Just literally somebody to help me. No big deal. And I first asked, and then I eventually had to beg somebody to come in. And even though a lot of people spoke broken English, nobody did come in because even if they thought they stepped inside the ward, they might get AIDS themselves. So I did what I fundamentally believe that any one of you would've done with great sincerity, is I went back to the ward.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And one of my greatest disappointments in life to this day is I actually did not know this gentleman's name, but he passed away in front of me. And this was my first experience dealing with death, and I've had that experience now many times. But it was my first experience, and seeing somebody take their last gasp of breath or close their eyes for the last time was a... Is, but in this case, was an extremely humbling experience. And the nurses came back, and I was crying, and they said, "What happened?" And I explained, and they said, "Mark, somebody dies here every day. At least they died with dignity and respect." And I said, "Wow, this is much more than what I can do." And I thanked them. I hugged them. I said, "You have so much more courage and so much more capacity than I ever will." And I said, "Thank you so much for what you do. I just can't do it." And I hugged them again, and I walked out.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And I went to the volunteer coordinator who sent me in the ward, and I picked up the phone and I called my mother and I explained what happened. I said, "I need you to get me out of here." And she called me back. She said, "There's a flight in two days, Mark. You're on the standby list. Go to the airport." And I was so excited to go. I was so excited to go. I wanted to go so badly. And what I did is I ended up going upstairs to my simple apartment where I simply had unpacked a few hours earlier, where I started to pack my bag. I wanted to go sleep on the floor of the airport. I wanted to leave so badly. And I was there ready to go sleep on the floor of the airport, and this kid, pictured behind me in the yellow T-shirt, he came up and he knocked on my door. And he said, "Mark, what are you doing?" And I said, "I'm leaving." I wasn't even paying attention.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And he said, "No, Mark, what are you doing?" And I said, "I'm leaving." And then he pointed down to his feet and he said, "You can't leave." And I said, "Why can't I leave?" And all of a sudden, it literally hit me like a ton of bricks because somebody had told me a week earlier that when a boy or girl from the slums of Thailand speaks English, it's not because they went to private school or any type of school at all. It's because they used to work as a sex slave for a foreigner. And this boy spoke perfect English with a European accent. And he said, "Mark, what are you doing?" And I again said, "I'm leaving." And he again said, he can't leave or I can't leave. And he pointed down to his feet and he said, "I'm a street kid." He said, "I'm so poor, I don't own shoes." He said, "I'm so poor, I don't know how old I am, and I'm so poor, I don't even know when my birthday is." But he said, "But it's no big deal.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: So what we do is we have a street kid government, kind of like a street kid student council. And what we do is, because we don't know how old we are and we don't know when our birthdays are, we come together one day of the year and we choose one day as all our birthdays, and we have one big massive birthday party. And it's coming up in two days. It's kind of like the biggest party of the year. You got to come." And he grabbed my hand and he made me walk downstairs. Next to the ward, there was this massive gravel pit. And there was a whole bunch of kids there, all of whom were between the ages of about eight and 18, none of whom knew when their birthdays were, and all of whom spoke English. And we played soccer, not with a new Nike soccer ball, but with a Coke can, a used Coke can. And at the end of this soccer game, the kids came around and they made me promise that I'd go to this birthday party. And I reluctantly, somehow emotionally distraught, agreed. And I said yes.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And the next day, I got up in the morning andI saw how the police would beat these kids up for kicks, and I saw how they would have to make money in the most horrible ways. And I just said, "You know what? I really need to go to this birthday party." So I went back to the volunteer coordinator, and I picked up the phone and I called my mother again, and I said something like, "Mom, I hate to do this to you, but I need you to change my plane ticket again because I need to go to this birthday party for street kids who don't have shoes." Now, my mom said to me something like, "Mark, I need you to be very honest with me. Are you doing drugs?" And I was like, "Mom, no." And she changed my plane ticket, and I went to this birthday party for street kids who don't have shoes. And what they do is they shine other people's shoes, and they buy simple things like watermelon and peanuts.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And they don't literally have enough money, so the center I was staying at actually matched their money that they were making so they could have watermelon. And a whole bunch of kids, including some of the boys here, were actually born with HIV, so they wouldn't have many birthdays of their own. And it was this incredible experience. It wasn't a birthday party full of stuff. I didn't have a lot of presents around. Nobody gave them things. It wasn't that kind of birthday party. But it was a birthday party like one I've never seen before. It was full of passion and compassion and love and excitement and energy, and it was really cool. And so I changed my plane ticket again, and I started hanging out with the kids. And I changed it again and again and again, and long story short, I ended up spending a year living and working in the slums of Thailand. And I had many, many, many, many AIDS patients pass in front of me. After 20-ish some odd, I stopped counting. But every single morning, I got out of bed, and I played soccer with these great kids.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And I eventually came back to North America, and I was really angry. I was really p\*\*\*\*d off. I couldn't figure out why people didn't care, especially people in my school didn't care. I just didn't think that people cared about these things or cared about humanitarian issues or were really engaged or were intelligent to have these conversations. I just didn't get it. And they didn't get it, at least what I thought. So I said, "Okay, there's two things I'm going to do. Option A, I'm going to go to G8 protests and throw things." That was option A. Very viable option, but that was option A. Option B was I was going to educate myself, and I was going to go get myself educated, so I could really talk about these issues in a very intelligent manner. And so after carefully weighing the options, I ended up choosing option B, and you still need people, to a degree, who are on the fringe, but I decided I'm going to educate myself, and I did that.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And I ended up getting a scholarship to Harvard and a Rhodes Scholarship to Oxford, and I'm a lawyer, but I don't practice. And the reason I share that is for a very important reason, is that by getting socially engaged and by having these conversations and by moving from me to we and really focusing on we, one of the great things happen, is that sometimes your greatest teachers in life can be those who you least expect. So sometimes the greatest teachers can be the ones who may not even have shoes. And I learned more about globalization, about compassion, and about leadership than I did from a bunch of street kids than from many of my professors. And it was a really interesting experience, and understanding this and really kind of growing from this conversation, which is just really so critical. The other reason I'm here, very quickly, is because of this photo. Now, Free the Children, the organization I so proudly represent, was actually founded by my younger brother, Craig. And I know probably some of the viewers, at least at a minimum, have seen him on Oprah. He's been on the show many times.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And as I like to joke, you now all know, for those of you who have seen him on Oprah, he's not as good-looking as I am. However, he did start the organization, and he started it when I was in Thailand. And what happened was Craig was 12 years old, and he was in grade seven, and both my parents are teachers. We kind of grew up in this small community outside of Toronto, like a white picket fence community without the fence. It was just one of these random places, and it was great. But nevertheless, so Craig was looking for the comic section one day in our local newspaper. And instead of seeing the comic section, my brother saw this picture, if you will. It's of a young boy from Pakistan. And this boy's story is the following. This boy's name is Iqbal Masih. Now, Iqbal grew up in a very poor family in a very poor community in Pakistan. And one day, a moneylender came to the village when he was four years old, and Iqbal's parents were very poor. Brothers, sisters, literally couldn't afford to feed him.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: So the moneylender came to the village, and they did what in so many cases, they promised Iqbal's parents that if Iqbal went off with them, they'd get $16, which is an enormous amount of money, and Iqbal would get a good job and a good education, and it was all here in the contract. And Iqbal's parents were illiterate, so they read the contract, but of course, couldn't read the contract. They signed the contract, not with a pen, but they put their thumb in ink and signed the contract, and Iqbal went away. And he did not, of course, get a good job and did not get a good education, and he ended up working as a carpet weaver, tying tiny knots in handmade carpets, carpets that would come to North America to adorn our floors. And when Iqbal's parents found out what happened, the moneylender said, "Oh, you didn't read the contract properly." And so Iqbal did this every single day, every single hour, day after day, hour after hour, for many, many years until he was 10. And so when he was 10 years old, he was lucky.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: He actually ran away, and he ran away, and he got hooked up with a human rights organization. And after understanding what happened to him, he started to speak out against this issue called child labor. And he went from town to town to village to village to eventually came to the United States and came to Boston and got something called the Reebok Human Rights Award, and then was reunited back with his family. And that same week, he was riding his bike with his cousin, so excited to be home, and he was very tragically shot and killed, and many people think he was shot and killed by the people who owned the carpet factory for speaking out. So Iqbal was killed at the age of 12. And my brother was 12 when he read this article because this went on the AP news wire and said, "Wow, I'm 12. This kid's 12. This is crazy." He looked at his life, looked at Iqbal's life, and said, "This is nuts." Took it to his grade seven class, said, "Who wants to help?" And a whole bunch of kids put up their hands.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And that's how the organization began 14 years ago, and now it's the world's largest network of children helping children, young people helping young people, high school, university students across North America getting engaged. We have about a million kids involved in Canada and another million involved in the United States. And what we do is empower young people to change the world, and Craig saw this firsthand. When he was 12 years old, he convinced my parents, but really my mom, because my mom makes all the decisions in the family, so convinced my mom, poor dad, thatHe would be allowed to go off to Asia to actually meet some of these kids. So we can't, of course, go off to Asia here this evening, and our friends watching via live web broadcast can't either as well. But let's go off to Asia with Craig when he was 12 to better understand this issue called child labor. The camera mic at this distance. This is the camera mic at this distance. This is low at the farthest possible distance at this point. This is low. Okay, great.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: When Craig Kielburger was only 12, he decided to take a seven-week trip to South Asia. It was a journey that would have important consequences for the rest of his life. He went with 25-year-old Alam Rahman, his friend and guide. Where? They took a camcorder and made a record of all their experiences to bring back to Canada to show other children. Craig is 15 now. This is the story of his life so far. The only time I was actually nervous on my trip was that one second when I'd said, "Oh God, what am I doing here? I'm 12 years old, and I've never taken the subway by myself." But after that, I loved it. You have a question? Why does he begin working in the mill factory if he was going to school before? Because of all the- Craig had become concerned about child labor through reading about it back in Canada. Now he wanted to find out everything he could firsthand. I had a million questions. I could've held a child there for hours and just asked them question after question after question.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: I wanted to know what it was like working in the conditions, how they felt having to get up each morning knowing that this was what they were going to do, what their dreams were for the future. I wanted to put myself in their life for a day and to learn exactly what went through their brain and exactly what they thought and exactly what they hoped and exactly what they feared. What is your name? How she ever cut herself? Yeah, sometimes. She sometimes cuts herself. Yeah. It's quite dangerous if you p\*\*\*k yourself when there's hundreds of these needles laying there. Those needles that she was sorting through, what are they used for? Use? They will collect the plastics. Only they collect these plastics. What are the needles used for before? What were they used for? Hospitals? Before, in the hospital. Maybe from the drug addiction. Is she ever worried about the spread of viruses like AIDS? Because she said she had cut herself before using. See what, just first aid. Just water. That's all. In the water. See what, if they get any treatment for that. And one- Just water. They don't get anything for it.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: So for those of you who couldn't see on the web or for those of you who couldn't see in the back here, Munila's job, of course, was to separate used syringes and needles for their plastics, and she did this piece by piece. And at one point in the footage, you actually see her stepping onto the pile of needles to get to the other side. And then the question is, "Do you cut yourself?" And she put up her hands, and what looked like freckles weren't of course freckles, they were pin p\*\*\*\*s all over her hands and her legs and her feet. And she says, "I cut myself all the time." And there was this blue bucket of brown dirty water in front of her. And she said, "I put my cut in this bucket of water because that's what I'm supposed to do, right?" And then she stopped, and she said, "I can't talk to you much longer because my master, not my boss, my master, will beat me again." And the reality is that there's about, give or take, 72 million kids of school ages who've never once stepped foot inside a classroom.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: About 200 million kids, again, depending on the statistics, but ballpark, who work in child labor, including this boy. This is a photo I had a chance to take, and this is the same job as Iqbal. This is a carpet loom. And you can't see very well in this photo, but his leg was actually shackled or chained to the carpet loom so he wouldn't run away. And what they do is they chain the kids down. And when they chain the kids down, then they can't escape. But then if they do escape, they only get one meal a day, typically. So if they do escape, and they start running, they actually can't run very far because they don't have any energy. So that's basically what happens. Or in India, we spend a lot of time in India, and in India, there's a high incidence of child labor. And in India, you meet kids, for example, this boy in the fireworks factories. And a lot of the kids actually make fireworks, and there's explosions all the time. For those of you who watch the BBC, you see this.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: This is one of the few news that was actually covered from an international perspective. And you can't see very well in this photo, many of you, but some of you can at least. This boy is very badly burned on the left-hand side of his body. So what they do is that when there are kids who are badly burned because an explosion goes off, and they often do because it's so hot and arid, and a spark goes off, and the gunpowder sets ablaze, is that then the kids are burned, and they take tar, and they put tar all over their burns so they will heal as quickly as possible, so they can go back to work as possible. So this boy actually was badly burned trying to save his younger brother who died in the fireworks explosion. And then, of course, they don't have time to grieve because they have to go back to work, and they put tar on the wounds, and that's what happens. Or the kids that work in the brick kilns or making the stuff that we import from Asia very cheaply.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: Often it's forced pregnancy tests or teenage girls who make the stuff and literally get paid like three cents a piece, and sometimes they make 90 cents a day in those circumstances. And as we gather here todayWe need to understand that as much as these issues are taking place, we as the young persons, we as the young generation, of course, people gathered here and watching, we have a huge responsibility. We have a massive responsibility because whatever you're studying, whatever you care about, whatever you're involving yourself in and part of these discussions, this is our calling. And just as there's the young person standing in front of the tank at Tiananmen Square or the anti-apartheid rallies in colleges, university campuses across America, I think this is our chance. This is our chance to come together to debate and discuss and actually end the worst forms of poverty. So that's my two cents on this issue. And when we understand these issues and we see that, you know what? Young people in Canada and the United States actually can participate and actually can be part of the solution and can be part of the challenge.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: One of the critical ways by doing this is making changing the world cool. And it's wonderful to be here, and obviously, you guys are part of the society, and you care about leadership. But you know what? I'm going to argue you're probably, maybe, a minority on the campus. And for those of the people who are watching, they're probably a minority on campuses across North America because changing the world is acceptable and it's important, but you know what? It's not hit that critical mass yet, and we have to hit that critical mass. We have to create the change to show that apathy is uncool and changing the world is so important, so engaging, and from a social perspective, so cool, like the whole concept that Malcolm Gladwell's been talking about. The way we do that as an organization is something called WE Day. So what we do is we start a little younger than college, university. We start at elementary school and high schools, and we take young people together, and we have these massive social events amongst many other things, but this is one of the things that we do.

speaker: Marc Kielburger
text: And we actually create this dialogue and this conversation. And we just recently had a couple WE Days, and they're very well known in Canada. We had 16,000 student leaders from 1,000 schools at GM Place, which is our big hockey stadium or arena in Vancouver. And then a week later, we had 16,000 student leaders from 1,000 schools in Toronto. And it was broadcast by our leading broadcaster, which is called CTV, and about 5.4 million Canadians watched the show or ancillary shows, which was an amazing experience. speaker: Oprah Winfrey
text: Please finish this sentence, "Oprah Winfrey taught me..." and remember to include your name, your school, and \#theNSLS. Okay, let's take a look at our last member video question of the night, here we go. - Good evening, Ms. Winfrey. speaker: Oprah Winfrey
text: How do I use it in service to somebody else?" You become a servant leader. And so it doesn't mean it has to be some big organization or some big cause or something. And that is one of the reasons why we were the number one show for 25 years. "We are in service to our viewer. How do we serve what it is they are looking for, desiring to see, to fulfill whatever their needs are." And so I love that question. - I agree with you.

speaker: Oprah Winfrey
text: So we have our final question of the evening, and it's one that we like to ask all of our guests. Oprah, why do you believe it's important for students to develop their leadership skills at organizations like the NSLS or other groups where they're identifying their passions and building skills to become a better leader? - Well, I think it's important. speaker: Oprah Winfrey
text: And then how do you use the leadership qualities that you've developed to have the life you want?" Who are you when you achieve all the stuff and the things around you to allow that stuff and things to be a reflection of who you are and not define who you are.

speaker: Oprah Winfrey
text: 'Cause I don't care how big your swimming pool is and how much square footage you got and how many cars you got in your garage. speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Paul Orfalea. It seems so simple. Back in 1970, when Paul Orfalea formulated a plan to provide college students with products and services they needed at a competitive price. And so near the University of California at Santa Barbara, the first Kinko's was founded in a space so small that they had to lug the copy machine out to the sidewalk in order to be able to use it. Today, Kinko's is in over 1,200 locations worldwide. So if you're interested in knowing what Paul Orfalea's secrets to success are for creating this huge success, he's going to share some of them today. Mr. Orfalea's business savvy comes apart from his passion for retailing, his eye for opportunities, and his care for both his customers and his coworkers. And Mr. Orfalea didn't stop there. His concern for environmental responsibility has proven him to be an exceptional business leader. His unique approach in creating a working environment that encourages active participation from all his coworkers, allowing them to share their ideas freely.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: And it's this environment which helped Kinko's be named one of Fortune Magazine's 100 best companies to work with in America in 1999, 2000, and 2001, three years in a row. Kinko's also has the distinction of being named one of Fortune's 500 biggest companies, and Working Mother Magazine named Kinko's as one of the best companies for working mothers. Something I admire about Mr. Orfalea is that his family has philanthropy at heart. They have the Orfalea Family Foundation. The Orfalea Family Foundation supports many organizations that are focused on child development, early care and learning, and differences in intergenerational programs. Mr. Orfalea recently wrote his autobiography, "Copy This\! Lessons from a Hyperactive Dyslexic Who Turned a Bright Idea into One of America's Best Companies." Copy that? It's a great book. I love it. And I want you to know, despite his tremendous success, Paul Orfalea remains one of the most down-to-earth, modern-day, what I would call adventurers. We are pleased to feature him tonight and grateful for him to share with us that which he has learned. Please, let's give a warm welcome, Paul Orfalea. Thank you very much. You're welcome, sir. Thank you. Thank you very much.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: How are you doing? Good. Good. Are you from California? Oh, ah. Hey, I'm very lucky in life. I think to be in leadership or be responsible, you should know what you have going for yourself. And I like to brag a little bit. Is that okay with you all? I'm very lucky to be a very bad reader. In second grade, I cheated on my alphabet test, and Sister Sheila found out I didn't know the alphabet. And I was held back in second grade. Then in third grade, my parents tried to convince me of the alphabet with my older brother and sister. That didn't work. Then I had to go to memory school. Then I went to school with nine kids. Two are 18 years old. I'm eight years old, and I kept thinking, "Now why am I in this school?" So I didn't belong there. Then my parents had me go to an eye doctor three days a week and he'd dilate my eyes, and I'd look at these stupid little eye circles. And they thought in those days bad reading had something to do with muscles in your eyes. Wrong. Finally, had a good tutor.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: My parents said every word I ever read cost them $50. Graduated from high school, impressively, eighth from the bottom of my class. I had a solid D average. And the only thing I really liked doing in high school was I was a woodshop major, and they had this thing called a lathe. You know what that is? It spins. I used to put my little chisel in there, and I'd go back and forth. I never really made anything. I just liked to go back and forth with a chisel. That's impressive for leadership, right? Now, back in those days out of high school, I was thinking about my future. And when you think of your future, you have places that want you. Then there was this one organization that really thought I was spectacular. You all wore the same clothes. You got to sleep outside. You got to go in the mud. You got to be in a lot of humidity and never take your clothes off because it was very hot and jungly, and you got to carry big guns, and there's a lot of explosions. That was called the war in Vietnam. That's choice A.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Okay, let me see if you guys can choose which choice I took. Choice B is go to college, flirt with women, and drink beer. What choice do you think I took? B, yes. I took B. So, I went to community college, and I went and saw the admissions officer because I wanted to go to USC. And I learned in life, if you want to be accepted by the in-crowd, you kind of got to dress like a Republican. You don't have to be a Republican, but at least dress like one, okay? So I went and saw the admissions officer, and I said, "I really want to go here." And for some reason, I was accepted. And I went to USC, and I graduated, and I remember the lowest day of my life because she said, "If you go to extension," that means USC at night, "we'll let you into the day school." So my first time, I was a sophomore. I wasn't accepted into the school, but the first time in my life, I was with the straight A students. I'm sure you guys are all very high academics. Well, I wasn't.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: I was never with you folks in school. So everybody, all summer long, I'm saying to myself, "I'm not that stupid. I can compete with these straight A types." And I had my pen out, my notebook, and there was 80 people in the class. And what I could tell, it might be an easier class because I knew that USC had a lot of football players.And a lot of them were in the class, so I figured I could do okay. I go to class, and the man is talking in a foreign language. He's using these big words I don't understand. All my life, socially, I was hanging around Aristotle, Socrates, and Plato. And I was thinking, trying to take notes. Everybody around me is taking notes. I give up and I go, "I should think of a homeless shelter or a drug to die from, because I'm just not going to go anywhere in this world.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: These people are a lot smarter than me." And at the break, my friend put his pen down and said, "I didn't understand a word this guy was talking about." And then he came back and said, "Well, I've been teaching at Yale, and evidently, I'm talking over your head." Now, isn't he stupid? Don't you think in the English language, there's enough words to use that you can convey it in a normal train of thought? We have a lot of words. Why do you have to use these big, stupid words? But that was my first experience in college, and luckily, I overcame that one because he came back and everybody couldn't understand him. And then I went to SC, and I can honestly say I never took notes. I'd sit in class, and the professor said something, I listened. And I just knew I was going to have my own business, so I could just, if he said subchapter S or LIFO, or in organizational behavior, there's theory X, theory Y. Ask me that a little later, I can go into it. I just sat back and listened to it. So that was my educational background.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Are you impressed? Now I want you to feel my hands. What do they feel like? Say it loudly. Soft. Yeah, that's soft hands. Because I have no mechanical ability whatsoever. My wife lent me the stick shift of her car, I destroyed it in one little trip. And I want to admit something to you. I started at Kinko's, and I worked there. I don't know how to run one machine at Kinko's, and I haven't known how to run a machine since the first copier and the cash register. They perplex the hell out of me, these machines. And at Kinko's, you know how you bind something? You punch the holes. I'd go like this with a punching machine. I'd pull it down, and I'd go, "Did I put the things this way that time, or did I put them this way?" I was never able to really fully bind. Can you imagine the founder of Kinko's doesn't know how to bind? No. Okay. I was going to keep that a big secret. But if you're lucky enough to have my skill sets, do you think I'm going to have a chance to get a job?

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: What do you think? No. There's not a whole lot of places that hire people that can't fill out forms or can't do mechanical things. Do you think the job opportunity market is really cool? And plus, I had three jobs in my life, and I lasted two days in every one of them. So I knew I was kind of incorrigible. Are you impressed with my leadership so far? I'm probably the ideal leadership candidate, right? So my third good quality is my family is Lebanese. You know anybody here know anybody who's Lebanese? Do you know anybody that's Lebanese that works for other people? They all have their own business. So I was always raised to have my own business. And my mother would always... Just part of our culture was... I was very lucky because my parents, if they were overly academic, I would've easily been defeated. But they never really looked at my report cards.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: My mother motivated us all to go to college by saying, "Now, doesn't it look like fun?" And we always had very interesting conversations at the dinner table, and it was more of an emphasis on learning than school and what others think of you. My brother one time was studying at 9:30 at night, and my dad walked in and said, "What are you doing?" My brother said, "I'm studying for a test." And my dad said, "You'll never remember it, so what's the good of learning it?" You'd think that that's kind of a weird comment, wouldn't you? But the emphasis was, "You're going to be out in the real world one day. You're going to school for a reason. Why don't you try to remember what you learn?" But we always were involved in the news, always interesting conversations. And I think my parents... If you ask a child, a child five years old comes home with a painting from school. What do you say to them? You're probably going to say, "That's a good painting," right? "I love it." That's the wrong thing to say to a child.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Because by telling them it's a good painting, you tell a child they have to please others rather than please themselves. What you want to say is, "Tell me about the painting and why did you do it?" And I think our system in education, with obsession with this pleasing others, has gone too far. It's about what you think of yourself. It's about why I did the painting and why did I want to do it. So I think I was ideally... What is the word I'm looking for? I was perfectly suited for my parents. I think if I hadn't had them and I hadn't had the background, I'd have easily been in a homeless shelter today or not alive. Now, if you're lucky enough to have my skill sets once again, and I want to leave the store, or I want to figure out how to treat the workers that are ringing the registers for my customers. Have you ever had a job where somebody mistreated you? What do you do? You go like this to the worker. What is a worker going to do to you? They hit you harder, aren't they? Does that make sense?

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: You ever had a job where someone mistreated you, don't you hit them harder?Does that make sense? So if somebody is ringing a cash register and your name is on the deposit slip, do you want to go like this to that precious hand or go like this? Do you get the feeling happy fingers ring happy registers? So that's been the spirit of how we've treated each other at our business. How I got into Kinko's is if you view the world as a successful place and you can trust people. Now, what choice did I have in life? Do I have a choice of being suspicious of other human beings? Or the place is really a dysfunctional planet Earth, everything is screwed up. Every time I go to a green light, I am worried about getting smashed. We live in a trusting world, don't we? Thing works. And it is an environment that breeds success. The most successful book ever written is the Yellow Pages. They wouldn't be in the Yellow Pages if they weren't doing something, would they? And they have to pay for the ad, so they have to be doing something right.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: We are surrounded by success. Every time there is a customer in line, is that an idea that some success is going on? Are you always in tune with, "Hey, why are they in line? What are they doing here? And how are they making a profit?" Do you do that? Well, I was at USC, and you could tell by now writing and academics wasn't necessarily my forte. You could tell. Could you say that? Yeah. So I made a deal with this group. If they wrote the paper, it was a big group project. I said... What do you think I did? I told the group, "If you write the paper, I'll get all the pizza, I'll buy all the Coca-Cola, I'll do everything so you guys can write, write, write, write, write." Because I didn't know how to. I really couldn't write very well. And so they Xeroxed double-spaced, they made this big, thick document, and I had to make a bunch of copies. And so I went to this place, and I saw a lot of people in line at SC making copies.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: So I figured if they were at USC making copies, why wouldn't they be like the guy, you know the guy who won the award in Santa Barbara? What's his name? Anton? Yeah. That's where we started our business. So I figured, well, if they're in one place, why wouldn't they be in another place? Does that make sense? So I started a little store, had a Xerox machine, and I figured, well, I've already got the Xerox machine. Why don't I sell notebooks and pens? Does that make sense? We could sell them. And it was the main artery of the campus. First day of school, I put these notebooks and pens on the sidewalk. Do you remember the first day of school? Do you need a notebook and pen? Of course. Do you think you sell about $2,000... I sold $2,000 a day worth of notebooks and pens back then. And back then, we had the quarter system at Santa Barbara. You got three times a year for back to school. Isn't that nice? And then basically, you don't have to go too far to figure out men want to meet women on college campuses.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Is that a stretch? So I put guys with backpacks, and they would go to the girls' dorms and sell notebooks and pens. They'd meet the future Mrs. Maybe, and I could get a commission. Isn't that a nice world? Okay. So that's how I started. Now, what do you think my favorite job at Kinko's was? My favorite job was leaving Kinko's. I didn't like being in those stores. Do you think I really enjoyed the hectic environment? There's a bunch of machines I don't know how to operate. Do you think I would really enjoy hanging around there? Now, if I reflect back on my contribution to Kinko's, I used to work with capable people, people that knew how to run businesses beautifully, like Jimmy Warren, Brad Kraus, a lot of folks that ran the business beautifully. Now, do you think with my ADD, I can't sit still, staying in the office was my thing? I like to wander. Wander, wander, wander. Now, do you think I could wander, and every store, they were doing something right the other stores could learn from. Wasn't that my job, taking an idea from one store and giving it to another?

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: How many of you have ever had a calendar done at Kinko's where you take 12 little pictures of your own family pictures, and you put them in a calendar? Have you ever had that? Just pretend like you did. Yeah, have you ever had a calendar like that? Yeah. Yes, you've had that calendar. We bought them. You did get one last week? No. You never got one of the personalized calendars? You've never seen one in your life? Yeah. Okay, good. Phew. Have you seen one? Yeah. Oh, good. Somebody did that in San Diego, Stanzak. What do you think? You look at it, and you go, "I think we could sell those." Do you think that might be a kind of cool thing? So my job was looking for opportunities and exploiting them. Now, do you think you can make more money looking for ideas or sitting in the office hovering? Ideas. Ideas. Isn't my business a savings account and a bunch of ideas? Uh-huh. Okay. So I like wandering, and it went to my strong suit. How many of you, you know what works...

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: I know you all can work hard, but you know what works 24 hours a day, seven days a week? Your ideas and your savings account. Isn't that interesting? What's your business? Isn't your business your savings account and your ideas? Isn't that kind of cool?Now, you ask about my leadership skills. You know what my leadership skill was? The best definition of management I ever heard came from my wife. Leaders, managers are to remove obstacles. The only reason you have a boss is to make what? Your life easier or harder? Yeah. Does it make sense for a boss to say, "Well, let's go out and burden these poor workers so they can be more unproductive?" And do you think the worker, if they had problems with your health insurance company because they were denied coverage, would be a little motivated or unmotivated? What? Angry. Angry. Their kids are sick, and your insurance company aggravates them over coverage. Is that a problem you have to have as a business? Yes.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: You get the whole package when you have an employee, and if you don't want interference on every aspect of them, and you don't remove obstacles on every aspect of their life, they're not going to have those little happy fingers ringing those wonderful little happy registers. Is that fair to say? So all of us business types that think... So my job was really removing obstacles and getting out of the way for the productive people that know how to run these machines. And really, why I was able to leave our business is, if any of you are patrons of Kinko's, you're basically a little uptight and confused, aren't you? When you walk in, you don't know what you want, you want it yesterday. Is that fair to say? So you walk in, and you talk to a worker, and then you go back and forth with the worker, right? The worker is a cool job because they can suggest something to you, and really, you're very appreciative of all the suggestion. The worker has all these machines around them, and the worker humanizes these machines, humanizes technology.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Then the worker sees the manufacturing process and is able to see the smile at the end. And most importantly, they see their contribution to the planet Earth. They see what they did and how it contributed. It helps somebody get a job, celebrate a life event. So I could see that was a cool thing, and all I could do was screw it up by getting overly involved in it. Is that fair to say? I'd go to the stores, and they would say, "Do me a favor, don't help behind the counter." So I think that one of the prerequisites is leadership is getting the hell out of the way. Don't over-manage your people. Now, I had a problem when we had two and three stores. It was very difficult because I didn't have enough to do. I'd go out and meddle too much in the stores, wouldn't I? Wouldn't you meddle too much if you only have two or three things to worry about? But the more I was in the stores, the less the self-esteem of the manager was. Now, I told you about Theory X and Theory Y, a lecture I had in college.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: It's an organizational behavior concept. If you're running a military organization and there's a vertical-- What do they call this, vertical axis? Yeah. And a horizontal axis? Okay, yeah, that's right. Got that right. The vertical is X, and the Y, this one here is the Y. Now, Theory X is you're running a military organization. You're going to have it pretty much, "You do what I'm telling you to do." Right? How many of you, you work at the university? Is it pretty hard to get anybody to do what you want them to do in a university? Faculty? Mm-hmm. It is? That's not a problem. Well, you can't just tell them what to do. You just can't tell them what to do, like blindly in the military, say, "Okay, I'll do what you tell me to do." I think the most independent organization on Earth is a bunch of faculty in a university. Are you going to use the same militaristic leadership quality to run a bunch of faculty? No. You got to use Theory Y, collaborative. I want to do it kind of a collaborative leadership style.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Do you think if you're dealing with a bunch of architects that are smart and independent, they're going to follow your military dictatorial style? But do you think if you're running a police department, you need more of a dictatorship style? So you kind of say, "What business am I going into?" And then you alter your style accordingly. Now, because I'm basically not a competent person, do you think I'm going to function very well in an X organization or a Y organization? I'm going to do much better in a Y organization. Kinko's was a great Theory Y organization. I had to rely on people wanting to open up that door every day in Fort Collins, Colorado, on their own initiative. Is that fair to say? Do you think I'd carry a big sledgehammer and say, "If you don't open it up, I'm going to beat the hell out of you?" Well, you could do that in the military. I couldn't do that in my business. I had to rely, because I didn't have a lot of money for overhead, on people's intestinal fortitude. That's called Theory Y.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: So whenever you own your own business or you're in leadership, think what style the organization needs, what kind of leader you are. That doesn't mean that in a Theory Y organization, I didn't have the steel fist. I had two. I had the steel fist and the velvet glove. What do you think I used mostly? I used the velvet glove, and I got people to work collaboratively. You think that's better off? Okay. Now, also, you have to figure out your tolerance for risks. Do you think I want a lot of risk-takers if I'm running a nuclear power plant? No. You want to say, "Look, you just do what we tell you. We wrote the manual. You push those buttons when we tell you to push the buttons," or follow the procedures. Is that fair to say? Now, what would a mistake cost me at Kinko's? Nothing. What?Well, so what? Big deal. I lose a little bit of money because they did a job bad. It's not like betting the farm on anything. I'm not betting like in women's clothes where you're betting on style. These machines don't go out of date. I'm not fighting my inventory.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: My cost of goods sold is relatively low. I could tolerate lots of mistakes. So what is your threshold for mistakes in your business? If you're not running a nuclear power plant and the stakes aren't too high, you could have what? A lot of mistakes. You want what kind of culture? An open culture. Does that make sense? Do you want a culture that celebrates success and is too punitive? If people stick their neck out, are they going to get in trouble? Why do all these great American companies eat it? Kodak, Xerox, Polaroid. Because you get the people that manage the career who won't manage the business. Do you think I want that if I own the business? Do I want people's candor? Do I want openness? Do I want people sticking their neck out if it doesn't cost me anything? Well, what can I make? I have 800 stores. If it works in one store, can't I take it to every one of those stores? Oh, yeah. If it works in one store, what was my biggest problem at Kinko's is people would say, "No, you don't realize. You're in California.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: It won't work here." Are you different in Florida? You have the same language. Come on. They don't want laminating in Florida? No, I would have those same stupid fights. No, if it worked in basically a few stores, it'll work in every store. But people are very reluctant to change. And I found that leaders are in the future, managers are in the present, and accountants are in the past, and a good leader is always aggravating their organization. You think a good leader is a very content person? They own their own business. If you run one of these big public companies like Exxon, do you think you're going to be a good old boy and be happy with the board of directors? Yeah, you got to wear the white suit, go to the country club, and do that little game because you got a what? A cush job? When it's your money, do you think you're going to be that cush and that cheerful? No. You want what? You don't want people around you to tell you what you want to hear.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
text: Like my friend Dean Zitkowsky says, "Executives like to be lied to." What do you want? My dad used to tell me a great story. He said, "A good salesperson sells you broke." You know what that means? If you listen to your salespeople too much, you'll have too much inventory and too much in your product line. You go broke because you got too much there. But if your salespeople aren't aggravating the holy hell out of you, what do you have? Problems. What do you want? You want people aggravating you. You own the business. You want people telling you the honest truth. You talk to lawyers, they're going to tell you not to do anything. You talk to marketing people, they'll tell you to do everything. What is it? A constant struggle of ambiguity. One of the big problems is I'm sure that you straight A types in this room all want easy answers, and life is very confusing. Now, is life very simple if you're a mother with a little baby? Yes. The baby cries, you do something about it. If it has a temperature, you take it to the doctor and a pill.

speaker: Paul Orfalea
