What a special story to share with us. We've got just a few more questions for you tonight, Rachael. This one is our final video question and it's from Isabella Estes from Lindenwood University. Go ahead, Isabella. \<v -\>Isabella, that's my favorite name. \<v -\>Hi, Rachael Ray. My name is Isabella and I go to school at Lindenwood University in St. Charles, Missouri. They say that people learn the most from their mistakes. I would like to know what mistake you learned the most from and why. Thank you. \<v -\>I think all of life is one big mistake we should all reveal to each other.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: And I think the reason I have been successful anywhere on local news, or Food Network or with books or, just in life as a waitress, as a dishwasher, is humility and just sharing what goes wrong with everyone. There's nothing wrong with being wrong. You learn more from being wrong than from feeling that you're right. Most people that go through life thinking they're right all the time are wrong all of the time. Because they have no humility. The people that really learn and have fun and go someplace in my experience, in the folks that I know, they're all people that admit all of their frailties and what's not the best or the most perfect about themselves. And sharing that will bring you not only great peace and freedom. It'll allow you to express your best self to everyone, to the world. Don't focus on your failures. They're not failures. They're gonna be your biggest successes. Truly, it really will be. Just share them with people in the right way. And think before you speak, don't put things out into the world that truly upset you or disturb you, or you think you need help with.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: That's not what I'm talking about. When you make a mistake with something you're trying to accomplish, that's something to share. If you're really hurt in life, that's something you keep very private and you share with people that are very close to you. But if it's just messes and successes of something you love to do all the time, put it out there, you'll feel terrific about it. And it'll help you build a stronger sense of self, whether that's on social media or in print, in art, in sculpture, in food, in science, in discovering the next great vaccine, you will be successful because you will have gotten over that little hurdle of not everybody's gonna like you. That's just life. But if you're sincere and you believe in it, focus on that. Don't focus on the naysayers, focus on what you do the best and stay true to it. \<v -\>Okay, all right Rachael. Well, before we do our final check-in with Nate, I'd like to ask you a question, that's one that we ask of all of our guests.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: And I just wanted to know why do you believe that's important for our students to develop their leadership skills at organizations like the NSLS or other groups where they're identifying their passions and building communication skills to become a better leader. \<v -\>Anything you can join or become a part of that helps you understand the humility of that and the responsibility of that. And that's where the crux is. You have to be humble to lead. You have to listen as much as you talk and you also have to have a direction. You have to know what you're trying to express, how to share it, how to be clear about it so the people you're asking to follow you can be successful at it. No one could be successful if you were an ambiguous leader, you have to give them a clear direction. It's a very difficult seesaw. You have to have humility and focus at the same time and you have to appreciate, this is the tricky part, you have to truly, in your heart with every breath you take and every sentence you make, you have to believe in both equally.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: The respect for others and what you might not know and the direction you want to take people. That is a very hard seesaw. Because you're admitting you might not know everything and you might still learn something. At the same time you're saying I have a clear vision of where we're trying to go. It's never about the money. It's about what you're learning and what you're giving. It's about the give and take, the light in the dark of the universe, of you and of the people around you. If you ever make it about money, you're wrong and you'll fail. In my opinion. \<v -\>That's great, thank you, Rachael. All right, it's time for our final check-in with Nate who is still in the NSLS Leadership Kitchen. Nate, how's it going? Are you done? \<v -\>I opened the window. I got some of the smoke out. There are no flames. I think things are going well. As the recipe says, I've got the chicken warming in the oven. So this is the big reveal moment where I'm gonna pull out the chicken. And then I'm gonna get a couple of pieces over here on a plate.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: So you can all get it sort of like, oh look, the cutlets, the chickens are running away. Why did the chicken cross the counter? To get onto the platter. Okay, here we go. Here we go. \<v -\>I love that. \<v -\>Drum roll, please. Here we go. Chicken Milanese, Escarole Salad. (cheering) \<v -\>Wow. \<v -\>Nate, you are the greatest. You are so darling. And you know what we do, we call it the upstate fan. John and I open the windows and the back door all the time. We hide dirty dishes out there. It is our fan. 'Cause you can't turn a fan on when you're taping. And we are so you. You did a beautiful job and that is gorgeous. Better than mine. \<v -\>That's too kind. And let me just tell you, you have taught a generation of people to cook. I mean, that's how I learn is watching "30 Minute Meals". And for everybody here, I'm not a chef. I'm not a cook. And if you could smell this kitchen right now and look at this dish, you'd think it would be.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: So Rachael, I'm just amazed at how you took your skills, how you took that life learning and you translated it in a way that people can get excited about it and all the love and care you put into this show. So thanks for sharing it with all of us. That's my sort of serious note. All the success you've had, I think what's amazing about it is that you put it back into good. So with your Yum-o\! organization, you are helping students. You are funding scholarships for young people who want to pursue a food-related career as they get older. So my one question for you is, for those students that are being benefited by Yum-o\! organization or for any student that's going after their career goal, all of these amazing things that I've heard you sharing as I've been cooking over here, what's the one goal that you think a student should go after in regards to their career? \<v -\>Be mindful of that.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: Everything you do matters, your stone that's skipping across the water and everything you do in life from being a dishwasher, to being on TV, to being a rocket scientist, everything you do in life is a stone that skips and that wave will come back. So be proud of it. Be mindful, think before you cook or speak or make any piece of your creative art and put it out into the world. Really do it with purpose and love and give as much as you get. Living that seesaw feels wonderful, whether it's time or 10 cents or a dollar, give when you get. When you feel good in life and when you have a good day, do something for someone else that same day, that same week, that same month, that same year. Share your life with other people in every way possible and never make it about the money. You'll never succeed if it's only about the money. It can't be. Everybody fails then. Some people have succeeded throughout history, but they're fewer than greater in numbers.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: I'm telling you, the people that you'll find along the way in life, more often than not, they were givers as much as receivers. That's my best advice. \<v -\>Nate, thank you so much for doing this tonight. You did an amazing job. I'm impressed, I know Rachael's impressed. I'm sure everybody watching this is impressed. And we appreciate you being a part of tonight. \<v -\>It is wonderful and amazing in the kitchen and made a meal that looks more beautiful than mine. So, okay hat's off. \<v -\>Thank you, Rachael. I'll expect you over to do my dishes now because this is really a big mess. \<v -\>I would absolutely clean your kitchen for you my brother, I clean mine four times a day. \<v -\>Bye Nate. \<v -\>Bye bye, thank you. \<v -\>Bye Nate the Great, love you. \<v -\>Rachael, thank you so much for this evening. This has been so much fun. It's truly been an honor having you here with us this evening. We learned so much and I think we'll all take some of the things that you impart with us, throughout, at least, the rest of the year for sure.

speaker: Rachael Ray
text: I mean, I feel like I took so much away from what you said tonight. Thank you so, so much. \<v -\>It was so special to be here and to be included in the conversation. Thank you. \<v -\>NSLS members, I'd like to thank you for watching this evening. And I look forward to being back with you tomorrow night for our chat with Academy Award winning actor, Jamie Foxx. But before we go, I wanna say thank you once again to Ms. Rachael Ray. (upbeat music)

speaker: Robert Gates
text: Hello, society members and our viewers from around the world. My name is Charles Knippen, I'm the President of the National Society of Leadership and Success. I'm happy to be hosting another "Thought Leader" series with you today. During this series, we sit down with world leaders, and we give you the opportunity to learn from them, to hear their stories, and to learn their tips for success. And today, I am joined by a leader with an unparalleled service commitment in the public sector. He is the former US Secretary of Defense. He is a former director of CIA. He is also an officer in the Air Force. He was also president of Texas A&M University, chancellor of William & Mary, and also in 2013, was named the president of the Boy Scouts of America. For over 50 years, he has been serving the public, but also the greater good. Today, I'm very happy to be hosting this session with Dr. Robert Gates. Dr. Gates, thank you for being with us today. Thank you for the opportunity. Great. Well, let's jump right in. During this series, we want to get your story.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: So if we could go back in time, for a lot of our viewers, they are students, traditional-age students, and we like to take you back to that timeframe. Can you give us the story of what were some of the critical moments for you, some of the critical decisions you made to get you from a student to where you are today? One of the questions that I often get from students is, "How do I get from where I'm sitting to where you're sitting?" And I like to take them back to when I was sitting where they are as a grad student. I think one of the mistakes a lot of young people make nowadays is trying to plan everything too carefully, and you just never know when different opportunities may arise. And I like to say opportunity knocks, but it doesn't knock the door down. And so grad student, CIA's recruiter is on campus at Indiana University, where I'm getting a graduate degree in Russian and Soviet history. And I decide to sign up for an interview with the CIA recruiter.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: I had every intention of using the interview, if I got the interview, to get a free trip to Washington, DC. I had no intention of going to work for CIA. I had no intention of making a career of it. I just thought it'd be a great way to get a free trip to DC. Well, one thing led to another. All of a sudden, I'm in CIA. I serve in the Air Force. CIA had a special program. It was during Vietnam. They gave no draft deferments, so you had to go into the Air Force, get commissioned. Very great incentive to be successful in officer training school because if you flunked out, you went straight to Vietnam as an airman basic. So it was highly incentivized. And then when I started at CIA, I went back to Georgetown or went back to school at Georgetown University to get a PhD because I had no intention of making a career of CIA. Literally within two weeks of getting my PhD in 1974, I got an invitation from Henry Kissinger and Brent Scowcroft to join the National Security Council staff as the Soviet desk guy.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And my bosses at CIA said, "There probably won't be a job for you when you come back." So the first lesson that I would offer from my life is I took a risk. I said, "Well, this looks interesting. I'm going to go do it." And I never really saw myself as a career person at CIA, but people just kept offering me interesting things to do. So I think that the fundamental lesson from my story is the willingness to take a chance, to understand that the only way you really get ahead is to take risks from time to time, sensible risks, but risks nonetheless, and to be open to opportunities that seem to come from nowhere and which were never part of your plan, and then you end up someplace else. I have one final example. I had no connection with Texas A&M University. And when the first President Bush called me, his museum and library is at Texas A&M, and they have a school of government and public service, a grad program, a master's program at A&M. And he said, "We need an interim dean," because it was a brand-new school.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: "We need an interim dean. Would you be willing to do this? It's only a day or two a month for nine months till we hire a permanent dean." Well, it ended up being two weeks a month for two years, but I got to know A&M. They got to know me. Lo and behold, I'm asked to be a candidate for president of the university. I become president of Texas A&M. I never anticipated being the president of a university. And I think had I not been president of Texas A&M and a little bit in the limelight, I'm not sure I would have ever been asked to become Secretary of Defense. So doing a favor for a friend, being willing to become the interim dean of the Bush School, at a fairly advanced point in my life, leads to a whole new set of opportunities and challenges that I never anticipated. So I think that the key in all of this, in addition to being willing to take a risk, is to be open to new paths that weren't part of your plan, and you never know where they'll lead.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: So have a great plan, but always be open and making sure. Yeah, and I would tell young people, I'd say, "The harsh reality is you've got to do all the hard work of preparation, and you may or may not be extremely successful. But if you don't do the preparation, you won't be successful. That's just a guarantee." Wise words. And the couple of things that you were just mentioning as far as looking for opportunity, taking risks, being open, those are things that you captured in a 50-year career here in your book, "A Passion for Leadership." And so, jumping right into that book, one of the things that struck me right away was your dedication at the very beginning. Dedicated the book to those who serve the public good. Can you tell us the inspiration behind that and the inspiration behind the book? One of the major reasons that I wrote the book was, I really didn't decide to do it until I was asked to stay on by President Obama.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And then I realized I had ended up with this rather extraordinary group of experiences that involved leadership of major organizations, and in particular, in every one of them, leading change and leading reform, making them better than they were, trying to adapt them to new circumstances, and trying to take care of the young people in my charge, whether it was at CIA or at Texas A&M or in the Defense Department. And my concern that because of our polarized politics and the paralysis that we see, that young people would be cynical about going into public service. "It's just a mess. Why would I get involved in that?" And what was especially tragic for me is I watched it at, particularly at Texas A&M, but I've seen it at William & Mary and elsewhere, is young people in college today are more involved in volunteerism and in doing public service as college students than I think they've ever been before in history. And yet, when they get out of college, they tend to put all that behind them.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And part of the book, part of the reason for the book, is to show young people that institutions can be reformed, can be changed. Because a lot of the reasons that young people don't go into government is because of the hierarchy, because of the bureaucracy, because it's seen as stifling. And what I try and point out in the book is that at these three very different places, I was able to change the bureaucracy. I was able to change things and make them better, make them more user-friendly, make them more satisfying for the people who work there. So I hope through the book to encourage young people to consider public service, if not as a full-time career, as some part of their life. President Bush has said, "No life can be complete without some measure of public service," the first President Bush, and I believe that. And for a lot of students who are sitting there, as you said, they're looking at the life in the public sector and kind of going, "Well, why would I do that?" With all the bureaucracy, red tape, and challenges that come into that, what would you say to them?

speaker: Robert Gates
text: As far as jumping into a career, what can they do to navigate that system and to create that change, to go in there and be that reformist in the system? Well, I think you have to have a certain measure of boldness. I wrote my first article for an in-house publication at CIA on how we could improve our analysis of the Soviet Union two years after I'd been there. So in 1970. So I'd been there two years. You can imagine how welcoming my supervisors were when I was telling them, it's two years in, how to do their jobs better. But you have to take measured risks, and you have to figure out how to navigate your way through the bureaucracy. One of the things that I advise young people is that when they get that first job, is to hang on to it for at least two to three years. Establish a reputation for competence, for innovative thinking, for doing the job really well, and as well as for kind of character and integrity.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And once you've established a reputation where people actually begin to have a stake in your success because you're a proven quantity now, that's the point at which you can begin to take some chances and try new things and ask for new opportunities from bosses. But the first thing is, you can't do that six months in or a year in. You really have to establish a strong foundation first, and then you have the opportunity to try a lot of different things. And I think that there's a lot of perception within the public sector for students that career advancement or moving ahead can be very stifling, or be stifled, be limited, held back. In your experience, though, you actually were given a promotion, I believe it was at CIA, above some other senior-level folks, and somebody took a chance on you. Can you talk a little bit about that experience and what you think you did to earn that? One of the things that's important, I think a lot of young people know the importance of having a mentor. And my point to them is, you need a lot of mentors.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And as you grow and as you assume greater responsibilities, the mentor you had when you were brand new is not going to help you grow. You always need to be looking two or three levels above you. "Who can teach me something? Who can I learn from? Who will help advance my career?" And so I like to tell people that my first mentor was a GS-14 at CIA, and my last mentor was President of the United States.And the problem is, if you just rely on one mentor, then you're going to plateau wherever that person is. And if you want to keep growing, you need to keep looking up. And by the same token, that will give you more visibility and more opportunity. But the other piece of it is, and this is what I did, was once you've established that foundation, the reputational foundation of being a very capable person, then take the opportunity to move around and get different kinds of experiences.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: I think that the main reason I was named Director of Central Intelligence was because in the nine years I spent at the White House, at the National Security Council, under four different presidents, I knew more about how presidents used intelligence than anybody else in the government, because I'd seen four very different presidents, Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, and then first President Bush. And that, I think, played a big part in President Bush's decision to nominate me to be Director of Central Intelligence. But I think the government is getting smarter about this, at least at the federal level. And one of the things the military is doing, for example, is taking young officers and giving them the chance to go to graduate school or to serve an internship or a year in a company, in a tech company or something like that. So I think taking advantage of these opportunities to get diverse experiences, and it will follow you all the way through your career.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: I would tell four-star generals, "I will not appoint you to be a combatant commander, the commander of Central Command or Strategic Command, because you've only done one thing your whole career. You have no perspective outside of your narrow window of visibility, and I need somebody who's got broad perspective." So once you, again, establish that foundation, taking on different kinds of jobs that give you a broader perspective and more diversity of experience in almost every organization, that will serve you well in the long run. So you have a student who builds a foundation, stays two to three years in their role, finds a mentor, starts moving around strategically to get that experience. One of the things you cover really well in your book is the limitations outside of their control, elected bodies within the public sector, that can be a challenge. So can you talk about the impact of elected bodies on the public sector, but then more importantly, how students can kind of navigate through that?

speaker: Robert Gates
text: So the key is figuring out how you or your boss can get public opinion on your side by doing things or framing the changes you want to make in a way that is so self-evidently beneficial to the public that it's very hard to oppose. Sometimes you're going to be able to get these people on your side, and one of the things that I have found in dealing with elected officials in particular is you often end up in front of them when something has gone wrong. And the best way to deal with it, and it's very hard for them to counter, is to go in, sit down, say, "Here's what went wrong, here's the problem, here's why it happened, and here's what I'm doing to fix it." Because then all they can say is, "Well, yeah, go do that." I mean, they can keep coming back at you, "Why did this happen?" And you can always say, "Well, as I said," and then you just repeat yourself. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: But if you grab the bull by the horns, as it were, if you take charge of the problem and say, "Here's what happened and here's how I'm going to fix it," it basically doesn't give them any place to go. You take that responsibility, you take that accountability, and it takes that wind out of their sails. And you also take all their talking points. That's fantastic. Thank you. So you have a leader who has stepped in. They're navigating the system around. One of the things that you focus on a lot are the tactics in being an effective leader within the public sector, and a unique part that I pulled from your book was about task force, the use of them and what you did at Texas A&M about culture, but then also the repeal of Don't Ask, Don't Tell. Can you talk about what task forces are, but then how they can be managed efficiently and effectively towards that end goal? Yeah. One of my favorite quotes is that a committee is a cul-de-sac down which ideas are lured and then quietly strangled.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: But I think that part of the problem with almost every organization is that vertical communication, especially, well, up and down works pretty well, but there's often very little lateral communication across different elements of an organization. So forming some kind of an ad hoc committee or a task force allow... I call them silo busters because it makes people from different parts of an organization talk to each other who normally wouldn't have an interaction with each other. And collectively, they can often come up with some really good ideas on how to fix problems. And you will establish relationships across the organization that last after the task force has gone away. Now, I believe task forces need to be very short in duration for the most part.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: When I was Director of Central Intelligence, I took over six weeks before the collapse of the Soviet Union, and I had to redirect the entire intelligence community away from the singular focus on the Soviet Union and the Cold War to a very different world.At one point, I had 24 different task forces operating simultaneously on every aspect of the intelligence business, but the longest deadline any of them had was three months. The longer you go, the worse the product, and you definitely do not want consensus. Consensus is an idea killer and a lot of people spend endless hours in meetings trying to get consensus. It's a waste of time. The key is to sharpen differences so that whoever's in charge can then make decisions and make choices. But task forces, there were a couple of task forces when I was Secretary of Defense that I kept for quite a while. One was trying to get immediate capabilities into the hands of the troops to deal with IEDs and other challenges where we needed solutions in weeks or days, not years.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And so I kept that task force in being because the Department of Defense is so huge and so many different parts of the department are involved in any decision that there's actually only one person who can bring them all together, knock heads, and make a decision, and that's the secretary. Because everybody has their finger in the pie and you've got to figure out how to bring them together, get the information you need, and then make a decision, and then make everybody go away and do their job. And so I use task forces a lot. But as I say, nine times out of 10, they need to have very short deadlines. Do not go for consensus. And the other virtue of task forces is to make sure you construct them in a way that the people who are going to have to implement the decisions are part of the task force because they will ensure that the solutions are actually workable. Because they've got to be the ones to go do it once the task force is done and the decision is made.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: So if you have people involved in the task force who are going to have to actually implement it, it helps make the results more practical and more workable. And it's really a new concept, I think, for a lot of young student leaders in thinking about going into an organization, creating that kind of change, but then how to do that and getting those task forces, getting the right players at the table. There's a lot of training programs or leadership programs and so on. It's in companies, in universities, you name it, in the military, on how to improve group dynamics, how to build teams, how to work together, and so on and so forth. That's all good and that's all very important. But every young person needs to know that at some point, they're going to have to stand alone. That they will have to make a decision that may be unpopular, that people won't like, won't agree with, and because they have the responsibility, they have to make that decision, and they're going to have to stand alone.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: Or people will be wanting to do something in a way that that young person knows is wrong or is unethical. And at that point, you have to plant your feet and say, "This is wrong," or, "This is not the right thing to do, and I'm not going to be a part of it." And you have to prepare yourself for that. You don't suddenly develop that kind of character and integrity at 50 years old. It begins even while you're in college, but in your jobs as a young person. And you don't want to be self-righteous about it, but at a certain point you will face those choices. When I made the decision to reduce the medevac time in Afghanistan from two hours to one hour, there wasn't a single senior person in uniform or civilian in the Department of Defense who supported that. And the reason was, they weren't harsh, they weren't being cruel, but their view was statistically it really wouldn't matter very much in terms of the number of people who survived. My attitude was, this is a matter of moral obligation and morale.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And only years later did we discover that it probably also saved somewhere north of 500 lives. Wow. What an impact. And so getting that student who's young in their career and getting them to the point where they are feeling confident enough, how can students approach the leadership training that they're going into? Whether it's an organization like ours, the Society, where they're building those skills, or any organization. How can they maximize those opportunities as they're seeking them out? Well, I think partly it's by observing other people. It's by observing people who have been successful leaders and the lessons learned from that. It's by observing and talking to their friends and peers, to their professors, to administrators at the college. It's mainly about what in the intelligence business they call situational awareness. It's being aware of what's going on around you and learning from every piece of the environment, that over time gives you those skills. And the key is, and particularly in these kinds of programs and others, is through exercises or through student government or something, just getting some experience in doing these things. Last question for you.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: I want to bring you back to the book. There's so many different tips, so many different tactics. When I was going through it and actually reading it, where you're taking them through vision, strategic thinking, attention to implementation, transparency. What do you want people to take away from this book? Beyond the tactics, beyond what you are giving them as tools, what do you want them to take away from this book? I think the major message in the book is thatPeople, not systems, make change and make the world better. And how you treat people is important, how you deal with people, how you take care of people who work for you and with you, how you look out for their interests, how you keep your ego under control. But it's all about understanding the people around you and treating them as colleagues and people who are valued, whose work is valued. And if they're subordinates, empowering them. So it's all about, if there's one underlying theme in the book is that it's at the end of the day, it's all about people. I'll give you one example of the importance of little gestures of respect.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: It was at the end of the Camp David negotiations for Middle East peace between Egypt and Israel, and the National Security Advisor, Zbigniew Brzezinski, and I flew into Cairo a day ahead of President Carter to nail down the final details with President Anwar Sadat of Egypt. Now, this was close to 40 years ago. And to this day, I will never forget Brzezinski introducing me to President Sadat as his colleague. Not his aide, not his staff person, but as his colleague. Just a tiny gesture of respect. But all the things that I've done in my life, I remember that to this day. So never underestimate the importance of small gestures of respect and of empowering people as you navigate your way through your career. What a great exclamation point and period to put on the end of that last question. Thank you so much for that. To our leaders and viewers, we hope that you've enjoyed your time in hearing the story and the tips from Dr. Robert Gates.

speaker: Robert Gates
text: And on behalf of our national organization, on behalf of 500 colleges and our 600,000 members, we want to present you as an honorary member of the National Society of Leadership and Success. Thank you. Thank you for joining us here today. Thank you very much. And to our leaders watching, we want to encourage you, as you take that next step towards your own success, we want to encourage you to make sure that you're also taking into account being a leader who makes a better world. Until next time. Thank you.

speaker: Slava Rubin
text: There's a concept of crowdsourcing. Crowdsourcing can really relate to anything, but crowdsourcing means getting lots of small bits of something aggregated so you get one lump sum of a concept. For example, right now you can see us because there's light, but let's say it was dark. What we probably would do is have everybody pull out their cell phones, and we would right away start turning on our flashlights on our cell phones. Similarly, crowdfunding is a concept of getting lots of small bits of money to accomplish a big bucket of money that is needed.This actually goes all the way back to the Statue of Liberty. So the Statue of Liberty by Jo was a gift from the French, but the base actually cost $300,000, and if we didn't afford the base, we wouldn't actually get the gift to put the statue on. speaker: Slava Rubin
text: The US was able to get half of it in the late 1800s, about 150,000 from private investors, but they were missing the other 150. text: I have no idea what it is, but if you're passionate and authentic about what you're trying to accomplish, you will be able to persevere through the ups and the downs. text: We're trying to build a lifelong relationship with each and every single customer. So if you go to the next slide, please. So you may think that our number one priority in the company is customer service, because that's what we want our brand to be about, but it's actually not. Our number one priority is company culture. Our whole belief is that if you get the culture right, then most of the other stuff, like great customer service or building a great long-term brand, will just happen naturally on its own. And so that's the business reason. And then there's also the personal reason for me. We made a lot of mistakes during my LinkExchange experience, and I just want to make sure that we don't make those same mistakes again. So what are the things that we do for company culture?

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: First of all, everyone that's hired in our headquarters, it doesn't matter what position you are, you can be an accountant or a lawyer or a software programmer, goes through the same training as our call center reps. And that's four weeks of training in our Las Vegas facility, where we go over company culture, our philosophy about customer service, how to use the customer service tools, and you're actually on the phone for two hours taking calls from customers. And after that, then we'll send you to Kentucky for a week, which is where our warehouse is, and you do all the different warehouse functions: picking, packing, shipping, receiving, and so on. And the reason we do that is because if we truly want our brand to be about customer service, then our belief is that customer service shouldn't just be a department. It should be the entire company. And then the other great thing about that, as a side effect, is that during our busy season, people from all different departments can hop on the phones and take calls from customers because they're already trained in doing so.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: The other thing we do as part of that training is at the end of the first week of training, we actually make an offer to everyone that's come through, and we say, "We'll pay you for the time that you've already spent training. But in addition, we'll pay you $2,000 to quit and leave the company." And that's a standing offer until the end of four weeks of training. And what we found is that-- Well, the original motivation for that was we didn't want people there that were there for just a paycheck. In Las Vegas, there's plenty of other call centers, and if you're looking to make money in the short term, then the right thing to do would be to take that offer and quit. And $2,000 for a call center rep is a pretty significant amount of money. And so actually, the first year we offered it, in 2000... Well, we've actually offered it for a few years, but we keep raising the offer. In 2007, we had about 3% of people take the offer. In 2008, we had less than 1% of people take the offer.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And the offer actually started at $100, and we keep upping it because not enough people are taking it. And so we may actually end up making the offer even higher. But there's the benefit of people leaving because if they're not really committed to the company and our culture and our core values and our mission about being about the very best customer service, then they're probably not going to last long anyways. They probably will be there for another six to nine months. So it actually ends up saving the company in the long run. But what we actually found was that the real value comes from the people that don't take the offer because they still have to go home and think about it, talk to their friends and family, and ask themselves, "Is this a company that I believe in? Do I want to be part of this culture? Do I believe in the long-term vision? Because I can make an easy $2,000 right now." And what we found was after they decide not to take the offer, they end up being a lot more committed to the company and a lot more engaged.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And that was just an unanticipated side effect and actually ended up being one of the, I would say, the biggest benefit from having the offer. We also have something called a culture book, which I have over here on the side. And we'll be happy to send you one for free, but this is something that we put out once a year, and we ask all of our employees to write a few paragraphs about what the Zappos culture means to them. And except for typos, it's unedited. So you get to read both the good and the bad. So think of it as kind of like customer reviews you might read on a website, except these are employee reviews of a company. And it's also organized by categories, by department, so you can see how the accounting culture might be slightly different from the warehouse culture. And then there's also pictures in there and so on. And this one is 480 pages, and we put it out once a year, and we ask employees to write something different every year.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And I'll give information at the end of this presentation about how to get a copy of that.And then we interview for culture. We actually do two different sets of interviews. The hiring manager and his or her team will do the standard set of interviews looking for fit within the team, relevant technical experience and ability, and so on. But then our HR department does a separate set of interviews purely for culture fit, and they have to pass both in order to be hired. So we've actually passed on a lot of really talented people that would have made a significant impact on our top or bottom line. But if we think they're bad for the culture, we won't hire them. And then the same thing goes for firing. Even if someone is doing their specific job function perfectly fine and performing well in terms of that function, if they're bad for the culture, we will fire them. And our performance reviews are 50% based on how much an employee lives or inspires the culture in others.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And even after they're hired, the whole training process, that four or five-week period, we're continuing to evaluate to make sure that people are right for the culture. In Las Vegas, it's actually pretty hard to hire for technical positions. And so we had this position open that was a pretty senior position technically. And so we were pretty happy that we finally found a candidate after looking for six or nine months to fill the position, someone that we were relocating from LA to Las Vegas. But by the end of the first week of training, it was very clear that he thought that customer service was beneath him. And so we actually just ended up firing him and then relocating him back to LA before he even started the job that he was actually hired to do. So we take culture very seriously, and I'll give some examples later on on how we interview for culture and how we exactly define our culture.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: So I wanted to share some of the things that we think are very important, but before doing so, wanted to share a couple stories to illustrate how the culture has really helped build our brand at Zappos and affected the customer experience. So the first story has to do with... This happened a couple years ago. We had a woman that was looking for a pair of boots for her husband. And she had gone to two or three different malls looking for this very specific pair of boots that she knew her husband liked, and after several days searching, came back empty-handed. And then she looked online and looked on a few different websites before she found Zappos and wasn't able to find them. But then she finally found them on Zappos, and she was very excited because she had been looking for these boots to surprise her husband with as a gift for a long time. And so she ordered them, and she got the surprise upgrade to overnight shipping, which we do for a lot of our customers, especially our repeat customers.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And she got them the next day, and she was very excited and ready to give them to her husband when he came home from work. Well, unfortunately, the husband actually never made it home from work the next day. He was actually killed in a car accident on the way home. And so he actually never got to see the boots that his wife had gotten for him as a surprise. And so, a couple days later, the widow called our customer loyalty team and explained the situation and asked for help with the return process. And like any good company would, the rep that she talked to stepped her through the return process and then basically gave her the step-by-step instructions, made sure she understood how to do everything. But then after the widow hung up, the rep took it upon herself to send flowers to the widow to show our condolences as a company. And when the widow received the flowers, she was so moved and touched that a company would actually care to do that.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And at the funeral two or three days later, told the 30 or so people, friends and family that were there about that experience, and then emailed us back and told us that not only was she a customer for life now, but so were those 30 or 40 other people. And clearly this type of situation doesn't happen very often. And we obviously don't have a process or procedure for it, but it's just an example where if you get the culture right, because the rep understood what our long-term vision was about what we wanted to build the Zappos brand into, and because we hire for culture and because we empower all our reps to do whatever they think is the right thing to do for the customer, they don't have to go get supervisor permission or so on. It's just an illustration of if you get the culture right, then most of the other stuff, like these stories that help build the brand, and we get 5,000 phone calls a day, and then we get emails and so on.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: So stories like these are being created every single day, thousands of thousands of times, and that's part of what builds the Zappos brand. Wanted to tell another story illustrating another department where we had a woman order a wallet from us, and she got it overnight as well, and tried it out for about a week or so.And then decided it wasn't quite right for her, and so she sent it back to us using the free return shipping. Well, what she didn't realize was that she had actually accidentally left $150 inside the wallet. And, well, she had two kids, and so she spent the next couple of days trying to chasing them around the house, trying to get one of them to fess up, because she was pretty sure it was one of them, or maybe they were in on it together. But she couldn't know, and none of them would fess up. And then a few days later, she received an envelope in the mail from the warehouse employee that had processed the return. And it said, "Dear so and so, Received your return. Thanks for shopping at Zappos.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: But you left $150 in it and thought you might want it back, so- ... here it is." And then we heard back, and then that customer called us and told us she was just completely amazed by that experience. Because this is a warehouse worker that is making close to minimum wage, could've easily pocketed the money, but because in the warehouse we also hire for culture and make sure everyone understands the long-term vision for Zappos, that just happened naturally on its own. And we could have developed a special process or procedure where people processing returns work in a high security area, and they're strip searched on the way out by their supervisor or so on. And that would have incurred additional costs, but rather than incur those costs, we've decided that it makes more sense to invest in the hiring and training process. And then these types of things just take care of themselves. So I want to talk about the four things that we believe at Zappos for building a brand that matters, for building a long-term brand. And the first thing is about vision.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: Actually, when we first started, we did not have this plan of Zappos being about the very best customer service. Really, this was back in '99 when all these other dotcoms were starting, and all we wanted to do was just try to sell some shoes online and make some money from it. And we kind of did that for the first few years, but then we sat around one day and asked ourselves, "What do we want to be when we grow up? Do we want to be about shoes, or do we want to be about something bigger and more meaningful?" And we all decided, let's try to be about something more meaningful. And that's really how we settled into being about the very best customer service and customer experience. And what we found was that when we decided that we were going to be not just about profits and not just about shoes, but about customer experience and something that actually mattered more in the world, that employees became a lot more engaged and passionate about the company.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And then when employees talked to customers and vendors, the customers and vendors could sense that employees were a lot more passionate and engaged, and that actually just made the customers and vendors more excited about working with the company or dealing with the company. And so in kind of a weird, ironic way, by trying to chase a vision that was bigger and not about money, that actually helped fuel our growth and become more dominant, and ultimately the money just followed. And so a lot of times when I speak at entrepreneur conferences, people ask me, "What's a good business to go into? What's a big market?" And so on. "Where do I have the chance of making the most money?" And my response is, actually, don't chase the money. Chase the vision. Chase your passion. And do something where you'd be so happy and passionate about doing it that you'd be willing to do it for 10 years, even if you didn't make a dime over those 10 years. And if you do that, then there's a few reasons for that.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: One is you're going to come across hard times no matter what, like every business does, and usually multiple times. And if you're not passionate about what you're doing, if you're doing it just for the money, you're not going to make it through those hard times. And then the second reason is because you'll just get employees that are a lot more engaged and customers that end up becoming a lot more engaged because they can sense whether you're doing it for the passion or for the money. And the really weird thing is that if you're doing it because you truly believe in the vision and you're passionate about it, then that will actually make you more successful. Craigslist is a great example where Craig did not want to-- He didn't set out thinking, "Oh, what kind of service can I create and make a lot of money at?" He was just truly passionate about the community he was building. And then kind of the success and all the traffic that he ended up getting was a result of people seeing his passion for what he was building.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: The second thing that I want to talk about that we think is really important is repeat customers. When Zappos first started, we actually did the same thing that every other dotcom was doing at the time. We spent a lot of money on high-profile advertising, all in the name of capturing market share, or trying to acquire as many customers as quickly as possible. I actually remember we spent $75,000 in the early days buying a billboard behind the home plate at the Giants baseball stadium in San Francisco. And at the end of the season, we tracked how many new customers we actually got, and it came out to a grand total of three new customers during the entire season. So we thought a $25,000 customer acquisition cost was a little high. But then this was during the whole period of the first dotcom crash, the recession. There was a war, 9/11. And so we couldn't raise money for the next several years. And so we actually were-Stumbled, I would say, into focusing on repeat customers because we didn't have the money to spend on marketing.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And so that actually ended up being a blessing in disguise because that's what led us to us really being a company about taking care of our existing customers, just being about the very best customer service. So basically, in March of 2001, it shows that 20% of our customers that bought in March of 2001 bought again over the next 12 months. And then of the ones that did buy again over the next 12 months, they bought one and a half times. And then the last column is just the two numbers multiplied together. And then you can see that in March of 2007, that number percentage of customers that bought again over the next 12 months increased to about 55%, and they bought an average of 2.7 times. And then the last column is just those two numbers multiplied together. And so that's really what we focus on at Zappos, seeing how with every improvement we make to the customer experience, whether it's getting them their order faster or answering phones 24/7 or extending our return policy to now it's 365 days, all of those things had an effect on increasing our repeat customer behavior.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And so then the third thing that we really believe in is transparency, and it's actually one of our core values at Zappos is to be open and honest. And companies with Web 2.0 and blogging and Twittering and so on, transparency is happening to all companies whether they like it or not. And I think that's why a lot of larger companies are actually having trouble nowadays because an employee or a customer that has a bad experience with your company could write up a blog and then suddenly it's read by millions of people. But the reverse is true as well. They can have a great experience with a company and then that's read by millions of people. And so at Zappos, we try to be as transparent as possible, whether it's with our customers or our employees or even with our vendors. So as an example, we work with about 1,500 different vendors, and they can log into our extranet and see the exact same information that our own buyers can see. They can see on-hand inventory, what sales are, what profits are, and so on. And we get questions from a lot of vendors.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: "Well, doesn't that actually-- Aren't you worried about that information getting into the hands of competitors?" And the answer is, yes, it's probably true that eventually some of that information does get into the hands of competitors. But on the flip side, we have an extra 1,500 pairs of eyes helping us manage our business together. And to them, they're much more invested because it feels like a partnership. And one of our buyers has a portfolio of 15 or 20 brands, they may miss this one style for a specific brand. Whereas on the brand side, if they have a rep that is dedicated to that brand, then they might see that something is running low on inventory and place that order again. And so our belief is that the benefits far outweigh any risk or cost to that. And for employees, we have a newsletter called Ask Anything, where it's literally that. Employees can email in and ask us any question they want about the company, and we'll answer them. They could be questions about financials, or they could be questions about when are we going to carry this brand?

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: Or sometimes they're just silly questions like why or do vegetarians eat animal c\*\*\*\*\*\*s? And then we'll research that and answer them and so on. And then the culture book is another example of how we're trying to be as transparent as possible. And I talked a bit about the tours that come through the office. We give tours every day, every weekday that is. And we've also had companies come in, such as Southwest Airlines or Lego or Best Buy, because they want to study either how we do customer service or what we do for company culture. And we're very open with all of them. We share whatever they want to ask. If they want to know what our interview questions are or what are our QA forms for scoring calls, we share all of that. And that's just part of our culture of being as transparent and open and honest as possible. And then I talked a lot about culture as well. And I wanted to actually talk a little bit about how we define our culture at Zappos. And it basically comes down to core values. And we have 10 core values at Zappos.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: A lot of companies have core values, or some companies might call them guiding principles. But the difference and the keyword here is committable core values. Most companies, I would say, especially bigger companies, their core values are something that it reads like a press release, and it's not really that meaningful. It's something you might learn on day one of orientation, and then it's kind of a meaningless plaque in the lobby. And by committable, what we mean is that you're willing to hire or fire people based on whether they're living up to those core values, even if they're doing their job function perfectly well. And so actually coming up with that list of core values is a very hard thing to do. It actually took us a year at Zappos to come up with a list of core values. And the way we went about it, it wasn't just a few senior managers sitting in a room and just at some offsite trying to figure out what our core values were. We actually asked all our employees, "What should we be when we grow up?

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: What do you want Zappos's core values to be?" And we got answers from almost every employee of what they thought the Zappos core values would be and compiled that original list. And that original list actually came out to a list of 37 core values. And we thought that might be a little hard for employees to memorize. And so we went back and forth and combined some of them and some that meant the same thing but were just different ways of saying the same thing.And then eventually came up with a list of 10 core values that we wanted Zappos to be for. You'll see our list of 10 core values and I'll talk about some of them and how we interview for them. So, number three is create fun and a little weirdness. And actually, when this first came out, that was actually the most polarizing core value because people either loved it or they hated it. But we've actually incorporated it into our hiring process. One of our interview questions is, "On a scale of one to 10, how weird are you?" And so, if you're a one, you're probably too straight-laced for our culture.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: If you're a 10, you're probably too psychotic for us. But for us, it's more of about a fun way of talking about how we really celebrate everyone's individuality. And you can see that through the phone calls that we have with customers because we don't have scripts. You might call twice, and the first time you call, you're talking to a rep that is chatty, loves to joke around, and is telling jokes while you're on the phone, and you walk away laughing. And then the second time you call, maybe it's someone with a different personality that's not quite as bubbly but still gives great customer service in his own way. And we don't really say you have to act this way or act this way. We encourage reps to let their own true personality shine, and as long as they're going above and beyond and the customer walks away thinking that was great customer service, that's all we care about. And when you come to our offices, you'll see that people decorate their cubes or aisles differently. Mine is themed after the Rainforest Cafe. There's vines and trees overhead.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And then in another aisle, there's a pirate theme, and people just come up with their own themes, and we really encourage employees to just express their own individuality. Number ten is to be humble. And actually, I would say during the interview process, this is the one that we come across the most. We come across a lot of really smart, really talented people that are just egotistical. And it's very easy when our HR department does their set of interviews for culture fit, they can tell whether they're egotistical and then just won't hire them. Now, what would happen in most companies is people would talk and say, "This person can add a lot of value for the company because they can. They're smart, they perform well, and so on. He might rub you the wrong way and might annoy a lot of people, but let's hire him because he's going to add value to the company." And that's how the company culture starts going downhill, and that's why so many large companies have bad company cultures.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And it's not like that one hire is going to make the company culture suddenly go downhill, but you keep making compromises like that over and over again, it all adds up. And then eventually, you wind up with the situation I wound up with at LinkExchange, which is it becomes a place where you don't want to go into anymore. Core value number four, be adventurous, creative, and open-minded. Our interview question for this is, on a scale of one to 10, how lucky are you? One, I don't know why bad things always seem to happen to me. Ten, I don't know why good things always seem to happen to me. So we generally don't want to hire the bad luck people because we don't want to bring bad luck to Zappos. And we try to hire as many of the good luck people as possible. But this was actually inspired by a research study that I had read about a few years ago, where they got a whole bunch of random people and actually asked that exact question, on a scale of one to 10, how lucky are you in life?

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And they got answers all over the board. And then afterwards, the researchers asked the subjects to go through a newspaper and count the number of photos there were in that newspaper, and then tell the researchers the answer at the end. Well, what the subject didn't know was that it was actually a fake newspaper, and sprinkled throughout the newspaper were headlines that said, "If you're reading this headline right now, collect an extra $100. And by the way, the answer is 37." And what they found was that the people that consider themselves unlucky in life generally just went through the task at hand and never noticed the headlines. And the people that consider themselves lucky in life generally noticed the headline, stopped early, and collected the extra $100. So, the takeaway is that it's not about people being inherently more lucky or less lucky, but a lot of luck is just about being open to opportunities beyond the specific task at hand. And so that's how one of the ways we look for people that are adventurous and creative and open-minded. So for Zappos, what do we want our brand to be about?

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: Most people know us for shoes, so one of the big challenges we have for our brand is how do we actually get people to think of us beyond just shoes? And we're actually making a big push into clothing this year. Clothing is actually four times the size of the footwear market, so we think, especially in this economy, it's a huge opportunity for us to continue growing. And so for customers that haven't heard of us, we really want them to know about our selection of clothing. And actually, we have a pretty good selection of clothing today. Anything from jeans to tops to everything else. And then for customers that know us for clothing, we want them to know about our customer service. And then for customers that know about our customer service, we want them to know us for our culture because ultimately, we think that really, it's all about culture. Our whole belief is that a company's culture and a company's brand are really just two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: Your brand may lag your culture, but eventually it's going to catch up, especially in this whole world where things are becoming more and more transparent. And building a brand today is very different from how you would build a brand 50 years ago. Fifty years ago, a bunch of people would-Sit around a room and say, "Okay, this is what our brand's going to be," and then spend a lot of money on TV advertising, broadcast that out. People didn't really have anyone to talk to except their neighbors, and so, whatever people advertised on TV that their brand was about, that's what their brand was about. But today, because consumers are so hyper-connected, you're no longer, as a company, in control of your brand. Your consumers are, and they're able to communicate with each other lightning-fast. So as an example, think about what is the brand of the airline industry as a whole, not any specific airline company, but the industry as a whole. If you ask a bunch of random people, most of them would probably say something about bad customer service or bad experiences and that is what the brand of the industry is.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And I don't think any airline actually sat in a room saying, "Hey, let's make our brand about being about bad customer service." And so that's why we really believe that if you get the culture right, then the brand will follow on its own, and if you care about customer service, then great customer service will follow on its own as well. And so whether it's about clothing or about customer service or about culture, overall, the Zappos brand, Zappos, is really just about delivering happiness to customers and to employees. And we really strive to make a personal emotional impact on our employees and with our vendors and ultimately on our customers as well. I began with a pizza story, so I wanted to end with a pizza story. This story actually happened a couple of years ago at a sales conference for Skechers. Skechers is one of the brands that we work with. And after the conference was over, a group of probably about six or seven of us went out bar hopping in Santa Monica. And it was probably about three or four Zappos people and three or four people from Skechers.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And I hadn't really been to Santa Monica before, so we wanted to hop as many bars as possible. And so we went to the first bar, had a drink, went to the second bar, had a drink, and then went to the third bar, had yet another drink. And we probably should've stopped then. But we continued hopping, and I would say probably had maybe one drink too many. And I know there's a lot of college students in the audience, so you may know what that's like. But we actually ended up shutting the bars down, and we went back to someone's hotel room in the hotel that we were staying at, all six or seven of us. And the woman from Skechers said, "You know what? I'm really, really hungry. I really would like a hot pizza right now." And so we're like, "Okay, well, why don't you go ahead and call room service?" So she called room service, and room service informed her that they only serve hot food only before 11:00 PM. And by now, it was, like, 2:00 or 3:00 AM.

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: And so she was all dejected and I told her, "Hey, did you know when I was in college, I used to sell pizza?" And she was like, "That's not helpful at all." And so the other Zappos people were like, "Well, call Zappos. Call Zappos. We're all about the very best customer service." And we thought it was the funniest thing at the time in our slightly inebriated state. And so she actually took us up on the dare and put it on speakerphone and called Zappos. And the rep answered the phone, didn't know that the rest of us were listening, and the Skechers person said, "I'm really, really hungry right now. I'm in Santa Monica. I want a hot pizza. The room service doesn't deliver after 11:00 PM. What do I do?" There was an awkward silence. And then the rep said, "You know you called Zappos, right?

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: We don't sell pizza yet." And so she's like, "Yeah, but I'm really hungry, and I really want a pizza." And the rep said, "Okay, hold on," and then put us on hold for two minutes and then came back and listed the five closest places in Santa Monica that were still open and delivering pizza. Now, I hesitate a little to tell this story because I don't want all of you to start ordering pizza. But I just think it's a fun story to illustrate my point that if you get the culture right, then most of the other stuff, like great customer service, just happens naturally on its own. And so my email address is tony,

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: presentation. I know we're going to have Q\&A, but if we don't get to any questions that you may have, feel free to email me. The culture book that I mentioned, we'll be happy to send you one, but we need your physical mailing address because it's a physical book. If you're ever in Las Vegas, come by for a tour of our offices. We give tours on Mondays through Thursdays. Or if you're looking for a job, we're hiring. And then next slide, please. And then here are some links to different websites. I'm very active on Twitter. Actually, our whole company is very active on Twitter. And we actually have over 400 employees that are on Twitter, and we have a page that aggregates all of them. But my Twitter name is just Zappos,

speaker: Tony Hsieh
text: It's actually a new subscription service that we launched, but there's a bunch of free videos there as well, as well as a list of suggested books that we have in our Zappos library, which we have right in our lobby, actually, and we give out to employees and visitors. And those are really just books that we really try to get all our employees to read. So those are all the different ways you can learn more about Zappos. And that's it. So thank you very much.

text: And so, as a startup business, he's looking for clients.
