Well, folks would come, and I would be present, and people would walk up to me and say, "Well, what do you do?" And I would say, "Well, I'm a housewife." I'd just recently gotten married and I was so excited and I saw the response. And the response was, "Oh." That didn't seem to matter, and as a result, it didn't make me feel so good. And what translated ultimately was that I realized that being a housewife wasn't impressive to others. And, honestly, to this day, I really struggle with when people ask me that question, "What do you do?" Like, in a matter of seconds, I'm supposed to decide whether or not I'm worthy. So, I really struggle. Instead, I like to ask people, "What's your passion?" You know, "What are you doing that you love?" That is something I can really connect to.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: So, so it happened, I didn't feel so good being always asked that question and having folks not being really impressed. So, my big breakthrough came when we were invited to this gentleman's home, and Randy was going to give him a presentation. We were going to have dinner. And I will tell you this was absolutely one of those experiences that truly was life-changing for me, in that, when we arrived, I see that we come to this magnificent, massive gate. And the gates open, and we go up the circular driveway to a very large, hand-carved door. And Sandy meets us at the entrance, and he welcomes us into his home. And his wife, we get a chance to meet. And she's putting the final touches on dinner. And so Sandy says, "Okay, let's go in the library." So I follow Sandy into the library, and I realize, as I'm walking down the hall, that Randy is not behind me and he must, obviously, still be in the kitchen with his wife. Well, I try to make myself comfortable and Sandy leads me into this beautiful library that's really got wood paneling that's not Formica.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And I try to sit down in this beautiful, supple leather couch that's not Naugahyde. And here I am, just, like, really nervous. And Sandy says, "Well, Debbi, "what are you doing with your life?" And I wanted to impress him. and I said, "Well, Sandy, I'm trying to get orientated." Sandy was absolutely appalled. He got up, and he walked over to a bookcase. And I saw he grabbed a very large -- and as he was approaching, I saw it was a leather-bound dictionary. And he stood before me, and he said, "Listen, "if you cannot speak "the English language, "then don't speak at all. "The word is not 'orientated.' "It's 'oriented.'" And then he left. And I sat -- sat there -- and I will tell you, I started to cry. And I thought, you know, Something that nobody ever realized is that I wanted to be a somebody. But how do you go through life wanting to be a somebody and not knowing how? And in that room, I thought and reflected about what my father said.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And that was, "Debbi --" it echoed -- it echoed through that room, It echoed through my heart -- and it was hearing him say, "Whatever you do, you've got to do what you love." And that's where I found this incredible energy that -- you know what? -- I sat there and I said, "I really make great cookies. "Every time I make "and share cookies, "I can do something "that's magical -- "something that money "can't even buy. "I can make people smile, "and all I have to do "is give them a cookie. "You know what? "That's what fills my heart. That makes me happy." And so I said, "You know, "I'm going to go "in the cookie business. "I'm going to do it. "I'm going to prove to Sandy "that I can be a somebody. "I'm gonna prove to those "that have never believed in me, "that have always thought "my dreams were too outlandish, "that the things that I hope for "were impossible to achieve," I was going to prove to them I could be that somebody. I survived that night out of embarrassment but absolute determination. And I started to work.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: I got home and I started to work, and I tried to find out and learn, "How do I open a business?" Okay, it's one thing to have a dream, It's one thing to have a recipe, but how do you take a dream and a recipe and try to build it into a store? Well, of course I knew that the first thing I needed, of course, was a business plan. So wrote a business plan. You know, that's on paper. That's something anybody can do, bottom line. Now I realized I needed money. So I had to meet with bankers to get financing. And what I did is I literally opened up the Yellow Pages and I sat up meetings with various branches. And before I went in to make my presentation, I wasn't going to give them my business plan, because that's what everybody does. They can't taste my business plan. They can't experience what I believe is going to be the best cookie that they're going to experience. The only way is to bring my products. So I would make fresh, wonderful homemade cookies.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And then I would put on my best begging and groveling clothes, and I would go in and I'd meet with the bankers and I would give them my presentation. And they would listen, they would eat the cookies, and they would consistently -- they would consistently smile and thank me and say, "No. No, we are not interested." Well, guess what? I honestly hate the word "no." It is one of those most frustrated words, because what you want to do, that you want to achieve "yes," you want break through barriers, but you need to find the people who say yes. Well, I was constantly getting, "No, no, no." And it was wearing on me, and I couldn't get launched. I was stuck. And so I had another moment, with my mom, who really changed my attitude. And she looked at me, and she saw how hard I was working, she saw how personally I would take it when I constantly got rejected. And she said, "Deb, it's not working. "Just give up. It's not meant to be." And you know what? That was music to my ears. I needed to hear that. Why?

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Because I realized that giving up is the easiest thing that any of us can do. We can throw in the towel anytime, anywhere. What's going to make us -- what's going to take us to our dream is that we never give up. You never give up. So I said, "All right. Here's what I need." I needed morning mantra. I needed a way to launch myself in the mornings. And what I did is I said, "Okay." Every morning, this was my mantra. "I will find "somebody who wants to say yes. "It means that "I have to keep asking. "I have to keep knocking, but I will find that person." And so I knew that the moment I stopped asking, it was going to end. So as the doors would close and people would say no, I kept believing in my heart there would be somebody out there, and ultimately I did. I found a banker who listened to my presentation, and he invested in me. And now I was truly rolling in dough. I was able -- I was able to secure a loan for $25,000, at 21% prime.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And I will tell you, that was the cheapest money I could get, and it was the best because now I was on my way. Now, what can I tell you about financing if you want to start a business? First and foremost, that whatever you do, you have got to believe in you, because people invest in you. And what you have to remember is, who's your audience? When you're going in to talk to a banker, you know what they're looking for? Are you going to help them succeed in their business career? It's relationship development. If they invest in you, and you don't come through, if you don't have the integrity to pay back, then that's what they're looking for, is, "Will you help me "so that I don't get in trouble with my boss?" So you're going in with integrity. You got to go in with belief that you've got to help the other person succeed, as well. Can't just be a one-ended road. So I knew that people were wondering whether or not they could believe in me. So you got to believe in yourself.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: The second thing is that you have got to take a product or service, and you've got to, in your heart, know it is the best. It is the best, not as good as. It has to be the best, 'cause that gives you marketing. That gives you the fortification and purpose to go out there and ask for that money. You don't want to be a "me too." And then the other thing that's very beneficial is look for very old, aging bankers, because they like to possibly give students a chance. And so that could help. So, now I have my money, And here the first store becomes a reality. In 1977, Mrs. Fields Cookies opens. And we have -- I have this bet with my husband, who says, "Hey, Deb, "what are you going to do for your first day in business?" You know, of course, I had a business plan, but I was so excited to just get this store open, and, you know, my husband said, "I bet you can't even do $50." And of course, I knew I could do $50, right? That's -- Yes.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And of course, this is when we were selling our cookies at 25 cents each. So, here I am, I open up the store and I am ready for customers. And what was I thinking? I just thought, "This is going to be an instant success." Well, guess what? I was an absolute failure. Anybody ever failed at anything? Well, let me explain something. The greatest thing was, 700 stores later, is I failed my way to success, because it was bleak, it was awful. I had no customers, I had no sales, and I had to pay back a loan at 21% prime, and I had nothing. Well, what am I going to do? You do the unconventional. You do whatever it takes. I mean, you're in the battlefield, and you're going to survive because you're not going to give up. And what does that translate to? It said, "Okay. I accept it. "I am failing. "If I stand in this store, "and no one comes in, "I'm going out of business. "So I'm going to try something else." And I placed cookies on a cookie sheet, and I left my store. And I was desperate.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: I was determined, and I had confidence in my product. And I walked out, I stopped people. I mean, I was a woman with a mission. I had a lot riding on this. And I stopped people. I said, "Hey, will you just try these cookies?" And some of these people tasted them, and they followed me back to the cookie store, where that day, I happily rang up $75. It was the best day of my life. And what I will tell you I learned was it was all about not giving up. It was truly understanding that you can celebrate when you have failure. You never know what causes success. Honestly, it could be multiple things that cause success. But when you're failing, you take that, you seize it, and you say, "Okay. Bring it on. "It's not working. "What I have to do "is be creative and find a way to make it work." And you keep finding a way until something sticks. So knowing that failure was okay and I wasn't afraid, I also learned that the whole Mrs.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Fields experience of marketing came with "try and buy." And as a result, I would literally, whenever the sales were slow, I would take into the streets and I'd give cookies away. And I wanted to allow people to try it. And if they liked it, they would come and buy the cookie. Well, it got to the point where I had customers literally that I knew they were going to come in at a certain time and want a particular cookie with their coffee, made in a certain way. And I will tell you the power of spread special. And that was, I literally had customers calling in sick. Now, think about that. Customers calling in sick. "Debbi, I won't be in today. I've got the stomach flu." What I realized is, I would never -- I had never been in the cookie business. I had never been in the cookie business. I'm in the feel-good feeling business. I am in the business of selling pleasure. I am in the business of creating "Wows." And it comes in the form of a cookie.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: So, here the store takes off, and my team is so wonderful and they want to encourage expansion. And Mrs. Fields grows. And we grow by realizing that it's got to be about perfecting quality. We got to love what we do. We've got to take great care of our customers. But we have to perfect quality. And people have said, "Now, "you know, Debbi, "I want to build a business. "I want to make a million dollars." What I can tell you is, you never start with money. You got to start with your heart. That's where it begins. It's the passion. What drives you? And it's really emphasizing that you need these four ingredients to get you to where you want to go. And for me, I will tell you, let's talk about the whole issue of passion. I love making cookies. I love eating cookies. I love sharing cookies. And as a result, that got me started. Because you know what? I did not have -- I did not have a pedigree of any kind. I had no money. I had not finished college. I had no business experience.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: I had all the reasons why I should fail. And more importantly I also had a stereotype of all the reasons why I should fail. But you know what? Don't ever give up on your passion. and then, when it comes to your product, for me, I knew, when I was building the product, that there was going to be competition. There's always competition. Embrace it, as long as you're the best. And what I did, when I started out, was I took the recipe and I built the recipe so that I took it to the extreme. Why? If you don't, somebody else will. And what I meant by that is, I added so much butter, to the point where, I swear, my cookies started to look like these huge pancakes, and I knew that I had to back it up. I added so much chocolate that you couldn't fit in any more chocolate chips. I decided I was going to get to the top and I was going to stay at the top. And in business, you have got to make that decision before you go in.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: You don't want to go in as a "me too." You want to go in and be the best, stay the best, and never compromise. Then, of course, once you build the recipe, then you need to have the people to make it work. And you know how I found my team? I found my team by focusing on their attitude. Because you know what? I needed people to help me build Mrs. Fields. I needed people to go out into the streets and give cookies away. And you know what? I never forgot that the most important thing is we were in the business of creating happiness and giving it in the form of a cookie. So, how did I get my team? I would audition them. People would come in, and they would be introduced, and instead of doing things in a typical, you know, manner, where you go in, you fill out your application, you sit down, I would get people, and I thought, "Let's use this recipe." People have to absolutely have the passion. They have to want to be here.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: So, I would say, "Okay, "here, sit down, tell me -- Eat these cookies." And some people -- the team -- I'm like, "Here, please eat these cookies." And could you imagine, some people would want to work for a cookie company, and they actually hated eating sugar and they despised desserts? Do you think they'd be very good at the counter? I mean, customer service absolutely comes from the heart. And so the last thing I wanted was somebody at the counter who said, "I don't eat these cookies." So I had to find people who loved the product, because I have to tell you, I'm very lazy. I don't want to write sales manuals. I want people to tell it the way it is from their perspective. And so if they loved it, they could sell it. The next thing is -- And so what does that translate to you? Don't ever work in a job you don't love. Pick things that you're great at and go in and get it.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And then the next thing was, if I knew they loved the product, then I needed them to take to the streets and give the product away, because that's the way we market it. That's the way we were able to create a customer base. And so I'd say, "Take this platter out. "Give cookies away. "And if you could bring "customers back, that would be a real positive." So they would. And sure enough, I knew that they were willing to help me build Mrs. Fields. And the third thing, it was the most important thing, is I needed to get people outside of their comfort zone. And I'm asking all of you, how often are you willing to get out of your comfort zone? And for those that are listening, we get caught into the safety net of like, "I don't feel comfortable doing that." Well, if you want to be in business, let me explain something. Whatever you decide to do, if you want to succeed, I have one bit of advice -- you got to be obvious. Nobody is going to discover your voice.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Nobody is going to know about you unless you are willing to be obvious and make a stand. And if you have a great product or a service, then you have to take that stand, because people will not discover you in your apartment. You have to get out. You have to communicate. And as a result, I was looking for people that would help me build Mrs. Fields, help me move mountains. And the way I found them was a simple question. And this was maybe the most critical. Best interview ever, and it really changed. If was asking my team, "I have one thing to ask you. "Would you be willing to sing my me favorite song?" That was part of the interview. "And I'm looking "at your response. How are you feeling right now?"

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: I love you\! Yes, you would sing it right now? Would everybody be willing to sing it right now? I love this group. Oh, my God. You entrepreneurs\! Yes\! Well, I will tell you, that was interesting, because I found that most people -- Here's what I was looking for, and I'm looking for it in you right now. You know the song. You know you can do it. But the question is, will you do it? And I found that those that were willing to do it were willing to do whatever it takes to build a company, because I wasn't asking them to do something that would harm a person. I wasn't asking if they had a good voice or not. I was only asking them to do something they knew how to do. But would they, to get outside of their comfort zone? If you could stand up and belt out "Happy Birthday," if you loved my cookies, and you were willing to go get customers, those were the only ingredients I needed for you to be part of my team. And once we had our team, we could launch anywhere. We could go anywhere.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: But I will tell you, there have always been challenges in building Mrs. Fields. And I always like to reflect on a book of poetry. And that is you can never experience joy without also experiencing sorrow. So, that's kind of where failure just echoes through my bones. I know that when I'm failing, I know that success will come. And when I'm having difficult times, I know that joy is around the corner. It's all attitude. And the better the attitude, the faster you get there. The other thing I could tell you is from Winston Churchill -- that success is never final. I always saw that I earned my reputation every day with every cookie and every customer. And as a result, I knew that it was grand-opening day every day. And you can never lose that spirit of launching every day in the moment, re-creating yourself and doing everything you can to be the best you can. And the other aspect is really coming into a close of how to take this recipe and really zero in on the critical elements of getting you where you want to go.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: As it relates to passion, true wealth comes in family and friends and absolutely loving what you do. I mean, and you know what? Whatever you do, I only ask you one thing -- give it everything you have. Give it everything. Don't compromise. And when it comes to perfection, I want to emphasize the whole emphasis that it's got to be about perfecting so that your products and service stands out. The next piece is that I also want to emphasize this whole issue of spread specials. When I started my company -- and I talk about the importance of people -- I called and I asked a very famous chocolate company in San Francisco -- I'm not naming names -- and I asked this gentleman -- I said, "Hey, I'm starting "a fledgling business. It's just very small." And the gentleman listened to the fact that I needed 25 pounds of chocolate to test in my cookies. And I said, "Is there any way I can get 25 pounds?" And he said, "Listen, "sweetheart, 25 pounds is "way too small for our trucks.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: "When you want to buy 10,000 pounds, you just call me back." And I went, "Oh, okay, thank you." And I then went to look for another chocolate supplier, and I found an industrial supplier. I called and I said, "Hey, look, "I have a very small order. "Is there any way I could get 25 pounds of chocolate to test?" And this gentleman said, "You know what? "It is too small for our trucks "to deliver, but where are you? "Because it's not too small for the trunk of my car." And I will tell you, he brought 25 pounds of chocolate, and it made all the difference. He brought them to me. He believed in me, and he made me feel special. And as a result, I will tell you, it was so powerful because that gentleman today sells Mrs. Fields over 25 million pounds of chocolate every year. And what I get back to is this whole emphasis on spreading special. And every person that you come in contact, I want you to think of them as the most important person you have ever met.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: I want you to think that if you could impact their lives in any way, it's what begins relationships. And for me, it's about touching customers' hearts and having that relationship that never ends. So focusing on how a phone call can change everything. The next part is, "No is an unacceptable answer." And I will tell you, everybody tells me no. I'm actually getting to the point where -- I told you I hate "no" -- well, I kind of embrace it now, because "no" is the easiest thing for anybody to say, because they don't have to commit, they don't have to connect. So guess what? You never want to ask a question that can be answered by a "no." Now, that's going to take some homework. Why? Because you always do tend to ask questions that can be answered by "no." Now catch yourself. As an example, when I need something done, what I do is, especially in customer service, I go to the person and I say, "Who "in your organization says "yes" to refunds or whatever?" And usually the organization knows. So you channel the people and you get the information.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And you say, "Okay, the person's "name is John Smith. "Great. Do you have his number? Yes. Perfect." So, "Hi, John Smith. "I understand you can say yes. Is that correct?" Start your questions always like that, Because guess how they answer? "Yes. Yes." You have to frame your question. "You can say 'yes to.' Am I correct?" Just start there. It will change everything, but "no" is an unacceptable answer. Remember that. Never, never stop. And then, of course, the next one is GENI. Hold on. I... GENI is "Good enough never is." And this is the philosophy of Mrs. Fields, and that is simply, "Never settle for mediocrity." Set your standards so high that even the flaws are considered excellent. I want you to think about that. Set your standards so high that even the flaws are considered excellent. And what does that mean? We had cookie orphans. We would have these beautiful cookies -- I'd call them edgies -- where they hit the side of the cookie sheet. And people would say, "Well, they're perfect." I would say, "No, they're not," because that would be called "compromise." A perfect cookie is round. It's not an edgie.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: So anything that wasn't perfect, we would donate to charity, and it would be given to blood donors. So I want you think that your standards are so high that the flaws are considered excellent. And more importantly, I want you to catch yourself every time you say, "Good enough" -- "That's good enough" -- because if you say it, it means it's not. And it means you can do better. And all I'm asking is that you give it your all. Give it your best. Don't compromise, because you can't build a company on compromise. You can't do it. So set your standards high. And then the last and maybe the most important thing is that the greatest failure is to not try. And I will tell you, I was a kid with a dream, with a recipe, and I had nothing to offer the business world that would give me the credentials. The only thing I had was my recipe -- my recipe for success. You take those P's -- the passion, the perfection, the perseverance, and the power of people -- and you never -- you never let anything stop you.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: I want you to reach for the stars, because the stars can be reached. Never lose sight. Never give up on you. Never give up on your dreams, because you will find them. This recipe will get you there. And I challenge -- I challenge each and every one of you in this audience and those listenings that if you follow this recipe, I challenge you to just tell me how high you go, because you'll get there. But you never give up and you never stop believing. If I had, I wouldn't be here today. So I thank all of you. It means so much to me that if I can change one person's life because I had a dream and a recipe and I refused to give up, then that means everything to me. And the last and the most important thing is, when you get told "impossible," remember that you're possible. Always remember, "I'm possible." Look at that word and see it differently. See it differently. Now, I also have some really exciting news. Today we have launched the Mrs. Fields

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: And I have something very special for you, and that is, we have a very special recipe that is -- we actually haven't named it. but it's a combination of chocolate and butter -- You know how much I love butter -- Butter is best -- and toffee and pecans. And honestly I think this cookie is better than my original recipe. Just saying. It's so good that I've decided I'm not going to make it a secret. I'm going to share it with all of you that are interested in letting me know you would like to have the recipe. And at the very end, we'll show you how to go

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: and ask for the recipe. And we'll send it out to you. And, hopefully, you will love it as much. In fact, I'm going to make Kevin taste it. So, we have a little test. Okay, where's Mr. Kevin? Oh, questions? Come on up.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Let's jump right into some questions. Cynthia from Kennebec Valley Community College asks, "What advice would you share "with anyone who is ready "to advance from "a cottage industry to a mass-production scenario?"

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Oh. Okay. Well, first of all, I will tell you, when I started my first store -- and actually, let's tell how it really started. It started in my kitchen. And my kitchen was -- and this is probably true of a lot of people, whether it's Steve Jobs in his garage, Debbi in her kitchen -- we have to start somewhere, right? And you have to start small. So for me, my first test was taking my cookies to my neighbor's house and having them actually purchase cookies and take them to a football game. And then, when she did, she came back with orders. And what that translated to me was, "I have something here that people want to buy." Okay. So I have a cottage industry. Now I want to open a store, which is what I did. And the next challenge is to go from one to two. I think, probably in the standpoint of the whole opportunity to succeed, you have got to see if you can reproduce yourself in two locations. That is the greatest challenge for an entrepreneur, is to let go and to trust.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Well, my first piece of advice is go ahead, get your first store open. And then, before you invest in another location or expansion, I want you to do one thing. I want you to go on vacation for three weeks. And let me tell you why. Most entrepreneurs do not teach, do not instill philosophy. so that the enterprise can go on. And as a result, if this cottage industry can last without the entrepreneur, then that means that this individual has success, because it can continue and it will operate. Every entrepreneur has to have a break. You have to focus on your family, you have to focus on taking care of yourself, because you give whatever it takes. But you need to learn how to develop skill-sets in others so that they can become as great as you want them to be or even better.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Oh, my gosh. How do you go about finding your passion? I will tell you. You just dial it in. You all have something special, okay? We were all born with that special ingredient of what we love. We know what we don't like. First of all, part of going through life is identifying what it is that you don't like, and steer clear of it. Don't try to be a master of something you don't enjoy. There is nothing worse when -- especially with customer service. I mean, truly. I am always shocked when there are people working in organizations, and they really hate customers. And you're like, "Who put them there?" You know? And I also have to tell you this. I have never, ever met a person that has gone to work and said, "I want to be fired." What happens is, you get caught up in making the wrong decision by trying to compromise, and compromise means, "Good enough never is." You settle. You take a job that you don't like, guess what? You're not going to be promoted, because you're not going to be obvious.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: You're not going to be great if you don't like it. So what my advice is, zero in. If you love music, then find places that love to play music. If you want to sing, sing in the elevator. I don't care what you do, but channel the gifts you've been given. We all have them. It's called "channeling it." And don't compromise. Let it come out, and that will build. And be mentored. I love the fact that most of the students said they wanted to work in an organization. Well, use that. Use that as your research and development to find out how to be the best entrepreneur. Learn what they do great, learn what they do wrong, and make it better.

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: Hello, my name is Danika Kime, and I'm in the Cal Poly, Pomona, chapter. My question for you is, "What's the one thing you wish "you knew before starting your own business?"

speaker: Debbi Fields
text: What's the one thing I wish? I will tell you -- I think I have to tell you that I knew that I was going into the -- It's like into this land of uncertainty. It was -- I knew that I had so many challenges. I think it was more the way I shaped it, being a woman in business. Here I am, 21 years old, trying to get financing. And guess what everybody told me? "Do it like everybody else." "Go in and wear that gray suit and try to fit in." And I thought, "Are you serious? "I'm going to celebrate "the fact that I'm a woman, "and I'm going to go in "and I want to be seen. "I want to be obvious. "I want to be heard. I've got great cookies." And so I got the biggest, most flamboyant colors to wear. And I didn't want to fit in. I didn't want to be like everybody else. And you know, they talk about glass ceilings. They talk about all the reasons why you can't. Impossible? I say you celebrate it. You say, "Yeah, "I know that's there. "But guess what?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: We are so excited to be here at the 2017 NASPA Annual Conference in San Antonio, Texas. We are also thrilled to have Anderson Cooper as part of the society's 2016-2017 speaker broadcast lineup, which I have the honor of hosting.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: For NASPA and society members, you can tweet your questions for Anderson using \#AskAC, \#NASPA17, and \#theNSLS. We'll be selecting questions to ask on your behalf during the Q and A, and at this time, I'd like to introduce again Lori White to the society members who are watching at home, the chair of the NASPA board of directors. Please give Lori a round of applause.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Welcome society members watching via live stream to this opening session of the NASPA Annual Conference. We are so excited to have you join us, and now, without further ado, on behalf of NASPA, and our colleagues in the society, we are thrilled to introduce the opening speaker for the 2017 NASPA Annual Conference. Anderson Cooper is the anchor of CNN's Anderson Cooper 360, which I watch every night. Well I have to tell him that, I really do. A nightly newscast that goes beyond the headlines, keeping politicians and policy makers honest, with in depth reporting and investigations. Since the start of his career in 1992, he has covered nearly all major news events around the world, often reporting from the scene. Most recently, he has extensively covered the conflicts in Syria, Iraq, Egpyt, the civil unrest in Baltimore, Maryland, and in Ferguson, Missouri, which is right around the corner from where I live in St. Louis. He has also covered Pope Francis' US visit, the terror attack at Charlie Hebdo in Paris, and the tragedy at the Pulse night club in Orlando.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: He's a Yaley, graduated from Yale University in 1989, he's also really young, with a bachelor of arts degree in political science. He also studied Vietnamese at the University of Hanoi. Please join me in giving it up for Anderson Cooper.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Thank you very much, alright, wow. Thanks. Wow, thank you so much, this is like the largest room I've ever seen, this is crazy. I must, it's a real honor to be here, I must admit I always find it odd to hear myself introduced as a television anchor, I never really set out to be a TV anchor, it's like a kid who tells me they want to be a politician, I think you should be a real person before you become an artificial one. When I graduated college I really had no idea what I wanted to do with my life, and in desperation I asked my mom for advice, which is something I rarely did growing up. Now, as you may know my mom is Gloria Vanderbilt, and she's a remarkable person, she's a fascinating person, but she's not the most practical person on the planet, as you might imagine.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: In fact the only time I can remember really as a kid asking her for advice was when I was applying for my first job as a waiter one summer, and I was going for a job interview, and I said, what should I do for the job interview, and she thought about it for two days, and then she came to me and she said, wear vertical stripes because they're slimming. It's not really great advice for a kid. Anyway, so it was a sign of my desperation my senior year of college when I asked my mom for advice on what I should do when I graduated. And she said to me, follow your bliss. Now, follow your bliss is, I was actually thinking of something, I wanted something a little more practical, like plastics, or something with a sense of direction, but follow your bliss turns out wasn't even original advice, my mom had been watching television, she watched Bill Moyers interview Joseph Campbell, who was a professor at Sarah Lawrence College, and Joseph Campbell came up with this term, follow your bliss.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: So, I'm glad my mom was not watching, I don't know, the Maury show, because god knows what sort of advice she would have given me, she probably would've told me to get a DNA test or something. The problem of course with follow your bliss, as you probably know, and for the students who are watching now, is figuring out what your bliss is, and at the time I really wasn't sure. I graduated in '89, so I appreciate Lori saying I'm young but I'm being ravaged by time here, so. I actually, I focused most of my studies on the Soviet Union and on communism, because I was a political science major and that was the big deal at the time, so my senior year, when the Berlin Wall fell, I was completely screwed, and, I mean I was happy for them, sort of, but for me, it was hard not to think I'd wasted four years of studying something that no longer was relevant to anybody.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: So when I graduated I really did not know what I wanted to do, and I had always been interested in news, and always, I'd watch, frankly, a lot of TV growing up. And I'd been interested in the experiences of war correspondence, particularly during the Vietnam War. And I'd actually left high school early, I'd left second semester of my senior year after I'd applied early to college, I didn't get in early, I got deferred, but I left my second semester of senior year, and I rode in a truck across Sub-Saharan Africa. And Africa had really opened my eyes and quickened my pulse, and I knew that I wanted travel to be a part of my life. So, because I'd watch a lot of news growing up, and I'd read a lot about war correspondence, I decided I would try to break into the news business.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Now, it's not a very easy business to break into and I applied for entry level jobs at ABC and CBS and I could not get the job, any job, which shows you the value of a Yale education I guess, but I got a job as a fact checker at a program called Channel One, which at the time was seen in about half the high schools and middle schools in the United States. And I was only there for a few months before I decided I should take a gamble, and that's when I came up with this plan. My friends called it a scheme, but I like to call it a plan. I decided that if no one was going to give me a chance as a reporter, I would have to take a chance. If no one was going to give me an opportunity, I'd have to try to create my own opportunity. I think when you're in an organization, that organization often only sees you in one way, so at Channel One they all saw me as a fact checker and they couldn't imagine that I could be a reporter on camera.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And so I decided that I'd have to change the way they saw me. And since I wanted to be a war correspondent, I decided I'd just start going to wars. Which my mom was obviously thrilled about, and I had a colleague at Channel One make me a fake press pass, and armed with that and a video camera which I borrowed I moved overseas, and I first snuck into Myanmar, in southeast Asia, and I hooked up with some students fighting the Burmese government. And from there I went to Vietnam, and then I ended up in Somalia, which at the time was plagued by both famine and civil war. Until Somalia I'd really never seen starvation up close. I was in, my first night in Somalia I flew in all by myself, I had a backpack basically with some video tapes, some chargers, some money, and I'd forgotten to bring food to Somalia which in the midst of a famine is really a stupid thing. And I went to a small town called Baidoa where about 100 people were dying a day at the time.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: In Somalia back in '92 in August when I was there, about 1,000 people were dying of starvation every day. And you'd see their bodies along the side of the road, sort of piled in makeshift morgues like so much kindling wood. I remember my first night I was sitting in a makeshift hut watching a man and wife fill a kettle with water, and in between them lay the body of their young son, and he was covered in a shroud. And I remember his arms were so thin, they were as thin as the twigs that made up the hut that they had been living in. And the man held the boy's head in his left hand, and his wife poured the contents of the kettle of water with her right hand over her son's body in order to wash his body before burial. And they'd already watched their three other boys die and this was their last child and he was only five years old.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And that was in August of '92 and he was the first child that I ever saw die, and since then there have been many many more and I've given up trying to count. In the last 25 years or so I've worked in 50 or more countries, and I've seen things as a reporter, I've seen more horror and hate than I can remember, but I've also found myself constantly surprised by what I've discovered in the far reaches of our planet. I've been surprised by the truths that are revealed in the dwindling light of day when everything else is stripped away. You know in war and disasters you expect to find darkness but you also find light. You expect to see horror but you discover humanity as well. It was in Somalia that I knew, that first trip, that I had found my calling. I knew that I couldn't stop the starvation, I couldn't save people's lives, but I can bear witness to their struggles, I could tell their stories.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I realize now that part of what motivated me in those early years, to seek out suffering, to seek out people who were struggling to survive was because in many ways I was struggling to survive, I was trying to understand how to survive. My brother who was two years older than me committed suicide my senior year of college. He jumped off the balcony of our apartment building in front of my mom, and it was, in many ways, it was my own grief that led me into my career. Now grief is not something that many people talk about here in this society, and when you're grieving you want to be around other people who speak the language of loss. And so I found myself propelled to go overseas because I wanted to be places where the language of loss was spoken, where life and death was not something that people feared talking about or were uncomfortable talking about, was something that they were facing and talking about every single day. I needed to learn other peoples' stories because they helped me to make sense of what had happened to my brother and what might happen to me.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I think one of the things that's so interesting about being a correspondent, especially in these times is that you see people do things, and you hear people say things that you can never imagine. One minute you're experiencing incredible joy and triumph, the next the depths of despair. And you can't allow yourself to become immune to the sadness of what you're seeing, and if you do then I think you have no business being out in the field because you can't do justice to the horror of, the reality of what you're there to report on. But you also can't allow the sadness to permanently alter how you see things. As a storyteller, you have to see things with fresh eyes. You have to see things with something called soft eyes. You have to be willing and able to walk in other peoples' shoes. I think those are the qualities that serve everybody, all those who are listening who are leaders on their campus and all those in this room who help students on college campuses.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: So many of our students today, you're all coming of age in extraordinary times, with opportunities and challenges that previous generations of people haven't faced. I think it's very easy right now to see the world that you're entering as worse off than ever before, as more polarized, more difficult. No matter what your politics are, we live in an incredibly polarized society. I think it's very easy, especially for young people today, feel overwhelmed. I was recently in a room of college students, a couple hundred, and I asked them to raise their hands if they felt that the world was worse off now than it's ever been in their lifetime, and in many people's lifetimes, if they believed that life for humans right now is more difficult and damaging than ever before. And nearly every single person in that room raised their hands, because they believed that.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And I understand, I think why they feel that way, but in truth the opposite is true, and that's actually the good news that I just wanted to talk about a little bit today, and I do hope this can be as much of a conversation as possible, so I'm going to leave a lot of time for the questions that people are tweeting in. But I know for many of you who are graduating, many of you are facing your futures with trepidation, and it's sensible to be concerned and aware, but I hope that fear doesn't paralyze you, because it really paralyzed me when I was graduating college. The good news today is that, you are lucky to be alive right now. As bad as things may seem, as polarized as this society may seem, as bad as wars may seem overseas, the good news is that life for humans as a whole on this planet is better than it has ever been and it's just getting better. It's better than it is for any previous generation in the history of the planet.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Now I'm by no means saying that aren't tremendous dangers and problems and disparities of wealth and poverty and access to medical care and threats to the planet, concerns over where the country may be headed, but by nearly all markers, life for humans is the best it's ever been, and it's just getting better. And all the statistics bare this out. In Syria, the barbaric acts of terrorism we witnessed, the barbaric, the war, the civil war that's going on there, the death toll is horrific. But the truth is, we are far less likely, everybody in this room is far less likely, and everybody on this planet is far less likely to die a violent death than ever before. Wars on this planet are less frequent, and they're not as deadly as they once were. We see them in ways we've never seen before, so they seem worse, but the reality is they don't last as long and they're not as deadly. The first day of the Battle of the Somme in World War I, 60,000 British soldiers died, the first day of the battle.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: It didn't seem like it, we see things up close now in ways that we never could before, and I think that's what makes it seem worse. Around the globe, people, human beings are living longer, we're living healthier lives, quality of life has improved even in countries that haven't seen enormous economic growth. Do you know that in 1820, 84 to 94% of the world's population lived in poverty. In 2010, it's down to 21%. Nick Kristof of the New York Times just pointed out the other day that back in 1981, 44% of the world's population lived in extreme poverty, which is defined as making less than a dollar a day. Right now, that's down to about 10%, according to the World Bank. And every day the number of people living in extreme poverty drops by 250,000. For all of human history up until the early 1960s most adults in the world were illiterate, they couldn't read. Now, 85% of the adults in the world are literate.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I was in a field hospital run by Doctors Without Borders in Niger several years ago during a malnutrition crisis and one of the heroic doctors there, a guy named Milton Tectonidis, talked to me about what he calls stupid death, which is a child dying because of a lack of access to an antibiotic that costs 15 cents, or 25 cents. Fewer kids today are dying than ever before. Nick Kristof points out that since 1990, more than 100 million kids' lives have been saved by simple things, vaccinations, diarrhea treatment, breast feeding promotion. In Niger, Doctors Without Borders was treating kids with severe malnutrition, in a revolutionary, miraculous new way, a product called Plumpy'nut, which is basically like a Clif bar, it's made out of peanuts. And they can just give it out in mass to mothers who can feed their kids and bring their kids back from the brink of death, it doesn't need refrigeration, it has a shelf life of several years. We may not feel like the world is a better place today than in the past, but I think part of that is that we're more aware than ever before of what's happening.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: We see it. All of you, people who are graduating now have more information at their fingertips than any previous generation in history. I mean when I was in college, we had libraries, are there even libraries anymore? It's amazing what this generation has at your fingertips, on your mobile devices. You have access to all the information that you need. What really gives me hope, besides these advancements around the world, is the power that each of us in this room has, the power that each student who's watching online has. The power of the individual. The power that each of us has to reach out, and to care for somebody else. It's what all of you do in your day to day lives, in your work on college campuses. The power and ability to walk in someone else's shoes, to live beyond just the confines of our own selves. And I've seen this, in the midst of tragedies and disasters, I've seen so many acts of bravery and selflessness by individuals. During the tsunami in Japan, people who, at risk of their own lives, reached out to complete strangers, being swept away by the rushing water.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: In the earthquake in Haiti in 2010, citizens who'd been abandoned by their own government for generations spent days digging through rubble with bare and bloodied hands to save strangers who'd been trapped beneath fallen concrete. Individuals make a difference. Each of us in this room can make a difference, and it's the difference between success and failure, the difference between hope and heartache, it's the difference between life and death itself. Individuals standing up, not waiting to be told what to do, but becoming leaders, taking responsibility. Too often, I think we dwell on the things that separate us, and this is certainly true of the media. We don't dwell on things, on the bonds that tie us one to another, and those bonds are the core of who we are or who we can be when everything else is stripped away.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Several months ago I found an online, an old radio interview that my dad had given, my dad died when I was 10 years old, but he wrote a book two years before he died called Families, and when the book came out in 1976 he did some radio interviews, and I guess he did a radio interview for a public radio station in New York, and I'd never heard it before, but I guess there's an organization that kind of re digitizes old radio interviews, and they put it online, and they sent me a tweet saying, we've digitized this interview your dad gave. And it was interesting because I clicked on the link, and I sat in my office and I heard my dad's voice for the first time since I was 10 years old. And I couldn't remember what he sounded like. And not only was it the shock of hearing his voice, but one of the things he said has stayed with me.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: He said, we are all of us separately and together engaged on the same tough journey, and each of us alike tastes of its joys and sorrows, each of us gets by as best he can, and we must, whenever possible, reach out to each other tentatively to touch, with our hands, with our eyes, and with our hearts. And I think that's what I try to do with my work as a reporter, and I think it's what all of you here do on college campuses every single day, and it's what the students who are watching now I hope will do as future leaders. I hope you continue to stand up, and reach out. We need you all. Thank you very much.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Your story, and we have some questions for you. So I will start. Our first question comes from Christina Elgy, from Dalhousie University in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and she asks, what are your thoughts on free speech on college campuses, and how do universities provide an open space for a spectrum of ideas without compromising their own mission and values.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Wow, something easy to start off with, that's good. Thank you, thank you for that question, I appreciate it. I thought you were gonna ask me is my hair naturally gray. And the answer is yes, thank you, it is. You know look, I don't know that I should be telling a room full of educators and folks who work on college campuses every day what college campuses should be doing, and frankly I'm a big believer, I should be listening to what you all, who are the experts, believe. Because you are in the trenches and in the front lines. Just as an outsider, somebody who looks at college campuses from afar, it's very, I went back to Yale recently for a meeting and I don't know how you do it every day, because I just felt so old. It just made me so depressed, I was like, first of all was I that young when we were there, they're children there, and I remember being much more mature when I was there.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: But, look, I think, look, it's a balancing act, I don't wanna sound cliche but I think it's, it is vitally important that the college campuses be a place where there are conflicting ideas, and where people feel, where people are kind of figuring out what they believe and who they are, and I think that's the amazing thing about a college campus. You know the things, I graduated college kind of sure of what my beliefs were, and thinking I knew a lot, and then I started traveling and I realized I knew nothing, and all these ideas that I had, they were really kind of limited and very kind of narrow minded. And so I think college campuses should always be a place where people are free to speak their minds, and the flip side of that is, I also think they should be a safe space for kids who do not feel welcome in other places, whether it's gender identity, whether it's sexuality, whether it's some sort of, really, whatever the issue may be.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And I think, you know, the term political correctness is thrown around a lot now, it's usually kind of spat out by somebody as a criticism. I think, anybody, usually people use it for something that they don't agree with, any idea they don't agree with is political correctness. I prefer the term human decency. I think there's something to be said for... I think there's something to be said for listening to somebody else's ideas, and walking in their shoes. I just think that's such an important quality, that quality of empathy to understand, and you talk about inquiry, to inquire about, to try to understand what somebody's ideas are. Even if those ideas, you disagree with them, you find them abhorrent, whatever it is, I do think it's interesting to try to understand where somebody is coming from, but that doesn't mean shutting down someone's ability to speak, or shutting down if somebody is feeling uncomfortable, I think that free expression is critical.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: So, I don't use the term political correctness, I just think we should be decent to one another, and I think college campuses, more than any place, especially for kids in that critical age range, I think that's something that is so important on campus.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Hi Mr. Cooper, my name is Grace Lim, and I'm from William Patterson University. I was wondering how your experience as a news anchor has effected your perspective on the globalization of world politics. We live in an era where events around the world can be broadcasted live anywhere in a matter of seconds. How have advances in technology changed the landscape of journalism?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Wow, that's a great question, I mean it's, we live, as I was saying, we live in this incredible time. When during the Vietnam war, something that happened, a camera crew would be out on a patrol, they were shooting on film, it took days for that film to end up back in the United States for it be processed and put on air, so information took days to move around the world. Now it's instantaneous, and everybody has the ability to become a broadcaster with their smart phone, everybody has cameras, we see the attack at Charlie Hebdo within seconds because someone was on a rooftop documenting the entire thing, and I think that's an extraordinary thing, I think there's a democratization of news which is terribly exciting. I do think it comes with great dangers as well, which is, it's more important than ever before to know where your information is coming from, to know, is this an actual, legitimate source, is this real, is it not real, I mean we all know about the term fake news, which is now thrown around by our president.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I did an interview with a guy who makes money creating fake news stories, and he was doing this during the campaign, he came up with a story that Democrats were being paid to go to Trump rallies and cause problems, he actually made a fake Craigslist posting to back it up as evidence, and it got, that became part of the news cycle, people started to cite that as real, and he thought it was terribly funny, and he was making quite a good living doing this. So, I do think it's more important than ever before to know where your information is coming from. But that ability to see things, I think it does make the world seem like a much worse and dangerous place than it really is, I do think it's important to see it in context, and to remember all the amazing advances that we are all benefiting from.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: \[Lori\] Well folks this is not fake news, we are real and live. And Walter Truelove Jr. from Devry University asks, with the result of the presidential election and how this country is divided, what can young leaders who are getting ready to take an active role in their communities and cities, what can they do to bridge the gap and bring the country closer?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Yeah, look, we've always been a country with great divisions, to pretend that the polarization we see now did not exist before, I mean, we saw the reaction, I mean you look at the reaction to the civil rights movement. You look at those films of freedom rioters down in Mississippi being spat on, little kids going to school being spat on and having horrible things, names hurled at them, people getting killed. James Chaney in Philadelphia, Mississippi. And so, going all the way back to the Civil War, I mean we are a country of a lot of divergent viewpoints, and so I think it's important to remember that this is not completely unusual. Our politics has always been a contact sport. The Vietnam war protests divided this country, Richard Nixon divided this country, so this is not new, I think for many of sort of the new generation who are coming of age now, it seems particularly startling because it is a departure in many ways from what we've seen just in the last 20 years or so.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: But I do think that idea for future leaders of walking in somebody else's shoes is, to me, it changed my life to start going overseas to sort of get out of the bubble on the campus that I was in.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I mean I grew up in New York in a very, we had a lot of different people, my mom and dad knew a lot of different people and a lot of different kinds of people and so, I was, the bubble I was in was a pretty big bubble but it was a bubble nevertheless, and to suddenly go to Africa, to suddenly go to places and start seeing how the majority of people are forced to live, it was an eye opening thing and it continues to be and I continue to learn and expand my mind every place I go, and I think that for any future leader, I think learning to walk in somebody else's shoes and not see everything as black and white, I think there is a lot of gray, and I think it's important to kind of listen to other people and not always be the one talking, but listening is a good thing as well.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: It looks like we have our first Twitter question of the evening, and it is from Thea, the associate director of student life at Stevens Tech asked, what do you feel

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Wow, these are really easy questions, so it's gonna, it's nice. Again, the hair is naturally gray. Look, I mean without a doubt, it's, I talked about the power of the individual, but there is also the power of government, and there are some issues which government has to take a role in, in which it can't be up to just individuals, the problems are too great, the problems are too institutional, and we've seen that throughout the history of this country, throughout the history of the world, I mean, you look at the hurricane Katrina, and there was this incredible outpouring of church groups and volunteers and people who went down to New Orleans and schools and students who went down to New Orleans and continue to, to help New Orleans rebuild. But there was also a tremendous influx of billions of dollars in government money that reworked the school system there, that helped to rebuild the city and rebuild the Mississippi Gulf coast. So I do think there has to be a role for, it can't just be individuals teaching people how to read, it can't just be one singular effort, one on one effort.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Though that's critically important, I think certainly, in the history of this country, when you look at the war on poverty, and obviously there's still a long way to go, but all those things have had impacts on, just on the numbers, and the preponderance of poverty in this country.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Anderson, you just talked about the fact that our country has faced challenging times throughout our history. And this question is from Caitlin K, from Connecticut College in New London, Connecticut, and she asked that given the recent shifts in government, higher education has been challenged in how to best support students, particularly those that may be facing discrimination, threats of deportation, and/or persecution. So what would you tell these students, who fear these severe and worrisome changes?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Wow. I mean again, I think everybody in this room, that I'm sure this is, I would much rather listen to you tell me what you would tell somebody. Look, I think these are understandable, absolutely rational concerns, I mean, clearly somebody whose immigration status is in question could, can be deported, more so now than in previous years, and I think that seems like it's only going to continue, so those are all rational, those are rational concerns. I do think it's important to...

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I can just speak as somebody who, when I was a young gay kid on a college campus, I wanted to feel part of the whole, but at the same time I felt, I felt apart from, and I think anybody who's part of any group that's been marginalized throughout the history has that sense of being an outsider, of not truly fitting in or not truly being welcome, and as much as anybody in a college campus can create a feeling, a one on one connection with somebody and make them feel that they do have friends, they do have people who are watching over them, who care about them, who are trying to help them. I think that's an incredibly important thing, I mean, when I was in college in the, it was the 1980s. I was, I was out to my friends, but I wasn't, most of the environments I was in were not particularly friendly environments for gay guys, for gay kids, and that didn't really, I mean I think it's a lot different now on college campuses but for many groups, that feeling of being separate from continues.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I mean to me being gay is one of the great blessings of my life, because it's allowed me to love the people that I love and to, but I think it's also afforded me a window on society that I would not have otherwise got. I mean I grew up a child of privilege, and I have the advantage of being white, and coming from a well off family, and I think being gay at least allowed me to kind of feel not like a, it allowed me to, I viewed myself as an outsider, I viewed myself as an observer. I think it made me a better reporter and a better person.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: So this question comes from Breana Sodano from Cal Poly Pomona in California, and she asks, how did you manage, through the election cycle, not to allow candidates' views about your personal identities affect you? Many of us in the field of higher education are doing work that is identity based, and it becomes challenging when it's personal as well.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Okay, you know, it's not my job to be offended by somebody, it's not my job, it's not about me. It's about the person I'm interviewing, it's about the person who has policies and my job is to ask questions to somebody, try to kind of confront them with things they've said which are not true, try to understand what their positions are, try to hold them accountable based on their past statements or based on their policies. So what I personally believe, I really work very hard to not let it affect how I interact with somebody or how I view somebody. I've spent tons of time with people who hate gay people, or would not like me personally. I've spent much of my life in very dangerous places, interviewing people who would, believe in killing gay people overseas.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And some even probably here at home, and so, I don't allow that to, I try not to allow that to, my job is to be a storyteller, my job is to be there because you all can't be there, and it's to bring you to a place that maybe you can't go to, or you don't wanna go to, or for whatever reason you're not there, and to kind of accurately convey as a correspondent what is happening there. So what I believe about somebody, it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter, and I think the same is true for anybody, I'm sure in your position as advising students on a college campus, it's what you personally may think about somebody's choices or even something which is not a choice, that shouldn't matter in how you treat somebody and how you interact with somebody, and as a reporter it certainly shouldn't matter. I want to treat everybody with the exact same respect, when they deserve respect, and disdain when they don't, but I wanna treat everybody in the same way, regardless of what I personally think.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And I've been doing this for 25 years, and I like not having to take a position, I like not having to, I think the last thing audiences need today is some overpaid blow dried anchor telling them what to think or how to feel or who to vote for. I think people want facts and information, and you're smart enough to make up your own minds. By the way I do not blow dry my hair. But I am way overpaid, I will say that.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Ethel Swanson Druger at Purdue University in Indiana asks, as you reflect on your personal professional journey, and some of the obstacles you've encountered, what are some of the biggest hurdles you've faced, and perhaps still face, and how do you rise above the negatives? What advice would you give others who may be facing some of those same struggles?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Oh that's interesting. I wish when I, looking back, I wish I... I'm 49 now, I love being 49, it's so much better than 39, and 29, and God knows 19. And I remember thinking when I was in college, you know you always hear people saying, oh college is the best four years of your life. I thought if this is the best four years of my life, I'm in serious trouble, because I did not feel, maybe other people on campus were confident and thought they were heading for great things, I was totally not confident, and much more insecure, and I wish I had had some of the confidence that I feel now, not arrogance but just, I'm comfortable with who I am, and I don't really have a skill, but in whatever minor skill I have, it's, I'm probably at the peak of it right now. So I wish I had sort of felt some of that comfort that I did not feel when I was younger, and so I'm not sure if that really answers the question but, I do wish that, wait what was the question again?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Oh, right, hurdles or challenges, right. Well look, I'm not going to pretend I had the toughest paper route growing up, I mean as I said, look, I was born into a family that had resources, I didn't have to take out a bunch of loans for college, my mom paid for college. My parents sat me down early on and told me look, we're paying for you up to college, and then after that you're on your own, and I appreciated that, I think you know, there's plenty of people who come from well off families who have trust funds and most of them seem not to really accomplish much in their lives, or they end up not doing so well, and I was very grateful that my parents sat me down early on and were like look, there's none of that. There might have been some Vanderbilts who had a lot of money back in the day, but they're dead.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And so I started working when I was 11 years old, I got a job and started earning money and saving up money, and I really liked that sense of, look we'll get you past college, but then you're on your own. And so I think for me the biggest hurdle was really one of overcoming an inherent shyness, I'm an introvert, it's very difficult for me to talk to people, I can't ask people for anything, it's very strange that I happen to be on television and talking in front of a crowd of 6,000 people right now, because this is exhausting for me and I will not talk to anybody for the next two days after this. But, I like it because it forces me to get up, and project myself and do it, and so I think the obstacle for me was really obstacles I placed in my own way of just being insecure, and uncomfortable in my own skin, and I wish I had sort of been able to rid myself of that sooner than I did.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Hello, my name is Tyler Clippel. I am a student at the College of Saint Rose in Albany, New York. My question is, what can honest media outlets do to combat the growing problem of fake news? Thank you.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Yeah, I mean, again look, the idea of fake news is, I mean what the term was actually used to describe was actual fake news stories that somebody in their basement put online and that those stories got aggregated and sucked into the news cycle and actually ended up getting picked up by legitimate news organizations and carried as real events, and I think that's, it is a real concern, when you have every, there is this democratization of information, people have access to put their own stories out there, and I think in many ways that's a great thing, but it's, I think the only way to combat it is for responsible news organizations to call it out, for internet providers to in some way, and I don't know how, to do it in a way that doesn't restrict free speech. But to police it.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: But I also think probably the most important thing is for consumers of news, viewers, readers, college students, to just be smart consumers, and to check, when I see something online, I always double back, I'm like, wait a minute what site am I looking at, what's the bias of this site or what's the angle of this site, and I like that there's, I don't think there should be a conservative newscast and a liberal newscast, I think there are facts and things which are real and those should be what are reported, but I like that people from different backgrounds and perspectives have access and that news is more diverse than it's ever been before, when I was growing up it was three middle age white guys, heterosexual white guys I assume, telling the country what was happening and newscasts were fifteen minutes long, and now you have a much greater diversity of faces and backgrounds, and I think that's only a good thing and I think that diversity in the newsroom, I mean it still has a long way to go, but it's, you have more diverse information than ever before.

speaker: Anderson Cooper

I think one, it would be confidence. I don't like being nervous about anything, so I have systematically, I was nervous a lot as a kid and so I've systematically tried to eliminate that butterfly feeling so the last thing that made me nervous actually was speaking in front of large groups, so that's why I started forcing myself to do it a couple years ago, and now I actually enjoy it. So I think that sort of sense of confidence is something I would tell myself. And also just to enjoy, I hate that word journey, because it sounds like such a bachelor word, you know, they're always on a journey, the journey for the rose and stuff like that.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: But I think, I do wish that I was more present in the days of my life, I felt like 20 years have gone by and I suddenly had woken up and been like wait a minute, it's like when you're driving a car for a long distance and suddenly you get to your destination and you're like I don't remember the last two hours, that's the way I feel about the last 20 years, I'm like where has that gone, and so, I wish I was more present for the moments of my life in that way, and enjoyed it more.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: My dad used to say when I was little, I couldn't sleep at night and then I'd go into his office, he had an office in the apartment and he was a writer, and I would curl up in his lap while he was typing, and he would always say, enjoy, enjoy, enjoy, and I wish I had sort of enjoyed all the ups and downs, because you started off with a video saying, what would you do if you knew you could not fail, and I actually have that on a thing on my desk, and I think it's a really interesting way to look at something, but when you're going through it, you can fail, and failure's actually okay. It's as important to learn about the things you don't want to do as it is to learn about what you do wanna do, and I think it's, it's only when you're looking back on stuff that you can kind of see that all the ups and downs did kind of lead you to where you're at, and I wish I'd sort been along, kind of enjoyed the ride a little bit more.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Okay. It looks like we have a Twitter question that comes from Caitlin Perrer via Twitter, and she asks what advice do you have for those of us feeling compassion fatigue due to our involvement in advocacy?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Wow that's interesting. Yeah, that's a really interesting idea, the idea of compassion fatigue, and as somebody who has spent 20 something years, and my first three years I was in war zones, mostly, and I started off in Burma, and then Somalia, and then Sarajevo a lot, I was in Rwanda briefly during the genocide and you see a lot of things, and you see, initially you see one child die and then suddenly you're in a place and you see 50 people who have died and then you're in Haiti during the earthquake and you're in a city where more than 200,000 people had died and they're being picked up by trucks and dumped into trucks and then dumped into mass graves. And it's very easy to start to get that sort of compassion fatigue, and I think the, I don't have any magic solution for it, other than to say I think it's very important to see things with fresh eyes every single time, and to be shocked by the horror of things you see, or to remain engaged if you're working with, on particular issues here at home.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: If you feel yourself becoming kind of immune to the suffering you're seeing or immune to the issues that you're trying to help people with, then you're not doing them, the people you're working with, any favors at all, and your job is to help other people, is to be compassionate and that compassion is important. And so whether it's taking a break, or doing a variety of things, it's a marathon, it's not a sprint, you want to be in this for the long haul.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: So I started, after three years of basically just kind of going to conflict zones I started doing more variety of reporting and anchoring and stuff, just because I found myself, after a while, very honestly I found myself in Rwanda during the genocide which lasted for about 100 days and about 800,000 to a million people were killed, and they were killed not with bombs and with bullets but very personal, it was very personal killing, it was knives and clubs, it was neighbors killing neighbors, husbands in some cases being forced to kill family members or their wives, kids having their Achilles tendons cut so they'd be hobbled for the rest of their lives.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: And I remember coming upon a group of people, five people who were dead on the side of a road and they'd been out there for a while, and I remember I took a camera I had, a personal camera I had and I started taking pictures of this little girl's hand, and the skin had peeled off her hand like a glove because she'd been out in the sun for so long, and I was taking pictures with my personal camera, and a friend of mine took a picture of me doing this and sent it to me after I got back, and I realized I had completely crossed a line, I realized that I was no longer viewing, I assume they were a family, I was no longer viewing this family as real people, as a family.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I didn't wonder what their names were, I didn't wonder about what their lives were like, I was fascinated by how the skin was peeling off this little girl's hand, and to me it was a wake up call of you know what, I should not, I have no business being there if I can not be shocked by seeing five people dead on the side of a road. So, to this day I have that picture up on my bulletin board right by work, I look at it every single day, and I think to that person who feels compassion fatigue, you know what, it's not about you, you have a job to do and you need to do whatever it takes to continue to feel that sense of outrage, or that sense of horror, or that sense of wanting to see justice, whatever it is, because that is your job, and that's what you are meant to do.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: Well thank you for sharing that part of your story, we appreciate it. And we have one last question we like to ask all of our guests, and it is, why do you think it's important for individuals to be a part of organizations such as the National Society of Leadership and Success or professional organizations such as NASPA?

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I think it's important to know that you're not alone in what you do, that there are others who are doing the same thing you are, who are facing the same obstacles you are.
