When I was a college student, I had this weird tick that I can not ask anybody for help, so I can't ask anybody for anything, I can't, I have a hard time ordering in a restaurant, like I literally, I have this weird obstacle to this day, and so my entire career was designed where I didn't have to ask somebody to let me be a news correspondent. I basically quit my job as a fact checker, moved overseas, put myself in war zones. It was a very passive aggressive thing to do.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I made it impossible for them not to use me, I started sending them free stories in war zones, which were very dramatic and they were like, yeah of course we'll put this on, because it's pretty dramatic. So I do think it's important to... I wish I had known that I was not alone going through these things and to know that there are others out there who you can consult with, who you, can be mentors to you, and who can help, and whether it's working on college campuses or you're a student out there, to know that there are advisors like you who are waiting and eager to be a part of a young person's life, I think that's, you're changing lives and I think to know that you're not alone, and to know that there are others going through what you're going through, and you're not the first person to have gone through this, that always gives me great hope whenever I feel really down about something.

speaker: Anderson Cooper
text: I'm not the first person to feel this way, I'm not the first person who has faced whatever obstacles it is, and there are others I can consult with and learn from.

speaker: Brené Brown

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Right now, I am pleased to introduce our guest for this evening Mr. Simon Sinek. Simon Sinek is an unshakeable optimist. He believes in a bright future and our ability to build it together. Described as a visionary thinker with a rare intellect, Simon teaches leaders and organizations how to inspire people. With a bold goal to help build a world in which the vast majority of people go home every day feeling fulfilled by their work, Simon is leading a movement to inspire people to do the things that inspire them. Ladies and gentlemen, here at NJCU and those watching all across the country, please join me in welcoming our guest for the evening, Mr. Simon Sinek.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: January 1968. Vietnam War. The North Vietnamese surprised the Americans with a surprise attack. On the day of Tet Tet is the Vietnamese equivalent of Christmas. And there's been a tradition for decades that there's no fighting on TET. But on this particular Tet in 1968, the North Vietnamese decided to violate that tradition and attack a hundred targets across the country simultaneously that day. They threw 35,000, sorry, they flew 85,000 troops at the American targets. Many of the commanding officers of the American bases were in town celebrating Tet and weren't there when the attacks happened. Most of the major fighting ended after about a week. Hue went on for about a month but most of the major fighting went on for about a week. And the Americans had repelled every single attack. And at the end of that week, the Americans lost fewer than 1,000 troops. The North Vietnamese lost 35,000 out of the 85,000 troops they had. In fact, if you look at the Vietnam War as a whole, America lost 58,000 troops over the course of those ten years. The North Vietnamese lost three million troops over the course of those ten years.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: America actually won nearly every if not every single battle it fought in Vietnam. So, it raises a question. How do you win every battle and lose the war? If you have at least one competitor, you have a game, and there are two types of games. There are finite games and there are infinite games. A finite game is defined as known players, fixed rules, and an agreed upon objective. Baseball. We all agree that whoever has more runs at the end of the game is the winner. The game ends, we all go home. Then you have an infinite game. An infinite game is defined as known and unknown players. The rules are changeable. And the objective is to keep the game in play, to perpetuate the game. When you pit a finite player versus a finite player, the system is stable. Baseball is stable. When you pit an infinite player versus and infinite player, the system is also stable. The Cold War was stable because there cannot be a winner or a loser.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Players drop outta the game when they run out of the will or the resources to continue to play, but the game continues with or without them. Problems arise however when you pit a finite player versus an infinite player. Because a finite player is playing to win and an infinite player is playing to keep playing. And this is what happened to America in the Vietnam War. America was fighting to win and the North Vietnamese were fighting for their lives. A very different set of strategic choices will be made. America did not lose the Vietnam War. America dropped out of the Vietnam War because they ran out of the will or the resources to continue to play. So it gets me thinking. Business, for example. If you think about it, business is an infinite game. There's no such thing as winning the game of business. It doesn't exist. Right? Companies come and go. They're introduced, they fall away, they run outta the will or resources to play. It's called bankruptcy. Or a merger acquisition. Where a company realizes that they cannot compete alone so they merge with another company so they can stay in the game.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: But the game continues with you or without you. But if you listen to the language of so many businesses, they don't know the game they're in. They talk about being number one. They talk about being the best. They talk about beating their competition. Based on what agreed upon metrics? Profit? Revenues? Market share? Number of employees? Square footage? Based on what agreed upon timeframes? A quarter? A year? Two year? Ten years? Five years? The life of the company? 50 years? Who knows? I haven't agreed to those rules. In other words, there's no such thing as being number one. There's no such thing as being the best. And there's no such thing as beating your competition. It doesn't exist. This came to life for me when I had a real life experience. I spoke at an education summit for Microsoft. I also spoke at an education summit for Apple. At the Microsoft summit, the vast majority of the executives spent the vast majority of their time talking about how to beat Apple.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: At the Apple summit, 100% of the executives spent 100% of their time talking about how to help teachers teach and how to help students learn. One was obsessed with where they were going, the other one was obsessed with beating their competition. Guess which one was in quagmire? So at the end of my talk at Microsoft, they gave me a gift. They gave me the new Zune when it was a thing. This was their competitor to the iPod. And I have to tell you, this was a remarkable piece of technology. It was beautifully designed. The user interface was simple and user-friendly. It worked flawlessly. It was an absolutely stunning piece of technology. Now I couldn't use it because it didn't work with iTunes but that's a different problem.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: But it was a miraculous, gorgeous piece of technology. So, I'm sharing a taxi with a very senior Apple executive at the end of the talk at Apple, and I decided to stir the pot. So I turn to him and I say, ya know, Microsoft gave me their new Zune and it is so much better than your iPod Touch.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Because the infinite player understands sometimes you have the better product and sometimes they have the better product. And sometimes you're ahead and sometimes you're behind. There's no such thing as winning. There's no such thing as being number one. There's no such thing as being the best or beating your competition. There's only ahead and there's only behind, and the goal is not to win every battle, the goal is to outlast the competition. And in this case, Apple was way smarter than Microsoft. This was in the Steve Ballmer days. The culture at Microsoft in those days was awful. People hated going to work. It was all about the numbers. It was all about winning. It was always about being number one. But based on what? How do you know? And this is the difference. Is organizations that understand the game that they're in and play by the infinite rules, not only outlast their competition, but they run innovation circles around them, and tend to be ahead more often than not, and they generally outlast their competition. So it begs the question, how do you play the infinite game? Well, there are five things, it's a checklist.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: It's literally one through five. If you have the bottom three but not the first two you will fall outta the game eventually. And that's exactly what happens to so many companies. Something like 80% of the DOW index are companies 35 years or younger. Where are all the old companies? They fell outta the game. 'Cause you can be ahead, you can be number one, you can win every battle, and you can still lose the war. That's the point. So here's the checklist. Number one, you have to have a just cause. Number two, you have to have courageous leadership. Number three, you have to have a vulnerable team. Number four, you have to have a worthy adversary. And number five, you have to have an open playbook. So let's go through them one by one. The first one, a just cause. Right? It's a reason to come to work every day. Now, ten years ago, I wrote a book called Start With Why and I attempted to articulate this thing called the why, this higher sense of purpose, cause or belief that drives every single one of us.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And over the course of my years trying to spread this idea, lots of people would come up to me and say, we know our why. I'd say, what is it? They go, it's to be the best. I'm like, no.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And so I've upgraded the language. That the why is a just cause. If I told you to come to work and the goal was to beat the competition, does that feel like a just cause? No, clearly not. Right? And that's the point. It should be something that inherently we know that we're motivated by and it's something we wanna contribute to, and even sacrifice for. A just cause is something we would willingly sacrifice for. Maybe it's something as simple as working late. Maybe it's something as simple as turning down a better paying job because you'd rather be at this company. But sometimes it means even sacrificing a promotion or sacrificing some of your own interests because it's the right thing to do and you believe in this. That's what a just cause does. It inspires us to want to give more, to commit to something bigger than ourselves. An organization must have a clearly articulated just cause first. Second, you need to have courageous leadership. Because a courageous leader is the kind of leader who has the ability to withstand the overwhelming pressures from the outside that are telling that company to advance the short term.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Push the stock price. Sell the company. Make the numbers. Whatever it is. And that courageous leader believes no, that what we're doing for this just cause is more important. That courageous leader understands that it's more important to prioritize the people over the short term gains, over the numbers. People over numbers. That takes unbelievable courage. The pressures are overwhelming on leaders and you have to have courageous leaders who have the wherewithal to do the right thing. No point in having a just cause if people aren't courageous enough to advance it. Number three, you have to have a vulnerable team. That doesn't mean we all walk around crying.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: A vulnerable team means you have worked to build a culture, you have worked to build a corporate environment in which the people who work there feel safe enough to say I made a mistake. I don't feel qualified to do the job you've asked me to do. I'm scared. I'm having trouble at home and I know it's affecting my work. Without any fear of humiliation or retribution. Without any fear that you will find yourself on some sort of shortlist for the next round of layoffs. That's what a vulnerable team means. The opposite of having a vulnerable team is having a team in which everybody feels that they have to lie, hide, and fake, every single day they come to work. Admit no mistakes, for fear that you'll be humiliated or put on some shortlist. Never admit that you don't know what you're doing, are you crazy? That's insanity. And definitely not admit you're scared or that problems at home are affecting you at work. Why would you do that? That's crazy. And unfortunately, that is the vast majority of corporate cultures today.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Most people come to work and lie, hide, and fake, every single day of their lives. And the problem is, it breaks the company. It weakens the company. I'll give you a few examples of what a vulnerable team looks like, right? (clears throat) So, we all know what happened with United Airlines, where they dragged a paying customer off the plane with a broken nose, two broken teeth, and a concussion, right? I feel sorry for that crew. I do not blame that crew. Because I can guarantee you every single person on that crew knew, knew that was madness, of course, it's obvious, it's common sense. But they feared breaking the rules more than doing the right thing. And it didn't just happen outta the blue. That is a culture that had been enforcing the rules and people being afraid to break those rules for years. And eventually, eventually, eventually, it breaks. That's what happens when people are lying, hiding, and faking every day, and refuse to admit mistakes. That's what happens. It builds and builds and builds until something really bad happens. I saw it happen years before. The same airline.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: I was getting ready to board that plane and I witnessed something that played out in front of me. Where one of the passengers attempted to board the plane before their group number was called. Which as everybody here know is a felony.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And that's exactly how the gate agent treated him. Step aside, sir, I haven't called your group yet. Please step aside and wait until I call your group. She said to a paying customer. So I spoke up. I said, why do you have to talk to us that way? Why can't you talk to us like we're human beings? And she looked me in the eye and said, sir, if I don't follow the rules I could get in trouble or lose my job. All she revealed to me is that she does not feel safe in her own company and her leaders do not trust her to do the job for which she's been trained to do. And guess who suffers? Customer and company. You do that enough, eventually what you get is dragging somebody off a plane in the way that they did. That was been building up for years because they do not have a vulnerable team.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: The reason we love flying Southwest Airlines is not because they have some magical gift to hire the best people, it's because the people who work there feel safe in their own organization and their leaders trust them to do that job they've been trained to do. And guess who benefits? Customer and company. It drives me crazy. One of the most frequent questions I get when I give talks is, Simon, how do we get the most out of our people? Like they're a towel that we just squeeze them. How do we get the most out of them?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: The question is completely flawed. It's how do we help our people work at their natural best. It is an entirely different question that gives you entirely different answers. One produces an environment in which people lie, hide, and fake every day, and one produces an environment in which people feel vulnerable every single day, which is a good thing. I saw it play out in front of me. I saw it played out in front of me. I was staying at the Four Seasons in Las Vegas and it's a beautiful hotel. And the reason it's a beautiful hotel is not because they have beautiful beds. Any hotel can buy a beautiful bed. It's because when you walk the halls of the Four Season, and someone says hello to you, you get the distinct feeling that they wanted to say hello to you, not that they were told to say hello to you. They happen to have a coffee bar in the lobby there. And so one afternoon, I went to buy myself a cup of coffee. And the barista working that day is a kid named Noah. Noah was wonderful. He was funny and he was engaging.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And I stood there for far too long buying a cuppa coffee 'cause I just enjoyed talking to Noah. So as is my nature, I ask Noah, do you like your job? And without skipping a beat, Noah says, I love my job. So immediately I followed up. I said, tell me specifically what the Four Seasons is doing that you would say to me that you love your job. And without skipping a beat, Noah said, throughout the day, managers will walk past me and ask me how I'm doing, ask me if there's anything that I need to do my job better. Not just my manager, any manager. And then he said, I also work at Caesar's Palace. And there the managers walk past us and catch us if we do something wrong. There the managers wanna make sure we are always doing everything right. There I like to just keep my head below the radar, I just wanna get through the day so I can collect my paycheck. He said, only at the Four Seasons do I feel I can be myself. That is what you call a vulnerable team.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And a vulnerable team is essential for innovation. It's essential for great camaraderie. It's essential for productivity. It's essential for teamwork. We cannot judge the quality of a crew by how well a ship performs in calm waters, we can only judge the quality of a crew by how well a ship performs in rough waters. The problem is it's the calm waters where you have to be building up the quality of the team. It's too late by the time the storm hits. I actually was doing some work with a large company and I was talking about this leadership stuff, and one of the senior executives raised their hand (chuckles) and said to me, you don't understand, I don't have time for this stuff, this is war. And I'm thinkin' to myself.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Your stock price is not war. Right? And you have no time for this leadership stuff in these hard times, my question to you is what we're you doing in the good times? That's when the team is built. All the time. Because when the team loves each other they will take care of each other and they will take care of the company. Because they believe in it. Vulnerable team. The next one is a worthy adversary. Right? You have to have a worthy adversary. What does that mean? It means you respect your competition. That's what it means. Your competition is there not to beat, your competition is there to make you better. That's why they're there. Rommel was the desert fox, the Nazi, the German soldier in charge of North Africa. Bernard Law Montgomery was the field marshal from Great Britain who was sent to North Africa to take on the desert fox. He said in his autobiography "I've heard great things "about this Rommel and I'm excited "to meet him on the battlefield." Think about that. His mortal enemy.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: "I have heard great things." How many of us hear our leaders say of our competition, I hear great things about what they're doing? We can learn from them. Montgomery actually had a portrait of Rommel hanging in his quarters, not to throw darts at but out of respect. It's very easy to rally people against something. And that's what we often do. We wanna beat our enemies. It's easy to rally people against something. The question is what do you stand for? And rather, you see your competition not as the thing to beat, you see your competition as standing in the way of the thing you believe in. I'll give you a perfect example. Let's compare the American Revolution to what happened in Egypt. Right? In the American Revolution, our founding fathers declared what we should believe in. They declared what we stood for. Right? All men are created equal. Endowed with certain unalienable rights amongst which include life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. They saw the monarchy, the dictatorial regime, of Great Britain, as standing in the way, inhibiting us, from spreading equality to all men and all women.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And they had to remove Britain from the equation. Hence the Revolutionary War. And then once Britain was gone, we've now continued to try and spread and advance that just cause, and we are at our best when we are advancing that just cause. Women's suffrage, civil rights, gay rights, universal education, universal healthcare, the ability for people to buy houses, get an education, whatever it is. Go to college. This is when we are at our best, when we're trying to advance the cause in which we believe in and the cause that we fought for. Now compare that to Egypt. Very easy to rally people against something. We saw it happen. Mubarak out, is what everybody chanted, and they got the whole country rallied against Mubarak, and they got him out. And then what? Nothing. They didn't stand for anything. We don't know what they were leading towards. Some abstract concept called independence? I don't know? Freedom? From what? And it's continued to fall apart.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: You have to stand for something and we don't see our competition as the thing to beat, rather we see our competition as standing in the way of the thing we're trying to advance, and when they fall out of the game, a new competitor will arise and we will then take them on. We saw it happen with Apple. First it was IBM, then they fell out of that game. Then it was Microsoft, then they fell out of that game. And now it's Samsung and Google and others. The competition changes in the infinite game. You don't run your best time when you run by yourself around the park. You run your best time when you run in a race. Your competition is there to make you better. Your competition is the pacer. Admire your competition. Study your competition. Learn from your competition. But the only true competitor is yourself. The goal is to wake up and be a better version of yourselves today than you were yesterday. The only true competitor is to say, how do we be better this month than we were last month?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: How do we make our company, our product, everything we're doing better this year than we were last year? And look how well they're doing on these things, we can learn from them. They outsmarted us this time but not next time. They're simply standing in the way of advancing the thing you believe. They're not there to beat. Sometimes you're ahead and sometimes you're behind. You have to have a worthy adversary that you respect and admire because they make you better. Finally, you have to have an open playbook. What does an open playbook mean? There was a young man named George Eastman who lived in Rochester, New York at the turn of the 20th century, 19th to 20th century. He worked in a bank. And his richest customers, he noticed, all owned land. So the young, enterprising George Eastman thought, if I wanna make money, I should own land. So he went out and started prospecting land in Rochester. And he took photographs of the land that he was prospecting.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: The only problem was, in those days, photography was exclusively something that only professionals did, and he had to take out all the chemicals and all the plates. It was cumbersome and it was dangerous and it was heavy and it was difficult. And the enterprising young Eastman who believed in simplicity and believed in making things simple, figured out a way to put all of those things on one plate, to make it easier for himself. As it turned out, there was a market for that. So he abandoned the real estate and started selling these photographic plates. And he improved his technology and he improved his technology until he invented film, the flexible form, of these plates, that could put a hundred photographs in one camera, that's what they did. And you'd send the camera in, they'd develop the pictures, and send them back to you. Now, he went to a photography show in London to show all of these professional photographers his new technology and they went crazy for it. They loved this new technology, this new thing called film, and no one bought it.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Because the quality wasn't good enough. It was too grainy. And as professionals, they wanted high quality photographs because it was their livelihood. So Eastman could've come back and said I can improve upon this technology to take advantage of the demand that's just sitting there. But he didn't. 'Cause he had an open playbook. He decided to do nothing to his technology. Instead, he started to sell his new invention to an audience that didn't care at all about the quality. The general public.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: George Eastman literally invented mass market photography. The reason we take our own pictures is because of George Eastman. Kodak went on to be a huge company. He became the sixth wealthiest man in America. Huge company, Eastman Kodak. By the way, he made up the word Kodak. He believed K was a strong letter.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: George Eastman had died and the company continued to grow without him. And in the late 1970s, in their R\&D department, Kodak invented the digital camera. Now they had an opportunity. Do they have an open playbook or a closed playbook? Well, the problem was they had a closed playbook. They said that the only way we make money is by selling film. So they actually suppressed the technology for fear that it would cannibalize film sales. They knew that somebody else would invent it and they gave themselves ten years. Do you know what they did over the course of those ten years? Nothing. They did nothing. Because it was too difficult. They didn't have the courageous leadership to understand that their company had to take a huge dip as they changed away from film to digital. They couldn't do it. They just didn't have the leadership for it. So they just didn't do it. Then, somebody else invented the digital camera and we all know what happened. Kodak is a shadow of its former self. It's a tiny, tiny little company now. Do you know what they do? The sell film to professionals.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: That's basically all they do now. Had they actually pivoted, actually had an open playbook, it's quite conceivable that all of us would demand to have Kodak digital technology in all of our phones. It's quite possible. But Kodak instead almost went out of business because of their closed playbook. Here's an example of an open playbook. Steve Jobs and Apple had already come off the success of the Apple 1 and the Apple 2. It was already a large company, already loved by people, and already considered the darling of business. Their next big innovation was a product that they called the Lisa. This was gonna be the next product they were gonna launch. As many executives do, they went on a tour of another company, as companies do. The executives visit each other. And they happened to go on a tour of Xerox Park. And Xerox showed them a technology that they had recently invented called the Graphic User Interface. Now understand, Jobs had a just cause. He believed in empowering the individual to stand up to Big Brother. Everything he did was about empowering individuals to challenge the status quo.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And he saw the personal computer as the perfect tool to do that which is why he went into the personal computer business. And now he saw this thing called the Graphic User Interface, and he thinks that this is the perfect leapfrog to empower individuals, because if more people can more easily use computers, that means more people can challenge corporations and take down the man. So after their tour, he gathers his executives and he says, guys, we have to invest in this Graphic User Interface thing. And they say, Steve, we've already invested millions of dollars and countless man hours in the Lisa. If we abandon what we've invested in, we will blow up our own company. To which Jobs responded "Better we should blow it up than someone else."

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: That decision, was the Macintosh. Macintosh revolutionized computers. It was the first Graphic User Interface company. And the entire platform of Windows was designed to copy the way a Macintosh works. He literally changed computers as we know it. Unlike the executives at Kodak, he was willing to throw it all away to do something that he saw was in the right direction of the future and he didn't even invent the product. That's an open playbook. You have to do and have all five of those things if you're gonna play the infinite game. It's the only way. All the infinite players obey all five of those checklists. So it begs the question, if that's how you build an infinite company, how do you live an infinite life? Now, clearly our lives are finite. We know that our lives are finite. But life is infinite. The game of life is infinite. And we will drop outta the game and new people will be born but the game continues with or without us.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: If you choose to live life by finite rules, that means you wake up every single day to be number one, to beat your competition, to make more money and accumulate more power than anybody else. And here's what happens. On the day you die, richer than everybody else, you've put all of your competitors to shame, more power than anyone you've ever known, you don't win life. You just die.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Whatta you want on your tombstone? Nobody wants the last balance in their bank account written on their tombstone. We want to be remembered for how we impacted the lives of others. He cared. She loved. Devoted mother. Loving father. That's how we wanna be remembered, for our contribution to the lives of other people. That's what it means to live an infinite life. That you will affect people in your life right now. That your life will actually live on beyond your own years. That after we're all long and gone, people will say, I am who I am because of you. That's what it means to live an infinite life. To build a organization that will outlast you, where the culture is strong enough that the people will want to continue your just cause not just without you, but for you, in your name. Look how we hearken our great leaders of the past. For Gandhi, for Martin Luther King, for our founding fathers. We do it for them. They have lived infinite lives. Their contribution has outlived them. Every single one of us has the choice to live an infinite life.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Why is that only second-term presidents become preoccupied with their legacies? Why not first-term presidents? Why is it that only people who reach their twilight years, when they're now in their 70s or 80s, they start thinking about their legacies? Why not a 20-year-old. Why not think about your legacy right here, right now? What kind of choices will you make from this day forth to live your life so that your life will be infinite? The contribution you will make to the lives of others will outlive you. The choice is yours. Thanks very much.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: He said the first question was a giveaway. We asked this following question. Simon Sidek is a multiple time New York Times and Wall Street Journal bestselling author. Now, according to one of his books, when should a leader eat? And he said it was a giveaway. And of course the answer is last. And this is of course a reference to his amazing book Leaders Eat Last and our winner tonight is Jerry Tinsley Simmons from Kennesaw State University. (clapping) Yeah, go ahead and give 'im a round.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Now let's take a look at the poll results. We asked you the following. In your opinion, what is the most important characteristic or skill a leader should possess? 5% of you said intuition. 39% said communication. 19% said confidence. 28% said integrity. And 9% said creativity. So, back to this gentleman right here. If you would, please give him another round of applause.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: You've done fantastic work and I know Twitter questions are jumping in and we're just gonna go ahead and jump in with our first Twitter question. And it comes from Elias Seigelman from Jefferson University and he asked how do you balance results and satisfaction versus fulfillment in the workplace?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: So, they're not mutually exclusive. It's not one or the other. You can have both. We are tangibly driven animals. Metrics are important to us. Targets and goals are important to us. And that's a good thing. Abstract is no good. It wasn't work. I mean you can't run a marathon with no mile markers. It's actually unnerving. I need to know and be able to measure progress. But we have to understand the role that metrics play. Metrics help us understand speed and distance. Right? And they're not absolutes, it's to help us gauge. The problem is, is when they become absolutes. So for example, can I get the pad back? Is that allowed? Or I can do without. So, let's say somebody gives us a goal. They say, if you hit this target. I'm a visual thinker, sorry.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: So let's say somebody gives us a goal. They say hit this target, right? If you hit this target, you will get a bonus. Right? And so one person on the team is making solid progress, building good systems, morale is really high, very low turnover. And things are going pretty well, right? It's a good team. And at the end of 12 months, they didn't reach the goal. We don't give that person a bonus. By the way, it's arbitrary that it's 12 months 'cause that's when we pay taxes. It could be anything. Versus somebody else on the team who they can't hold on to employees, morale is terrible, they're begging, borrow, and stealing, who knows what they're doing, they drop the price, and on the right day, on the right time, look at that. They hit the goal. And we give that person a bonus. And that sends a message to the rest of the organization which is we don't care how you got there as long as you got there. I think that the goal is important.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: It helps us measure and it helps us gauge, but if we miss the goal, we have to look at how we're doing. How we got there. And I think that's one of the things we don't consider. So how we get there will manage the satisfaction. These people are very satisfied and love coming to work. These people, not so much. They might be making more money, for now, but in the long term, these people are your better employees. And so it's not one or the other, it's both. And understand the role of money inside an organization. Money is fuel and fuel is very important. I think there's nothing wrong with money, it's just we have to understand the purpose of money. So the company is the car and money is the fuel. So I don't care how amazing your just cause it and how wonderful your culture is, if you have no money, you don't go anywhere. You might have bought the most beautiful car, you got no gas, you got nowhere to go. The purpose of a car is not to buy gas. The purpose of a company is not to make money.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: The purpose of a car is to go somewhere. And fuel helps you get there. The purpose of a company is to accomplish something, to advance a greater cause, to contribute to society, and money will help you get there. Very necessary, very important, but it's not the reason we bought the car in the first place.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: In your research do you find that companies hire invdividuals who are probably more likely to be on the up and down level or versus the individuals who has thoughts and ideas that are driven by that. - Oh we know the answer

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: They hire these people. They hire these people. Because they drive results. And they ask me questions like how do I get the most out of my people. Ya know? And they have a proven track record, right? It's just an unfortunate thing. Now you're gonna get me all soapboxy. (all laughing)

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Okay, so I talked to a guy on SEAL Team 6. And I said, how do you choose who from the regular SEALS gets to be on SEAL Team 6, 'cause SEAL Team 6 is the higher echelon. And he said we look at two axes. We look at performance and we look at trust. Now the way they define these things is performance is on the battlefield. So this is trust on the battlefield and this is trust off the battlefield. The way they say it is, I may trust you with my life, but I don't trust you with my money or my wife. That's what they say. (all laughing) So when people say, I'm a high performer, I trust him. Sure, at work. But what about when we're not working? When we're going out. Do you really wanna be friends with that person. That's what they're talking about. Of course, nobody wants this person, the low performer of low trust. Of course, everybody wants this person, the high performer of high trust. What the SEALS learned is that this person over here, the high performer of low trust, is a toxic leader.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: They would rather have a medium performer of high trust, sometimes even a low performer of high trust, it's a relative scale, over this person. Now think about most of our companies. We have a million metrics for this and we have negligible to no metrics for that. So we keep promoting those people and then we wonder why our companies suffer in the long term and why we hate going to work, 'cause we're promoting high performers of low trust. That's what we do. Here's the joke. These people are incredibly easy to find. Go to the team, ask them who the asshole is.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And they will all point to the same person. They're very easy to find. So are the natural leaders. Also go to the team and say, who do you trust more than anybody on the team? Who always has your back? And in hard times, you know they'll always be there for you. They will also all point to the same person. And it's probably one of these people who may not be one of your highest performers but they're your best natural leaders. But in business we tend to overlook these people in favor of those. The highest performing organization on the planet, SEAL Team 6, knows this, but companies think that they have it figured out.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Question-- No, you're fine. From our member Tara Lamb, a student nurse at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, who works in ER and Intensive Care unit. And she says, I have so many reasons why I love what I do and it's why I strive to be the best nurse that I can be. But not all healthcare workers are pleasant to work with and I often find if difficult to go to work in the mornings. How do I stay focused on my whys?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Okay, so she needs to be the leader she wished she had. One of the problems in healthcare is that we have broken cultures, in healthcare. And that senior doctors, or especially hospital administrators, don't know what their job is. When you ask them, what's your priority, they say patients. No, it's not. It's to take care of the people who work in the hospital. You take care of the people who take care of the people. That's what you do. Every administrator and every senior doctor and senior nurse should be preoccupied with one thing and one thing only, are my doctors okay, are my nurses okay, is my staff okay. And if you get that right, they will devote all of their time and energy to taking care of each other and the patients. The problem is, we have cultures, in which they think money is more important or patients are more important or anything else other than the doctors, the nurses, and the staff, and so the doctors, and nurses, and staff are forced every day to expend time and energy to protect themselves from their own leaders.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And take energy away from doing the right thing for the patients. It goes right back to that poor gate agent who she's more concerned about breaking the rules than she is about taking care of me. If anybody works in an organization where after you make a decision, you have to send a CYA email, ya know, just in case. That is proof that you work in a culture, I mean if that's standard fare, it's proof that you work in a culture where people feel it's important to take time and energy away from doing my job in order to do something to protect myself from my own leaders. That's what that is. That's what's happening. If you work in a company where it's standard practice for most people to keep a folder of all the good things you've ever done, just in case you need it, that is a sign that people are taking time and energy out of their day, away from doing their job, in order to protect themselves from their own company.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And that's what's happening in our hospitals. And I've seen it. I have a friend who went through a horrible experience in a hospital, and the doctors and nurses were more preoccupied about looking good or not breaking a rule rather than taking care of her and her medical needs. And we wonder why healthcare is broken in this company. It's not that we need some massive legislative overhaul, what we need is cultural overhaul inside the hospitals. We need to teach leadership to people we put in positions of leadership.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: I guarantee it. I guarantee you. When they take a doctor who happens to be a high performing surgeon, you're now in charge. Do you know how much leadership training he gets?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Zero. He went to school for 15 years to become a surgeon, so what makes you think you can just be a leader without any training? It's really, really hard. And if you studied that, why wouldn't you study this?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: It just makes you a good surgeon. And I know how hospitals work. If they're offered a fantastic leader, who's the third best surgeon in the world, or they're offered the best surgeon in the world, but everybody knows he's a compete bastard, do you know who they choose? Number one.

text: So I like the American education system because you don't have to declare your major until junior year. speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Yeah, so I think the education system is great and so what I would recommend is in those years that you have to make your decision, try lots of things. (all laughing) And that was basically it.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And I didn't do very well my freshman year 'cause I was bored outta my skull, right? 'Cause I was taking courses based on low course work. speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Yeah, I would think because people are so young and still have so much growing to do that eventually it'll change. 'Cause 50% of people end up changing majors but to go to the professor who has the best ratings.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: All the professors, and try different subjects. Do something that, it's not quite what you imagined but the professor is like the best rated professor on campus, I'll take one class. speaker: Simon Sinek
text: So, we're gonna take a question from the audience and this is gonna come from Pretha Pornima, who is here with us this evening, and she asked, if the reality in most companies is finite thinking, and they are obsessed with the what and the quick wins, can the infinite survive within the finite? Don't you think that at some point you need to walk out and if so, does walking out mean that it's a failure to adapt to reality?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Raise your hand, who is it? Okay, so I can talk to you. Your question's a good one. There are multiple options, obviously. One option is always to leave. And if you work in a culture that is absolutely untenable, that is a viable option. But it's not the only option and it's definitely not the first option. The first option is to be the leader you wish you had. You've heard me say it before. You have to be the leader you wish you had. In other words, you may be able to affect the people at the top. They are preoccupied with whatever they're preoccupied with. And so you ignore them. You worry about the person to the left. You worry about the person to your right. And it's not about you anymore. You now preoccupy yourself with ensuring that these people go home and love coming to work the next day. That is within your control. One of them might even be your boss. Sometimes our bosses are difficult, it's not because they're bad people, maybe they had bad role models, maybe they don't know any better, maybe there's overwhelming pressure.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: In other words, we can exercise empathy. Are you okay, boss? You came down really hard on us in the meeting yesterday, are you okay? We wanna see you do well. We're trying to help you. And you can break people down when they realize that you actually do care for them. So you have to learn to care about the people to the left and the people to the right and ensure that these three, four, five, ten people love coming to work because you're the leader they wanna come to work for, even if you don't have the formal authority. And what you start to see is the tail can wag the dog. In time, this group becomes very high performing. One of those people leaves, goes to another group, takes all the lessons they learned and what you start to see is eventually it starts to grow.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Let's see, we have another Twitter question from you, from Nick Elsas, and he asks, what do you recommend a student do the day after graduation to be successful in the future? (all laugh)

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: So, look, at the end of the day, when you're young and junior in your career, it's the most confusing, exciting, wonderful, awful day of your life. Because now it's you. It's life's journey, right? You work your way up to eighth grade, then you have to start again at ninth grade. And you work your way up to senior and you have to start again as a freshman. You work your way up and you grad-- And then now you're nothin' again.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And ya don't. Because there's something wonderful about being junior inside a company. You probably don't have as many responsibilities as other people. You may or may not have a spouse. Probably don't have kids. Vast majority of people don't have kids at this time. In other words, you can do anything. You can go try stuff out. Also, your cost of living is a lot lower. And you can't really break anything at a company and bring the company down. This is the best, like if you're senior and you make a bad decision, you can break the whole company. When you're junior and you make a bad decision, ehhhhh. Maybe you lose a little bit of money. (all laughing) There's not much you can really do that'll break the company. And so this is an amazing opportunity to practice and learn and practice and learn. Find a mentor. And a mentor is not someone who is your champion, who will put in a good word for you so you get the promotion.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: A mentor is somebody who's probably not even at your company, and if they are at your company, they don't have to be in your chain of command. They're somebody who likes you and you like them. And they believe in you and they see maybe a little bit of themself in you and they wanna see you do well. And they give you candid and honest advice. In other words, come to learn, come to be a better version of yourself. Too many people start off trying to prove that they are worthy of being there, trying to prove that they should be in charge, and yet everybody knows that you have no experience. (Shon laughs) We know, we saw your resume. Your resume says your GPA and what you grad-- You have no jobs.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: \[Shon\] Right. So this is the best time to try things out and experiment and push the boundaries and make sure you're making friends and make sure you're taking care of others and make sure you find a mentor. And enjoy the journey. If you take that route, you're more likely to be successful than not. I'll give you a personal example. Whenever I would interview when I was junior, they would always say, what're you looking for? And my answer was always the same. A mentor. I'd always say, I know it's like looking for love but I'm looking for somebody who hopefully will take me under their wing and grow me. And I would turn down high profile, amazing jobs to take something that was kinda rinky-dinky because I liked the person I would be working for more. And I remember working with colleagues who all they cared about was the high profile job with the high paycheck, and every decision they made was, which one's gonna pay me more. Their lives, I know what happened to them, 'cause I've stayed in contact with some of them, they're the unhappiest people I've ever met.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: They made a lotta money in the short term but then they ran out of passion and they ran outta love and they ran out of friends, and their careers went like this and plateaued. And it's because every decision they made was money. You talk about people who have no joy in work. Where the people who try to make the decisions based on who I worked for and the kind of work, they made less money in the early days. I'm tryin' to do it with my hands. They made less money in the early days but then it went like this later on. To a tee. Every time.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: That brings me to the next question I have because it's related. When I think of people graduating from college, a lot of importance was placed on, what are my peers doing? As soon we graduate and this person got the great job and I'm still out here looking. And it takes me to this question from Jennifer Mankin, from Central Community College, she asked, do you think social media negatively impacts success? And I ask because that's where we are and a lotta people - Yeah, of course. use it to compare.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: I mean, everybody's vacation is better than mine. Everybody's friends are better looking than mine. And everybody's weekends were way more exciting than mine. I just sat at home and binge-watched Stranger Things 2. I mean like, that was my whole weekend.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: So yeah, of course. Look, human beings we can't help ourselves but compare ourselves to others. And comparison is the deadliest thing we can do to ourselves. Because we will always come up short. And all it does is exaggerate all of our insecurities. It's okay to enjoy other people's success but let them live their lives and you live your life. Oh and by the way, they're curating their social media, that's not really their life.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And so you're making decisions based on how you feel based on their curated things. I know, I've talked to so many millennials, I know somebody who's out of work, really depressed, and yet she goes and does all these things so she has the appearance of this amazing, successful life. And so now she may be making those decisions based on what her friends, who knows what sort of weird, twisted, exaggerated, circle of depression this is forming. So go back to the rules of the infinite game. Your friends are there to admire. Your friends are there to say, God, I'm so happy for them, what are they doing that I can learn from? I'll give you an example. We can all fall into this trap. So in my business, authors and speakers and folks like us, we're all comparing ourselves to each other and sometimes it can get silly and competitive. And sometimes I go on Amazon and I check the rankings of my books to see that I still have a job.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And I would check the rankings of his books. And when I was ahead, I'd be like, yesssss. (all laughing) And when he was ahead, I was like (growls) It would drive me crazy. And I had this weird abstract competition. Same thing, right? Social media happened to be Amazon rankings. And I would check in all the time. I'd always check in, mine/his, mine/his, nobody else, just mine and his. (all laughing) Anyway, I was at an event and we were interviewed together on the same stage. And the interviewer decided to let us introduce each other. So I went first. I had to introduce him. And this is what I said. I looked at him and I said, you make me very insecure.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: I said, because all of your strengths are all of my weaknesses. And every time I see you do well, it just reminds me what I'm bad at. That's how I opened up.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And now we love each other. (all laughing) Because I realized that he's really good at what I'm bad at, so by me getting to know him and really learning to love him, I'm realizing I'm getting better at those things. And I'm taking more pride in the things that I'm good at, rather than thinking I have to be good at everything he's good at. So it's healthy to grow our own strengths rather than be intimidated by the strengths of others.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: It's also something to be said about how you were able to go to him and be authentic about how you really felt. And it just kinda broke that ice between you two.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Yeah, I probably couldn't think of how to introduce (mumbles) (all laughing) But anyway, he and I are now very close friends and I love him, I've gone and stayed at his house and we hang out whenever we can and it was all from that, it was all from that. When I learned to put the competition aside and now when I see that he's doing well, I am so excited. And so I think when we compare ourselves to others, it reminds us of our own insecurities, and that's a bad place to be.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Okay, cool. I'm gonna go to our next question then. And this one is going to be from Cindy Gonzales from the University of Laverne. And she asked, what advice can you give future leaders who feel defeated and are about to give up?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Leadership is a sometimes lonely experience. And I think it's not just leadership, I think careers, life, is difficult. And anybody who thinks they can do something as difficult as life, or as difficult as work, by themselves is crazy. We are just not that good. Human beings are just not that strong. And so, we have to foster and build relationships with others because every single one of us, I don't care how successful, I don't care how powerful, you absolutely will have days where you're consumed by self-doubt. You will absolutely have days where you are defeated. You will absolutely have days where you wanna throw in the towel. And only if you have somebody in your life who comes to you and says, I got your back.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: You have to have somebody who loves you. And the only way you'll have someone in your life that loves you is if you're willing to love somebody else. And that you have to find somebody that you believe in and you want to be there for them, to encourage them and inspire them. Then the odds are pretty high that they'll come to you. And in those times of loneliness and weakness, that you do call someone and say, I'm struggling. So this book nearly didn't happen. It was the most difficult thing I ever wrote. I was looking at the social science, the biology, of how the human brain worked, and overlapping that on corporate culture, and I couldn't understand why all the social scienti- All the biologists, they weren't social scientists, all the biologists that I was interviewing, why none of them hadn't written this book. It seemed so obvious. Take the biology and overlap it on a corporate culture. And I realized, 'cause it was impossible to write. Because every chapter coulda been its own book. It just went on and on and on and on. It just was never ending. It was impossible to organize.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And I actually got to the point where I quit. I couldn't do it any more. I couldn't figure it out. I was not a happy person. And I stood up from my desk and I went for a long walk, and I literally was planning my exit. I knew I'd have to give the money back to the publisher for my advance. I'd have to pay them back. I knew I'd be humiliated 'cause I'd have to tell everybody, oh yeah, I'm not writing that book. And I was literally planning the steps of my exit. Including rationalizing, look, there's 10,000 books published every year, if one doesn't get published, no one will notice. I was literally planning my exit and rationalizing that it was okay for me to quit. Ya know sometimes you have to know when it's time to quit, that whole thing. I don't know why, but I called a buddy of mine who was in the Air Force Special Forces. I don't even think I said hello. I just called him I said, he picked up the phone, and I said, what do you do when you can't do the mission?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And as is his nature, he started telling me a story. And he said that he used to fly Pavelow helicopters, big Special Forces helicopters, and he said, there was a mission that they were ordered to go on that everybody knew from the intelligence that it was a suicide mission. And it wasn't like a kill Hitler mission where we were all gonna die but we'd kill Hitler, this is we were all gonna die and we wouldn't achieve our objective. Like everybody knew. The defenses were too strong. Our everything was too weak, we were too weak, it was a suicide mission. And they were prepping their helicopters and his wingman says to him, what do we do? Do we refuse to go? They had wives and kids. He said, do we refuse to go? And my friend turned to him and said, no, this is what we sign up for, we go. So he said to me, is this book more powerful or less powerful than Start With Why? I said, it's affecting me more intensely. The research is incredible. It's more powerful than Start With Why.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: He says, okay, I gotta a funny story to tell ya. He said, before I met you, I wanted to drop outta the Air Force. And I read this crazy little book called Start With Why and it reinspired me and now I love being in the Air Force and I'm really become the leader that I wanted to be. He says, if you're telling me this book is more important, we need this book. He said, this is what you signed up for. You have to do this.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: So he never had to fly that mission. Cooler heads prevailed. But yeah, he said this is what you signed up for, you have to do it, so I turned around and went back and finished. And so this is the same thing. If you're gonna commit yourself to a course of action, you gotta make sure you have that person that you can call and say, I can't do it. That's what I did. If I didn't call him, I would have quit.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: I called him and said to him, I can't do it. And he said, I gotcha. I gotcha. - Support system. Ya gotta have it. Ya gotta have people who love you. And the only way you have people who love you is if you love people. That's the only way it works.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Hello Mr. Sinek, my name is Nick Rooney and I'm a soccer player at Chapman University, with a major in business and a minor in leadership. My question for you, is you have a quote that says "Dream big, start small, but most of all, start." when do you think is the right time for someone to start finding their why and do you think the educational system does a good job of helping kids find and understand their why? Thank you so much for taking the time to answer my question. I'm a huge fan. I've seen all your videos. And I hope to meet you one day.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: Aww, that's so nice, thank you. The time to find your why is when you wanna find it. I never believe that somebody should be forced to find it. I would never tell somebody you have to find it. When you're ready to find it, then find it. If it's when you're 18, do it when you're 18. If it's when you're 24, do it when you're 24. If it's when you're 50, do it when you're 50. But when you are ready, like my rule for me is I won't help anybody find their why unless they ask me. Because you have to want it. You have to want it, right? And I believe that, I would love to see our education system offer that opportunity. It is currently not offered in almost every high school or university.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: I would love to see the why discovery process introduced into universities, so that juniors and seniors or maybe sophomores when they're choosing their majors, but definitely juniors and seniors, that as a parting gift from the university, they actually get to learn what inspires them and who they are, what makes them tick, so that they can make those decisions when they leave school. I think that would be an amazing thing to build into an education system. It doesn't exist, it should exist, and in terms of when you should do it, when you're ready. If you want it now then do it now. I'm very proud of the fact ... So the biggest complaint I got when I wrote Start With Why is I make the case for the existence of this thing called they why, but I don't tell anybody how to find it.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: And I'm very, very proud of it and here's why. Because I understand that there's not enough of my team to go out there and help everybody. And it's a high quality, high price product. And I'm really proud of the fact that we have this book that basically takes word for word our entire process and put it in a book that you can get on Amazon for like 12 bucks. I'm proud of that. And that is well within the reach of every university student. So if your university doesn't offer the actual sort of high intensity, human to human way of doing it, then go out and spend 12 bucks and get together with a friend and do it with each other. Somebody should form the Start With Why club at your university, where you buy one book, you can all share it, and you all help each other find your why. And the only people who join the club are people who wanna find their why.

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: That's good. That's really good. And it makes me think, speaking of universities and students being on campuses, finding your why, we like to ask this question of all of our guests. Why do you think it's important for students to be a part of organizations such as the National Society of Leadership and Success, that helps to build leaders and put them in situations or organizations or around people that can help them find their why?

speaker: Simon Sinek
text: We are social animals and we thrive when we're amongst people who believe what we believe. We're all very connected in this world but we're not connecting, and I think to show up with human beings, in a room like this, every single one of you could've tuned in online, and I know a lot of people did tune online, but it's different when you're here. I can look you in the eye. You can feel it. As can I. And there's something to be said for doing something with common pursuit with other people, that I fundamentally believe in. And the idea of teaching people leadership, I love that it's happening here, 'cause we've already discussed, it's not happening in hospitals, it's not happening in companies, so let's at least make it happen at a university level. So that the future leaders will be way better equipped to lead than the current leaders.

Working for The Today Show, on NBC.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: This national platform that was just amazing. Doing really cool stories. Again, a stage that I was able to find myself on, whether it was covering a group of refugees down in Clarkson, Georgia or a girl with down syndrome who was swimming across Lake Tahoe. I was able to tell stories and develop relationships with the world, along a path that I didn't expect. Remember, I wanted to be an astronaut, then I wanted to be a programmer, and then I was a football player. And now, all of a sudden, I'm in media on one of the biggest shows in the world. The Today Show, the morning show. And it's my story of reinvention. And it all comes from opportunities and the relationships that you make. Now at the end of the day, sometimes, you have to create your own opportunities. And that's, ultimately, what happened to me. My success story was great until it wasn't. In 2009, I started having trouble in my marriage. Ultimately, I divorced in 2010, and with four kids, it was rough. It was difficult. And despite what looked calm on the outside, I was struggling inside.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: I went through what I now know was a depression, 'cause I didn't leave my apartment. I stayed at home and watched reruns on Netflix. I think I watched every episode of Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman and Cheers, and all these antiquated shows that I had no interest in but I just watched because I needed to see the end. And I was stuck, until I realized that if I wanted to get out of it, I had to create my own opportunity. So I got up, went back and started working out with my strength trainer. He got me nice and strong and big, and like I was a football player again and here I was at 35 years old, saying, "I can come back to NFL." It didn't work out. It wasn't my fault though, they locked out. They locked out the players so that's what I keep telling myself. But it got me off the couch, right? I recreated this energy, this vigor inside of myself and it started opening up opportunities again because of relationships that I had. So back to my days at the University of Virginia. I went to school with this...

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: This guy's name was Rick Gerson. And he called me when he saw that I was trying to come back to the National Football League and he said, "What in the hell are you doing?" He said, "You don't need to be playing football anymore. "Go talk to my brother. "You guys'll figure something out." And so we met at Club Macanudo on 63rd Street and Madison Avenue in New York. We smoked a cigar and... Started talking about the problems that athletes, former athletes, face when they retire and pondering whether there was anything that we could do about it. And a week later or two weeks later, or three weeks later after these continued meetings and building this relationship, we started a company called Thuzio. Thuzio means "Enthusiast." Everyone is an enthusiast of somebody, and if you can find a way to connect with that icon in your life, why would you not do it? And so Thuzio was built as a marketplace. Interestingly, it was a turn back to that second dream, that second opportunity I had at the University of Virginia as a programmer.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: And so we created a platform for consumers, whether it be individuals or businesses, to interact with former athletes. And it was things like playing flag football or going to lunch, or going to a business conference, or anything you could conceivably think of, we had created. And so when you think about the life and the path that you're going to take, whether it's succinct and you're straight in line, you know exactly what you're doing, don't forget that you might fall off for a variety of reasons. One, cause you find a better opportunity. Two, you might fail out of it. You need to seek another opportunity. But ultimately, when failure comes about as it undoubtedly will, because that's life, you have to sometimes recreate yourself. And when I mentioned earlier that sometimes you don't know what those opportunities will look like. As I stand here on a stage, elevated above you guys, I can't help but think about probably the greatest opportunity that ever came to me.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Last year, actually about a year and half ago, I got a call from my manager, who told me, "You know, I know you did a little bit of stage acting "at one point in your life. "Would you be interested in being in a Broadway show?" And obviously, I said yes. Who wouldn't wanna be on The Great White Way? And so he asked me and I agreed to do a stint in Kinky Boots. And so as I stand here on stage, I'm remembering like the dance that I had to do in six-inch, thigh high, red stiletto boots, and the song that we sang at the end. With Raise You Up where everybody gets emotional and brought into it. The beauty of that performance and that show is that we on stage were pushing out all of this love and eventually you get it, and then all that love comes right back on top of me. And, of all the things that I've done, outside of having kids and raising a family, professionally.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Playing in the NFL, starting businesses, being on a radio show, getting talk about why the Jets and the Giants stink this year, of all those things, doing a Broadway show with a message like Kinky Boots was probably the greatest opportunity that ever came my way. "Oh and he was a football player for The New York Giants. "Oh he's a broadcaster." But life is so much deeper than that, and my life is so much deeper than that, and it all came about because I saw opportunities and I tried to capitalize on them. I saw relationships that were built over years and when things got hard, and when failure started to takeover, you lean on those relationships, right? There's that whole song, right? ♪ That's what friends are for ♪ it's true, right? It lasts, it lives in your heart and in your mind because it's true. We say cliches in football, like, "Oh, we gotta give it our best.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: "You know, we just gotta play one play at a time." It sounds corny to you all, but it's the truth\! That's why they keep saying it. As you all think about where your life is going to go and the path that it's going to be on, not just you in the audience, but all of you out there watching in cyberspace, think about your opportunities. speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Hello, my name is Ronald Abdul Holland. A senior student at City College and this question is for Mr. Barber. Being a businessman and a entrepreneur, could you please explain to us the failures you went through as a businessman, and how did you overcome them? Thank you.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: That is a great question. So I have started three businesses now. And the first one was a fun one. It was with Stephen Ross of The Related Companies, doing affordable housing. Now the problem with the business is that we started it in 2007 and we all know what happened in 2008. It was a correction in the market and we felt stuck. Now the lesson from that business was that timing matters. I said that about the Giants and winning a Super Bowl but it really matters in life and in business. You have to be really aware of the macro issues even though you're focused, when you're an entrepreneur, on the micro, right? You look right now. All you can see, sometime myopically, is what you're trying to create but you have to take in the macro factors which we kinda didn't do. Fortunately, Steve Ross was our business partner. He let us out of the deal, he personally guaranteed it and guess what? In two, three years, it turned around and he made a ton of money. So I think it's...

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: One of the things you have to think about is the, are all of the market forces but also, partner well. And when I started Thuzio, my partner in Mark Gerson, who was my friend, Rick Gerson's brother, had already started a big company called GLG, the Gerson Lehrman Group, which is the largest collection of experts, so he had been enormously successful and the beauty of that is that there was no pride in ownership. It wasn't like, "I'm starting this myself, "I'm bootstrapping and I'm gonna do it all on my own "and I don't want any help from anybody else." It was, "Let me find the best people to partner with "and work with, so that when we have to pivot, "as every business has to do, "you're not driven to profitability." I think one of the hardest things that young entrepreneurs get faced with is giving up equity for sustainability, and it's a really hard equation. Because when you start going to VCs and private equity firms, you end up giving up a little bit of control and get driven down a path that might not necessarily be the right path to success.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: You know, you said to partner well and I feel like a lot of times, we feel like a good partner would be someone in our family or a good friend-- - Usually not\!

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Yeah, so one of the things that... I think one of the greatest skills I learned, and I alluded to it when I was talking, at the University of Virginia, was that I met so many different people from different walks of life, and so I learned how to communicate with anyone and everyone and I always tell people, when I get into a room and I'm uncomfortable, smile, right? It'll drive people to you. It will make you seem approachable, even if you're scared out of your wits or angry, or whatever. It's deceiving but it makes it real. It makes you approachable. And so finding the right partner is all about having too many friends, you know what I mean? And I'm not talking about friends you go to dinner with every night and you talk to every day, but people who you can call on who've had a meaningful relationship with you and have a sense of you. That allows you to have options 'cause you gotta have options. - Absolutely. Okay, so our first Twitter question.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: True. Well, it depends on what you're talking about 'cause I have many walks of life, but I'll give you a football analogy quickly. In the NFL, there's an immediacy. No, you better be ready because there's 52 other guys that are, that you are accountable to. That are expecting you to play at a certain level. And so that expectation, because of the immediacy of success and failure, pulls you up even when you're not, when you're not ready. But if you're not in an industry like that, and by the way also, you get hit one time in football, you kinda get mad and you get ready. But most people aren't in that type of industry. I think when... In my other walks of life, like for instance, when I was Broadway or when I get ready to do a show for my radio show, and I don't feel up or ready, I stop thinking about it, right?

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Because what makes you feel anxious and unready, sometimes, is that you don't feel prepared, and you're like, "Oh, I can't think straight "because I gotta think about the A "and then I gotta think about B and C and D," and so when I get to that point, I just, I quit it all. And become that procrastinator that all of us have been at some point, and, interestingly, life finds a way to work itself out. And if it doesn't, it'll be okay, right? The next hour will come. The next day will come. It will work itself out. I think we sometimes stress too much in day-to-day life, whether in school or work or whatever it may be. And sometimes you just gotta relax.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Yeah, I know I've definitely been guilty of feeling like it was the, that something was the end of the world when it was far from the end of the world, and then you get in your head, and get yourself crazy and you're right. Life will go on, the next day will come, the next hour will come. That's great advice. - And you fix it, tomorrow.

text: And so, I often get asked, you know, "Why did you retire when you did? "What made you... "You were so good at the end of your career. "Why did you retire?" text: That's a great question. So I'm trying to, so... You wouldn't know it, because of what I do for a living, but I was really shy when I was young. I mean painfully shy. speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Like, nervousness about having to talk to all these people, until I said to myself, "Like, embrace this." Again, smile into it and embrace it. text: Right, there's just a different energy and if you, if you cast it off, again, back to the Kinky Boots, you send out this tidal wave of whatever it is. speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Okay, so Caroline on Twitter asks, "How do you know which is the right path for you "and, for example, how do you know..." Sorry. Caroline on Twitter asks, "How do you know which is the right path for you? "For example, how do you know you declared the right major?"

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: No, you don't. You don't. You absolutely don't. And you can change, nobody says you can't. Again, I told you guys, I wanted to be an engineer 'cause I wanted to be an astronaut. And along the way, I found that I loved something else more. And so, declaring is, I guess, you have to do it, but I almost feel like not declaring is what life is about. And it's back to the last statement that I said to you guys in my address. Don't jump into a box, right? Don't let someone put you into a box. And so, certain professions require it. Like, you're gonna be a doctor or a lawyer, you kinda gotta stay in the box. But for my experience, and whether this is, you know, hugely successful entrepreneurs or whether it's accountants or whatever it may be, they've made their best decisions by not being defined and focusing on the relationship first as opposed to, you know, the title. So if you're declaring a major and you're not quite sure that the one that you declared is right for you, it's probably not right for you, right? And so, it's one of those questions.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: I also feel like a lot of people don't end up doing what their major was anyway, so like, you know, it doesn't matter these days and so why not just declare something that you're interested in so you can learn about it?

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: You can be whatever you want. I had lunch yesterday, actually, with an entrepreneur and I ask him, you know, "how did you get into this space?" I was like, that's true, because the world is just interactions, and I think about, like, all of these business folks who have had ridiculous success. They didn't get there on their own. They got there because they had a good relationship with someone who helped them along the way and they connected. And so, don't stress over it because it, ultimately, likely won't matter, unless you're a doctor or a lawyer.

And some people just aren't cut out for it. They're better following and being diligent that way. But being a leader takes, I think, a couple of things. One, a very clear direction. You can't waffle. You can't say, "Oh, this is where we're going. "Yeah, but nah, now we're gonna go here. "Nah, we're gonna go here." So it takes a very clear direction. It takes a skill to relate to people. Like, I consider myself a people person. Like I could sit in a room with anybody and have a conversation.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: I learned that from Bob Tisch actually, who was one of our former owners who passed away in 2005, and he would walk into a room and be okay with everybody, and have a real conversation with everybody.
