And I asked him, I was like, "Why are we going to this event "and why am I hosting this event for you?" And he said to me, he goes, "Because he's gonna win." And it was, it was just, it was like a genius response. But that's leadership. It's understanding how to fit and how you help others fit into the mold that suits them the best. And so, having a clear direction but also being relatable. It's the most important part of being a leader. Because if you can't talk to everybody, then, at some point, they're not gonna follow you.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: People don't wanna work for you. (murmurs) try hard. - You gotta be on the level. Be on the level, right? The same level, you have to be. At least perceived same level. - Absolutely. text: Hi, Tiki. I'm Marisa Carpenter. A sophomore at University of The Pacific. Thank you.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Awesome question, Marisa. So she's right. I was in the McIntyre School of Commerce, my concentration was management information systems, which was studying database design and programming, C++ and COBOL, which are obsolete languages now by the way, so it's like when I tell people, "I know C++," they're like, "(sniggers) okay, and? "I know my ABCs too." She asked a very good question. How do you balance it? At UVA, I did a lot. I was in a couple of societies. The Rotunda Burning Society, which is a service society and, you know, The Imps and, you know, all these things and I also played football, I ran track for a year while I was there. But obviously, being a student was the most important thing for me. Time management became the hardest, mainly because of, football was so structured.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: It was, you gotta be at the facility by, you know, 02:30 and you're gonna get outta there at 06:00, and you gotta go to a study hall, and then you gotta go to the training table 'cause they make sure you eat, which was a good thing 'cause I wouldn't, but then you have to go finish your homework and start the whole day over again. And I think the short answer, and I wouldn't espouse this really, is I didn't sleep a lot when I was in college. Mainly because I loved it so much. And, I mean, I loved the programming stuff. Nobody knew what HTML was. Like, nobody, it was, like, "How is this stuff on this screen?" And then Doom came along and then all the computers were taken in the computer lab. But when you love something, as I grew to love it, you find time to do it. And I didn't sleep a lot, and it probably... I was probably able to get away with it because I was 19 and 20, 21 years old. But learning how to manage your time and make priorities is the most important thing.

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: So block off, you know, two hours where this is what you're going to do every day and get on a schedule. Whether it's in the morning, I'm gonna get up, I'm going to go do my programming work and I have my practice from this block, and then afterwards, I have to go to study hall and then I'm gonna get back into the lab and finish up that work then I'm gonna sleep. You have to block it. You can't let it meander. You can't be like, yeah, you know, I'll get to it in a second. Yeah, I'll do that homework then. Yeah, I'll work on that project then. You have to really block it. And I think one of the great things about our advisors at UVA is that's what they would do. They would give us simple sheets, like blocks of time. Like, what are you gonna do here? What are you gonna do here? What are you gonna do here?

speaker: Tiki Barber
text: Put in front of you. - It's in front of you, it structured you. It's like the kid who puts his goals on his wall, and he sleeps and looks at it every night. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Valerie Jarrett, is the longest serving senior advisor to President Barack Obama, and the current senior advisor to the Obama Foundation. She oversaw the White House offices of public engagement and inter-governmental affairs, and shared the White House council on women and girls. She led the Obama administrations efforts to expand and strengthen access to the middle class and boost American businesses and our economy. She championed equality and opportunity for all Americans and economically and politically empowering women in the United States and all around the world. Ms. Jarrett came to the White House with a background in both the public and private sectors, having served as chairman of the Chicago Transit Board, commissioner of Planning and Development, and Deputy Chief of Staff for Chicago Mayor, Richard M. Daley. Ms. Jarrett serves on the board of Lyft, the John F. Kennedy Center for the performing arts, and is the board chair for when we all vote. She's been name one of Time Magazine's, most influential people. And if that's not enough, she's also, a best-selling author. NSLS members here at Montclair State University and those watching all across the country, please welcome Ms. Valerie Jarrett.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Oh absolutely this is such an honor, thank you so much for being here this evening, I know it's an honor for me, myself and to our members and we're all looking forward to hearing from you. You know I felt so inspired when I was introducing you just now, you've had this incredible career, both public and private sectors, but I read that growing up, and I heard you actually speaking in the green room, that you were painfully shy. Really really scared to speak up for yourself, and for others, a feeling I'm sure many of the members have felt before and can relate to. So, how do the stories about, you know the struggles and accomplishments of your family members, help you find your own voice and what advice can you give our members, to find their voice?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Practice, practice, practice. I was so shy, I said this to some of the students who I just met with, when I was your age, I never raised my hand in class, I think it has to do with and I don't wanna do the spoiler alert but I was born in the Middle East and we moved to the United States when I was five, after having been in London for a year and we moved, overseas initially because my father was looking for a job, in a major teaching hospital in the United States and as an African American, he couldn't find one, comparable to his white counterparts. So he and my mom took this huge leap of faith, and they went halfway across the world, and I was the second baby born in the hospital that he helped start.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And so then we went to London for a year, and them moved back home as my parents called it, to Chicago, and I think, just starting school I was a couple years ahead of myself, I had a British accent for that one year I spent in Great Britain, I was from a country no one had ever heard of, and I just felt different.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I got bullied, I got beat up for a whole host of reasons after school, and I had a younger cousin who had to come to my rescue, that was embarrassing, and so it kind of made me withdraw, and I didn't wanna speak up 'cause I was afraid somebody would say, oh you're the different one. And that painful shyness stayed with me well into adulthood to tell you the truth, and it wasn't until I swerved, as I like to talk about in my career, and found a job where I first started advocating for other people who particularly those who didn't have a voice.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Well of course I knew he'd be president one day, didn't all of you? No, so all right so this is the setting. It is the summer of 1991, and I have been working for city government for four years, three mayors in four years, and mayor Daley had just promoted me to Deputy Chief of Staff and I was trying to hire people to come work in the mayor's office. And a dear friend of mine who was a lead lawyer for the city, sent me a resume and across the top it said, "Brilliant young lawyer, "has no interest in being in a big law firm, "wants to explore public service." And I had been at a big law firm too kinda following the path of least resistance, and had left because I was miserable, so when I saw this wonderful resume and heard that this other woman was interested in leaving the law firm I thought I wanna meet her.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: So I call her in for an interview and Michelle Robinson walks in my office, she's about, she's just not much older than all you, she's 27, tall, elegant but simply dressed all in black, she had her hair pulled back, barely any makeup on, and she saw her resume sitting on her desk. And she never mentioned anything about Princeton undergrad, or Harvard Law School, none of that, she told me her story. Which is a good lesson when you're interviewing, people could read your resume they don't need you to resuscitate that, just tell them your story and it's what you all now know is the quintessential American story. Growing up on the south side of Chicago, working class family, parents who hadn't gone to college but believed that she and her brother could have a better life with a good education, and instilled in them this core sense to those who much as give and much as expect it. And then she told me how her father, and her best friend had died within the previous year. And that it was wake up call. And she thought you know life is short. I should do something purposeful.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And interestingly I left my big law firm right after I had a baby, and I used to look at this baby who now just had a baby so that tells you how long ago that was,

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: and I thought well, will she every be proud of me? If I continued to do something that, for which I feel no passion. And I thought, I'm leaving her every day to go do something I don't enjoy, why don't I go and find something that makes me feel good and it's the first time I actually listened to the quiet voice inside of me. And I joined city government and it changed my life. And so I was so impressed with Michelle Robinson, I gave her a job offer on the spot. I had no authority to give her a job offer (laughs) but I thought who would turn her down right? She's magnificent. And she said wisely, "Let me think about it." And then a few days later I said well what about that job, are you gonna come and work with us? And she said, "Well my fiancee doesn't think it's such a good idea." And I said well who's your fiancee, and why do we care one bit what he thinks?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: and she said, "Well his name is Barack Obama, "and he started his career as a community organizer "on the south side of Chicago, "and he's a little uncomfortable with me "going straight from a law firm into the "political environment in the mayor's office. "Would you have dinner with us?" and I said yes and that was such a good move. And I will tell you, at the dinner he really got me to open up about myself and as I mentioned to you I didn't really like to talk about this country that's the answer to the question because it was a controversial country by that point in time. And I usually had a lot of explaining to do so he starts out and he goes, "So where are you from?" I said Chicago. He said, "Did you grow up here?" I said yes, he said, "Were you born here?" and I went, no. And then I told him where I was born, and as opposed to a lot of people who reacted kind of weirdly to it, he said, "Well that's interesting, tell me about it."

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And then he started telling me about his life growing up in Indonesia for several of his early years and we compared notes and we found, that we had similar experiences, I don't know how many of you in the audience or watching have lived outside of the United States, but sometimes we take this place for granted. And there's nothing like getting outside of it, particularly in an undeveloped country such as the one I lived in, to see how much we should appreciate what we have, not perfect by any stretch of the imagination, but a lot better. And we also talked about, how both feel like we can walk in a room and find something in common with whoever's in the room, because we grew up with people from all over the world.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And so you kind of expect to find commonalities, not withstanding all these differences, and we also finally agreed that the United States is a fabulous country, but it's actually not the only country on Earth.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And that you can learn a great deal beyond our shores. And so, at the end of the dinner, I remember thinking, ugh my gosh, this couple they're so in love, they're so happy, the perfect couple, they listen to one another, they communicated well, and they both were so committed to public service and he had expressed a little bit of an interest in politics.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Oh my gosh okay well that is an amazing story and just that, you know what's amazing great about this organization, and these talks specifically is, is that it gives our members all over the country, the opportunity to learn from accomplished leaders such as yourself. So many of you guys sent in questions and we're gonna first start out with a video question.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Hello my name is Savannah Lambert, and I go to ACTC, a technical college in Ashland, Kentucky. And my question is, what was it like being a woman and working in the White House, in a male dominant environment?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: That's a good question. Well I am proud to say, particularly 'cause I co-chaired President Obama's transition team, that we didn't have the male dominated environment. He believed that diversity is a strength and so he surrounded himself in the White House, and throughout his administration with people who were diverse. He thought he would make better decisions if he was hearing from a variety of perspectives. But I will say, early on in the White House, we noticed, that the women's voices were shrinking a bit.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I would remind you, when President Obama took office, we were in the middle of the worst economic crisis since the Great Depression, we had two wars under way, we had a lot going on on our plate. The banks were on the verge of collapse, millions of people were losing their homes, millions of people losing their jobs, the automobile industry completely in the tank. And tensions got kind of tense, when he wasn't around 'cause he's very zen-like, and calm and he brings out the best in people. But when he walked out of the room, people got really kind of loud, shall we say. (laughs) some people got loud, the men got loud let's put it that way. And so the women began to shrink and when I told him that he said, "Well that's not the culture I want in my White House." and so he invited the women to dinner and I went to each of them ahead of time and said you better be honest, and tell him what the issues are because culture has to be, built by openness and communication and trust.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And they did, and he said, "Listen you know what, "don't think that you're fighting for yourself. "You're fighting for your ideas. "And your ideas are important to me. "And your ideas are gonna be different "than they guys' ideas. "You each have subject matter expertise "and different life experiences. "And so, go in there and just fight for me. "Knowing that if your ideas get a fair hearing "and are presented to me, "I will make a more informed decision." and that was so empowering to the women and at the end of the first term, someone said to him, "How would you compare your White House at the beginning "when you first took office and everyone came in "and no one knew one another, to the end of the first term?" And he said in the beginning, he had the smartest, best players on the field. At the end of the first term he had the best team.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And team takes trust and communication and one of the ways that I think that the women dealt with some of the tensions that we were experiencing is, we started all having dinner together, after the dinner we had with him, I invited the women and we would open up and we would do just what Michelle Robinson did. We would tell each other our stories and when you walk into a meeting or a classroom and you've had dinner with somebody the night before, and they're at the table, it gives you so much more confidence to speak up. And so, you are, all those of you who are on campuses all across our country, take times, study hard, you know don't go back and tell your parents I said don't work hard, do work hard.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: But take time to build friendships and relationships because, these folks will be with you throughout your life and just think about it, what if I had said to Michelle Robinson, no this is a job interview and I'm not interested in meeting your fiancee. I might not be sitting on this couch with you today.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I think that also means you also have to be willing to make yourself vulnerable, and I hope you all read my book but it is all there. I tell the good, the bad and the ugly in part because I want people who are younger to appreciate I just wasn't born sitting on this couch. That there was a lot that went into this and there were some challenges that I had, there were failures, there was, there was a lot of mess in there. And that's, and I had parents who loved me, unconditionally gave me a lot of support, so there was both love and there was challenge, there was disappointment, there was failure, there was adventure, as I mentioned to you, and I think if you open up and tell your story, then it's easier for people to actually hear what you have to say when you have some messages for them.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And not ever to be ashamed of any parts of those stories because they all make who you are, it's all part of the journey so even the failures right?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Absolutely. The failures have taught me so much and if nothing else they're taught me that I'm resilient. And that I can get back up and I think that's again the advantage of age, and I'm trying to rationalize how it's so good to be my age. It's because you've had some bumps along the road and you see oh that's not the end of the world. You get another chapter. And the question is really not as every chapter perfect, but through the chapters add up to a whole life. I mean, did you love, were you loved? Did you feel as though, the short time that we have on this earth that you made a difference. In somebody else's life, did you make it a little easier for them. And I think that's really, sometimes we're too hard on ourselves in terms of what we expect, perfection, it's not perfection, we're all human. Just try.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: So, in your book "Finding My Voice", which is right here and you absolutely should all read it, you write about your efforts to stay grounded while in the White House pressure cooker, which I can only imagine and I feel as though we all have our own pressure cookers right? Whether it's school or your own job, we all sort of know that feeling. But what advise would you give our members, to keep them focused on their true North, even during the days when that pressure feels absolutely, and completely overwhelming?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Well find your true North first. And that's part of finding your voice and that begins with listening to the most important voice and that's the quiet one inside of each of us. And when I decided to ban in this 10-year plan that I created when I was your age, that I had executed flawlessly and then woke up after 10 years completely miserable in both business life and my personal life, and I veered off into another direction, that's really when things began to happen and I think what you have to do, is to take a good sense of who you are, know where your true North is, doesn't mean you shouldn't be flexible and swerve along the way, but don't let anybody throw you off center and one of the things that I did in the White House, is try to ground myself every single day. And, during President Obama's campaign in 2008, we met a gentlemen in Austin, Texas, who gave President Obama a patch from his military uniform, while we were, he would operate the elevator for us, while we were going up and down in the Hyatt hotel for three days.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And on the last day, at 7:30 in the morning, when President Obama's actually not a morning person, he said, "Let me give you this." And, I was in the elevator, I'm very nosy I don't know if I've mentioned that to you yet, so I was looking to see what it was and when I realized what it was, I was taken aback and so was then Senator Obama who he says, "Well I can't accept it" they go back and forth back and forth, long story short, finally the gentleman said, "I've carried this patch with me for 40 years."

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: It made me strong when I served in our Army and it made me resilient when I faced the vicissitudes of life, and it's been really treasured possession and I want you to have it. Well you know I burst into tears (laughs) and it was a small elevator and it wasn't those pretty tears it was like tear tears where you can't catch your breath, you know those kinda tears,

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And later I said, "What'd you do with that patch?" and he said, "I put it in my pocket." and I thought typical man I don't mean where did you put it physically, I mean, how did it make you feel? 'cause this is before people used to send newborn babies ten-deep over a photo line, you know, here President Obama hold my baby, and I'd go, you don't know those 10 people between you and the president. They might drop that baby.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: So this was before any of that kinda stuff started happening and so when I challenged him, well how did it really make you feel, he pulls out all these trinkets that people had given him.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Keeps them in his pocket 'till this day. All along the campaign trail and he told me the name of the person, if he knew it, why it was so special, and why he put it in his pocket. So I decided every day when I came to the White House, 'cause you can get caught up, 'cause it's chaos in there, that I would as I came through the gates, I would think about that man, and just like ground myself, and look at the Washington monument blinking and thinking, oh my gosh I'm going into the White House. And I would say, do something to make him proud, today. Just like I wanted to make my daughter proud, when I went into public service I wanted to make that sacrifice, that act of generosity from that gentleman worthwhile. And that helped me. It just helped me tune out the noise and the clutter, and to appreciate that it's not about you, you are a public servant and I learned a local government, which I commend everybody to try because your constituents are proximate.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: They know your phone number, they know your address, they come down to city hall and yell at you in person, they go to community meetings and yell you they protest in front of your home, as was my case one time and my daughter said, "Why do you do this?" and I said, "I'd rather be the one making those decisions." and I learned how to listen to the people that were there to serve, and I think that skill, that value set, was important in the White House, where people can seem a long way away 'cause it is such a isolating ivory tower.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And so, I worked hard to bring people in to bring voices in from outside, that was one of my responsibilities, to make sure, that we stayed in touch that we had the pulse and that keeps you grounded too.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: All right so speaking of skills, I'm not sure if you've heard but before you came on stage, we asked our audience both here and those watching across the country, a trivia question, and a texting poll question, so I'd like to take a look at the results right now with you here. Here was the trivia question. Valerie Jarrett was born to American parents who at the time were living and working in which Middle Eastern country? Name the country. The answer is Iran. And our winner is, Lillian Toney from Northeast Lakeview College. Congratulations.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Good job, Lillian. All right so we're also gonna take a look, at our texting poll results. In the beginning of the broadcast we asked you the following, in your opinion, what is the most important characteristic or skill a leader should possess? So 6%, we're gonna have the results right here. 6% said communication, 17% said confidence, 75% said integrity, and 2% said creativity. So I'm very curious to hear your opinion on these results but let's discuss after we watch a related question from Natalie James from the University of Texas at San Antonio.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: I think that leadingship is about motivating people and I would've added one, motivating people to move in a direction where they might not have gone but for your leadership. So if they're prepared to go down that path, then you're not influencing then that's actually not leadership. And so you have to first again, to yourself be true, you have to be authentic, they have to believe you, and you have to feel passionately about the direction that you wanna take them. If you don't care about it, people can feel that, they have to know that you are authentic because you're asking them to do something different than what they're already doing right and they're not gonna do that, also if they don't trust you. And so you have to have good communication skills, you have to have confidence, you have to believe in what you're saying, if you're at tentative then they're gonna go, why am I gonna follow you? You better know what you're doing, right? And I think, I'm so delighted to see integrity poll as high as it did.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Because, I think, regardless of whether we're talking about leading an organization or a campus or we're talking about world leaders or local leaders or business leaders, integrity, you have nothing more important than your reputation. My dad used to tell me when I was very young, very very young, color well within the lines. And if you color well within the lines then you'll always be safe. And sometimes I would call home with an ethical question, as a young adult or maybe even in college, and my father, you know, this is back when you had different lines and he'd pick up the line after my mom and I've been talking, and he'd say, "What are ya'll talking about?" And I'd describe and he said, "So you're calling here 'cause you're not sure what to do." and I said yeah. He said, "If you're not sure what to do, "you do know what to do, don't do it."

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And that was just a good core principal to stick with you, so I think integrity is really, really important. Because if people are following you, often times they're putting their life in your hands, their future in your hands, their profession, their personal life in your hands. Have integrity, have character. Have core values.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Right, and when we say leadership we're talking about good leadership, which means to me, be kind. Be decent. I think you can be very strong, and very decent. It's part of why I was drawn to work for President Obama. There were a lot of people who used to say to me, "Why doesn't he get angry and yell?" It takes a lot more strength, to stay calm and focused, than it does to fly off the handle.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Yeah. So you said that your decision to leave private law for public service was a surprise to many, including yourself. And I'm sure many of our viewers are thinking, about maybe making some changes in their life, whether it's personal or professional.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Well so Nicole in a word, what drove me, misery. I was very unhappy. It's a great motivator, I always wonder like, what if I had been just, a little unhappy might I have stayed. So let me tell you about that 10-year plan I described to you. So my plan was to go right to law school, because I couldn't figure out what else to do, I slept through the GMATS, it was a good party the night before, I went to Anatomy class with my boyfriend I was scared of the cadaver, I was scared of organic chemistry, that was the end of pre-med, and so my best friend was in law school and she said go to law school. And everybody at college had a plan and I thought well I need a plan. So I made a 10 year plan. Go right to law school, figure out what my passion in the law is, probably move back home to Chicago, get a grade job, fall in love, get married, have a baby by 30, thinking about that biological clock, thank goodness it ticks later now don't worry, and live happily every after.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I did everything on that list, I married the boy next door, and that our moms had grown up in the same apartment building, our fathers were friends he was a doctor, my dad was a doctor, I had a crush on him since I was eight and he was 12, what could go wrong. Oh, plenty, plenty could go wrong. Trust me, plenty could go wrong. I did have my daughter just shy of my 29th birthday best thing I ever did, and I had this great job at a big law firm and everybody thought my life should be perfect, including my parents. I was the first lawyer in our family and so they were really proud of me. And I was not. And I think sitting in that, I begin my book in my office in tears. Beautiful office, great view of Lake Michigan, wonderful salary, and I just was miserable. And I thought, I have got to figure out, what's really in my core. And I had to do some soul searching and it's a very lonely experience, particularly when everybody else thinks you should be happy and you're not.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And a good friend of mine said, "Why don't you consider joining the administration "of Mayor Hill Washington?" He was the first black mayor of Chicago, and he was a progressive and he was delicious he had a vocabulary you wouldn't believe, everything had three or four syllables and they were all in the dictionary, real words. (Nicole laughs) He just was mesmerizing and it's the first time I really thought, seriously about city government, I didn't know who my elderman was, I didn't know how many there were, I didn't know how government worked, because I never felt connected to the people who were leading the city. And when he was selected I started reading the newspaper, the Chicago Lens section and I started figuring out how things worked. And so when my friend said, "Why don't you veer", I listened to that quiet voice and it took, courage and in fact, the first day of work, my mom took me to work I don't know why, I'm grown adult with a child, married.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And she drove me to work at City Hall, I think it was so she could say to me when we pulled up in front, "I can't believe I spent all that money on tuition, "for you to do this." (Nicole laughs) and I just said, Mom, I think this is gonna be the right thing for me. And it takes a lot of strength, and I love my mom and she's always right, except this time I thought you know I was doing what everybody else thought was good, and it wasn't right for me. And I think the thing about the swerve which I, I am really big on is that, the advantage of having an education for all of you here and those of you who are listening, a good education is it gives you a safety net where you can take some chances. I'm not saying do something stupid, but you can take some chances, you can take some calculated risks, knowing that if they don't work out, you can then do something else and then you will have learned something even with the bad experience.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: I'm really glad I spent six years, miserable at a big corporate law firm. I learned a lot that was invaluable when I was a lawyer for the city. And that's the other piece of it, even if you don't think you're enjoying what you're doing, work hard at it, try to figure it out, take in what you can from the experience, and then don't be afraid to move on and particularly don't fear yourself. Don't fear failure so much that you're unwilling to try.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Yeah, that's amazing. You've obviously had many stressful jobs, at least they seem stressful to an outsider like us. So our fist Twitter question, comes from Laura Ann Jimenez, and she wants to know if you have any tips on how to handle stress, what works for you.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Yeah and I think this is again very personal. And I think part of it is, you have to, keep that long view, what I was saying earlier your true North and recognize that there is gonna be some bumps along the way and then you have to surround yourself by people who wish you well. And I think we've probably all had experiences with friends, so called friends, that don't actually wish you well, that aren't there for you when you need them, that aren't supportive and kind to you. And I think one of the advantages of getting older again is that you kind of lose all of the ones that were just kind of not really in your corner. And, build strong, deep relationships with people who are rooting for you.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I found you know there's this whole sense of, particularly for women, is there balance, can I have it all, well no, no none of that is true, nothing's every balanced in any relationship I've ever been in or in life, and certainly you can't have it all if it means right now, all at the same time, which usually means you're doing it all yourself but again, it's back to those chapters and at each chapter along the way, did you have people in your life, that were enhancing it and were you enhancing the lives of other people? And that I think gives you a reservoir of support and then I also think you have to, like for me, I exercise in the morning, and I started doing this really and earnest after I had my daughter and I was trying to lose the 90 pounds that I gained, and I would get up every morning before she got up and that would be my hour of the day, and I kept that habit.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And the endorphins worked I guess, I don't enjoy working out but the endorphins to make you feel better and if I start on the treadmill and I'm just obsessing about something that has upset me from the day before, by the time I'm done, I don't know maybe I'm just so exhausted but I've forgotten what I was so upset about. And it kind of is restorative to me and so you have to figure out, what is restorative to you, and just as they often say the analogy, if you're in an airplane and the oxygen gets thin and they drop the mask, put it on yourself first, you do have to figure out how to take care of yourself. And you also have to figure out and this took me a while, how to laugh at yourself.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: I do the dumbest things sometimes and I used to take them so, I'd be mortified back to the fear of speaking in public and now you see I literally cannot shut up, right? (Nicole laughs) But there was a time where, wherever I asked a question if I didn't think it was brilliant or wasn't phrased exactly correctly or if I did a speech and I think well, I blew it, I didn't say that word or I didn't make this point that was in my talking points and I drive myself nuts and I'm like just give yourself a break.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I worry because we're seeing metal health issues particularly among college students are becoming more acute and I think that some of it is social media and I know we love social media, we're using it today, it can be an incredible force for good. But it can also be very isolating and make people compare themselves to everybody else's better life and not learn, you'll see a constant theme here from me today. The richness and texture of human interaction. I would much rather be sitting here talking to you, and seeing your face and your body language so why it's so great to have the videos with these questions too, it's just more to it than just texting as opposed to talking to and with somebody.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: I mean I know for myself that it's definitely been hard to let certain people go because you think growing up, all these people are gonna be a part of my life forever and like you said, not all of them want you to do well and it's hard to you know, to just move through life and let some of those people go but it's a really important thing for your success.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Let them go nicely and give and you know what? And then give them a chance 'cause they may grow and you know, someone who was selfish when you were in college, might've seen what it feels like on the other end of that stick and grow and so, I'm not saying don't be forgiving, but you do have to protect yourself.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: So what is your relationship with Lucile Davins, a confident black woman who worked as an assistant to Chicago's Mayor Washington and Mayor Dayley teach you about the importance of mentorship and how did you apply those lessons during your mentorship to the Obamas?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Oh my goodness, so that's the book. So, where does it begin. So Lucile Davens was a very confident African American woman who worked in the Mayor's office when I worked in the law department, she was my client. And she was a badass, she really was and everyone was terrified of her and the person who recommended to me that I go work in city government was a good friend of hers and he called ahead and he said phone a friend and said, "Look out for Valerie," which was really helpful. Again, because I had a relationship with him, he was willing to do that for me and she had a relationship with him so she was willing to take me under her wing and she helped me in more ways than I can ever describe to you. She brought me to meetings with senior policy people so I could understand how the law tied into the policy as it was being developed.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: She let me go and see Mayor Washington who I already told you I loved dearly and take me into his office and, and I was really a fly on the wall for everything that she did and I learned a lot watching her and she would always say to me, "Valerie, every thing we do, in city government, "is designed to improve the lives "of the citizens of Chicago." That's the litmus test, if we're not doing that, then we're not doing our jobs. And it just she drowned it into me in such a powerful, effective way. And then she mentored me by one day, well one other thing, so I told you, I think I mentioned to you I was a single mom by that point in time, and I finally took the nerve to say, well look I gotta get home by bed time 'cause I've gotta put Laura to bed, I'll come back but I at least gotta tuck her in, 'cause she's old enough to say where are you mommy. And Lucile said, "Well how about if I stop at your home "on my way home?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: "It's on the way and we can work from there "after you put Laura to bed." And then I started fixing dinner for her so she did get something out of it. (laughs) But, you know who does that for you? It was just incredibly sensitive and she had a 16-year old daughter and remembered what it was like probably to be a young working mother, and then, one of the most important things she did for me was she said to me one day, "You should go ask for promotion". Never in my wildest dreams did I ever consider doing that, and I said well when my boss decides I'm worthy of a promotion, she'll give it to me. And she said, "First of all, you should ask for double promotions, "so you can't go to your boss, you need to go to your boss' boss' boss."

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And, he's not thinking about you either and I am your client and I know your work and I know the experience you had, the six years at the law firm.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: So go and ask for the promotion. Well I just wouldn't do it. And I just kept, not doing it and not doing it not doing it and finally she said, "You gotta go," and I thought well I'm losing her confidence, she's just disappointed in me so I thought, let's get it over with. So I go in, I make an incoherent pitch I think, for why I'm deserving this promotion, and the chairman of the department said, "Okay." just like that. So I go back to Lucile and I said, "He said okay\!" and she said, "That's great\!" 30 years later, I call Lucile Davens and I say, I've written a book, and you're in the book and I wanna tell you everything that's in the book, but one thing's been bothering me all these years, and she said, "What?" I said, did you every say anything to Judd before I went in there and asked for that promotion? and she said, "I might have."

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: All these years I was thinking I made that powerful case, right? And she didn't tell me which means that she understood the importance of me asking for myself. That that's a part of my growth, that she recognized I didn't have the confidence to do. And she knew if I asked I would get it. But she made me go in there and do that myself and that was so empowering for me. Particularly since I thought I made this compelling case all those years. So yes, and so I think the lesson, the lesson that Lucile taught me is to get to know the people who you're working with, as she had gotten to know me, and I had opened up to her. And then then you're gonna be able to bring the best out of them.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And so for my teams of, whether it was working running the department of planning and development, sharing the CTA, being the C of a real estate company or working in the White House, the teams that I've always had, have gotten to know the people on my team and I want them to be open with me and tell me their story and let me understand what's going on in their life because I think too often, we try to compartmentalize our lives, And it doesn't actually work. I realized that like when I was trying to, close a real estate deal at two in the morning and I kept getting up to leave and, I'd say I'm going to the vending machine or I'm going to the Xerox machine or I'm going to check voicemail. I'll give you a hint I was nine months pregnant. Where was I going? The bathroom 'cause that's what you do when you're nine months pregnant. You're laughing 'cause you know right? But I didn't feel that I could tell the guys anything about my pregnancy and I just, nothing's happening below my neck.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Because I thought that if they knew me, and they knew how messy everything else was, they wouldn't think I was as serious about my work, and what Lucile helped me understand is, by opening up and saying to her I'm in a divorce, I'm a single mom, I'm this that, she figured out how to accommodate me. And in return, to this day I am loyal to her and the, the other lesson I think I learned in city government along these same lines, is you do have to advocate for yourself, not just by promotions but by what you need in life.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Mayor Dayley who used to terrify me when I first brought me into his office and then he made me the Commissioner of Planning, I was in a meeting with him, with the same person who sent me Michelle Robinson's resume who was a dear friend of mine, and we were sitting across from each other and we keep, kept both looking at our watches and he caught me and he looked and he said, "What's going on here, what's so "important that you're looking at your watch, "you have somewhere to go?" And I was terrified and I'm not sure, I'm not sure, Nicole, what I would've done if Susan hadn't been across the table.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Because if I said, "Sir, the Halloween parade starts in 20 minutes. "And we are 25 minutes away." and I held my breath and I didn't know what he was gonna do, right? I was terrified of the man and he said, "Then what are you doing here, get to the parade." and Susan and I go racing down Lake Shore drive our children were in second grade together, the Halloween parade, little costumes, darlings come out of the school, and the door opens and the parents are standing out waiting for the kids to parade out and our kids come out and they're looking through the audience and we were there, because I spoke up and because there was somebody across the table for a meeting, who said speak up, speak up, speak up. And if you don't tell people what you need, how can they accommodate you and unfortunately, this kinda gets into policy, I think we have some structural impediments that keep working families from being able to thrive, in the workplace.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And part of what I've dedicated, the last 30 years of my life is to try to remove some of those impediments and so it's everything from raising the minimum wage that our families have a living wage to equal pay for women, to paid leave we're the only developed country in the world that doesn't have a national paid leave policy, how on earth are we gonna compete for talent and retain that talent if we don't recognize the fact that we have sick parents, we have babies, we have things that happen in our lives where we need to take off and we can't do it unless we get paid for it. Workplace flexibility, I surely needed that as a single mom. Affordable child care, two thirds of our state, childcare is more expensive than in-state tuition, for state schools. And, and a work environment this applies on college campuses all across our country, we need an environment free of sexual harassment and violence. One in five women, are gonna be sexually assaulted while in college. That is outrageous. And that, predatory violent behavior continues into adulthood.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And so, we have to shape our workplace where the culture is one where everyone can thrive and that means you have to take care of all of that and have a culture of respect.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And just back to what you were saying before for a moment, wouldn't you say that you're a better worker, a better employee, if you speak up and talk about who you really are outside of the workplace? If people don't know who you are and the things that you're dealing with outside of there, then like you said they can't help and you can't be the best person that you can be in that job.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And they will not invest in you if they don't know you. Part of why, I am so close to the Obamas to this day, is because we did have that dinner.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And at the dinner we didn't just talk about the narrow corners of what her job description would be, we got to know one another. And they were trying to figure out, could they trust me? You know would she thrive in this environment, and there were a lot of people who said to me since, "Well why on earth did she need to have her fiancee, there?" But having been at the table for every decision he's made in his career, she's right there too and so it was really more of a reflection of their partnership. So you do have to, and what I'm telling you is not easy. You gotta make yourself vulnerable. And people might, you might tell them something and they might look at you peculiarly just as people looked at me for years, and still do sometimes when I say I was born in Iran. But that experience is part of what has made me who I am, and so don't shy away from who you are.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Yeah. And also nice experience you know you mentioned your early experiences facing racism and discrimination in your book. I know you were bullied for your skin being both too dark and too light. How did those experiences inspire your life long goal of making communities more fair and just?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Well I think once you felt like another, it gives you a level of empathy. And, I remember growing up you know my parents kind of instilled in me these values, that I was talking to you about earlier, but whenever I would say well something's not fair, my parents would say, "Well who told you "that life was fair?" And I used to always think but it should be. And then they would say, "Well then go make it fair." And I'll tell you a very funny story about my mom. I mean my parents, they just they were, well my mom's still alive, incredible people, in so many ways, the risks that they took, their integrity, their character, their core values, but, the weekend after President Obama was elected in 2008, they were, the Obamas were on "60 Minutes". And that was back when being on "60 Minutes" was like, a really big deal.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I watched them and they reminded me, with my parents we watched it together, and my parents had known them as long as I had so, and my parents never in their wildest dreams did they think that in their lifetime the country would elect a black president. Particularly not somebody that they knew so intimately. And in fact during the campaign there would be times where my mom, my mom in particular would say, "You know, this was such a good experience for him, "next time around, I'm sure it'll be better." And I'm like you don't know Michelle Obama, they'll be no next time. If he doesn't nail it this time we're done, he has to get a real job. (laughs) So uh, so the night of the "60 Minutes" when it was finished, you could've heard a pin drop. And my dad had been very ill and we were, actually in his hospital rehab center room, and at the end of it, my mother looked at me, and she said, "How on earth did you know that he could win?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: "Not that he would win, even that he could win?" And I said, Mom, you raised me to say if you're willing to work twice as hard, and you're resilient and you have a dream, and you stick to it and you have a little bit of luck, anything is possible, so, of course I thought he could win. And she looked at me and she said, "Well I never believed any of that."

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And then my father said, "Me either." And I realized, it's crazy. I know I was shocked when they said that, but I realized it was like a thunder bolt went off in my head I said, oh my gosh. They raised me aspirationally. Not as the world that they know, not shackled by their reality, growing up under Jim Crow and segregated Chicago and D.C. where my dad couldn't get a job in the United States and he had to go halfway across the world. That's not the reality that they raised me. They raised me aspirationally to find my reality. To find my own reality and I think, that's part of what we wanna do with young people in college campuses, we don't wanna shackle you with our reality, you are so much smarter. You're so much more worldly you have every bit, everything at your fingertips. The only thing you don't have that I think that we encourage you to do, you don't have experience and you're not as patient as perhaps you should be.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: 'cause you haven't had to be patient, we used to, I sound like people who used to walk to work or walk to school five miles a day but, you have to go to the library and look something on index card and then go find the book and the encyclopedia, you remember that right? You guys just pull out something and it's right there.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And that's great and a lot of respects but it's also, doesn't teach you like the grit of hard work. And that sometimes you work on something that you might not live to see come to fruition. One year for my birthday, president Obama gave me the best gift, Nicole. He gave me the petition for universal suffrage, signed copy of the petition, no idea where he got that but beautiful signed copy, by Susan B. Anthony and all, framed and it was signed in 1866, framed along side the resolution that was proposing the 19th amendment, to give women the right to vote. Signed, 53 years later, 1919. And, he inscribed something sweet about you know you're part of the journey towards mending that ark towards equality, but the lesson in it for me was really you know what, the women who led marches and hunger strikes and were alienated by their husbands, and were jailed to give women the right to vote, back when that first petition was signed, many of them did not live to see us have the right to vote.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And that that's part of what we have to recognize is that we do our part, we carry the baton as far as we can carry it. And if you're lucky, like we were with something like marriage equality, my God people have been working on that for decades, and like a thunder bolt, it happened on our watch. And that was great, but you have to give credit to the journey that it took to get there and you can't expect, particularly big swings in change to happen overnight.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Hi I'm Cassie from Trevveca Nazarene University, and I was just wondering how you advocate for women in the workplace, regardless of your occupation? As well as how you embrace new leadership that you weren't necessarily expecting?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Well advocating for women in the workplace is something we all have to do. And, men have to be a part of the solution let's face it. Men are still, disproportionately represented at the top of all organizations. And so, part of our job as women is to educate them and I talked earlier about how if you're going through something you have to be able to help people understand what you're going through so that they can give you the support that you need, and you have to meet people where they are and so one of, one of my strategies lately, for advocating for women in the workplace, I've changed the paradigm a bit. I used to think back to, you know life should be fair, that I should just simply be able to say, this is the fair thing to do. And then I realized no, that actually doesn't work. You have to explain to the person why it is in their self interest to do it. And so the case I make now for why I advocate for women in the workplace, is it mounting studies show that diversity is actually a strength.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And that you, if you build the diverse workforce, they're more productive, they're more efficient, they if they have the support in terms of the structural impediments being removed that I mentioned earlier, they will be more loyal to you and in the private sector, more profitable. So I make a business case for why, yes it's good for working families to support women in the workplace, but you will have a stronger business, if you do it. And the other reason why I make it a business case is because, lets say you have an initiative, a nice to do for women, and then they budget gets tight, because the economy gets tough. What's the first you cut? You cut the nice to do? You don't cut the business imperative. And so I wanna make sure that a sustainable change over a long time. And I think that we need women's voices in there, and we also need men who appreciate the fact that diversity is a strength, to be our partners in this advocacy.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: I watched them all. (laughs) You can't name a show about the White House that I have not watched and devoured and for different reasons. So "West Wing" was the first one that I really watched. And I thought, oh my gosh, that what every White House must be like, right? And to some degree I have to say, if I had to pick one of those shows, "West Wing" would be more like our White House than any of the others and then, the team of people, we had a great president, who's moral center was where we thought it should be, wasn't a perfect person, none of us were. But they noodle throughout issues in a very similar way to the way that we did. So we really weren't' like "Scandal" at all, but I watched "Scandal". It was my, what do you call it, hidden pleasure, when we were in the White House and we wouldn't always watch it on Thursdays but I would always tape it, and then whenever I just needed a minute to relax 'cause I love Kerry Washington I thought it was great storyline, I also did watch "House of Cards".

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: I'm glad that it's done now because I wasn't very happy at all with how Kevin Spacey behaved. But if you haven't seen the show, it, it is nothing like, well I could say it's not like any White House, it's not like our White House was.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: I'm going to ask my question to Valerie Jarrett. How do you see to yourself as a woman, as a leader, within the business world and within your personal endeavors? And also, how do you keep pushing when the odds are against you and keep telling you no, when in your heart you have a passion to go further? Thank you for your time.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: So, I think again, experiences taught me that most hard things seem impossible, until they seem inevitable. And, once you have enough things that went from hard and impossible to inevitable, in reality, you begin to go okay, what hard things are hard, but you can move the needle. And I think one of the hardest things that we did in the White House was pass the Affordable Care act, and I never really understood why it was that people were against providing affordable health insurance to every American, but they were and mostly it was political, and we just kept pushing and pushing and pushing and there were many times where people said to President Obama, "Your poll numbers are dropping, "because of this. "Why don't you just insure children. "Why don't you compromise?" and he kept saying, "What is the point in having political capital, "unless you're prepared to use it to be a force for good." And seven presidents before him had tried to pass it and failed.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And he also said, "I'm not gonna let perfect "be the enemy of the good." I mean part of what we're hearing in the democratic debates for the president right now is, ways of changing, changing the Affordable Care Act and it should be strengthened and improved. There are parts of our country that do not have sufficient private health insurance carriers to make their rates competitive and cost should come down. But at the time, for example, I wanted a public option. I wanted people to have a choice of using a government plan or a private insurance. But guess what? We didn't have the votes for the public option. And so then you're faced with, you just said no, I'm gonna get a 100% what I want, or I'm gonna compromise a little bit. And his, his mantra was always, don't let perfect be the enemy of the good. Good is better. And if we'd held out for that public option, or universal medicare for all, then 20 million people today wouldn't have health insurance. You all wouldn't be able to stay on your parents' plans until you're 26.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: People with pre-existing conditions would run into discrimination with either higher premiums or being uninsurable all together. You couldn't come out of school and go start a business because you would, or leave an employer to start a business 'cause you would be tethered to the insurance plan, women couldn't get preventive care without a co-pay. There's a lot of Affordable Care Act that's good, nobody said it was perfect. And so please if you're, in your life's journey, recognize that if it's more than just one person having to make the decision, if you don't have veto power, then you're gonna have to listen and you're gonna have to make some compromises. And I think part of one of the challenges in our current climate is that we're not giving each other room to move.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And I mean that's not how we did things. I worked with a lot of people when I was, both in local government and certainly in the White House about whom I might've disagreed on 99 issues. 'Cause that's what was in the best interest of what Lucile taught me, the people that were there to represent.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Yeah. Okay so, while you were in the White House you were able to do a lot of amazing things. You got to meet the Dahli Lama, you got to attend state dinners hosted by Queen Elizabeth, attended the Olympic games, what was your big, pinch-me moment, while you were at the White House?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Honestly every single day. (chuckles) I have to say the queen was very cool, the pope was really cool, the Dahli Lama was really cool. So in terms of world leaders, those were probably the coolest people. The queen was really cool because that year I lived in London and then I went back and lived there a summer when I was in college, I used to love the changing of the guards at Buckingham Palace. And I would just stand outside of that rod iron fence for hours on end, watching the guards changing and my parents you know in the rain would say, "Valerie let's go," and I no one more time. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And the queen has on those long gloves, and I thought her dress was very sparkly and then I looked up close and I was like, oh those are diamonds all over that dress.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And she couldn't have been nicer, and part of what I think I learned from the people who I had admired from afar, and I had a chance to meet, is that they're all human. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: There you go. Okay so, through writing "Finding My Voice", you were able to sort of reflect on your life, and occasionally noting things that you wish you knew, which I think that we all do. text: Oh my gosh. I wish that I had experimented with a whole wide range of classes that I had no thought that I would be good at. And I tried it with that organic chemistry. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: You know I am woman, I am mighty, let me roar, and I took on so much and I tell the story, in my book about, working all day, coming home, putting Laura to bed, and then, and then working some more, and in the wee hours of the night, making baby food from scratch. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Okay we have just two more questions for you this evening. So you once thought about running for mayor for Chicago. Would you consider running for public office in the future and what is next for you?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: No. In a word no. And I've given, I hasten to say it but you should never say never, 'cause I also said I would never ever work for the federal government, ever under any circumstances. And that's when I worked in local government and I thought the federal government was so removed from us and they were trying to get us to tailor the needs of the citizens of Chicago into their programs and I couldn't understand why their programs couldn't be tailored to the needs of the citizens and so, but then what did I do? I went and worked for the federal government. So I feel at this stage of my life, that what I enjoy most is helping advise other people. I really, enjoy talking to people who are thinking about running for office, thinking about public service, trying to figure out what to do in their careers, I mean, this generation's part of why I wanted to come up here and talk to those of you who are here with us today, and certainly those of you who are watching around the country.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: You have so much potential, and so to help you unleash that potential is really, what I care most about. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: And so don't hate on me for that because I know not everybody in this room gets to do that, but I do feel like I earned it and what do I wanna do I care a lot about gender equity and so I launched an organization called The United State of Women, that's a non-for-profit organization geared to sharing best practices around the country for how we close the gender gap and we had a huge summit when I was still in the White House and shared the White House council and women and girls and we called it the United State of Women to say well this is the work we did and these are challenges that lie ahead and here is how we address those challenges and then we had a huge summit in 2018 in LA, more people came and we're

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: and find out about, we're having galvanizing sessions around the country and then we'll have a big summit place to be announced shortly. I care about the fact that in the last presidential election, 43% of eligible voters did not vote. 43% just proportionally, young people and I know that because this is a leadership group that that's not this group, but you all have the ability to go on your campus, campus by campus, and make sure everybody registers to vote and the organization was launched by Mrs. Obama. I chair the board. Its non-partisan.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: It's not that I don't care whether you vote Democrat or Republican, I really do want you to vote Democrat, but mostly I want you to vote and I think the challenge that we have in our country is the culture doesn't support voting and so we're looking for ways of starting with young people. I used to go in the voting booth with my parents and I just thought it was like the most exciting thing in the world and then I took my daughter in with me and we need a culture that appreciates the fact that our country is only going to be as good as the citizens demand that it be. We the people have to hold our elected officials accountable, we have to know who's running for office and not just the President, my goodness, it matters who's on your school board who's on your city council, who's the mayor, who's the alderman, every elected office matters. They're all spending your money. They're all making policies that affect your lives. Why won't you wanna care about who it is and I think that in this environment, politics is so messy and I get that.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: It's horrendous. I mean it's just I have to steel myself sometimes to turn on the news, but the only way that changes is if we engage. You can't shun these institutions that are so important in our lives. You have to embrace them and make them better. I care about criminal justice reform and I am soon to be announced going on the board of a very important organization that's fighting for criminal justice reform and the final issue I care an enormous about is gun violence We have a health epidemic in our country on gun violence and it is these mass shootings, the worst days that we had in the White House, were ones where we were confronted with gun violence from Sandy Hook, which I felt was such a wake up call for our nation, but shortly after I went up to New Town with President Obama to mourn the 20 kids, first grade kids, and six adults who were murdered, but then I accompanied Mrs.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Obama to our hometown of Chicago, and went to the funeral for Hadiya Pendleton, who had marched in the president's inauguration parade three weeks earlier and was shot a mile from where our homes are in Chicago. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: So that's what I care about, it's a mouthful and then in my free time, I am on the faculty of the University of Chicago law school, just 'cause I love to be on college campuses talking to really smart people. And they make me think about things I hadn't thought about before, and they test me and push me, and it's an enriched environment and I wish I were a kid again.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: All right so in that light, finally we'd like to ask all of our guests this question, why do you think it's so important for a student to participate in an organization like the National Society of Leadership and Success, which teaches you know skills such as effective communication, and leadership, while also encouraging them to discover and follow their passions?

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: Well, why on Earth wouldn't you, right? I mean, it's the most obvious thing in the world is that part of why you go to school is that you wanna have the skillset that's gonna make you productive adults, and if you're a really productive adult, you wanna be a leader. That's what you're trying to do. And so, if you have an opportunity to participate in an organization like this that will help you hone those skills and be a more effective leader, a better leader, a leader that reminds, where you are reminded that it's not about you, it's about service, then I can't imagine why you would pass this up. And so I say, I know it probably is time-consuming. Those of you who are here to today with us and those of you who are watching, it means you weren't studying during this hour we were together, but I hope that that, coupled with maybe taking a gander at my book, will give you some of the tips that you need to be a more effective leader. We are hungry for your leadership. You are the change that we have been waiting for.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: This country needs this next generation to seize the reigns and get out there and be a force for good, and I am confident that you have all the tools that you need to do it. You just have to make up your mind that it's a priority for you. And so, I say go out there and change the world. President Obama, we know he was all about hope and change and people said, sometimes they they thought it was kind of "Pollyanna"-ish. You know, hope and change, and the reason why one of his books was called "The Audacity of Hope," is that it is audacious to be hopeful.

speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: You have to have grit and determination and resilience to be hopeful. There are a whole lot of reasons why you could be cynical and pull back into your own little echo-chamber and never venture out 'cause it's scary out there. And so, the qualities of leadership that you need, that were a part of what was a part of the question that was posed to you, each of those qualities are so important, and when you add passion to it, it is a lifelong journey. I don't know a leader who is an effective leader that doesn't challenge his or herself every single day to be better. You can never just say, okay, I got this. speaker: Valerie Jarrett
text: The adventure, as I said, is in the swerve, and leadership only comes out of people who have the courage to get out there, go against the wind, go against the crowd, and convince people that there's a better way, and I am counting on you to help lead that path for a better way. That's your challenge.
